How large can an archimedean derivative be?

At order P, let VP be the span of vectors obtained from tensors of lowest compact-type vectors by applying at most P derivatives. A derivative in direction X is ∂Xw = (d/dt)σ(exp(tX))w at t = 0. A direction supported at one real place v belongs to the Lie algebra of its unitary group. Write ‖X‖HS for its Hilbert–Schmidt norm. Use the indefinite counting hypotheses. In particular n ≥ 8, the representations are unitary discrete series, and each coordinate of the Harish-Chandra parameter λ at each real place satisfies |λᵢ| ≤ b².

Derivative bound. The spaces VP are finite dimensional and preserved by the product of the maximal compact groups. Their vectors are differentiable along every real one-parameter subgroup, and one derivative takes VP into VP+1. For w ∈ VP and any one-place direction,

‖∂Xw‖ ≤ ‖X‖HS βP ‖w‖,   βP = √n b² + (3/2)n3/2 + 3P.

Here is why the dependence on P is linear. At one place write Eij for the operators representing the matrix units in the complexified Lie algebra. The compact roots eᵢ−eⱼ join two coordinates with the same signature sign. The noncompact roots join opposite signs. Let ρc and ρn be the half sums of the respective positive roots (i < j). The starting compact highest weight is Λ = λ + ρn − ρc. The counting hypotheses separate opposite-sign parameter coordinates by a common gap h ≥ 120nq3/2, where q is the real Witt index. The lowest-type multiplicity and infinitesimal-character theorems identify this compact type and give the scalar of the full quadratic Casimir operator on its generated module. Harris, Kobayashi and Speh, §2.3, formula (2.24)[59].

Moving a compact generator past a noncompact one adds their commutator, which is again a sum of noncompact generators. Thus words of length at most P lie in the compact-stable space obtained by applying at most P noncompact generators to the starting compact type. In one such step, the tensor-product rule with the off-diagonal block permits the old compact highest weight or a shift by a root joining opposite signs. The root eᵢ−eⱼ has Euclidean norm √2. By compact-type decomposition and induction, every highest weight μ seen by order P satisfies ‖μ−Λ‖ ≤ √2P. This bound on possible compact types holds for the entire span of words.

How does a bound on weights control every vector?

In matrix-unit coordinates let Ω be the sum of Eᵢⱼ Eⱼᵢ over all pairs and let ΩK be the same sum over same-sign pairs. On the common space of smooth vectors, unitarity gives Eᵢⱼ* = Eⱼᵢ for equal signs and Eᵢⱼ* = −Eⱼᵢ for opposite signs. Summing the squared norms therefore gives the energy identity

∑i,j ‖Eᵢⱼ w‖² = Re ⟨w, (2ΩK−Ω)w⟩.

On a compact type μ the scalar of ΩK is ‖μ+ρc‖²−‖ρc‖². On the generated module the scalar of Ω is ‖λ‖²−‖ρc+ρn‖². Put L = ‖λ‖ and A = ‖ρn‖ + √2P. The preceding weight bound gives ‖μ+ρc‖ ≤ L + A. Since the compact action is unitary, its finite-dimensional space splits orthogonally into compact types. The same upper bound for the compact Casimir quadratic form then applies to their sum, including linear combinations w.

The full half sum has coordinates (n+1−2i)/2 for 1 ≤ i ≤ n, giving squared norm n(n²−1)/12. Each coordinate of ρn has absolute value at most n/2. Thus ‖ρn‖ ≤ n3/2/2, and L ≤ √n b². For a unit vector the energy is consequently at most

2(L+A)²−L²+n³/12 ≤ (L+2A+0.3n3/2)² ≤ βP².

For the first inequality, (L+2A)² already exceeds 2(L+A)²−L² by 2A², and 0.3² ≥ 1/12. For the second, 2√2 ≤ 3 and 1 + 0.3 ≤ 3/2. This proves a bound on the sum of the squared generator norms. Applying Cauchy–Schwarz to ∂Xw = ∑ Xᵢⱼ Eᵢⱼ w gives the one-place estimate. Tensoring with the other places preserves the squared bound, as one sees by expanding in an orthonormal basis of the other factors. For simultaneous directions X = (Xᵥ), the derivative is the sum of the one-place derivatives. The product rule, the triangle inequality and Cauchy–Schwarz therefore give

‖∂Xw‖ ≤ √f (∑v ‖Xᵥ‖²HS)1/2 βP ‖w‖.

The descent in the cusp starts at order P₀ = 8qN, where N = n²f, and uses the simultaneous-direction bound. The Sobolev estimate at the starting order needs up to N more derivatives, each in a unit direction supported at a single place. Since βP increases with P, β = βP₀+N works for both steps. For example, the dimensions n = 8, f = q = 1 give N = 64 and P₀ = 512. Taking one constant through order 576 contributes 1728 to β from differentiations. This example counts orders and leaves the parameter gap and the bound b in force.

How an integral controls the starting value

The mean-zero argument starts with a bound for evaluation at every point y in a neighborhood of a deep point x. The available norm is an integral over the whole quotient. To pass from that norm to a value at y, we first average along short curves through y, then count how often their coordinate neighborhood can cover the same point of the quotient.

Evaluation along one curve. For a continuously differentiable complex function h on [0, s], integration of its derivative and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give |h(0)| ≤ |h(t)| + √s (∫ |h′|²)1/2 for every t in that interval. |h(0)|² ≤ (2/s) ∫0s |h(t)|² dt + 2s ∫0s |h′(t)|² dt.

There are N = n²f real directions, an orthonormal Lie algebra basis of size n² at each of f places. Write Fw for the continuous representative of one automorphic image of a test vector w. Along the jth one-parameter subgroup the derivative of Fw is F∂ⱼw. Differentiating raises the allowed order of the vector by one. Suppose the integral of |Fw|² on the full parameter cube is at most C(y)‖w‖² for all vectors through order P + N, and ‖∂ⱼw‖ ≤ β‖w‖ at the orders where a derivative is taken.

Use the subgroups in a fixed product order. For fixed values of the first N − 1 parameters apply the endpoint estimate in the last one, then integrate in the first N − 1. The two full-cube integrals are bounded by C(y)‖w‖² and C(y)‖∂Nw‖². Thus removing one parameter costs at most 2/s + 2sβ². The bound on the smaller cube holds through order P + N − 1. After N removals the cube is the point y, and all vectors through order P are still covered. With s = 1/β each removal costs 4β. The stated estimate rounds (4β)N up to (6β)N.

For 12n³s ≤ 1 and 8n⁵s ≤ 1, the quantitative exponential-coordinate theorem bounds the parameter integral of any nonnegative measurable function by efP∞ times its Haar integral on a set S at the real places. Any two matrices in S differ multiplicatively by a matrix of operator norm at most 2 at each place. The factor ef allows a Jacobian loss of at most e at each place.

When we fold the translate y(S × Kg) into a fundamental domain, each point z is counted once for each rational translate γz inside it. Fix one such γ₀ if any exist. The ratios γγ₀−1 are distinct rational transformations that preserve the finite lattice at y. In coordinates at y their operator norms are at most 2 at each real place.

The lattice separation inequality gives a lower bound t(y)² for the geometric mean over the real places of the operator-norm distances between two distinct such matrices. To see the two factors, take the difference of the corresponding rational transformations. It sends the lattice at y into itself and has nonzero image. For such a map between lattices, the geometric mean of its local operator norms is at least the least size of the target divided by the largest size of the source. Here the target has least size τ(y). The Hermitian lattice is self-dual, so duality reverses the filtration and replaces each size by its reciprocal. The largest size of the source is 1/τ(y). Their quotient is τ(y)², which is at least t(y)² after truncation. At least one local distance is therefore ≥ t(y)². In the maximum of the local norms, the open balls of radius t(y)²/2 about the matrices are disjoint. They lie in the ball of radius 2 + t(y)²/2. Volumes scale with exponent 2N, the real dimension of f spaces of complex n × n matrices. Their volume ratio bounds the multiplicity by (1 + 4/t(y)²)2N. Enlarging 4 to 4√n gives the bound used in the count. Dividing by the finite volume introduced above gives the cube constant

The top rows of the resulting matrix represent the rational arithmetic map after a common invertible row change and a word-dependent invertible column change. At the chosen complex place a single simultaneous conjugation may be necessary. It preserves absolute squares. Invertibility explains how to recognize the arithmetic map. How many independent directions do the period maps detect?

Start with one word u. Its normalized period map Au = cu−1/2Pu takes du columns into the common row space. Its Gram matrix is Kuu = Au∗Au. Choose an orthonormal basis of the kernel and extend it to the source. For each unit vector x in the kernel basis, Aux = 0 gives (Kuu − I)x = −x. It contributes exactly 1 to the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm Q(Kuu − I). The remaining basis vectors contribute nonnegative terms. By the dimension formula for a linear map,

dim ker Au ≤ Q(Kuu − I),   rank Au ≥ (1 − e0)du   if   Q(Kuu − I) ≤ e0du.

The weighted count of minor lists bounds the contribution at each intersection defect. Squaring the norm pairs two terms, so the two sums over defects give the square of a single sum. In the resulting estimate, the factor du bounds the row mass multiplied by the local representation dimension and its Gram normalization. It counts the source columns, whose number is known before applying the period map. The scalar bound on that square gives Q(Buu) ≤ ξdu, where ξ = exp(−kf log k).

Write D∗ for the positive reference mass of the whole row space and Γ for the family scale with log Γ = CΓm⁵fL. The complementary estimate gives Q(Kuu − Buu − I) ≤ Γdu²/D∗. The chosen word sizes satisfy duΓ²/D∗ ≤ C0. Multiplying by du/Γ gives a complementary error of at most (C0/Γ)du. Applying ‖X + Y‖² ≤ 2‖X‖² + 2‖Y‖² gives e0 = 2ξ + 2C0/Γ. For example, the coordinate map from ℂ⁸ to ℂ⁷ that drops the last coordinate has squared error exactly 1 and rank 7. Appending zero rows leaves its Gram matrix unchanged. An upper bound for the number of available rows therefore needs additional information.

What happens when all the words share the same rows?

Their mixed Gram entry is 1, and F has diagonal entries 2 and 0. Move the second column to (0, 1). The two diagonal Gram matrices still equal 1, but the mixed Gram entry vanishes, F becomes the identity, and the span has dimension two. In both cases tr F = 2. The second trace moment tr(F²) falls from 4 to 2 as the repeated direction is replaced by an independent one.

Cycling the factors under the trace gives tr F = ∑u tr Kuu and tr(F²) = ∑u,v Q(Kuv). Put a = √e0. On the diagonal, Cauchy–Schwarz gives |tr(Kuu − I)| ≤ √du ‖Kuu − I‖ ≤ a du, with the Hilbert–Schmidt norm throughout. The triangle inequality gives ‖Kuu‖ ≤ (1 + a)√du. The family meets the lower bound on R by choosing ⌈C₀Γ²/σ⌉ words. Each contributes at least D∗/(C₀Γ²) columns. Multiplication gives R ≥ (C₀Γ²/σ) · D∗/(C₀Γ²) = D∗/σ.

To see where this hypothesis enters, consider a smaller family. Take one word consisting of a single unit column in ℂ100 and set D = D∗ = 100. Its Gram matrix is (1), so its diagonal error is zero. There are no distinct-word pairs and the row count is exact. Yet F is the projection onto that one column, with both traces and rank equal to 1. At σ = 1/100 the theorem requires at least 10,000 columns in total. Controlling the minor lists gives the error estimate. The independent supply of columns allows the trace ratio to force a large span.

5.18Counting matrices at one prime

Let q be either auxiliary prime. The number of invertible n-by-n matrices over the field of q elements is qn²Πn(q), where Πn(q) = ∏j=1n(1 − q−j). Choose the columns in order. Once i independent columns have been chosen, their span excludes precisely qi out of the qn choices for the next column. An index divides this count by the number of allowed level matrices. On the column side, these are upper triangular with diagonal entries 1. The strictly upper triangle has k(k − 1)/2 free entries.

The row has a central block of size k + 1 flanked by (m/2 − 1) singleton blocks on each side. Between different blocks all entries above the diagonal are free. Within the central block the first k positions have a free strictly upper triangle. Its final column has zeros in all k positions above its diagonal within that block. Thus the whole row matrix has r(r − 1)/2 − k free entries. Every choice has determinant one. Subtract the exponents of q in the two indices. The difference is r(r + 1)/2 + k − k(k + 1)/2 = A, where A = mk + m(m − 1)/2. The first k factors of Π cancel.

row index / column index = qA P(q),   P(q) = ∏j=k+1r(1 − q−j).

Check at q = 2, k = m = 2. The two invertible groups have orders (4 − 1)(4 − 2) = 6 and (8 − 1)(8 − 2)(8 − 4) = 168. Each level subgroup has one free binary entry, so its order is 2. The quotient of indices is 84/3 = 28, exactly 25(1 − 2−3). This checks the local identity in small ranks. The estimates for the full family use m ≥ 44.

5.20How a volume becomes a sum over lattice classes

The formula for the word scale uses the volume of a unitary group on the row side and a Hermitian genus mass on the column side. To compare ranks, we need both in the same units. A genus consists of lattices isometric at every finite place. Its mass is the sum of 1/|Aut(Λ)| over its global isometry classes. The proof starts in positive definite rank two, where the automorphism groups are finite.

Let Γ be the rational unitary group, G its adelic group and K the subgroup preserving the completed lattice at finite places and unrestricted at infinity. In the definite case the prescribed archimedean measures are probabilities. Applying the product normalization to the whole compact group at each infinite place gives μ(K) = 1. Pick representatives gi of the finite double quotient Γ∖G/K. In the class of gi, exactly |Γ ∩ giKgi−1| translates of a point by Γ land in giK. Weight that coset’s indicator by the reciprocal. Its sum over Γ is one on that class. Integrating the weighted indicators over G now gives the volume of a fundamental domain. The stabilizers are the lattice automorphism groups, so the result is the genus mass.

A finite model. Take G = S₃ and Γ = K = {1, (12)}. The two double cosets have representatives 1 and (13), with stabilizer orders 2 and 1. Their weights add to 3/2. Directly, μ(K) = 1 gives mass 1/2 to each element and a Γ-fundamental domain has three elements. This explains the inverse stabilizer in the formula. A deeper finite level K′ ⊂ K has measure 1/[K:K′]. Renormalizing that subgroup to measure one therefore multiplies the covolume by its index. In the word count the row uses its own index and the column uses its own, so their quotient is row index divided by column index.

5.21Why adjacent ranks have a predictable mass ratio

Write M for the new rank, f for the number of conjugate pairs of complex embeddings of the CM field, and v for half its root discriminant. The quadratic extension of its totally real subfield is unramified at every finite prime. For a totally positive definite integral Hermitian lattice Λ, count vectors whose squared lengths are at most j² at every embedding. Sum these counts over the genus using the reciprocal automorphism weights above. The zero vector contributes the mass μΛ. Grouping the other vectors by their represented value gives the same sum, now expressed through representation counts. Divide by j2fM and let j grow. The two ways of counting give

μΛ (πM/M!)f / (vfM δ) = (cM−1 λΛ/δ) M−f Lη(M) / √((2v)f).

On the left, πM/M! is the volume of a unit ball in ℂM, and δ is the positive square root of the absolute norm of the lattice discriminant ideal. On the right, cM−1 is the mass constant for the preceding rank, λΛ is a product of local lattice corrections, and Lη(M) is the Euler product of the CM field. This second limit uses the representation-density formula and the asymptotic sum of its local factors. The zero vector’s separate contribution tends to zero after division. Cancel δ and use M!/M = (M − 1)!. For a lattice with an orthonormal integral basis every local lattice correction is one. The two standard masses consequently satisfy the following identity for the ranks M ≥ 3 used here.

massM / massM−1 = [((M − 1)!)(v/π)M]f Lη(M) / √((2v)f).

For instance, take M = 3 and a finite prime of the totally real subfield of residue size 2. If it is inert, the unique prime above it has norm 4 and its Euler factor is (1 + 2−3)−1 = 8/9. If it splits, its two primes of norm 2 each contribute (1 − 2−3)−1/2, giving 8/7 together. These are factors at a single prime. Across the rank increments, the same positive rank-one constant occurs in both standard masses and cancels in their ratio.

To reach the indefinite row, the normalized unit-vector unfolding supplies the same ratio for a space and the orthogonal complement of a vector of norm +1 or −1. From definite rank two, use +1 to compare successive positive definite ranks. For a constant signature (P, Q) with P ≥ 2, induction on Q uses a −1 vector, whose complement has signature (P, Q − 1). The two inductions identify the row volume with the standard mass of its rank r. In the word-scale formula the column mass then cancels the common ranks, leaving exactly the increments M = k + 1, …, r. These are the factors estimated in the lower bound for each word.

5.23What survives in the quotient of dimensions?

Fix a place. Write its row as λ = (c0, …, ck−2, −b0, …, −bm−1) of length r = k + m − 1. Its first block is nonnegative and decreases in steps of at least one. The bj are positive and increase in steps of at least one. The column u0 > ⋯ > uk−1 belonging to the word interlaces the first block, with ui > ci > ui+1. Write V(y) = ∏i<j(yi − yj). Each cross-block gap ci + bj is at least bj, and each gap within the negative block is at least one. This proves the first inequality below.

V(λ) ≥ V(c)∏j bjk−1,   V(u) ≤ D2k−3V(c),   D = 8xeL.

For the second inequality, the column has k − 1 gaps touching its first entry and another k − 2 touching its last. Each is at most D. Each remaining gap ui − uj is bounded by the distinct gap ci−1 − cj. The unused adjacent gaps of c are at least one. Dividing the inequalities now cancels the factor V(c). For a small check take c = (4, 0), u = (6, 2, −1) and b = (3, 5). The row has gap product 7,560, the column has gap product 84, and their ratio is 90. This example illustrates the interlacing calculation alone.

The local factor in the mass identity is dρFr/V(u), with formal degree dρ and Fr = ∏h=0r−1h!. At the required separation between parameters of opposite signature, the discrete-series estimate with tolerance 1/3 gives dρ ≥ (2/3)V(λ)/Fr by Weyl’s dimension formula. Thus the row factorials cancel as well. The source allows a logarithmic loss of 2k log D + 2k(1 + log k) in the Vandermonde comparison. At the family threshold, 2(log 8 + 1 + log x) ≤ L and log(2k) ≤ L, so this loss is at most 5kL.

5.24Adding the losses in the mass identity

The geometric weights satisfy 0 < bj < wjρ ≤ (1 + 1/x)bj and wjρ ≤ 2eL. Then k log w − (k − 1) log b = log w + (k − 1) log(w/b) ≤ 2L + k/x. Each rank increment M = k + 1, …, r contributes a positive mass Euler product Lη(M). Group its local logarithms by the rational prime p. A prime ideal of residue degree d above p contributes at most (d/2)[−log(1 − p−M)] in absolute value. The residue degrees above p sum to at most the field degree 2f. Summing over p gives |log Lη(M)| ≤ f log ζ(M) ≤ f, since M ≥ 2. Averaging over the f places leaves a total cost at most m − 1 for the r − k rank increments.

Subtract S + mG from log Xu and multiply by k. In the mass identity the surplus m(m − 1)[log(v/π) + G]/2 is nonnegative. The two remaining discriminant terms cost at most kL + (m − 1)L/2, using 0 ≤ log(v/π) ≤ L and log(2v) ≤ L. The two auxiliary primes together cost at most 2. Add these amounts to the place and Euler losses.

8kL + (m − 1)L/2 + m + 2 + k ≤ 11kL,   log Xu ≥ S + mG − 11L.

Indeed, (m − 1)L/2 ≤ kL/2 and m + 2 + k ≤ 5kL/2 because 44 ≤ m ≤ k and L ≥ 1. For fixed family and constants ε > 0, C0, CY, a single threshold works for every admissible scale above it, every family index, every choice of spacing and weights satisfying the stated data, and every word. 5.25Why a real-place degree has the size of a Vandermonde product

The placewise mass estimate compares a row with the column belonging to a word. The row supplies a discrete series of the real unitary group U(p, q), an irreducible unitary representation σ with square-integrable matrix coefficients. For a nonzero vector w, its formal degree is ‖w‖4 divided by the integral of |⟨w, σ(g)w⟩|2. Multiplying the Haar measure by a positive number divides the degree by that number. The numerical comparison therefore requires a specific measure.

Let N = p + q with both signs present. The parameter λ has strictly decreasing entries indexed from 0, with λi − (N−1)/2 integral. Each index carries a sign, with p positive and q negative. Write Fn = ∏0≤a<na! and V(λ) = ∏i<j(λi − λj). On the normalized measure one has the following equality for the large-gap parameters used here.

d(λ) = V(λ)/FN,   FN = ∏i<j(j−i).

5.26How an integral fixes the missing constant

Imagine moving λ by integer steps. When an admissible step raises one coordinate by one, the degree and the Vandermonde change by exactly the same ratio. Along λi(t) = λi + t(N−1−i), for integers t ≥ 0, the steps can be ordered so that decreasing order and the gap survive. Thus d(λ(t))/V(λ(t)) stays constant. To find its value, let Tt be the lowest compact type, the finite-dimensional representation of U(p) × U(q) selected by the weight λ(t). Form Yt = tpq dim(Tt)/d(λ(t)).

Put A = ∏(j−i) over opposite-sign pairs i<j. On the algebraic side the compact Weyl dimension formula cancels the same-sign factors of the moving Vandermonde up to ratios tending to one. Indeed, if the moving gap is g, its ratio is (g+b)/g, where b counts opposite signs strictly between the indices. Each opposite-sign pair leaves t/[λi−λj+t(j−i)], tending to 1/(j−i).

On the analytic side, polar coordinates use probability measure on the compact group and one complex coordinate per opposite-sign pair. The Haar density includes the constant c = FN/(πpqFpFq). Rescaling each complex coordinate by 1/√t absorbs tpq. The limiting squared coefficient has a Gaussian factor exp(−(j−i)|z|²) in each coordinate, whose plane integral is π/(j−i). The coefficient supplies a lower limit and an integrable upper bound supplies the matching upper limit. Comparing the two values of the same limit gives the stated degree.

V(λ)/[d(λ)FpFqA] = lim Yt = cπpq/A = FN/(FpFqA).

5.28An upper bound for the scale of every word

Relative variation alone can leave all the words equally large. To bound their absolute scale, start again from the mass identity used for the lower bound. It gives fk log Xu as a sum of six terms. For an upper bound, a term of known negative sign can be discarded. The remaining positive contributions must be estimated even when the word and the family member vary. Assume 44 ≤ m ≤ k, r = k + m − 1, L ≥ 9 and log(2k) ≤ L. Write CY for the bound log gi ≤ CYL on each of the two auxiliary primes. The following budget is divided throughout by fkmL, so its sum bounds log Xu/(mL).

  • The coefficient of log(v/π) is f[(m − 1)k + m(m − 1)/2]. Since 0 ≤ log(v/π) ≤ L and m ≤ k, the normalized contribution is at most 3/2. The term in −log(2v) is nonpositive.
  • At most m Euler values enter. Each logarithm is at most f by the comparison with ζ(M) at integers M ≥ 2. Together they cost at most 1/(kL). The finite corrections log(1 − gi−j) are nonpositive.
  • The positive prime term has coefficient fm(2k + m − 1)/2. Since log(g0g1) ≤ 2CYL, it costs at most 3CY.
  • At each infinite place, separate the logarithm of the ratio of representation dimensions from the factorial products in Weyl’s formula. The gap estimate for the real-place degree and the column estimate bound the first by km(log 3 + 5 log(2k) + 5L + 10). For the factorials there are r − k additional factors j!. Each is at most rr. Since r ≤ 2k, their logarithms total at most 2kmL. Summing over f places costs at most 12/L + 12 after normalization.

These four bounds imply

log Xu/(mL) ≤ 3/2 + 1/(kL) + 3CY + 12/L + 12 ≤ 15 + 3CY.

For the last inequality even the looser k ≥ 5 suffices. The constants independent of CY sum to at most 3/2 + 1/45 + 4/3 + 12 = 1337/90, strictly below 15. Take the maximum of the thresholds for this estimate, the lower estimate, the real-place gap and the mass inputs. Thus the same threshold works for all words. To pass to the chosen prime Tu, its window has center XuΓ−2/(fk) and upper multiplicative allowance 1 + 1/(fk). With Γ ≥ 1 this gives log Tu ≤ log Xu + 1. The construction absorbs the additive allowance into its common counting constant. The existence of a prime in the window is a separate arithmetic input.

The term Ωlog in the main-term calculation has a geometric meaning. At a single complex embedding, the norm of a generator of a differential line depends on the generator and the elliptic lattice. The proof first measures the line in a way that survives a change of generator. It then computes its mean using complex multiplication and carries that mean into the bounds for the columns of a theta kernel.

5.30Which changes of scale cancel?

Let K0 be the imaginary quadratic host field of discriminant −dK, and E the extension used in the host. Take a nonzero integral ideal 𝔠 of K0 with norm prime to 2dK. If Δ is the discriminant of its embedded elliptic lattice and δ12 = Δ, the rescaled lattice Λ = δ·φ0(𝔠) has discriminant one. Take any number field M inside ℂ containing the specified images of E and the Weierstrass invariants g2(Λ), g3(Λ). For each embedding ρ of M, transport those two invariants and let Aρ > 0 be the area of the corresponding period lattice.

Fix a host embedding label τ. The source spans the vectors of conjugates of elements of the host fractional ideal and intersects the resulting module with the τ-coordinate line. Write ℓτ for the resulting module inside M and DM = [M : ℚ]. For a nonzero s in ℓτ, put I(s) = [ℓτ : 𝒪Ms]. The measured quantity is

mρ(s) = log(π |ρ(s)|² / Aρ),   Ω̄τ = (2 log I(s) − ∑ρ mρ(s)) / DM.

When ℓτ has generator a, every such s has form ca with 0 ≠ c ∈ 𝒪M. The index is |NM/ℚ(c)|. Meanwhile each local logarithm increases by 2 log |ρ(c)|. Their sum increases by twice the logarithm of precisely that index. Thus Ω̄τ equals the average of −mρ(a). For a small check, take the free line ℤ[i] and use the test element s = 1 + i. Its multiples form a sublattice of index 2. Each of the two embeddings contributes an extra log 2, cancelling the finite contribution 2 log 2. This example checks the normalization in a free line.

5.31Why the root discriminant appears

Write n = [E : ℚ], h = [E : K0] = n/2. Let b be the absolute norm of the product of the host fractional ideal with the relative different of E/K0. The ideal-index calculation gives I(s)n bDM = |NM/ℚ(s)|n. Taking logarithms and summing the local metrics eliminates the norm of s. Hence

Ω̄τ = (1/DM) ∑ρ log(Aρ/π) − (2/n) log b.

Set B equal to the absolute norm of the relative different. Its half-different identity gives b² = B. The discriminant tower formula gives |disc(E)| = B(dK)h. Since rd(E) = |disc(E)|1/n, the correction (2/n) log b equals log rd(E) − log √dK.

For the area term the proof compares the conjugate lattices with a family indexed by ideal classes. Over a common extension their homotheties give 6 log Aoriginal = 6 log Afamily + log |ρ(u)|, with u a discriminant unit. The unit contributes zero to the sum over embeddings. Averaging over the extension gives the same mean as over M, because each embedding occurs with the same multiplicity. The Chowla–Selberg class-sum formula then evaluates the area mean as γ + log(2π/√dK) − dχ, where dχ = Re(L′(1,χ)/L(1,χ)) for the host quadratic character. This dχ is the scalar denoted d in the main-term calculation above. Subtracting the correction cancels log √dK. For every compatible M and every τ this gives

Ω̄τ = γ + log(2π/rd(E)) − dχ = Ωlog.

This identifies the scalar that occurs earlier with v = rd(E)/2. The calculation uses the CM family of period lattices, the Chowla–Selberg evaluation and the ideal-index formula as inputs.

6Theta lifts, local factors and the Galois input

How can a theorem attaching Galois representations in odd dimension give one in even dimension? Lift the same automorphic representation twice to a larger odd rank, adding different character lists each time. The shared part can then be recovered. Both global theta integrals must produce a nonzero form for this argument to start.

What is being lifted? · Two parallel lifts · Recovering the even-dimensional row · The iterated chain · Whittaker factors · Split and inert places · The finite test vector · Real places · Continuation · Split lattice calculation · Inert cell calculation

6.1What is being lifted?

A Hermitian form measures lengths using both a field and its conjugation. On two complex coordinates the example is ⟨x,y⟩ = x₁y₁ + x₂y₂. Its unitary group consists of the changes of coordinates preserving this pairing. For a number field we can make such a change at each place. An adelic group element collects these choices, integral at almost every finite place. A rational change of coordinates gives the same change simultaneously in all completions.

An automorphic form here is a function on the adelic group, invariant under those rational changes on the left and satisfying additional finiteness and regularity conditions. Translating its argument on the right produces a space of functions carrying a group action. The irreducible space being lifted is U, and φ is one vector in it. A theta kernel converts φ into a function on another group by integration. To show that this conversion retains some information, one proves that a resulting vector has positive squared norm. At a good finite prime the commuting Hecke operators then provide a list of spectral parameters, with multiplicities, which can be compared on the two sides.

6.2Two parallel lifts to odd rank

Let E be a CM field, a totally imaginary quadratic extension of its totally real subfield F. The version used here assumes that E/F is unramified at all finite places, that E contains a square root of a negative rational integer, and that [F : ℚ] is even. At every nonsplit finite place the underlying prime of F has odd residue characteristic, norm greater than three and does not divide the absolute different of F. Take an even rank n ≥ 1 and an automorphic representation U of the definite unitary group of rank n. Fix its highest weights λ at the complex embeddings and a finite split place w₀ of E.

For a Hermitian source with identity Gram matrix and signature (n, 0), the lifting theorem gives a rank threshold d₀. The proof chooses t = 2(d₀ + n) + 1. Both targets are definite skew-Hermitian models of rank D = n + t, an odd integer above the threshold. Each lift uses its own compatible pair of splitting Hecke characters. The proof takes a common lower bound b for the components of λ at the chosen complex embedding above each real place and chooses their target exponents so that mW,j(v) ≤ 2b − D. Thus every required archimedean inequality D + mW,j(v) ≤ 2λv,k holds. Applying the same rank theorem once for each pair produces U₁ and U₂.

There is one common algebraic Hecke character κ, and two lists ψj,h of t algebraic Hecke characters. No character from the first list equals any character from the second as a global character. At a split place w where κ and list j are unramified and U has a Satake multiset, write B(w) for its algebraically normalized eigenvalues. Unramified means the character is trivial on local units. Its value at a uniformizer is then well defined. The target eigenvalues obey the following multiset identity, with multiplicities retained.

Bj(w) = κ(w)−1B(w) ⊔ {ψj,h(w) ∣ 0 ≤ h < t}.

At infinity the target weight jumps are the union of the original jumps shifted by the weight of κ and the negatives of the weights of the added characters. At the chosen w₀ the construction specifically guarantees that κ and every member of list 1 are unramified. Distinct global characters can agree in value at an individual prime. The proof compares their associated global Galois characters.

6.3Why each global theta lift is nonzero

The lifting theorem first obtains a real threshold L for integrability of a height power against Haar measure. Taking an integer N > 2L and d₀ = max(N, 2n) gives both D ≥ 2n and L < D/2. For splitting characters with the prescribed restrictions and archimedean exponents, the real-place pairing supplies a nonzero vector f∞ in the Weil model and a nonzero automorphic form φ with matching type. The outstanding choice is the finite-place Schwartz vector ffin.

Let ω be the Weil representation of the source and target adelic unitary groups on test functions on adelic n-by-D matrices over F. For a source group element g and a target element h, its theta kernel sums the translated test function over rational matrices, diagonally embedded into the adeles. With DX the model’s source integration domain, the lift of φ is the function of h given by

Θ(Φ, φ)(h) = ∫DX (∑ξ∈Matn×D(F) [ω(g, h)Φ](ξ)) φ(g) dμ(g).

This convention conjugates the source form. The matrix coefficient used to test nonvanishing pairs ω(g, 1)Φ with Φ using additive Haar measure on the adelic matrix space. The source coefficient pairs the right translate of φ with φ on DX.

Set Φ = f∞ ⊗ ffin. Write cΦ(g) for the Weil matrix coefficient and mφ(g) for the source matrix coefficient. The Rallis input says the following integral converges and must vanish if the theta transform of (Φ, φ) is identically zero.

I(Φ, φ) = ∫ cΦ(g) mφ(g) dg.

Choose a finite set S containing enough places to control the level of φ, the ramification and the tail estimate. Use a local bump vector at each place of S and the model's vacuum vector elsewhere. The proof decomposes the integral into archimedean, finite-in-S and outside-S factors. The Schur calculation supplies a nonzero scalar and the chosen coefficient is nonzero at the identity. A compact open set of positive measure supplies the main contribution. A bound on the outside-S tail gives the strict estimate that prevents cancellation. This proves I(Φ, φ) ≠ 0 for the chosen data. The resulting theta transform is an automorphic form. An equivariant projection onto an automorphic constituent preserves a nonzero component, yielding a target representation to which the weight and local-parameter statements apply. The finite vectors may be chosen separately for the two lifts.

More explicitly, after integrating the archimedean and selected finite-place factors, the last integral has an integrand equal to a constant r > 0 on a compact open subgroup K. Its norm away from K is bounded by r times a nonnegative function w. The tail choice makes ∫Kᶜ w dμ < μ(K). Thus the contribution from K has absolute value rμ(K), strictly larger than the maximum possible contribution from its complement. The other factors are a positive Haar volume and a nonzero scalar.

6.4Recovering the even-dimensional representation

The goal is to remove a prescribed character line from each comparison without losing continuity or local data. Two different characters can take the same value at a prime. The four-element example lets you see how a vector passes one test yet fails to transform by that character on the whole group.

Apply the available odd-rank Galois theorem twice, each time in dimension D. It attaches continuous semisimple ℓ-adic representations ρ₁ and ρ₂ to U₁ and U₂. Let χj,h be the ℓ-adic character attached to ψj,h, and Pj(g, X) the characteristic polynomial of ρj(g). Injectivity of the Hecke-to-Galois character map preserves disjointness across the two lists. Comparing normalized Frobenius data at good split places and using density gives, for every Galois element g,

P₁(g, X) ∏h(X − χ2,h(g)) = P₂(g, X) ∏h(X − χ1,h(g)).

The representations ρ₁ ⊕ ⨁χ2,h and ρ₂ ⊕ ⨁χ1,h consequently have the same characteristic polynomials. The whole-group comparison and semisimplicity give a line χ1,h from ρ₁ and retain a comparison identity for the complement. Induction removes all t lines, preserving continuity, semisimplicity and the required local conditions. The remaining dimension is D − t = n. Tensoring with the ℓ-adic character of κ restores the original normalization. Given a source Satake multiset at w₀, unramifiedness of the first list supplies the local conclusion there. In the construction used here, the places lie in a prescribed set of split primes whose Frobenius classes stay dense after finite exclusions. For each place of that set carrying Satake data, weak compatibility identifies the representation obtained there with a fixed one. Transport across this isomorphism gives the local conclusions on the same representation.

6.5Which primes can test the two lifts?

The two lifts must be compared at enough places to determine a representation of the entire Galois group. We first specify the places using the field alone. Fix a CM field E, its maximal real subfield E⁺ and a positive integer d for which E contains an element x with x² = −d. For a finite place w of E, write q for the rational prime below it and c for complex conjugation. The set used in the comparison is

Qd = {w : cw ≠ w and −d is a square in ℚq}.

The first condition says that the prime below w in E⁺ has two distinct primes above it in E. The second concerns a square root in the rational completion. A prime of absolute residue degree one has residue field 𝔽q, or equivalently absolute norm q. We claim that every such w with q ∤ 2d belongs to Qd.

Indeed x is integral since it solves the monic equation X² + d = 0. Under any complex embedding its image is purely imaginary, so cx = −x. Choose an integer a reducing to the same element of 𝔽q as x. If cw = w, both x − a and −x − a lie in w. Their difference gives 2x ∈ w and multiplication by −x gives 2d ∈ w, contrary to the choice of q. Also a² + d ≡ 0 modulo q, with 2a nonzero modulo q. Hensel’s lemma lifts this simple root to ℤq. Both conditions follow. Sutherland, Lemma 9.15[63].

A split prime that fails the square test. Take E = ℚ(√5, i) and d = 1. The prime 3 is inert in ℚ(√5) since 5 is a nonsquare modulo 3. Its residue field is 𝔽₉, where (√5)² = 2 = −1. The two simple roots ±√5 of X² + 1 lift over that real field’s completion, giving two places in E. At each of them the first condition holds, while −1 has no square root in ℚ₃ since it has none in 𝔽₃. At 29 both 5 and −1 have simple square roots, 11 and 12 modulo 29. Every place above 29 has degree one. The first lifting step sends 12 to 41, with 41² + 1 = 2 · 29².

6.6Why does a single automorphic vector give Satake data at almost every split place?

Fix the source representation U of the adelic unitary group and choose a nonzero smooth automorphic vector φ in it. Its stabilizer at the finite adeles is open. To see what openness gives, view a matrix g through the entries of both g and g−1. Around the identity, choose additive neighborhoods of the entries small enough that membership in all of them puts g in the stabilizer. There are only finitely many entries. Their neighborhoods contain a common neighborhood N of zero for the entry differences. Shrink once to a neighborhood N′ with N′ + N′ ⊆ N.

A basic neighborhood of zero in the finite adeles allows every integral value outside a finite set of coordinates. Thus an integral entry supported at just one place w belongs to N′ for all but finitely many w. Exclude also the conjugates of those exceptions. For a split pair w, cw, put Kw = GLn(𝒪Ew). A local matrix from Kw acts on the conjugate coordinate by the conjugate inverse transpose in the standard unitary model. Its entries and those of its inverse are integral at both places. Every entry of either matrix minus the identity is the sum of at most two integral entries supported at single places. It belongs to N′ + N′. Consequently every element of this local compact group fixes φ.

w, cw outside a finite set   ⟹   Kw φ = {φ}   at split w.

The automorphic representation has irreducible admissible local factors in its restricted tensor product. At a split place the local unitary factor is GLn(Ew). The local component theorem supplies an embedded irreducible smooth representation σ of this factor. Translations by the other factors commute with it, so they carry this copy to other copies of σ. Their span is invariant under the full group. Irreducibility of U makes the span all of U. In particular, φ lies in a finite sum of these copies. D. Flath, Theorem 2 on restricted products[64] and J. Getz, Theorem 7.5 for the finite adèles[65].

To see why at least one copy contains a fixed vector, add the copies in order until their sum first contains φ. Write W for the preceding sum and V for the final copy. The local group preserves W ∩ V. Irreducibility of V makes this intersection zero, since V ⊆ W would leave φ outside their sum. The projection of φ from W ⊕ V onto V is therefore nonzero and fixed by Kw. Thus σ is spherical. The Satake isomorphism identifies its spherical Hecke character with an unordered multiset of n nonzero complex parameters. This supplies the source multiset at every split place outside a finite set depending on φ. Satake, Theorem 2 on spherical functions[66] and Theorem 3 on the spherical transform[67].

6.7Can these places realize any finite Galois test?

Let Γ = Gal(Ω/E) for an algebraic closure Ω. An open neighborhood of an element g in the Krull topology contains all automorphisms agreeing with g on some finite Galois extension L/E. Several simultaneous restrictions are one such test after taking the compositum of the fields involved. Write h for the restriction of g to L. Density amounts to producing an inverse Frobenius with restriction exactly h, even after an arbitrary finite set S of places of E has been discarded.

V(L,h) = {g′ ∈ Γ : g′|L = h}.

Apply Chebotarev to the conjugacy class of h−1 in Gal(L/E). The unramified places it gives have positive Dirichlet density. Those of absolute residue degree at least two have Dirichlet density zero. Indeed their sum of (Nw)−s is bounded for real s > 1 by [E∶ℚ] ∑q prime q−2, since Nw ≥ q² and at most [E∶ℚ] places lie over q. Dividing by log(1/(s−1)) and letting s decrease to 1 proves the assertion. We may therefore choose a degree-one place outside S and the finitely many places over 2dℓ. By the square-root argument this place belongs to Qd. Sutherland, Theorem 28.9 (Chebotarev)[68].

At such a place w, changing the prime of L above w conjugates its arithmetic Frobenius. Choose it so that Frobenius is h−1 itself. Extend the prime to Ω and take a lift σ of the residue-field map z ↦ zNw in its decomposition group. Since L/E is unramified at w, all these lifts have the same restriction there. Now σ−1 lies in V(L,h). The freedom to choose the prime over w is what turns a conjugacy class into an element of the specified open set. Sutherland, Proposition 7.18 on the Frobenius class[69].

Two witnesses for one test. Continue with E = ℚ(√5, i) and take L = E(ζ₇), d = 1 and ℓ = 13. Ask for the inverse Frobenius that sends ζ₇ to ζ₇³. At 61 and 89 both 5 and −1 are nonzero squares modulo the prime. For 61 one may take the roots 26 and 11 respectively, and for 89 the roots 19 and 34. Thus both give places of norm the rational prime. In the residue field of L, arithmetic Frobenius raises ζ₇ to the 61st or 89th power, respectively. Both exponents are 5 modulo 7, whose inverse is 3. Reduction distinguishes seventh roots of unity away from 7 because the roots of X⁷ − 1 remain distinct. After excluding all places over 61, a place over 89 still realizes the same test.

Absolute degree one gives enough witnesses for the density proof. Some places of degree two also pass the good-place test. For example 5 is a nonsquare modulo 17 and 4² ≡ −1 modulo 17. A place above 17 has norm 17², splits over the real subfield and belongs to Q1. Its inverse exponent is 4 modulo 7, so it answers a different finite Galois test. The figure lets you vary both the candidate prime and the finite exclusion.

6.8Why impose large gaps on one auxiliary weight?

Fix an odd positive rank m. To approximate a Hecke system by one arising from geometry, the construction allows the weight to change at two auxiliary places u and v above ℓ. Their primes in the maximal real subfield E⁺ are distinct. At one embedding inducing v, the new dominant weight is a nonincreasing list λ₀, …, λm−1. Its desired filtration jumps are the integers jk = k − λk, with indexing from zero. Consecutive jumps differ by at least one. The additional separation imposed by the approximation theorem is

jk+1 − j₀ > m(jk − j₀)   (0 ≤ k < m−1).

This inequality ensures that any two disjoint nonempty subsets of the jumps have different arithmetic means. The rank-extraction theorem below uses precisely this property, called lacunarity. To prove it, subtract the smallest jump from every jump. This translates both means equally. Let M be the largest shifted jump in the union of the two sets and call the set containing it A. For every entry b of the other set B, the gap inequality gives mb < M. The other entries of A are nonnegative, so the mean of A is at least M/|A| ≥ M/m. Every entry of B is smaller than that lower bound.

A rank-three weight. The weight (0,0,−2) has jumps {0,1,4}. The largest jump divided by three is 4/3, already greater than the next jump 1. For the unshifted weight (0,0,0) the jumps {0,1,2} satisfy mean{0,2} = mean{1}. At the conjugate embedding the dual weight has coordinates −λm−1−k. Its jumps are the reflected set (m−1)−J, here {−2,1,2}. Reflection sends every mean b to (m−1)−b, preserving unequal means. This explains why the construction may use either prime of E above the auxiliary real-subfield prime.

6.9Which part of cohomology carries the auxiliary Hecke system?

Let U′ denote one of the auxiliary automorphic representations. Fix an algebraic closure Ω of the CM field E and write Γ = Gal(Ω/E). The geometric input supplies a smooth projective variety with finite étale correspondences over E, the eigenvalue θh prescribed for each correspondence h, and an algebraic Hecke character κ. The existence of these data with the required automorphic eigenvalues and local comparisons uses a holomorphic Lefschetz formula. Start with the sum of the étale cohomology groups of the geometric fibre, with coefficients extended to an algebraic closure of ℚℓ. Only finitely many degrees contribute, their dimensions are finite, and Γ acts continuously. Milne, Lectures on Étale Cohomology, Theorems 15.1 and 19.2[70]. Brinon and Conrad, Example 1.2.3[71].

The holomorphic Lefschetz input has a concrete local term. Over ℂ let c₁ and c₂ be the finite étale maps of the correspondence to a smooth projective variety Z. Suppose they agree at only finitely many points y. At each one, use c₁ as local coordinates, let Ay be the derivative of the resulting local map c₂ ∘ c₁−1, and assume det(I−Ay) ≠ 0. For each holomorphic degree a, the theorem equates the alternating sum over b of the traces of c1∗c₂∗ on Hb(Z, Ωa) with the sum of the fixed-point contributions. At y the contribution is the coefficient of ta in det(I+tAy) divided by det(I−Ay). On a complex elliptic curve take c₁ to be the identity and c₂ multiplication by two. Only the origin is fixed. Its derivative is 2, so the two contributions are −1 and −2 for a = 0 and 1. This illustrates the Hodge trace calculation required in the construction of the geometric data. Atiyah and Bott, A Lefschetz fixed point formula for elliptic complexes II, the holomorphic fixed-point formula for a map[72].

On the étale cohomology space H, take the simultaneous eigenspace of the correspondence operators Th. Pullback and trace along a finite étale correspondence defined over E commute with the Galois action, since acting on the geometric fibre carries each of the two correspondence maps to itself and permutes the points in each trace. Consequently, Th(g x) = g Th(x) = θhg x whenever x has the prescribed eigenvalues.

Hθ = ⋂h ker(Th − θhI),   g Hθ = Hθ   (g ∈ Γ).

Make this representation semisimple as follows. Starting at zero, choose an invariant space of smallest possible dimension strictly larger than the previous space and containing it. Dimension increases at each step, so the process reaches Hθ. The induced representation on each successive quotient is irreducible, since an intermediate invariant space would contradict minimality. In a basis extending the flag one step at a time, the matrices are block upper triangular. Taking their diagonal blocks respects multiplication and inversion, so the direct sum of the quotient actions is a representation. Its entries are entries of the original matrices in a fixed basis and are continuous. The determinant of a block triangular matrix is the product of the determinants of its diagonal blocks. Thus every group element has the same characteristic polynomial before and after passing to the quotients.

For a two-dimensional example inside a three-dimensional space, take the operator diag(3,3,7). Its eigenvalue 3 selects the first two coordinates. Let g ∈ ℤℓ act there by the matrix with diagonal (1,1), entry g above the diagonal and zero below. On the third coordinate let it act trivially. Both the first coordinate line and the quotient of the selected plane by that line are trivial representations. The associated graded action on the plane is therefore the identity for every g. Before and after, the characteristic polynomial on that plane is (X−1)².

A rank-one twist restores the normalization used by U′. Fix a spherical good prime w away from ℓ and outside the finite exceptional set for this realization. Put R = (Nw)(m−1)/2Bw, where Bw is the Satake multiset. The local geometric comparison gives a polynomial with roots R/κ(w) that annihilates inverse Frobenius on the semisimple piece. The ℓ-adic character attached to κ multiplies that matrix by κ(w) under the chosen coefficient identification. For a monic polynomial P of degree m, set Q(X) = cmP(X/c). Then Q(cM) = cmP(M) = 0, and the roots of Q are those of P multiplied by c. At an embedding τ, a geometric jump prescribed at j+tτ moves to j, since the character line has jump −tτ and tensoring with a filtered line adds its jump. As a numerical check on both normalizations, roots {1,3/2,5/2} with κ(w) = 2 become {2,3,5}. Raw jumps {3,4,7} with tτ = 3 become {0,1,4}. The dimension D of the resulting representation ρ is still the dimension of the cohomological piece. Recovering rank m takes one more theorem.

How can a prime avoid every prescribed place and still split the quadratic field?

In the geometric construction ℓ is already fixed. A second rational prime p serves a different purpose. The geometric group is described away from p, so we must be able to remove its components without affecting the places reserved for a test. We also need a square root of −d in ℚp, where ℚ(√(−d)) is the imaginary quadratic subfield of our CM field. The list of primes to avoid is only known after choosing an automorphic form and a point at which it has nonzero value.

Auxiliary prime lemma. For any positive integer d and nonnegative integer B, there is a prime p greater than both B and 2d for which X² + d has a root in the ring ℤp of p-adic integers.

Put c = (max{B, 2d})! and take any prime divisor of d · c² + 1. Every prime up to max{B, 2d} divides c and hence leaves remainder 1 when it divides into d · c² + 1. Our prime p is larger than all of them. In particular it is odd and divides neither d nor c. The residue m = dc satisfies

m² + d = d(d · c² + 1) ≡ 0 (mod p),   2m ≢ 0 (mod p).

The derivative at this root is a unit. The simple-root form of Hensel’s lemma lifts the root to ℤp. One can see each new digit directly. If a² + d is divisible by pk with k ≥ 1, substitute a + pku. After division by pk, the congruence for the next digit is (a² + d)/pk + 2au ≡ 0 modulo p. The coefficient 2a stays invertible, so this determines a unique digit. The compatible residues define a root in the complete ring. For d = 1 and B = 3, we get c = 6 and p = 37. Starting at 6 gives 1 + 12u ≡ 0, so u = 3. The next lift is 117, and 117² + 1 = 10 · 37².

Where the finite exclusions come from. The integral arithmetic datum provides a positive integer e such that a prime at which −d is a square is good for the datum whenever it does not divide e. Fix a nonzero value of the chosen form at a finite adelic point g₀. By the restricted-product definition of the finite adèles, the matrices of g₀ are integral invertible outside finitely many places. Collect the rational primes under those exceptions, the level exceptions of the form and all the requested test places. Take B at least their maximum and at least e. The lemma supplies a good p outside that list, at which every component of g₀ is integral invertible. Thus the nonzero evaluation is still available when the stabilizer construction removes the p-component. The arithmetic datum and its integer e are inputs to this application.

How can one tell whether two test places choose the same quadratic root?

Let K = ℚ(x), with x² = −d and d positive, inside the CM field E. Two places of E can induce the same prime ideal of the integers of K. This matters at a rational prime q where the construction must choose one of two local roots. We need a test that works even when the chosen integral generator ω generates a proper subring of the integers of K.

Quadratic residue test. Suppose K = ℚ(ω), with ω integral of trace t, norm n and discriminant Δ = t² − 4n. Let q be a rational prime coprime to Δ for which X² − tX + n has a root modulo q. For every place w above q, there is a unique one of the two residue roots r for which ω − r belongs to w. A second place u restricts to the same prime of K exactly when it lies above q and ω reduces to r there. Complex conjugation exchanges the two roots.

In the residue field at w the quadratic factors as (X − r)(X − (t − r)). Its roots differ because (2r − t)² ≡ Δ modulo q. Reducing ω singles out one root. Since the conjugate of ω is t − ω, the conjugate place singles out the other. To see why testing this one generator detects every integral element y of K, write y = α + βω over ℚ. The traces of y and ωy are integers. Indeed they are rational sums of algebraic integers, and a rational root of a monic integer polynomial has denominator one. Evaluating the two traces gives the linear system

(2α + tβ,   tα + (t² − 2n)β) = (Tr(y), Tr(ωy)).

The determinant of this system is Δ. Eliminating α and β shows that Δy = A + Bω with A, B integers. Since Δ is invertible modulo any place above q, membership of y in that prime is equivalent to A + Br ≡ 0 modulo q. The criterion depends only on the residue root, proving the assertion for the whole ring of integers. Conversely the contraction records both q and whether it contains ω − r.

For example, take K = ℚ(i), ω = 2i and q = 5. The order ℤ[2i] misses i, but Δ = −16 is a unit modulo 5. The two roots for ω are 1 and 4. At a place where ω reduces to 1, the missing generator i reduces to 3, since 2 · 3 ≡ 1 modulo 5. At the conjugate place it reduces to 2. This explains why several distinct places of E can be assigned the same residue parameter in the integer level construction.

How deep must a level be to fix the chosen automorphic form?

The automorphic form Φ carries a local character χ at a distinguished place w₀. An element of its level can therefore act by a scalar. To make Φ invariant we must also put its component at w₀ in the kernel of χ. We now choose a single depth that enforces both conditions before passing to the geometric tower.

Let E be the CM field, n the positive rank and p the auxiliary rational prime. At a finite place u write 𝒪u for the local ring of integers, 𝔪u for its maximal ideal and Ku0 = GLn(𝒪u). The chosen form specifies a finite set S containing w₀ and open subgroups Ku for u ∈ S. At w₀ put J = Kw₀. The character χ of J has open kernel. In its global level the similitude multiplier is a unit at every rational prime, the components at u ∈ S lie in Ku, and the components at places outside both S and its CM conjugate lie in Ku0. Right translation by a level element h multiplies Φ by χ(hw₀).

The comparison of lattices gives a surjection j from the finite adelic unitary similitude group to the group used for the level away from p. Its kernel consists of the elements whose matrix components away from p are all the identity. The comparison also supplies local changes of basis au, integral with integral inverse at almost every place and at all places above p. The choice of p keeps every place in S away from p. In the construction one also chooses p so that some nonzero value of Φ occurs at an argument integral above p. The stabilizer calculation below uses the disjointness of S from the places above p.

Uniform stabilization lemma. Put T = S ∪ {u ∣ au ∉ Ku0}. This is a finite set away from p. There is an integer e ≥ 0 with the following property. Let g be an adelic similitude whose image j(g) preserves the level-one lattice. In lattice coordinates write

Cu = au gu au−1.   Assume Cu ≡ I modulo 𝔪ue for every u ∈ T.

Then j(g) has a lift h such that its inverse-transpose transform belongs to the global level of Φ and has w₀-component in ker χ. In particular, writing h∨ for that transform, Φ(z h∨) = Φ(z) for every z. This involution inverts the similitude multiplier.

Choosing the depth. Preservation of the level-one lattice is equivalent to Cu ∈ Ku0 for every u away from p. In these coordinates the lattice consists of the integral local columns. Applying the lattice action and its inverse to the coordinate columns tests integrality of every entry of Cu and its inverse. Conversely, these entry conditions preserve every integral column in both directions.

Every open neighbourhood of I in GLn(Eu) contains all integral matrices sufficiently close to I modulo a power of 𝔪u. Indeed, powers of the maximal ideal are a neighbourhood basis at zero. If C ∈ Ku0 and C − I has entries in 𝔪ur, so does C−1 − I = −C−1(C − I). Thus both matrices approach I entry by entry as r increases. This gives the assertion in the topology of the group of units. The Stacks Project, §15.37, adic neighbourhoods.[73]

At each u ∈ T apply this observation to the conditions that au−1C au be integral with integral inverse and, if u ∈ S, that its inverse transpose belong to Ku. These conditions define an open neighbourhood of I. Conjugation and inverse transpose are continuous, and the valuation ring is open, so entrywise integrality for a matrix and its inverse is open. Call the resulting depth ru. At w₀ use also the preimage of ker χ under the same conjugation followed by inverse transpose. This kernel is open in the open subgroup J, hence in the full matrix group. Write r₀ for the resulting depth. We may take

e = r₀ + maxu ∈ T ru.

For a local example, let a be diagonal with entries ϖ and 1, where ϖ is a uniformizer, and put C = I + ϖrE12 with r ≥ 1. Here E12 has its only nonzero entry, a one, in position (1, 2). Undoing the change of basis gives I + ϖr−1E12. Its inverse transpose is I − ϖr−1E21. A condition requiring congruence to I modulo ϖ² in the original coordinates thus requires r ≥ 3 along this family.

Constructing the lift. The level-one condition controls the coordinates away from p. To prescribe those above p, let ε be the rational finite adèle equal to 1 at p and 0 elsewhere. Its image over E is fixed by CM conjugation since it has the same value at conjugate places. Apply x ↦ εx + (1 − ε)I to the matrix of g, and apply the scalar version to its multiplier. This defines a homomorphism πp of the similitude group. Indeed ε² = ε and ε(1 − ε) = 0, so multiplication and the similitude relation hold separately on the two components. The new element agrees with g above p and equals the identity elsewhere. Consequently

h = g πp(g)−1,   j(h) = j(g),   hu = I above p,   hu = gu away from p.

The two lifts have the same image because πp(g) lies in the kernel of j. At u ∈ T the chosen depth now puts h∨u in Ku0, in Ku when prescribed, and in ker χ at w₀. At u away from both p and T, the two integral matrices au and Cu belong to the group Ku0. Therefore hu = au−1Cuau and its inverse transpose belong to that group as well. Above p the inverse transpose is the identity.

It remains to check the multiplier of h∨. At each place of E, the unitary similitude relation expresses the multiplier times I as a product of the conjugate transpose matrix from the conjugate place and the local matrix. Both factors have integral entries. A diagonal entry therefore shows that the multiplier is integral, since the rank is positive. Applying the calculation to (h∨)−1 proves that its reciprocal is integral. Every rational prime has a place of E above it. At that place the additive valuation of a rational local scalar is its rational valuation multiplied by the positive ramification index. Thus the multiplier has valuation zero at every finite rational prime. All the global level conditions now hold. The transformation law of Φ evaluates the remaining scalar at w₀ as χ(h∨w₀) = 1, proving invariance. The Stacks Project, Lemma 10.36.17, lying over for integral extensions.[74]

One integer level for all the prescribed places

At each place in a finite set T, we know how close a matrix must be to the identity to stabilize the chosen automorphic vector. We want a single integer M that imposes all those congruences. At a place w where we shall apply a Hecke operator, we also need a level ideal prime to w. Simply removing the entire rational prime below w from M can lose a required congruence at another place above the same prime.

Level and site theorem. Work over the CM field E with its chosen integral lattice and coordinates, the auxiliary prime p and the automorphic vector V of the uniform stabilizer theorem. Its level support S misses the places above p, and the form takes a nonzero value at a point integral above p. Let K = ℚ(x) = ℚ(ω) be the quadratic subfield specified by the integral generator ω. Fix a finite set Q of test places. Each w in Q lies over a good rational prime q ≠ p. Here good means that the quadratic polynomial of ω has two distinct roots modulo q and the trace pairing is perfect at q and the coefficient of the lattice form is a unit there. Write ū for the CM conjugate of a place u. Assume that w is split over the real subfield, that w and w̄ lie outside S, and that neither w̄ nor any ū with u in S has the same restriction to K as w. All test places over the same rational q must restrict to the same place of K. The two places of the quadratic subfield above q.

For every positive integer c prime to p, there is an integer M ≥ 3, prime to p and divisible by c and by every test prime. The principal subgroup of level M stabilizes V in the sense of the uniform stabilizer theorem. At every test place w we can also choose a site, consisting of its rational prime q, an integer root r modulo q, an auxiliary ideal 𝔞 and the subgroup of the associated ideal level. This subgroup has the same stabilizer property. Sites above the same rational prime use the same integer representative r and the same auxiliary ideal 𝔞.

From a depth to an integer. The uniform stabilizer theorem supplies a finite T away from p and a depth e ≥ 0. Each member of T belongs to S or has a nonintegral change of coordinates. Write 𝔭u for the ideal of u and ℓu for its residue characteristic, so ℓu ∈ 𝔭u. Take B to be p + 3 plus the largest test prime, with the last summand zero for an empty list. A prime divisor t of B! + 1 exceeds B, since every prime at most B divides B!. Any prime larger than B will do. Form the products

P = (∏u∈T ℓu)(∏w∈Q qw),   b = e|T| + e + 1,   M = ctPb.

All factors are positive and prime to p. The factor t gives M ≥ 3 even if both products are empty. The exponent b is at least 1, at least e and at least e|T|. Thus every test prime divides M, and ℓue divides M for every u in T. In particular (M) ⊆ 𝔭ue. For any nonzero ideal 𝔟 inside all these powers, a matrix in the subgroup of level 𝔟 belongs to the integral level-one subgroup. Its difference from the identity has entries in the extension of 𝔟 to each local integer ring away from p, measured in the frame coordinates. Those entries lie in 𝔭ue at every u in T, so the uniform depth applies. Taking 𝔟 = (M) proves the assertion for the principal level.

Keeping the congruences at the other places over q. Fix a test prime q. Choose one test place over it and choose an integer rq lifting the residue of ω on its side. The quadratic splitting criterion gives the same root at every test place over q. Let Tq be the places of T above q and let M(q) be the integer left after removing the full q-power from M. Set

𝔞q = ∏u∈Tq 𝔭ue,   𝔟q = (M(q)) 𝔞q.

Three containments explain this choice. First, (M) ⊆ 𝔟q. Indeed q divides P, so its exponent in M is at least b ≥ e|Tq|. For each u in Tq we have (q) ⊆ 𝔭u. Multiplying those inclusions, each raised to e, places the removed q-power in 𝔞q. Multiplication by M(q) gives the claim. In particular 𝔟q is nonzero.

Second, 𝔟q ⊆ 𝔭ue for every u in T. Above q, the right-hand ideal occurs in the product defining 𝔞q. Away from q, ℓue still divides M(q). The subgroup of level 𝔟q therefore satisfies the same stabilizer condition as the principal subgroup.

Third, (q, ω − rq)e|Tq| ⊆ 𝔞q, while 𝔞q is prime to each test ideal 𝔭w over q. To see both assertions, take u in Tq. The frame is integral over a good prime, so u must belong to S. Its conjugate cannot be on the side of w by hypothesis. There are only two sides, and conjugation exchanges them. Hence u is on the side of w, and q and ω − rq both belong to 𝔭u. Multiplication gives the required power containment. Since w is outside S, each 𝔭u is a maximal ideal distinct from 𝔭w. Their powers and their product are consequently prime to 𝔭w. This also covers the empty product, when 𝔞q is the unit ideal.

Finally M(q) is prime to p and q, and it is at least 3 because it retains t. The local pairing condition holds by goodness of q, and ω reduces to rq at w. These facts give all the required site data. Their construction uses q alone for the shared root and auxiliary ideal. The eigenvalues for the geometric correspondence still require the spectral and Hodge arguments.

An example with two places on one side. Let E = ℚ(ζ), where ζ is a primitive eighth root of unity, and take ω = i = ζ². At q = 17 the polynomial X² + 1 has distinct roots 4 and −4. The ideals 𝔭w = (ζ − 2) and 𝔭u = (ζ + 2) each have index 17, since the absolute determinant of multiplication by their generator on the integer lattice is its norm, 24 + 1 = 17. They are distinct since their generators differ by 4, a unit at primes above 17. The index calculation uses the ideal norm formula. Both residues send i to 4. The field discriminant is prime to 17 since the power basis of ζ has discriminant 256, the norm of the derivative 4ζ³. For example the integral trace pairing twisted by −i is perfect at 17, and the real coefficient −(ζ + ζ−1) is a unit there since its square is 2.

To illustrate the ideal construction, take T = {u}, Q = {w}, e = 2, p = 5, c = 2 and t = 29. Then P = 17², b = 5 and M = 58 · 1710. Removing the 17-part leaves 58, which is a unit at both places. The site ideal (58)𝔭u² reinstates depth two at u and remains a unit at w. The shared quadratic root is represented by 4. This calculation takes the stabilizer support and depth as inputs.

How can a Hecke trace detect a prescribed system of eigenvalues?

Let K be the compact open subgroup at the integer level N. A Hecke function at this level is bi-invariant under K and supported on finitely many right cosets. Write ∗ for convolution. Let ψj be the functions attached to the chosen correspondences and θj their prescribed complex scalars. A polynomial in words is a finite linear combination of ordered products of the ψj. The empty word acts as the identity. For such a polynomial s, let s(ψ)f mean the result of applying its convolutions to a test function f, and let s(θ) mean its scalar evaluation.

Spectral trace test. Use the odd-rank unitary datum and the nonzero automorphic form of the prescribed local type at w₀. The rational prime below w₀ is good for the datum, and its chosen quadratic generator generates the same field as √(−d). No prime above p occurs in the level support of the form, and the form has a nonzero value at an argument integral with integral inverse above p.

Given any finite set of excluded rational primes, the auxiliary-prime construction chooses a good prime r outside this set, distinct from p and away from the level support of the form. Take an admissible multiple N of r whose principal level lifts to the stabilizer with trivial type character. Use the stabilizing deck operators belonging to the principal subgroup at r, with scalar 1, or the spherical operators at eligible places away from r, with their prescribed index and character normalization. The assembly of the local tests specifies which operators to include. For each such family there is a Hecke function f such that g−1 carries the integral lattice into itself whenever f(g) ≠ 0. The ψj commute on all words applied to f. There is one polynomial A such that whenever s(θ) ≠ 0, the test (As)(ψ)f satisfies the regularity and vanishing conditions of the trace formula and has nonzero definite automorphic trace.

From the form to a finite space. The local type gives a Hecke idempotent e, so e ∗ e = e. Transport of the given automorphic form supplies a nonzero vector φ fixed by e on which each ψj acts by θj. It belongs to one of the spaces of definite automorphic forms at this level and weight. Take their direct sum M over the finitely many definite Hermitian classes in the trace formula. For each class the double coset set at the specified level is finite. Evaluation on representatives determines a form, by its rational transformation law on the left and level invariance on the right. Each summand therefore embeds in a finite product of copies of the coefficient space. In particular M is finite dimensional, and the sum of the traces on its summands is the trace on M. Finite class number and evaluation at representatives.

For a Hecke function h, write T(h) for its action on M. Convolution becomes composition. Put M₀ = im T(e). The local Hecke relations imply that each T(ψj) preserves M₀ and that their restrictions Tj commute. At the chosen auxiliary places a second construction supplies functions u and u′, with e ∗ u = u ∗ e = u and u′ ∗ u = e. On M₀ the operator B induced by u commutes with every Tj and has a left inverse. It is thus invertible on this finite-dimensional space.

Choosing the multiplier. Start with M₀, which contains φ. Whenever Tj − θjI fails to be nilpotent on the remaining space, restrict to its generalized θj-eigenspace there. The dimension decreases and φ survives. Each restriction is a polynomial projection. Indeed, on M₀ factor the minimal polynomial of Tj as (X − θj)kb(X) with b(θj) ≠ 0. The Euclidean algorithm gives a multiple of b congruent to 1 modulo (X − θj)k. Evaluated at Tj it fixes the kernel of (Tj − θjI)k and maps into it, since the full minimal polynomial annihilates Tj. These projections commute. Their finite product A(T) projects onto a nonzero space L on which every Tj − θjI is nilpotent. The product uses finitely many indices even when the family of correspondences is infinite, and A(θ) = 1.

Choosing the function. The operator B preserves L and is invertible there. Put tm = tr(Bm|L). Some positive m has tm ≠ 0. In fact the minimal polynomial of B|L has nonzero constant coefficient. Taking the trace of its annihilating identity shows that if all positive power traces vanished, its constant coefficient times t₀ would vanish as well. But t₀ = dimℂ L > 0. Fix such an m and take f = u∗m ∗ e. On L the difference s(T) − s(θ)I is a polynomial without constant term in the finitely many commuting nilpotent differences occurring in s. In a sufficiently high power every resulting monomial contains a power of one of these differences large enough to vanish. Thus the difference is nilpotent. Its product with the commuting Bm is also nilpotent and has trace zero. The trailing e removes the kernel of T(e), and A(T) removes the complementary summand to L in M₀. Consequently

trM T((As)(ψ)f) = s(θ) trL(Bm).

For example, let one operator have diagonal entries 2, 2, 5 and let B have diagonal entries 1, −1, 1 in the same diagonal basis. To detect θ = 2 take A(X) = (5 − X)/3. On the selected two-dimensional space the first power of B has trace zero and the second has trace 2. With s(X) = X + 1 the resulting trace is 6. The common eigenvector φ establishes that the selected space is nonzero. The scalar-valued function f supplies a trace that detects that space.

The passage from this trace identity to a geometric test uses two local results. The auxiliary Hecke function puts the support of each positive convolution power into a regular set. The inverses of points in the support of each power carry the integral lattice into itself. The regular set is stable under left multiplication by the supports of the ψj, so their words retain regular support. Cuspidality of the type at w₀ and separability of the local characteristic polynomial at an auxiliary place kill the orbital terms from marked pairs with reducible polynomial and from elements of the definite forms outside the regular irreducible locus. The construction of these local functions and the orbital vanishing theorems enter here as inputs. The Hodge comparison uses the resulting trace test to obtain a joint eigenclass.
