How does one level carry all the requested spectral tests?

A test of Hodge weights needs good reduction at its place. A polynomial test needs the Hecke operators at its place. Write H for the finite set of places of the first kind and C for those of the second. We shall require H and C to be disjoint. We now construct the family of operators used for both purposes and compute its polynomial.

Hypotheses on the field and representation. The CM field E contains x with x² = −d for a positive integer d. The element −d is a square in ℚℓ, the maximal real subfield E⁺ has even degree over ℚ, and each finite place nonsplit over E⁺ is unramified over it and lies away from ℓ. Fix an identification ι of the algebraic closure of ℚℓ with ℂ. The representation U is irreducible automorphic on the definite unitary group of odd rank a. At a designated place w₀ above ℓ it has a cuspidal type. Here a torsion-free compact open subgroup maps onto a cyclic group of ℓ-power order. A nontrivial character of this quotient occurs on a nonzero vector of U, and every smooth irreducible local representation containing that character is cuspidal.

Write K = ℚ(x). Each place in H ∪ C is split over E⁺ and spherical for U, has a different restriction to E⁺ from w₀, and lies over a rational prime q for which −d is a square in ℚq. At a common rational prime the test places must all induce the same place of K. Above ℓ this must be the place induced by w₀.

Assembly theorem. Given the integral group datum, its automorphic vector and the spectral and local comparison inputs specified below, there is one level with one family of correspondences and one system of scalar values. It passes the group-side good-reduction and weight tests at every place in H and the polynomial test at every place in C. It also passes the polynomial test at all eligible spherical places away from ℓ outside one finite exception set. Here the group-side tests are the hypotheses that the geometric transfer theorem uses to obtain its conclusions about a tower.

Choosing the form and its level. Call a place u allowed if its conjugate has a different restriction to K from every requested place. At least one of u and its conjugate is allowed in each split pair. Indeed, if both were forbidden, two requested places of the same residue characteristic would induce opposite primes of K, contradicting the quadratic residue test and the compatibility hypothesis. The place w₀ is allowed for the same reason. The automorphic vector construction with this choice of sides supplies a nonzero form, an auxiliary character κ and a finite exceptional support S. At each requested place w, sphericity and separation from w₀ keep w and its conjugate outside S. The choice of sides also keeps the conjugates of the supported places away from the required prime of K. These are the freedom conditions used by the level construction.

Choose the geometric prime p outside the residue characteristics of the requested places, those of the full support S, and those where the argument of the nonzero evaluation is nonintegral. The spectral construction supplies a second prime r₀, distinct from p and from the requested residue characteristics. At this point only the prime and the spectral assertion for levels divisible by it are fixed. Apply the integer-level theorem with c = r₀. It gives a level N divisible by r₀ and a compatible site at every requested place. Their stabilizer property permits the spectral trace test at that level.

Choosing the operators. Include the eligible deck transformations (changes of level structure) with value 1. Include each eligible local Hecke correspondence at a place outside H whose site is compatible with all the requested sites. For each such entry record the scalar provided by the local action on the chosen form. The spectral assertion applies to this entire indexed family. It supplies a test function f on whose convolution words the operators commute. For each polynomial nonzero at the recorded scalars, a further polynomial multiplier gives an admissible convolution with nonzero trace. The simultaneous eigenclass in cohomology is obtained later by geometric comparison.

At a place w in C, write Q for its residue field size and B for any multiset of spherical parameters of U there. Write ei(B) for the elementary symmetric polynomial of degree i, with e₀ = 1. For each i from zero to a there is an eligible local operator. Its scalar is a subgroup index times ι(ϑi), where

ι(ϑi) = Qi(a−i)/2 ei(B) κ(w)−i.

The index counts the cosets in the correspondence and is removed in the local congruence. The coefficient of Xa−i in its Hecke polynomial is (−1)iQi(i−1)/2ι(ϑi). The two exponents of Q add to i(a−1)/2. This is precisely the exponent obtained by multiplying each of the a parameters by Q(a−1)/2 before evaluating the elementary symmetric polynomial. Thus the roots are the algebraically normalized parameters divided by κ(w), with their multiplicities. Here ι(ϑ₀) = 1, so the constructed polynomial is monic.

For a rank-three check, take Q = 5, B = {1, 2, 3} and κ(w) = 5 in the coefficient formula. The four values are 1, 6, 11/5 and 6/125. The Hecke polynomial multiplies the last two by 5 and 125 before applying the alternating signs. It gives X³ − 6X² + 11X − 6, whose roots are 1, 2 and 3.

At a place v in H, all the non-deck operators in our family come from different places and compatible sites. These are the hypotheses of the group-side good-reduction criterion. Deck transformations at its site have scalar 1. Indeed the site subgroup stabilizes the chosen vector and lies in the level at r₀, because r₀ divides the part of N prime to the residue characteristic of v. The weight comparison for the automorphic vector then supplies, at each embedding above v, all the shifted exponents required for the Hodge test. Such embeddings induce places over ℓ through ι. For a place in H away from ℓ this exponent condition is empty, while the good-reduction and unramified-character conditions still apply.

Finally exclude places whose residue characteristic divides Nep, together with those whose characteristic occurs in S. Here e is the defect integer of the arithmetic datum. The exception set is finite because the factorization of each rational prime has finitely many prime ideal factors. At every remaining eligible spherical place away from ℓ the local site may use the principal subgroup of level N. Its residue characteristic differs from those of all the prescribed sites, which divide N. The same coefficient calculation applies there. The direct calculation at each w in C is essential because its characteristic was deliberately made to divide N. The arithmetic datum, the choice of automorphic vector and frame, and the geometric comparisons still have their own existence theorems.

Which places must be tested on the same geometric tower?

Two places above ℓ have fixed roles from the start. The place w₀ carries the cuspidal type. The place v′ carries the weight test that will later be used in rank extraction. They have different restrictions to the maximal real subfield E⁺ and the same restriction to the quadratic field K. Assume the field and type hypotheses and sphericity at v′. In the application U is unramified at nonsplit places off a finite exceptional set, and spherical at split places whose restrictions to E⁺ avoid the type place and the specified exceptional places. To select the extra tests below, sphericity at each named place is given explicitly.

For a place in H we obtain an unramified auxiliary character, the group-side good-reduction condition, and the prescribed exponents for every embedding above it. For a place in C we obtain the polynomial for every multiset of spherical parameters there. Each row gives a single application of the level construction.

Places that share one level and one system of scalar values

Base choice{v′}∅

Why the choices satisfy the hypotheses. For the base choice, every place above ℓ is split over E⁺ by the field hypothesis, and −d is a square in ℚℓ. The two specified restrictions of v′ give the remaining compatibility. At an additional spherical place w away from ℓ, assume it is split over E⁺ and −d is a square at its residue characteristic. That characteristic differs from ℓ. Consequently w cannot lie above the same prime of E⁺ as w₀, and there is no common residue characteristic with v′ at which to compare quadratic roots.

For an additional spherical w above ℓ, assume its real-subfield restriction is different from both those of w₀ and v′ and that its restriction to K equals that of v′. Transitivity gives agreement with w₀ on K. This checks the common-root condition in each of the last two rows. The different real-subfield restrictions imply w ≠ v′, so H and C in the last row are disjoint.

To see the two restrictions separately, take a primitive eighth root ζ, put E = ℚ(ζ) and choose ℓ = 17. We have K = ℚ(ζ²) = ℚ(i) and E⁺ = ℚ(ζ + ζ−1) = ℚ(√2). The discriminants of the displayed quadratic generators are −4 and 8. At 17 their residues determine their primes by the quadratic residue calculation, whose trace argument applies also to the real quadratic generator. At the type place take ζ ≡ 2. The choice ζ ≡ −2 has the same square and the opposite real trace. The choice ζ ≡ 2−1 has the same real trace and the opposite square. There are just two primes of E⁺ above 17 in this example. They exhibit the choice of v′ relative to w₀. The extra w in the last two rows requires a third prime of E⁺ above ℓ. At 2 the polynomials (X + 1)⁴ + 1 and X² − 2 are Eisenstein. The local fields generated by ζ − 1 and √2 therefore have ramification indices four and two. Their relative index is two, so this example illustrates the local test at 17. A. V. Sutherland, Number Theory I, Lecture 11, Lemma 11.4 and Theorem 11.5.[75] The level example computes the prime ideals.

Their levels, auxiliary characters and finite exceptional sets can be chosen separately. After the auxiliary character of each tower has been removed, the underlying spherical parameters again belong to the same U. The later comparison on a dense set of Frobenius elements uses this agreement. The large gaps in the weight enter when extracting a representation from cohomology.

How do the field labels determine the base of the tower?

The level and its operators are defined using a field F in the group datum. The tower is to be taken over the CM field E of the automorphic representation. Fix the supplied field isomorphism η from F to E. Before a geometric fibre power can be chosen we need a root ρ in E and a map from the integers of F into E for each label of the datum. They specify how the coefficient field acts on the base. In this construction the datum has a single label. The unitary rank can still be any of the positive odd ranks under consideration.

Standard base lemma. Let ω be the integral element in the datum, with ω + ω̄ = t and ωω̄ = n. When there is one label, the standard base exists over E. Its root and labelled homomorphism are given by the following formulas.

ρ = η(ω),   t₀(y) = η(y)   for y ∈ 𝒪F.

Indeed, expand ω² − (ω + ω̄)ω + ωω̄ to obtain zero. Applying η gives ρ² − tρ + n = 0, since a field isomorphism fixes the rational integers. The map t₀ sends ω to ρ by construction. For a general datum, the differences of the maps belonging to two distinct labels must generate the unit ideal. A single label has no distinct partner, so all conditions on the base are now verified.

These equalities are used again after choosing an embedding τ of E into ℂ and its field automorphism σ from the weight test. That test arranges σ(τ(η(y))) = τ₀(y) for the distinguished embedding τ₀ of F. For any integral y this verifies the required embedding of t₀(y). Setting y = ω verifies the required image of ρ. The Hodge comparison can therefore be applied with both labels fixed once the geometric fibre power and its comparison theorem are available.

Which maps of abelian schemes give the transitions in the tower?

Fix the standard base over the CM field E and the auxiliary rational prime p. For each integer N ≥ 3 prime to p, choose a moduli scheme XN over E with universal abelian scheme aN ∶ AN → XN. A point of XN specifies an abelian variety with an action of the order in the unitary datum, a polarization compatible with its involution, and a level marking. In a family the polarization is recorded by a symmetric line bundle on the fibre square, trivial on the zero axes and relatively ample on the diagonal. The action on tangent spaces has the prescribed labelled multiplicities. The marking αN sends the fixed lattice Λ into torsion sections. At each geometric point it extends to compatible torsion coordinates respecting the action and the Weil pairings. In particular it identifies Λ/NΛ with the N-torsion there.

Existence of the generic model. The Harris–Taylor integral moduli theorem used here supplies a representing scheme with its universal object at each such level over a Noetherian base satisfying the integral datum. A Noetherian ℚ-algebra with the standard labels qualifies since all nonzero integers are units. In characteristic zero the comparison of moduli problems keeps the abelian scheme, its action, line bundle and sections. The full Tate-coordinate theorem supplies the required coordinates on every geometric fibre. Conversely, the polarization kernel condition and the prime-to-p torsion coordinates recover the integral moduli conditions. Both descriptions use the same Cartesian maps preserving the structures. Thus a family over an E-scheme S has a unique classifying morphism S → XN, along which its structured abelian scheme is the pullback of the universal one. Representability of the integral problem and the two torsion comparisons are inputs to this deduction. The classical construction at the unitary levels is given in M. Harris and R. Taylor, The Geometry and Cohomology of Some Simple Shimura Varieties, Chapter III[76].

The pair to construct. Write KN for the principal subgroup of level N and Λ̂ for the adelic lattice away from p. An adelic element h gives a transition from N′ to N when hΛ̂ ⊆ Λ̂ and hKN′h−1 ⊆ KN. Realizing this action on the moduli data requires a base map πh ∶ XN′ → XN over E and a map of total spaces Φh ∶ AN′ → AN. To specify the second map, pull back the target abelian scheme to XN′. We seek an isogeny ψh from AN′ to πh∗AN. Composing it with the projection to AN gives Φh and proves the equality

aN ∘ Φh = πh ∘ aN′.

The isogeny commutes with the order action. It pulls back the target polarization bundle to a positive tensor power of the source bundle, whose exponent is prime to p and agrees with the similitude multiplier of h up to an integral adelic unit away from p. The torsion condition uses geometric coordinates extending the source and target markings. For every positive m prime to p, the source point labelled x maps to the target point labelled y precisely when hx ≡ y modulo mΛ̂. This specifies the action even when the source and target levels differ.

Building the isogeny at a deeper level. Clear denominators in the inverse action of h by an integer k > 0 prime to p. The lattice construction supplies compatible additive maps Fm on Λ with hFm(x) ≡ kx modulo mΛ̂, together with the order and pairing compatibilities. Work first at level Nk. The subgroup of sections by which to quotient has elements αNk(N FNk(x)) for x ∈ Λ. It is a subgroup by additivity, and multiplication by k sends every one of its elements to zero because αNk kills NkΛ. The Hecke quotient theorem for a locally Noetherian base gives the quotient ψ ∶ A → A′ with its descended polarization and level-N marking. Multiplication by k on A is constant on the fibres of ψ and descends to a map χ ∶ A′ → A. Thus χ ∘ ψ = [k]. Composing with ψ on the left and using that ψ is a surjective quotient gives ψ ∘ χ = [k] on A′. In characteristic zero such a pair gives a finite étale surjective isogeny. The universal property of XN now classifies the quotient family.

The quotient is first available with this additional marking. To use it over the original source, one must show that changing the extra marking leaves both maps unchanged. The descent argument below proves this on the overlap of two lifts. It produces the pair (πh, Φh) at the required level.

Uniqueness and composition when the maps exist. Two transitions for the same h agree on geometric points by the marked-isogeny criterion applied with the identity change of marking. Reducedness of the source and separatedness of the target give equality of the base maps. The same argument on the smooth total spaces of the abelian schemes gives equality of Φ. In particular an element of KN at unchanged level induces the identity. If the first step has label h and the second h′, pull the second isogeny back along the first base map and compose. A possible change u between the intermediate torsion coordinates belongs to the middle level subgroup. Admissibility of h′ puts h′u−1(h′)−1 in the final level subgroup, where it can be absorbed in the target coordinates. Thus the composite acts on the marked lattice by h′h. Uniqueness gives

πh′h = πh′ ∘ πh,   Φh′h = Φh′ ∘ Φh.

For a simple case, take p = 5, source level 12, target level 3 and h = 1. If a lattice vector gives a point P of order 12 in the original marking, it gives 4P of order 3 in the new marking. The abelian variety over this geometric point is the same. The map of moduli schemes forgets the finer marking. This is the transition that yields Cartesian squares when one passes to the fibre powers.

Descending a transition map to the prescribed level

Keep the moduli schemes and their universal abelian schemes over the standard base field. Write K(N) for the principal subgroup and Λ̂ for the prime-to-p adelic lattice. Fix a power k ≥ 0. A point of the fibre product ZN specifies a point of XN and k points of its abelian variety. At power zero only the point of XN remains.

Transition theorem. Let h be an adelic element. Assume hΛ̂ ⊆ Λ̂ and hK(N′)h−1 ⊆ K(N). Then h induces a map Th from ZN′ to ZN over the ground field. It is independent of the finer level used to construct it. An element of K(N) acts as the identity at level N. For successive admissible elements h and g the composition is Tg ∘ Th = Tgh.

Choosing the common cover. Write d for the denominator used in the preceding isogeny construction. It is prime to p and clears h−1 on Λ̂. Such a d exists because the adelic lattice and its transform are commensurable away from p. If u is congruent to the identity at level Nd, apply u − 1 to dh−1Λ̂ ⊆ Λ̂. Its image lies in NdΛ̂. Applying h and cancelling d puts the image of huh−1 − 1 in NΛ̂. The same calculation with u−1 gives the full subgroup condition. Pull the pair constructed at level Nd back to level M = N′Nd. Its two maps are now defined on a cover of the prescribed source.

Descent and independence. Forgetting level gives a finite étale surjection c from XM to XN′. Two geometric lifts of a point differ by a change of level u in K(N′). The target change huh−1 belongs to K(N), so the transformed objects agree at level N. Rigidity of a polarized isogeny with its action on the prime-to-p Tate modules gives agreement on the abelian varieties as well. For the map on moduli points, the two pullbacks to XM ×XN′ XM therefore agree on all geometric points. This fibre product is reduced, since it is étale over a smooth scheme over a field. The target is separated, so the equalizer is closed and contains this entire reduced scheme. The map descends uniquely along c. On total spaces the forgetful map is the base change of c. The same argument descends the map of abelian varieties, using smoothness of the source and separatedness of the target. The endomorphism, polarization and Tate-module compatibilities descend with it. The Stacks Project, §35.13, descent of morphisms along faithfully flat covers.[77]

Denote the resulting pair by (πh, Φh). Two constructions can be compared after forgetting from a common multiple of their fine levels. There they have the same transformed moduli point and the same map of its abelian variety by the uniqueness just used. Since the common cover is surjective and étale, the descended pairs coincide. The pair for g composed with the pair for h realizes the transformation for gh, by composition of the isogenies and of their level structures. An element of the level subgroup realizes the identity pair. Applying these statements to the base point and then to each of the k coordinates proves the composition and identity laws for the fibre powers.

Which level changes give finite étale covers?

Fibre theorem. Suppose K(M) ⊆ K(N) for two admissible principal levels. For the transition with h = 1, forgetting the finer structure gives a finite étale surjection at every power k. The power at level M is its cartesian pullback from level N. More explicitly,

ZM ≅ XM ×XN ZN.

When N divides M, the map on moduli schemes forgets the additional level structure. Its geometric input is the finite étale surjectivity of the full-level forgetful map. For an inclusion of principal subgroups, the level MN maps to both. The two composites to XN agree by the transition theorem. Finiteness and étaleness thus descend along the finite étale surjection to XM, and every point of XN lifts from level MN. In the forgetful transition the abelian variety is unchanged after base change, so its square with the moduli schemes is cartesian. Giving k points of the pulled-back abelian variety amounts to giving their common base point at level M and their images at level N. This proves the displayed isomorphism. Finite étale surjections remain finite étale and surjective under base change.

The quotient acting on a fibre. Assume K(M) is normal in K(N). Each element u of K(N) acts at level M because it normalizes the finer subgroup. The composition law makes this a left action, and K(M) acts trivially. Given two geometric lifts of the same moduli point, their level structures differ by an element of K(N). If the lifts give the same point downstairs in the fibre power, the cartesian square shows that this element also takes the first lifted tuple to the second. Conversely, an element fixing a tuple fixes its level-M moduli point. Rigidity identifies its action there with the identity on the abelian variety, and the full level structure forces u ≡ 1 modulo M. Thus K(N)/K(M) acts freely and transitively on every geometric fibre.

For an intermediate subgroup K(M) ⊆ H ⊆ K(N), forgetting the choice within an H-orbit gives an intermediate finite étale cover. To see this, pull the cover back along itself. The free transitive action identifies the pullback with a disjoint union indexed by the quotient group. Taking the orbits of H/K(M) gives a finite set of components compatible with descent. The descended cover has that orbit set as its geometric fibre. Here normality of K(M) in K(N) provides the group acting on the fibre. The construction of the intermediate cover imposes no normality assumption on H. The Stacks Project, §95.6, descent of finite étale covers.[78]

A common normal refinement is available for finitely many prescribed levels and translates. For each pair (Nj, hj), the principal-level congruence theorem gives a positive factor cj prime to p such that conjugation by hj carries level Njcj into level Nj. Taking M = N ∏j Njcj imposes all these inclusions. The principal kernel K(M) is invariant under conjugation by the integral level-one subgroup, hence normal in K(N).

We can now count a fibre even when the given inclusion is not assumed normal. Write H ⊆ J for the two level groups and take a common finer level L normal in J. Over a point at level J there are [J : L] lifts to level L by the normal case. Each lift to the intermediate level H has [H : L] such points above it. Dividing gives [J : L]/[H : L] = [J : H], since every H-coset in J is a union of [H : L] cosets of L.

The geometric correspondence uses an intermediate subgroup in a specific way. Given K(N) ⊆ K ⊆ K(1), it takes one copy of ZM for each coset of K(N) in K. Here N divides M and the datum requires (hu)K(M)(hu)−1 ⊆ K(N) for every u in K. On the copy labelled by a representative u, the two arrows are the forgetful transition and Thu. Both have principal level N as their target. This description defines the correspondence using the principal-level models already constructed.

How many points lie over a point of the Hecke correspondence?

At a principal level N, write ZN for the fibre power constructed above. A Hecke correspondence gives two maps from one scheme to ZN. To apply it to a point we first take all its lifts by the source map s, then take their images by the target map t. We can count the lifts before specifying where t sends them.

Degree theorem. Let K(N) ⊆ K ⊆ K(1) and let the finer principal level M be a multiple of N. Assume the admissibility conditions of the transition theorem for each translated target map. The source map is finite étale. Every point over an algebraically closed field has exactly

d = [K : K(N)] · [K(N) : K(M)] = [K : K(M)]

lifts. The space ZN is smooth over the ground field. For the compact unitary datum used here it is projective.

Proof. For each coset c in K/K(N) take one copy of ZM. On this copy s forgets level and t uses the translated element h times the chosen representative of c. The first index in the formula counts copies. It is finite since K(N) has finite index in K(1). A point above x specifies its copy c and one lift in that copy. By the fibre calculation there are exactly [K(N) : K(M)] such lifts. Summing over the copies gives the product. Each copy maps by a finite étale morphism. Their finite disjoint union is again finite étale, since over an affine open its algebra is the finite product of the algebras of the copies and étaleness can be checked on each copy.

For instance, if the two indices are 2 and 3, take a point x and label its lifts on one copy u, v, w. Above x in the whole source are the six pairs (1, u), …, (2, w). Some of their images under t can coincide. Those images then enter the correspondence with their multiplicities.

For smoothness, start with the smooth principal-level moduli scheme and its smooth abelian scheme. Taking a further fibre factor is a base change of the abelian scheme followed by composition. Both operations preserve smoothness. The zeroth power is the moduli scheme itself. For projectivity, the compact-datum moduli theorem gives a projective base. The polarization gives a relatively ample line bundle on the abelian scheme. The exterior product of its pullbacks to the factors gives a relatively ample line bundle on the fibre power. Projectivity over the base and projectivity of the base over the field now give the asserted projectivity. This uses the compactness hypothesis at the moduli step. The degree formula uses the level indices.

Which integral model receives the tower?

At principal level N, the moduli space XN and its fibre power ZN are defined over the number field E. To study reduction at a place w, we need a space over its local ring R = 𝒪E,w. We build it by keeping two pieces of the full level marking. This specifies the target, as well as the map from the tower to its generic fibre.

Integral model and comparison theorem. Take the compact unitary moduli datum of the standard base theorem, with one distinguished embedding on each side of the link, algebra degree one and odd group rank. The identification F ≅ E carries the place 𝔴 of the datum to w and gives the chosen generic labels. At the good prime q ≠ p, the quadratic polynomial of ω has a simple root r modulo q, the lattice pairing is perfect over ℤq, and 𝔴 contains (q, ω − r). Use the level factorization 𝔫 = (N0)𝔞, where N0 ≥ 3 is prime to pq, 𝔞 + 𝔴 = 𝒪F, and 𝔞 contains a power of (q, ω − r).

There is a smooth projective R-scheme M representing the integral level-N0 moduli problem. A finite étale cover Y → M records, in addition, a marking of the torsion killed by every element of 𝔞. Write AY for the pullback of the universal abelian scheme on M. For k ≥ 0 its k-fold fibre product 𝒵 over Y is smooth and projective over R. At any principal tower level N prime to p with N ∈ 𝔫, a choice of auxiliary generator a as below gives a comparison

πN ∶ ZN → 𝒵E, 𝒵E = 𝒵 ×Spec R Spec E.

Construction. First extend the standard labels to R. The integral labels are the images of ω and the integers of F under the given field identification and localization. Integers prime to q are units in R. The degree-one algebra splits at q, so these labels define the same unitary datum there, with residue field of order qf at w. The integral representability theorem supplies M, of relative dimension n − 1 for lattice rank parameter n. Compactness gives properness, hence projectivity with the quasi-projective moduli embedding. The finite-level representability theorem applies to 𝔞 by its support and coprimality conditions above. It supplies Y and identifies its universal family with the one pulled back from M. These two representability results are geometric inputs. For the unitary moduli construction see Harris and Taylor, The Geometry and Cohomology of Some Simple Shimura Varieties, Chapter III[76].

The finite map makes Y projective over R, and étaleness preserves the relative dimension of M. The polarization gives relative projectivity of the abelian scheme. Forming another fibre factor pulls back a smooth abelian scheme of relative dimension g = dim(AY/Y). Starting at 𝒵 = Y when k = 0 gives relative dimension (n − 1) + kg over R. The Stacks Project, finite morphisms are projective[79] and smooth morphisms under composition and base change[80].

It remains to specify the two markings. Since N ∈ (N0)𝔞, the rational number c = N/N0 belongs to 𝒪F and hence is a positive integer. In the Dedekind ring 𝒪F, write (N) = 𝔞𝔟. One can choose a with (a, N) = 𝔟 by prescribing its valuation at the finitely many primes dividing N using the Chinese remainder theorem. Thus

N = N0c, (a, N)𝔞 = (N), η0(y) = ηN(cy), λ(y) = ηN(ay).

Here ηN is the full level marking on the lattice Λ. The first mark retains level N0. To read the second, localize at a prime dividing N. If N and 𝔞 have valuations s and b, multiplication by a on Λ/NΛ has the same image and kernel there as multiplication by a uniformizer to the power s − b. Its kernel in Λ is therefore 𝔞Λ locally, and its image in Λ/NΛ consists exactly of the classes killed by 𝔞. At primes away from N the quotient vanishes. The full marking now identifies Λ/𝔞Λ with the required torsion on geometric fibres.

The two marks belong to the original polarized abelian scheme, with its prescribed endomorphisms. The representing property gives a map jN ∶ XN → Y over R and identifies the original family with the pullback of AY. Level-N0 rigidity makes this identification unique for the chosen marks. Applying it to each of the k points gives a map to 𝒵. Its structure map already factors through Spec E, so the universal property of the generic fibre gives πN.

Why does changing the full marking leave the comparison unchanged?

Let K0 consist of the elements preserving the prime-to-p adelic lattice Λ̂ in both directions and inducing the identity modulo 𝔫Λ̂. An element u of this group can move a full level-N marking. We show that the two marks seen by Y, and the images of the points in the abelian scheme, survive such a move.

Invariance under transport and refinement. Keep c and a at level N. Let N′ = Nt be another admissible principal level, with marks given by ct and ta. These satisfy the same ideal identity, since (ta, Nt) = (t)(a, N). For every u ∈ K0 and every defined tower transition Tu from level N′ to level N,

πN ∘ Tu = πN′.

Proof. The transition on abelian schemes is an isomorphism to the transported family. Indeed, u and u−1 preserve Λ̂, so the inverse-isogeny construction can use the integer 1 in the two composites. The polarization is preserved with exponent one as well. The transition formula expresses its similitude multiplier as a positive integer d prime to p times an integral adelic unit away from p. The multiplier of a lattice automorphism and its inverse are themselves integral away from p. Hence d has zero valuation at every prime away from p, and coprimality also gives zero valuation at p. This forces d = 1.

The ideals (N0) and 𝔞 are coprime because N0 is prime to q and 𝔞 contains a power of (q, ω − r). The Chinese remainder theorem splits the congruence on u into the congruences modulo those two ideals. The first identifies the transported ηN′(cty) with ηN(cy). For the second, (a)𝔞 ⊆ (N) gives u(ay) − ay ∈ NΛ̂ for every y. Under the transition the mark ηN′(tay) therefore becomes ηN(ay). The two maps into Y classify the same marked object. Uniqueness identifies both their base maps and their maps of abelian schemes. Applying the latter to every point in the fibre power proves the formula.

At t = 1 this gives invariance at a fixed level. When K(N) ⊆ K0, the action descends to the finite group K0/K(N). With the right-action convention, z · δ is the transition for a representative of δ−1. Invariance shows that every such orbit lies in a fibre of πN. The finite étale comparison and the description of its fibres by the graphs of this action give the converse. A relation among correspondences after reduction at w requires the separate special-fibre congruence.

For example, take 𝔞 = 𝒪F, N0 = 3 and N = 6 at a site with p = 5 and q = 17. We can choose c = 2 and a = 6. The auxiliary marking is zero and the retained marking is η6(2y). At level 12 the choices become 4 and 12. Forgetting from 12 to 6 sends η12(4y) to η6(2y), two descriptions of the same 3-torsion point. This checks the factor t in the comparison.

Why is the map from the tower to the generic fibre finite étale?

Work over the valuation ring O at the chosen place, with fraction field E. Keep the integral models Y → M and their universal abelian schemes. Write 𝒵 = AYk and 𝒫 = AMk for the two fibre powers. A subscript E denotes the generic fibre. At the admissible principal level N = cN₀, choose the generator a and the quotient with its two level markings as in the invariance lemma. This gives the comparison πN from the tower space ZN over E to 𝒵E.

Finite étale comparison. The map πN is finite étale for every such quotient and every k ≥ 0. Let K₀ be the level subgroup defined by the integral model’s level ideal. If two geometric points z, z′ of ZN have the same image, then some u ∈ K₀ carries z to z′ by the tower transition Tu. The word “separation” here describes what the level marking can distinguish in a geometric fibre.

The comparison at the reference level. At N₀ the generic moduli comparison identifies the tower base with an open and closed subscheme of ME, and its universal abelian scheme with the pullback of the integral one. Taking k factors preserves this pullback. It gives an immersion ρ ∶ ZN₀ → 𝒫E onto an open and closed subscheme. This is the sense in which the reference-level comparison is trivial. Each point of its image has a single lift and points on the complementary components have none.

Let t ∶ ZN → ZN₀ forget the refinement of principal level, and let v ∶ 𝒵E → 𝒫E forget the auxiliary marking. The maps satisfy

v ∘ πN = ρ ∘ t.

To see the equality, first compare the induced maps on the moduli bases. Forgetting the auxiliary marking of the chosen quotient and first descending to N₀ give the same quotient object. The identity transition identifies the abelian schemes and sends the sections labelled cy at level N to those labelled y at level N₀. The representing property of M thus makes the two classifying maps equal. Over this common map rigidity of the quotient gives equality of the maps of universal abelian schemes. Taking the same k-fold product gives the displayed equality on the tower.

The map t is a finite étale change of principal level. The immersion ρ is finite because it is closed and étale because it is open. The map v is finite étale because AY is the pullback of AM along the finite étale map Y → M. The same pullback description holds for the fibre powers and after base change to E. Thus both v and v ∘ πN are finite étale. For finiteness, the graph of πN over 𝒫E is a closed immersion because v is separated. The projection from its ambient fibre product to 𝒵E is finite by base change. For étaleness the same graph is an open immersion because v is unramified, and the projection is étale. Their composite is πN. Stacks Project, finiteness of a morphism over a separated target[81] and the graph argument for étaleness[82].

Separating the points in a fibre. Suppose πN(z) = πN(z′) over an algebraically closed field. Applying v and using the injectivity of ρ gives t(z) = t(z′). The subgroup K(N) is normal in K(N₀). Indeed, if an element acts as the identity modulo N on the lattice, conjugating by a lattice automorphism preserves this property. By transitivity in a principal-level fibre, we obtain u ∈ K(N₀) with z′ = Tu(z). We still have to show that u preserves the auxiliary marking.

Project z to the moduli base XN by forgetting the k fibre coordinates. Projecting z′ gives the translate of the same base point. Equality of the πN-images forces the two corresponding marked quotients to have the same base point in Y. Pull their universal objects back to this geometric point. By rigidity their quotient maps agree there. In particular the level sections indexed by ay agree for every lattice vector y. The pointwise description of the level structure says exactly that u fixes those marked vectors modulo N in the completed lattice. The congruence criterion for the auxiliary ideal identifies this condition, together with u ∈ K(N₀), with u ∈ K₀. These are the two markings compared in the quotient calculation.

How do level transformations split the pullback of the cover?

Let π = πN ∶ ZN → 𝒵E be the finite étale comparison. Assume also that the chosen level satisfies K(N) ⊆ K₀. The latter group lies in K(N₀), since its level ideal is N₀ times an integral ideal. It preserves the lattice and hence normalizes K(N). The quotient Δ = K₀/K(N) is finite, since its order divides the finite index [K(N₀) ∶ K(N)].

Splitting theorem. There is a right action of Δ on ZN over 𝒵E. A pair of points in the fibre product consists of two lifts of the same point. The second lift and the unique transformation which carries it to the first specify that pair. On schemes this gives the isomorphism

∐δ∈Δ ZN ≅ ZN ×𝒵E ZN,   (δ, z) ↦ (z · δ, z).

The action and its fibres. On a fixed principal level the transitions obey Tv ∘ Tu = Tvu, and Tu is the identity when u ∈ K(N). For δ represented by u set z · δ = Tu−1(z). Replacing u by another representative gives the same transformation by the identity at principal level. The inverse in the definition gives (z · δ) · ε = z · (δε). The invariance of the quotient gives π(z · δ) = π(z) as an equality of maps. The preceding separation argument gives a transformation between any two geometric lifts. On a given geometric point two transformations can agree only if the quotient of their representatives fixes that point. Freeness of the principal-level action puts this quotient in K(N), so their classes in Δ agree.

From points to schemes. The second projection of the fibre product is étale by base change from π. The map from each copy of ZN in the display is a section of that projection. Its graph is an open immersion, and the map from the disjoint union is therefore étale. We just proved that it is bijective on points valued in every algebraically closed field. For an étale map, uniqueness makes the diagonal surjective on underlying points. Its diagonal is also an open immersion, hence an isomorphism. The map is therefore an étale monomorphism, an open immersion. Existence of a preimage for each geometric point makes this open immersion surjective, hence an isomorphism. Stacks Project, Lemma 35.25.2, on universally injective étale maps[83].

Every nonempty geometric fibre of π now has exactly |Δ| points. Outside its open and closed image the fibre is empty, and both sides of the graph isomorphism are empty there as well. The restriction to the image is the step that produces a surjective cover. The base model 𝒵 is smooth and projective over O. The self-product in the display and its splitting are over its generic fibre.

For example, take L = ℚ(√2) and let Spec L map to the first of two copies of Spec ℚ. Its two transformations over ℚ are the identity and conjugation. Over the first component, L ⊗ℚ L ≅ L[T]/(T² − 2), where T comes from the first factor. Evaluation at √2 and −√2 gives L × L, since their difference is invertible in L. Thus the self-product consists of the two graphs even though the original generic cover is the spectrum of a field. Over the second component the fibre is empty.

Which Hecke operators realize the transformations? Assume the list of operators contains, for every u ∈ K₀, an entry at level N whose subgroup is exactly K(N), whose translating element is u, and whose prescribed scalar is 1. Choose such an entry for a representative of δ−1. Its correspondence has one coset, so its source map sj is an isomorphism. Changing that coset’s representative multiplies the translating element on the right by an element of K(N), which acts trivially. With aδ(z) = z · δ, the two legs consequently satisfy

tj = aδ ∘ sj,   θj = 1.

This equality identifies the target as a morphism on the whole correspondence. Every simultaneous eigenclass with the prescribed values is therefore fixed by the action of these cover transformations.

How does a Hecke transition lift to the integral correspondence?

Fix a tower of fibre powers over a number field E. Write ZN for its kth fibre power at principal level N. At a place w of E, keep the marked integral moduli scheme Y and the fibre power 𝒵 of its universal abelian scheme. The two markings give the comparison πN ∶ ZN → 𝒵E. In identities with integral maps we compose πN with the generic-fibre inclusion into 𝒵. Fix the residue characteristic q at w, distinct from the auxiliary prime p of the tower. The chosen prime ideal 𝔴 in the coefficient integer ring and the place w both have residue cardinality Q = qf. Put n equal to the rank in the local Hecke datum.

Here are the level and isogeny hypotheses. The site supplies an ideal 𝔞 and a level N₀ ≥ 3 prime to p and q. The subgroup K₀ consists of the elements of K(1) acting as the identity modulo (N₀)𝔞 on the completed lattice Λ. Take N, M ≥ 3 prime to p, with N = N₀c, M = Nτ and K(N) ⊆ K₀. The marking uses an element a of the coefficient integer ring satisfying (a, N)𝔞 = (N). At level M, the new choices cτ and τa satisfy the same ideal identity after multiplication by τ. Choose quotient data at these two levels.

Choose a Hecke index 0 ≤ i ≤ n and its integral adelic element h. Integrality means hΛ ⊆ Λ. The prescribed local type requires h to act trivially modulo the positive integers prime to q and modulo the ideals prime to 𝔴 containing a power of the chosen split ideal (q, ω − r). Here ω and r specify the quadratic generator and its chosen root modulo q. For some scalar α outside 𝔴, α𝔴Λ ⊆ hΛ. The index of hΛ + 𝔴Λ in Λ equals Qi, the similitude multiplier is Qi times a prime-to-p adelic integral unit, and QiΛ ⊆ hΛ. For every u ∈ K₀ assume (hu)K(M)(hu)−1 ⊆ K(N), so the translated transitions are defined. Fix the integral moduli correspondence for these isogenies and its pullback to the chosen level structure. On fibre powers denote its maps by P, R ∶ Ti → 𝒵.

Lifting theorem. Let b be a coset in K₀/K(N) and choose its representative rb. On the copy of ZM labelled by b, let s forget the finer level and let tb be the transition for hrb. There exists a morphism κb ∶ ZM → Ti with

P ∘ κb = πN ∘ s,   R ∘ κb = πN ∘ tb.

Construction. Start with the marked isogeny representing the transition for hrb on the generic moduli scheme. Make the two marked quotient objects at level N₀. Their cartesian comparison maps identify the abelian schemes over the source, so the isogeny transports to a map between the quotient objects. On the prime-to-p torsion, compatibility of the two markings gives the level condition. The multiplier condition gives the polarization multiplier Qi, and the lattice kernel condition gives the prescribed Hecke type. The transported isogeny therefore defines a point of the integral moduli correspondence over the generic source, where q is invertible.

Pull that point back to the finer integral level structure using the source quotient. This gives the first identity on the moduli schemes. On the target, both candidate maps classify the same quotient with the same level marking. Indeed the congruences for h and rb fix the marked lattice vectors modulo the level, and the torsion comparison transports their markings across the isogeny. Uniqueness in the moduli problem gives the second identity. Applying the morphisms in each of the k factors proves both equations on fibre powers, including the zeroth power. The universal integral correspondence and its pullback along the auxiliary level are the geometric inputs. The construction assigns to each translated transition a morphism into that correspondence. The invariance of the quotient comparison gives πM = πN ∘ s for the two chosen markings.

How many tower lifts give the same integral Hecke point?

Retain the lifting hypotheses. Put H = K₀ ∩ h−1K₀h. Assume Qi divides M, and that the index d = [K₀ : H] equals the number of i-dimensional subspaces of the n-dimensional residue vector space over 𝒪/𝔴. The integral correspondence supplies this same Grassmannian cardinality for the geometric fibres of its source after pullback to the tower in characteristic zero. Thus the number of possible integral lifts of a fixed tower point is known before their multiplicities are calculated. The prime ideal 𝔴 is maximal here.

Fibre theorem. Let U be the disjoint union of the copies of ZM and write κ for the map given on each copy by κb. A point of ZN ×𝒵 Ti specifies a tower point z and an integral Hecke point ζ with πN(z) = P(ζ). Over any algebraically closed field the number of tower lifts of this pair is

#(s, κ)−1(z, ζ) = m = [H : K(M)] > 0,   d m = [K₀ : K(M)].

Proof. Admissibility for the identity representative gives K(M) ⊆ H. The principal subgroup K(M) is normal in K₀ because conjugating a level congruence by a lattice automorphism preserves it. By the free transitive action on the forgetful fibre, choose a lift z₀ above z and label all lifts in one copy by uK(M), with u ∈ K(N). Across the copies each lift has a label x = rbu modulo K(M). These labels exhaust K₀/K(M) once.

Suppose two lifts give the same ζ. Projecting from the fibre power to the moduli scheme gives the same marked isogeny point. For a lattice vector v, the corresponding marked torsion point belongs to the isogeny kernel for label x precisely when hxv belongs to MΛ. The two labels therefore give identical kernel tests for every lattice vector. The hypothesis Qi ∣ M ensures MΛ ⊆ hxΛ for each label, since x preserves Λ. To see what these kernel tests determine, write gj = hxj. The lattice completion lemma represents every element of Λ modulo MΛ by an ordinary lattice vector, since M is prime to p. Each gj satisfies gjΛ ⊆ Λ. The tests therefore agree on all of Λ. Moreover each preimage gj−1(MΛ) is contained in Λ by the divisibility just proved. The two preimages coincide. Cancelling the nonzero scalar M gives g1−1Λ = g2−1Λ.

Thus g1g2−1 is a lattice automorphism. It also acts trivially modulo the level ideal. Indeed h acts as the identity modulo both parts of the level. The level congruence theorem combines them into the congruence modulo (N₀)𝔞, which also holds for x1x2−1. Since the conjugate is now known to preserve Λ, reduce the equality (g1g2−1)h = h(x1x2−1) modulo the level ideal. It gives g1g2−1 ∈ K₀. Equivalently, x1x2−1 ∈ H.

Fix one ζ. If any label maps to it, every other such label lies in the same right coset Hx. This gives an upper bound of [H : K(M)] labels there, including the case of an empty fibre. There are d possible ζ. Counting the whole source by its labels gives [K₀ : K(M)] = d m by multiplication of subgroup indices. A single fibre below its upper bound would make the sum smaller than d m. Every fibre therefore attains the bound. In particular, every ζ occurs. This recovers the total from the tower degree theorem.

For a finite example of the count, let K₀ be the permutations fixing 4 in the symmetric group on four letters, take h = (3 4), K(N) the three even permutations in K₀, and K(M) the identity subgroup. The intersection H fixes 3 and 4, hence has two elements. The two copies carry three labels apiece. Grouping these six labels by the right cosets of H gives three fibres with two lifts each.

Finally, (s, κ) is finite étale. Its source is finite étale over ZN by the tower degree theorem. Its target is also finite étale there by the integral correspondence theorem after base change, since q is a unit on the generic tower. A morphism between schemes finite étale over a common base is finite and étale. The restriction to the image of the generic tower uses exactly this positive degree m to lift a compatible pair, then preserves the same multiplicity on the restricted correspondence. The calculation gives the comparison on the generic tower. The integral relation at residue points also needs the separate special-fibre point identity. Stacks Project, Lemma 29.45.14[81] and Lemma 29.37.19[84].

What does a deformation at the generic point of the special fibre remember?

The residue-point identity is tested over a generic point of a component of the special fibre. The local ring there lets us compare an abelian variety with an infinitesimal deformation of it. Both come from one object over a field, although the two maps from that field can differ.

Factorization at the generic point. Let R be a discrete valuation ring with maximal ideal 𝔪 and let X be smooth over R. Write Xs for its special fibre and let z be the generic point of an irreducible component of Xs. Suppose a morphism v ∶ Spec T → X from a local ring sends the closed point to z, and the structure map R → T kills 𝔪. Then v factors through Spec κ(z), where κ(z) is the residue field at z.

Proof. The assumption on 𝔪 puts the whole test scheme in the special fibre. Its local ring at z is 𝒪X,z/𝔪𝒪X,z. Smoothness is preserved by base change, so Xs is smooth over the residue field and hence reduced. In an affine neighbourhood of z in this fibre, the prime defining z is minimal. Localizing at it leaves just one prime ideal. That prime is the nilradical, which is zero because localization preserves reducedness. A local ring with zero maximal ideal is a field. Thus

𝒪X,z/𝔪𝒪X,z = 𝒪Xs,z ≅ κ(z).

The map v corresponds to the local homomorphism 𝒪X,z → T. This homomorphism kills 𝔪𝒪X,z, so it descends to the displayed field. Taking spectra gives the claimed factorization. The Stacks Project, smooth schemes over a field are geometrically reduced[85] and morphisms from the spectrum of a local ring[86].

In the application the test point first lies on a space flat over the underlying moduli scheme. Flat morphisms lift generalizations. Any generalization of its image within the special fibre would lift to another generalization in the special fibre upstairs. The original point is already generic in its component, so the lifted point, and hence its image, must be unchanged. This permits the same argument on the moduli scheme. The Stacks Project, going down for flat ring maps[87].

An example with dual numbers. Take the affine line over ℤ(5) and the generic point of its special fibre. Its residue field is 𝔽5(t). Take k = 𝔽5(u) and let ε² = 0. The map t ↦ u + ε gives a point with values in k[ε]. Every nonzero denominator b(t) has invertible image because its reduction b(u) is nonzero. Thus the assignment extends to the whole residue field. Reducing modulo ε gives t ↦ u. Both points factor through 𝔽5(t), and the coefficient of ε still distinguishes them.

Why is the geometric generic point ordinary at the chosen place?

Generic ordinarity theorem. Let R be a discrete valuation ring of characteristic zero and residue characteristic q. Take the smooth integral moduli scheme M for the unitary datum with algebra degree m = 1 and principal level N ≥ 3 prime to q. Choose one of the coefficient maps 𝒪F → R of the datum. Its inverse image of the maximal ideal is a prime 𝔴. Write Q = |𝒪F/𝔴| = qf. The prime contains q, so it is nonzero, maximal, and f ≥ 1. Let y ∶ Spec k → M be a point over an algebraically closed field with image the generic point z of a special-fibre component. For the abelian variety A at y and the rank parameter n,

#A[𝔴](k) = Qn−1.

Here A[𝔴](k) consists of the geometric points killed by every element of 𝔴. This cardinality is the meaning of ordinarity at 𝔴 in the congruence argument. For example, when Q = 5 and n = 3, the theorem counts 25 geometric points. Describing how kernels above these points reduce is the further geometric input to the ordinary subspace lemma.

The alternative if the count fails. The local length calculation and the action of Frobenius give the alternative used in the deformation argument below. Let P be the space of primitive classes in first de Rham cohomology of A, and let L be its intersection with the first Hodge filtration. Primitive means that pullback by the group law is the sum of the pullbacks by the two projections. We work on the dual H = P∨, with Hodge subspace Fil = L⊥. Write Φ for the q-semilinear Frobenius on P and ρ for the coefficient action there. Reduction at the chosen embedding gives the character χ ∶ 𝒪F → k with kernel 𝔴.

The local parameter calculation chooses coefficients e and d. The action of e projects to the factor at 𝔴 modulo q, and ed = d modulo q. The torsion and Frobenius calculation gives the following alternative. Either the stated count holds, or

ρ(e)L ⊆ W, W = spank{ρ(d)Φf(v) ∣ v ∈ P}.

This implication uses the local structure of the finite 𝔴-torsion scheme. If the point count fails, the local coordinate at the identity gives a nonzero tangent vector with a lift through the Qth-power map. Comparing Frobenius with the endomorphism on the 𝔴-factor then constructs a preimage of each projected Hodge class. In the alternative under consideration the nonzero projected Hodge line lies inside W. Its vanishing under Φ detects a loss of rank. The separating eigenvector lemma uses that loss and the coefficient annihilator relations to produce a simultaneous χ-eigenvector y0 in the image of ρ(d) outside W. Given y0, extend a basis of W by this vector and choose a functional ξ vanishing on W with ξ(y0) = 1. Put x = ξ ∘ ρ(e). Since ρ(e) fixes both W and y0 pointwise, x still vanishes on W and x(y0) = 1. For each l ∈ L, the inclusion gives ρ(e)l ∈ W, so x(l) = ξ(ρ(e)l) = 0. This is exactly x ∈ Fil. Idempotence also gives x ∘ ρ(e) = x.

A deformation that moves the Hodge subspace. Let φ be the nondegenerate skew-symmetric de Rham pairing from the polarization. It represents evaluation at y0 by a vector α in H, so φ(x, α) = 1. The local Lie-algebra calculation supplies a vector b outside Fil in the image of the dual projector. Its pairing with x is zero. Indeed, the quadratic generator acts by the chosen root on both projected vectors, and adjointness for conjugation gives the other root on the opposite side of the pairing. The two roots are distinct in the residue field. Define

D(v) = φ(v, α)b + φ(v, b)α, D(x) = b ∉ Fil.

The polarized direction lemma checks the infinitesimal moduli conditions. The coefficient actions are adjoint under conjugation, and the eigenvector relation for y0 makes D commute with these actions on Fil modulo Fil. The two quadratic root spaces give the prescribed Lie relation. For the polarization, the two summands cancel in φ(Dv, w) + φ(v, Dw) by skew-symmetry. Realizing the Hodge graph with its order action, polarization and level marking gives a deformation over T = k[ε]/(ε²). In the crystalline comparison with the special point the lifted filtration has an element with constant term x and first-order coefficient D(x). The coset of this coefficient in H/Fil measures the motion of the filtration.

Why the same coefficient must vanish modulo Fil. Representability gives a morphism Spec T → M reducing to y. Both maps kill the maximal ideal of R. The generic-point lemma factors them through κ(z). Thus A and its deformation are pullbacks of the same marked abelian variety over κ(z). The Frobenius-span inclusion descends from k to κ(z) and then extends to T. For descent, de Rham base change identifies the filtration and the coefficient actions, and extension of fields detects membership in a subspace. For ascent, the pulled-back Hodge subspace is generated by pullbacks of its elements, and Frobenius commutes with these pullbacks. Using the common residue field is essential here because its two maps can send elements to different first-order lifts.

In characteristic q, (a + εb)q = aq. Because f ≥ 1, at least one Frobenius occurs in every generator of W. Under the crystalline comparison, its value against the constant lift of x is the constant lift of its value at the special point, hence zero. The inclusion over T shows that the functional obtained by applying the dual projector to this lift annihilates the lifted first Hodge subspace on the primitive classes. It therefore belongs to the lifted filtration on the dual. On constant classes it evaluates as x ∘ ρ(e) = x with first-order coefficient zero. This constructs a second lift of x in the very same filtration.

For a fixed x, two possible first-order coefficients of a filtered lift differ by an element of Fil. Indeed the difference of the two lifts has zero constant term and lies in ε Fil under the Hodge comparison. Our two coefficients are D(x) and 0. Their equality in H/Fil contradicts D(x) = b ∉ Fil. The second branch of the alternative is impossible at z. This proves the point count, with the local torsion calculation, the coefficient-space calculation and the unitary deformation and crystalline comparison theorems as its geometric inputs.

How much of the torsion lies at each geometric point?

Let A be the abelian variety at a geometric point of the unitary moduli problem in characteristic q. Write k for its algebraically closed field. Take the algebra degree m = 1, the rank parameter n ≥ 1, and a principal level N ≥ 3 prime to q. Choose a coefficient map 𝒪F → R of the base and compose with the map R → k of the point. Call the resulting character χ, its kernel 𝔴, and the size of its residue field Q = |𝒪F/𝔴| = qf, with f ≥ 1. This calculation works at every such point, including those where the ordinary count is still in question.

Local length formula. Put K = A[𝔴]. For every k-scheme T, its T-points are the points of A(T) killed by all elements of 𝔴. Let M = #K(k) and let ℓ be the length of the local ring B = 𝒪K,0 at the identity. Then

Qn = Mℓ,   M = Qj,   ℓ = Qn−j   (0 ≤ j ≤ n).

Proof. The arithmetic input is the ideal-torsion degree theorem for this unitary datum. It gives a finite flat subgroup A[𝔴] of rank (Norm 𝔴)mn, here Qn. Its proof chooses an auxiliary ideal 𝔟 prime to q and coprime to 𝔴 with 𝔴𝔟 = (g). The two coprime factors split the kernel of [g] into its 𝔴-torsion and 𝔟-torsion. Dividing the degree of [g] by the known prime-to-q degree for 𝔟 gives the stated rank. We use these two isogeny degrees in this step.

The coordinate ring of K is a finite-dimensional k-algebra. It is Artinian, hence a product of its local rings. Every residue field is a finite extension of the algebraically closed field k, hence equals k. Each factor therefore accounts for one point of K(k). Translation by that point identifies the identity with it and gives an isomorphism of the two local rings. Each factor has length ℓ and also dimension ℓ over k, since every simple quotient in a composition series is its residue field. Adding the dimensions of the M factors gives Qn = Mℓ. The Stacks Project, Lemma 10.53.6 on Artinian rings[88].

Finally 𝒪F acts on the abelian group K(k), and all elements of 𝔴 act by zero. Thus K(k) is a finite vector space over the field 𝒪F/𝔴. If its dimension is j, its cardinality is Qj. Since ℓ ≥ 1, we have j ≤ n, and division gives the last equality. To determine which exponents can occur, we now look inside the identity factor.

Why does the tangent at the identity force a dichotomy?

Tangent and point count. Under the hypotheses of the local length formula, the tangent space of K at its identity has dimension one over k. Thus ℓ > 1. Either ℓ = Q and M = Qn−1, or ℓ ≥ Q2. The first case is precisely ordinarity at 𝔴.

Proof. By the defining property of A[𝔴], its tangent vectors are those v ∈ Lie(A) killed by every coefficient in 𝔴. We identify this space using the Lie conditions of the moduli problem. Write λj for the coefficient characters at our point, with χ = λi. The datum has a quadratic element ωF whose polynomial splits modulo q. Its two roots in 𝔽q are distinct because its discriminant is prime to q. All λj send ωF to the same chosen root r. The first Lie condition says that every vector on which ωF acts by r is a sum of vectors vj on which all coefficients act by λj. The second says that each of these simultaneous eigenspaces has dimension m, here one.

Take a vector v killed by 𝔴. If z is an integer lifting r, then ωF − z ∈ 𝔴. Consequently ωFv = rv, and the first Lie condition gives v = ∑j vj. The coefficient characters have pairwise distinct maximal kernels by the separation condition on the base. The Chinese remainder theorem therefore gives a coefficient e which is 1 modulo 𝔴 and 0 modulo every other labelled kernel. Applying e to the sum leaves exactly vi. Since e − 1 ∈ 𝔴, the same operation fixes v. Conversely, on the χ-eigenspace every coefficient in 𝔴 acts by zero. Thus the entire tangent space is exactly the χ-eigenspace. Its prescribed dimension also supplies a nonzero tangent vector. The Stacks Project, Chinese remainder theorem[33].

In the de Rham description used in the deformation argument, the dual H of primitive first de Rham cohomology maps onto Lie(A) with kernel Fil. This map commutes with the coefficient action. A generator of the χ-line therefore lifts to some h ∈ H, and eh still lifts that generator, so eh lies outside Fil. This identifies the nonzero tangent direction in the Hodge quotient. Berthelot, Breen and Messing, Théorie de Dieudonné cristalline II, §2.5 and Proposition 5.1.10[89].

To read this direction in the local ring, let c ∶ B → k be the residue map and 𝔪 = ker c. A tangent vector is a point over k[ε]/(ε²) reducing to the identity. Its map on functions factors through B and has the form b ↦ c(b) + εδ(b). Multiplicativity gives δ(ab) = c(a)δ(b) + c(b)δ(a), so δ kills 𝔪². Conversely any linear functional on 𝔪/𝔪² extends by zero on k to such a δ. Thus 𝔪/𝔪² is dual to this tangent line. If ℓ were one, B would equal its residue field and every δ would vanish. We conclude ℓ > 1. The Stacks Project, maps from a local scheme[86] and tangent spaces and dual numbers[90].

Now ℓ = Qn−j with positive exponent. If ℓ ≤ Q, the exponent must be one, giving the ordinary count. If ℓ > Q, the exponent is at least two. This extra length is the hypothesis for the construction of a lifted tangent.

Two groups of rank nine. Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 3, μ3 × (ℤ/3ℤ)k has three points, one for each element of the constant factor. At each point the multiplicative coordinate u = t − 1 satisfies u3 = t3 − 1 = 0, so the local ring is k[u]/(u3). The product formula reads 9 = 3 · 3. For α9, the kernel of x ↦ x9 on the additive group, the only geometric point is 0 and its local ring is k[x]/(x9). Here 9 = 1 · 9. In each ring the maximal ideal modulo its square is generated by the class of the coordinate. These finite group schemes illustrate both numerical outcomes at Q = 3 and n = 2. Realization of a particular group in the unitary moduli problem is a separate geometric question.

How does the local length give a coordinate for the torsion?

Suppose the count at the identity gives local length ℓ > Q. A field-valued point sees only the residue of a function. We need to recover the original linear coefficient from the term of degree Q in a Qth power. We first construct the ring in which to evaluate functions.

Local coordinate lemma. Let B be a finite-dimensional commutative local algebra over a field k, with maximal ideal 𝔪, residue field k via the structure map, and a one-dimensional tangent space. Choose x in 𝔪 with nonzero class in 𝔪/𝔪². If ℓ is the length of B over itself, then

k[X]/(Xℓ) ≅ B,   X ↦ x.

Proof. The dual-number description of tangent vectors identifies the cotangent space 𝔪/𝔪² with the dual of the tangent line. The class of x spans 𝔪/𝔪². Nakayama’s lemma, applied to the finite B-module 𝔪, gives 𝔪 = (x). The Stacks Project, Lemma 33.16.5[91] and Nakayama’s lemma[92].

Finite dimension makes B Artinian, so its maximal ideal is nilpotent. Let h be the first positive exponent with xh = 0. Write b as its residue plus xb₁ and repeat with b₁. After h steps this expresses b as a polynomial of degree less than h in x. These expressions are unique. In a nonzero polynomial relation of degree less than h, factor out the lowest power Xa. The remaining polynomial has nonzero constant term and so evaluates to a unit. This would give xa = 0 with a < h. Thus B ≅ k[X]/(Xh). Each successive quotient (xa)/(xa+1) for 0 ≤ a < h is a copy of the simple module k. This gives ℓ = h. The Stacks Project, finite-dimensional algebras and nilpotence in Artinian rings[93].

Now put T = k[t]/(tQ+1). Since ℓ ≥ Q + 1, sending x to t defines a surjection u ∶ B → T. In T, the class tQ still survives. For instance, a local coordinate of length nine gives a quotient of length four when Q = 3. This quotient is all the next calculation needs.

Where does the first derivative go under a Qth power?

Let k have prime characteristic q, let Q = qf with f ≥ 1, and write Δ = k[ε]/(ε²). The quotient u just constructed gives a point of the torsion group with values in T. Restricting it to Δ gives a tangent vector. The following two ring maps track the vector through Frobenius.

τ ∶ T → Δ,   t ↦ ε,  j ∶ Δ → T,   a + bε ↦ aQ + bQtQ.

The map τ fixes k. The map j acts on its coefficients by the fth iterate of Frobenius. It is additive because raising a sum to a qth power distributes in characteristic q. It respects multiplication because (tQ)² = 0 in T. Since 1 and tQ are linearly independent over k and a field has no nonzero nilpotents, j is injective. The Stacks Project, absolute Frobenius[94].

Write z = a + bt + t²c(t) in T. Its Qth power retains only the terms in degrees zero and Q. Thus

j(τ(z)) = zQ,   τ(j(a + bε)) = aQ.

For a coefficient example, take Q = 3 and k = 𝔽₃(ω), where ω² = −1. This field has nine elements since −1 is a nonsquare in 𝔽₃. If z = 1 + ωt + t² then τ(z) = 1 + ωε. Cubing gives j(τ(z)) = 1 − ωt³ because ω³ = −ω and t⁶ = 0. The quadratic coefficient has disappeared. The linear coefficient can still be recovered because Frobenius is injective on k.

The restriction τ ∘ u sends the local coordinate x to ε. Its derivative is therefore nonzero. The original T-point factors through the torsion group, so every element of 𝔴 kills it. These two properties and the identity j ∘ τ = Frobf give the lifted tangent used in the proof that the image tangent is constant. The strict threshold matters here. If ℓ = Q, every lift would satisfy u(x)Q = 0. The identity and injectivity of j would then force τ(u(x)) = 0.

What happens to the lifted tangent after Frobenius?

Let A be the abelian variety at the geometric point of the unitary moduli problem. Its ground field k is algebraically closed of prime characteristic q. We keep the algebra degree m = 1 and level N ≥ 3 prime to q. The chosen residue character χ of 𝒪F has kernel 𝔴 and image of order Q = qf, with f ≥ 1. Denote the action of a coefficient b on A by [b]. Write Fr for absolute qth-power Frobenius on A. We first show why [a] factors through Frf for the coefficient a chosen at 𝔴.

The coefficient and the Hodge space. The local ideal calculation supplies a ∈ 𝔴 and e, s ∈ 𝒪F with e² ≡ e modulo q and a(1 − e) = qfs. Let L be the first Hodge filtration on primitive de Rham cohomology in degree one. The pullbacks ρ(b) = [b]∗ preserve L and give it an action of 𝒪F modulo q. Thus E = ρ(e) is a projector. The unitary Lie algebra calculation gives the following input at the geometric point. Its selected Hodge summand EL is a line on which every b acts as χ(b).

Extracting one Frobenius factor. Suppose θ is a group morphism on A over an automorphism σ of k, and θ∗L = 0. Invariant one-forms are dual to the tangent space at the identity, so θ has zero differential there. Translations give zero differential at every geometric point. Locally the pullback of each regular function is therefore a qth power by the degree-zero Cartier isomorphism for smooth schemes over a perfect field. These roots are unique on the reduced scheme A. They agree on overlaps and define a map θ′ with θ = θ′ ∘ Fr. Uniqueness also gives the group law for θ′, and its action on scalars is λ ↦ σ(λ)1/q. Katz, Nilpotent connections and the monodromy theorem, Theorem 7.2[95].

Extracting all f factors. Start with ψ0 = [a]. Suppose [a] = ψj ∘ Frj for j < f, with scalar action σj(λ) = λ1/qj. We show that ψj∗ kills both summands of L = (1 − E)L ⊕ EL. Since [q]∗ acts as zero on L, the one-step argument factors [q] through Fr. Taking the jth iterate and using naturality gives [qj] = νj ∘ Frj. It follows that [1 − e] ∘ ψj = [qf−js] ∘ νj. Indeed precomposition with Frj gives [a(1 − e)] on both sides. We may cancel this precomposition because Frobenius fixes the underlying points and is injective on functions. Now q divides qf−js, so pulling back the equality gives ψj∗(1 − E)L = 0.

On EL the first pullback ψ0∗ acts as χ(a) = 0. For 0 < j < f, the same cancellation shows that ψj commutes with every [b], since [a] does. Its pullback preserves the Hodge filtration and commutes with E. The image of a vector of EL therefore lies in EL, with character χ. Semilinearity also gives that image the character σj ∘ χ. A nonzero image would force all Q values of χ to be roots of Xqj − X, whose degree is less than Q. This proves the vanishing and permits the next extraction. At j = f the induction gives [a] = ψ ∘ Frf, where ψ = ψf lies over λ ↦ λ1/Q.

Constancy lemma. Write Δ = k[ε]/(ε²). Suppose the point count has given a nonzero tangent v ∶ Spec Δ → A at the identity with a lift u ∈ A[𝔴](T). The truncated-ring calculation supplies a k-algebra map τ ∶ T → Δ and an injective ring map j ∶ Δ → T satisfying v = u ∘ Spec τ and j(τ(s)) = sQ for every s ∈ T. Then ψ ∘ v is constant in the infinitesimal direction. More precisely, let v0 be the constant tangent given by the identity section over Δ. Then ψ ∘ v = ψ ∘ v0 as maps of schemes.

Proof. Precompose with Spec j. The composite of Spec j with Spec τ is FrSpec Tf. Naturality of absolute Frobenius therefore gives

ψ ∘ v ∘ Spec j = ψ ∘ FrAf ∘ u = [a] ∘ u = 0T.

The last equality uses a ∈ 𝔴. Replacing u by the identity section gives the same calculation for v0. To cancel Spec j, observe that Spec Δ has a single point and Spec T is nonempty since j is injective. Both maps from Spec Δ have the same image point in A. Choose an affine open neighbourhood of it. On the coordinate ring of this neighbourhood the two maps become equal after composing with j, so they were equal already. This proof also accounts for the action of ψ on the ground field. The Stacks Project, §33.36, naturality of absolute Frobenius[94].

Which Hodge classes does the constant tangent detect?

Put P = H1dR(A/k)prim and L = P ∩ Fil1. A primitive class pulls back along addition to the sum of its pullbacks along the two projections. The classes in L are represented by differential forms. Let ρ(b) = [b]∗ act on P. The coefficient e for 𝔴 satisfies e − 1 ∈ 𝔴, and E = ρ(e) is idempotent. The unitary Lie algebra calculation says that EL is a line and that every coefficient b acts on it by χ(b).

Vanishing on the selected Hodge line. If v has the lift in the constancy lemma, then ψ∗(Ex) = 0 for every x ∈ L.

Indeed the Lie–Hodge pairing identifies tangents at the identity with linear functionals on the classes of invariant one-forms. In the dual P∨, a representative h of the tangent v is defined up to the annihilator L⊥. Its restriction to L is nonzero. A pulled-back form evaluated on v evaluates the original form on the image tangent, with the scalar twist of ψ. The image tangent is constant, so h(ψ∗x) = 0 for all x ∈ L. Pullback preserves L. Because v is killed by 𝔴, [e] fixes v. Evaluating forms on this equality gives h ∘ E = h on L. For any functional λ on P, the restriction of λ ∘ E to L is a scalar multiple of h|L. In fact all these restrictions factor through the line EL, and h gives a nonzero one. Finally ψ commutes with [e]. After precomposition with FrAf this follows from naturality and [a][e] = [e][a]. Frobenius on the smooth, hence reduced, scheme A is the identity on points and is injective on functions, which permits cancellation on affine opens. Thus

λ(ψ∗Ex) = (λ ∘ E)(ψ∗x) = 0   (x ∈ L).

Linear functionals separate the points of P. This proves the vanishing on the whole selected line using a single nonzero tangent.

How does Verschiebung supply the last Frobenius preimage?

Pointwise Frobenius inclusion. Let Φ be the q-semilinear Frobenius on P. With the same hypotheses and a nonzero lifted tangent, for every x ∈ L there exists z ∈ P such that

ρ(e)x = ρ(d)Φf(z).

Here d is the coefficient in the Frobenius-span alternative. Two other local coefficients c and c′ satisfy ad = qc and c′ce ≡ e modulo q. Write U = ψ∗. Multiplication by q also factors through Frobenius. The factor is the Verschiebung from the Frobenius twist of A to A. UΦf−1ρ(d) = Vρ(c),   ker V ⊆ im Φ.

Indeed naturality and the two factorizations reduce their composites to [da] ∘ FrAf−1 and [cq] ∘ FrAf−1. Cancel Frobenius and take pullbacks in reverse order. The index here counts Frobenius iterates of the one chosen character. A generalized eigenvector is killed, for each b, by some power of ρ(b) − χj(b)·1. Commuting endomorphisms over the algebraically closed field k give a direct sum of such spaces. Indeed their linear span in End(P) has a finite basis taken from the coefficient operators. Decompose successively into the generalized eigenspaces of those basis elements. Commutation preserves each summand already obtained.

Why do these spaces have the same dimension? Write C = 𝒪F. The characteristic-polynomial comparison for abelian varieties, applied to the prime-to-q lattice of the moduli datum, identifies the characteristic polynomial of ρ(b) with that of multiplication by b on C, raised to the power mn and reduced in k. Here m and n are the parameters of the unitary datum. Choose b by the Chinese remainder theorem so that its residue at 𝔴 is a nonzero generator of the residue field over its prime field and its residues at the other primes above q are zero. The conjugates χj(b) distinguish the embeddings at 𝔴, and they are nonzero. Thus the multiplicity of χj(b) in the characteristic polynomial counts precisely dim Pj. By the comparison, this is mn times the dimension of the corresponding generalized eigenspace for multiplication on k ⊗ℤ C. In this last space the bijection λ ⊗ c ↦ λq ⊗ c carries each character summand onto the next, so their dimensions agree. We have proved equality of dimensions before asking whether Φ carries one space onto the next.

We have Pf = P0 because χ takes values in the field with Q elements. The Hodge–Frobenius identity gives ker Φ = L. Since Φ commutes with the coefficient action, semilinearity sends Pj to Pj+1. On all these spaces E is the identity since E is idempotent with generalized eigenvalue 1. For 1 ≤ j < f, any element of Pj killed by Φ therefore lies in EL, where the character is χ. But χj ≠ χ since the polynomial Xqj − X cannot vanish on all Q field elements. Distinct generalized eigenspaces meet only in zero. Thus Φ is injective on Pj for those indices. Since the spaces have equal dimension and every scalar has a qth root, the image of a basis is a basis. We can therefore lift from P0 back to P1 through f − 1 applications of Φ.

This preserves the equality because ρ(d) preserves every simultaneous generalized eigenspace. The preceding lift now gives w ∈ P1 with y = ρ(d)Φf−1(w). For f = 1 take the projected b itself.

By the vanishing on the Hodge line, Uy = 0. Commuting ρ(d) with Φ and using the displayed operator relation gives Vρ(c)w = 0. Frobenius–Verschiebung exactness supplies z0 with Φ(z0) = ρ(c)w. Together with the torsion count this proves the alternative used in the generic ordinarity argument.

Which eigenvector can a functional separate from the Frobenius image?

Let P be the space of primitive de Rham classes over the algebraically closed field k of characteristic q, and let L be its first Hodge subspace. The coefficient ring 𝒪F acts by ρ. Write χ for the residue character at 𝔴, Q = qf for the size of its image, and ΦQ = Φf for the iterated Frobenius, with f ≥ 1. This additive map commutes with each ρ(c) and sends λz to λQΦQz. Separating eigenvector lemma. The local coefficient and Hodge data give a vector y in the image of D and a linear functional x on P such that

W = spank{DΦQz ∣ z ∈ P},   ρ(c)y = χ(c)y   for every c,
x(W) = 0,   x(y) = 1,   x ∘ E = x.

Write P = G ⊕ G′, where G′ is the sum of the other simultaneous generalized eigenspaces. For one coefficient, the Chinese remainder theorem applied to the relatively prime powers of the linear factors of its minimal polynomial gives the projections onto its generalized eigenspaces. The commuting coefficients preserve every summand. Repeatedly splitting a summand whenever a coefficient has two distinct eigenvalues terminates in finite dimension. This gives the asserted decomposition. The Stacks Project, Chinese remainder theorem.[33]

The map ΦQ sends generalized eigenvalues ψ(c) to ψ(c)Q by semilinearity and commutation. Every χ(c) belongs to the field of Q elements, and raising to the Qth power is injective on k. Therefore ΦQ preserves both G and G′. On G, the idempotent E acts as the identity because its only generalized eigenvalue there is 1. Write πχ for the projection onto G along G′. Extend it to a basis of G. The images of the remaining basis vectors span U, so dim U < dim G.

The projection of s lies in U because ΦQ preserves both summands. The projection of Sb is S applied to the projection of b, and the last term has zero projection because E acts as 1 on G. This gives G ⊆ U + SG. Both summands lie in G, and S preserves U because it commutes with ΦQ. Iterating gives G = U + ShG = U, contrary to the dimension bound. Choose u ∈ G with y = Du outside W.

The first has derivative −1, so their greatest common divisor is X − χ(c). Indeed the ideal generated by these two polynomials is generated by its monic element of least degree, since division with remainder would otherwise produce an element of smaller degree. That generator is their greatest common divisor and so is a polynomial combination of the two. Hence ρ(c)y = χ(c)y.

This proves the lemma. If the Frobenius inclusion EL ⊆ W holds, then x also vanishes on L. It belongs to the dual Hodge subspace used in the deformation at the generic point.

A two-dimensional example. Take k to be an algebraic closure of 𝔽₃, with 𝔽₃ acting by scalars on k². Put Q = 3, E = D = 1, S = 0 and ΦQ(λe₁ + μe₂) = μ³e₁. Take L = ke₁. Choosing y = e₂ instead gives the required functional x(λe₁ + μe₂) = μ.
