How can a Hodge class move while the polarization is preserved?

Keep the eigenvector and its separating functional. Write y₀ for the eigenvector in primitive cohomology P, and x for the functional with x(y₀) = 1. We are testing the longer local-ring case. In that case x vanishes on the Hodge subspace L ⊂ P and hence lies in Fil = L⊥ ⊂ H = P∨. To rule out this case we will make the image of x move out of Fil to first order. The motion must preserve the given symmetries, since the deformed variety will belong to the same moduli problem.

Polarized direction lemma. There is a linear map D ∶ H → H of rank at most two with D(x) ∉ Fil. On Fil it commutes with the coefficient action modulo Fil, and it satisfies the first-order polarization identity below. It also kills the relations defining the prescribed splitting of the Lie space.

Finding the two vectors. Denote the polarization pairing by φ and the action on H by σ. The pairing is nondegenerate, φ(u,v) = −φ(v,u), Fil is isotropic, and the adjoint of σ(c) is σ(c), where the bar is the coefficient involution. These properties come from crystalline duality. The polarization induces an isomorphism on the q-divisible group because its kernel is killed by an integer prime to q. Duality identifies the dual Hodge filtration with the annihilator of Fil, and the polarization carries Fil into that annihilator. The adjoint identity is the compatibility of the polarization with the action of the order. Chai and Oort, Theorem 2.11.[98]

Nondegeneracy identifies H with its dual by placing a vector in the second slot. Take the unique α with φ(v,α) = v(y₀) for all v. Then φ(x,α) = 1. Since y₀ has character χ, evaluation gives φ(σ(c)v,α) = χ(c)φ(v,α). Adjointness therefore gives σ(c)α = χ(c)α.

Let E = σ(e) be the dual place projector. By the Lie calculation, its image in H/Fil contains a nonzero character line. Choose b = Eh₀ outside Fil. For every coefficient c, σ(c)b − χ(c)b lies in Fil. For the distinguished quadratic generator ω the stronger identity ΩE = rE holds on H, with Ω = σ(ω) and r the chosen residue root. The conjugate operator is t − Ω, where t is the trace of ω. Put r′ = t − r. The square of r − r′ is the discriminant of the defining quadratic, a unit at the residue prime. Since Ex = x, the adjoint identity φ(Ωx,b) = φ(x,(t − Ω)b) gives rφ(x,b) = r′φ(x,b). Thus φ(x,b) = 0, including in characteristic two.

D(v) = φ(v,α)b + φ(v,b)α,   D(x) = b ∉ Fil.

Checking admissibility. The image lies in the span of α and b. Expanding the next sum gives two pairs of opposite terms, by skew-symmetry, so

φ(D(u),v) + φ(u,D(v)) = 0.

For v ∈ Fil the error in σ(c)b ≡ χ(c)b modulo Fil pairs to zero with v by isotropy. Substitute this and the character identity for α in the formula for D. The commutator D(σ(c)v) − σ(c)D(v) reduces to φ(v,α)(χ(c)b − σ(c)b), which lies in Fil. The algebra-degree-one assumption ensures that every element of the acting order is the image of a coefficient c.

The remaining constraint concerns the subspace Z of Lie relations. It is spanned by vectors of the form ∑j λjσ(cj)(Ω − r′)h, where the same sum ∑j λjχi(cj) vanishes at every labelled coefficient character χi. Such a vector pairs to zero with α because χ is one of those characters. It pairs to zero with b term by term. Indeed σ(c)b is again an Ω-eigenvector of eigenvalue r, so the adjoint t − Ω − r′ kills it. Both coefficients in the formula for D vanish on Z. The next step turns these three checks into equations for a moving subspace.

Which part of the derivative does a moving Hodge subspace determine?

Over the dual numbers Δ = k[ε]/(ε²), a lifted vector has a constant term and a first-order coefficient. To compare two lifts we must first put their Hodge subspaces in the same ambient module. Evaluate the dual de Rham crystal of the special fibre on the square-zero thickening k ← Δ, with its trivial higher divided powers. Constant crystalline base change identifies this evaluation with HΔ = H ⊗k Δ. In these coordinates every vector is uniquely u + εv. The coefficient action sends its two entries to σ(c)u and σ(c)v. The filtration of a deformation is the part that can vary.

Graph lemma. For a linear direction D, the submodule G obtained by moving Fil in that direction is characterized by

u + εv ∈ G   ⇔   u ∈ Fil   and   v − D(u) ∈ Fil.

In fact 1 + εD is a Δ-linear automorphism of HΔ with inverse 1 − εD. Applying it to u + εw with u, w ∈ Fil gives u + ε(D(u) + w), proving the formula. It takes a basis of the constant Fil and any complementary basis to bases of G and a complement. Thus G is a direct summand, its quotient is free and reducing G gives Fil. For u ∈ Fil, the possible ε-coefficients of lifts of u form exactly one coset D(u) + Fil. In particular εv belongs to G exactly when v ∈ Fil. Two directions give the same graph precisely when they give the same map Fil → H/Fil. This is the local graph chart for a Grassmannian. The Stacks Project, Grassmannians, Lemma 27.22.1.[99]

For the polarized direction, the commutator on Fil lies in Fil. Hence acting on a graph vector preserves its membership condition. In particular the whole order acts on the quotient. The distinguished vector x has a lift x + εb in G. The constant vector x has ε-coefficient zero, so it could lie in G only if b belonged to Fil. This is the test we will use after realizing the graph by an abelian scheme.

Splitting a class. Let [h] denote a quotient class with Ω[h] = r[h]. Put δ = r − r′. Replacing h by h′ = δ−1(Ω − r′)h preserves this class. Both coordinates of h′ now lie in the image of Ω − r′. If g is a finite linear combination of coefficient actions that evaluates to zero at all labelled characters, then both coordinates of gh′ lie in the relation subspace Z by its definition. The original Lie signature gives Z ⊆ Fil. Indeed on the original Lie quotient, the image of Ω − r′ lies in the r-part by the quadratic relation, and this part already splits into the labelled characters. Since D(Z) ⊆ Fil, the graph membership formula gives gh′ ∈ G.

The labelled characters are distinct on the residue coefficients by the separation condition of the datum. Extend their evaluations to the commutative k-algebra of formal finite linear combinations of coefficients, with multiplication induced by multiplication of coefficients. Each evaluation is onto k and their kernels are distinct maximal ideals. The Chinese remainder theorem supplies elements pi whose values are 1 at the ith character and 0 at all others. Both 1 − ∑ipi and (c − χi(c))pi have zero evaluations. Applying the preceding paragraph first to one expression and then to the other gives

[h] = ∑i[pih′],   σ(c)[pih′] = χi(c)[pih′].

The sum is direct because applying pj to a sum of eigenclasses selects its jth term. The multiplicity calculation will identify the ranks after realization. The Stacks Project, Chinese remainder theorem.[33]

How does the Hodge graph give an abelian scheme with an action of the order?

Fix the abelian variety A0 at our geometric point of the unitary moduli problem. Its field k is algebraically closed of characteristic q. Put Δ = k[ε]/(ε²) and extend the map from the coefficient base to k by the inclusion k → Δ. Let Fil be the Hodge subspace of the covariant first de Rham module H of A0. The graph construction starts from an admissible endomorphism D of H and produces a summand G in the crystalline module over Δ. This module records the de Rham homology of a lift before its Hodge subspace has been specified.

Realization with endomorphisms. There is an abelian scheme A over Δ, with its fibre identified with A0, whose Hodge subspace is G under crystalline comparison. Every endomorphism in the prescribed order 𝒪 lifts to A, and these lifts form an action of 𝒪.

Proof. The ideal (ε) has square zero and carries the divided powers with γ1(u) = u and γj(u) = 0 for j ≥ 2. The crystalline deformation theorem says that, on such a thickening in characteristic q, a direct summand lifting the Hodge subspace specifies a lift of the q-divisible group. Its morphism criterion says that a homomorphism on the special fibre lifts precisely when its crystalline map carries the source summand into the target summand. Such a lift is unique for fixed source and target lifts. Here the q-divisible group is the system of kernels of multiplication by q, q² and all higher powers, with their inclusions. The Serre–Tate theorem gives the corresponding statements for abelian schemes with identified special fibre. These results apply also when q = 2 with the divided powers just specified. Here the constant abelian scheme A0 ×k Δ already supplies a reference lift for evaluating the crystal. Under this comparison, G is a direct summand and reduces to Fil, so the theorem gives the required A. For a coefficient b ∈ 𝒪, apply its action σ(b) to a graph element x + ε(D(x) + u), with x, u ∈ Fil. Its reduction is σ(b)x ∈ Fil. The difference between its first-order coefficient and D(σ(b)x) belongs to Fil by the order condition. Thus the crystalline endomorphism preserves the graph, so [b]0 lifts uniquely to [b]. The identity, sum and composite of lifted homomorphisms reduce to the corresponding operations on A0. Uniqueness now gives [1] = id, [b + c] = [b] + [c] and [bc] = [b] ∘ [c].

Why does the polarization lift, and what happens to its degree?

The polarization datum on the special fibre is a line bundle P0 on A0 × A0. It is trivial on the two axes through the identity. It is symmetric under exchange of the factors, its pullback to the diagonal is ample, and its adjoint on the order is the prescribed involution b ↦ b∗. For each point y of the second factor the restriction to the first factor gives a point of the dual abelian variety. Denote the resulting homomorphism by λ0 ∶ A0 → A0∨.

Polarized realization. If the graph is isotropic for the crystalline pairing of P0, the lifted abelian scheme carries a bundle P with these same properties and with restriction isomorphic to P0. The corresponding isogeny λ has the same degree as λ0. An integer e prime to q that kills ker λ0 also kills ker λ.

Proof. The dual abelian scheme A∨ represents rigidified families of line bundles algebraically equivalent to zero. Its universal family on A × A∨ is the Poincaré bundle. The associated perfect crystalline pairing identifies the Hodge subspace of A∨ with the annihilator of the Hodge subspace of A. Hence λ0 respects the two lifted filtrations exactly when its crystalline pairing vanishes on G × G. Indeed, for each second argument v in the graph the pairing with u is evaluation of the image of v under the crystalline map induced by λ0 against u. Vanishing for every u in the graph says that this image lies in the annihilator. The morphism criterion now lifts λ0 to λ ∶ A → A∨. Pull back the Poincaré bundle along (id, λ) ∶ A × A → A × A∨ to obtain P. This construction accounts for its restriction and its trivializations along the axes. Robert, Theory of abelian varieties and their moduli spaces, Theorem 2.3.7 on the dual abelian scheme[102], and Berthelot, Breen and Messing, crystalline duality, Proposition 5.1.10[89].

Symmetry identifies λ0 with its dual. The two lifts λ and λ∨ are equal by uniqueness, so exchanging the factors carries P to an isomorphic bundle. Similarly the special-fibre relation λ0 ∘ [b]0 = [b∗]0∨ ∘ λ0 lifts to the same identity over Δ. It says that acting on one argument of P by b has the same effect as acting on the other by b∗. Finally the diagonal pullback of P reduces to the ample diagonal pullback of P0. Ampleness is detected on this nilpotent thickening. The Stacks Project, Lemma 32.11.4 on restriction of an ample line bundle[103].

The kernel. The moduli datum supplies an integer e prime to q annihilating ker λ0. In particular this kernel has zero tangent space, since the differential of [e] is multiplication by the unit e. The differential of λ0 between spaces of the same dimension is therefore invertible. Its lift remains invertible over Δ, and translation gives the same conclusion everywhere. Thus λ is étale and, being proper and quasi-finite, finite. Its kernel is finite étale over Δ, so its rank equals that of its special fibre. This rank is the degree of λ. Moreover, multiplication by e and the zero map on this kernel agree after reduction. A finite étale target has unique infinitesimal lifts, so these two maps agree over Δ. The conclusion concerns the same annihilating integer e for all test schemes. The degree is determined by the special-fibre kernel and need not equal e. This argument uses the invertibility of e also when q = 2. The Stacks Project, finite morphisms and proper quasi-finite morphisms[104] and the infinitesimal criterion for étaleness[105].

How do the level, the Lie conditions and the prescribed first derivatives fit together?

Realization in the moduli problem. Let the principal level N ≥ 3 be prime to q. The abelian scheme with order action and polarization constructed above admits a level structure lifting the original one and satisfies the two Lie conditions of the original unitary datum. Together these give an object over Δ whose reduction is identified with the starting object. For every x ∈ Fil, the lifted filtration contains a vector with reduction x and first-order coefficient D(x).

The level. If Λ is the lattice of the datum, its original marking sends v ∈ Λ to a section η0(v) killed by N. The differential of [N] is multiplication by N, which is invertible over Δ. Thus [N] is étale and there is a unique N-torsion section η(v) above η0(v). The sum of the lifts for v and w and the lift for v + w reduce to the same section and are both killed by N. They coincide by uniqueness. The same argument applied to [b]η(v) gives compatibility with 𝒪. At every geometric point, the original prime-to-q Tate markings, their transition maps and their Weil pairings are transported across the identified fibre. Indeed a ring map from Δ to a field kills ε, and the line bundle defining the pairing restricts to the original one. Thus η also meets the geometric level condition. The Stacks Project, Lemma 37.8.10 on formal étaleness[105].

The Lie conditions. Let ω be the quadratic element of the datum, r its selected root and χi the coefficient characters. The first condition is an identity of tangent vectors after every scalar extension Δ → S. Each vector in Lie(AS) on which ω acts as r must be a sum of vectors on which the central coefficients act through the individual χi, with the scalars mapped into S. Over Δ this is the signature calculation in the graph quotient. To pass to S, the projector onto the selected root is (σ(ω) − r′)/(r − r′), where r′ is the other root. Their difference is a unit. On its image the coefficient labels are separated, so the operators selecting the individual characters add to the identity and obey the character identities there. These identities persist after extension of scalars. The tangent module of a smooth group commutes with base change, so the resulting sum is the required decomposition over S, including when S has nilpotents.

The second condition prescribes the dimension m of each labelled tangent eigenspace at every geometric point. Every such point of Spec Δ factors through Spec k, and the fibre identification respects the order action. Its tangent eigenspaces therefore have exactly the dimensions prescribed on A0. In the ordinarity argument m = 1. Decomposition must hold over every test algebra, whereas multiplicity is prescribed on geometric fibres.

The prescribed derivative. Under crystalline comparison the lifted Hodge filtration is exactly G. Taking the element x + εD(x) in this graph realizes the required coefficient. More generally x + ε(D(x) + u) lies in the same filtration for every u ∈ Fil. Thus the intrinsic first-order coefficient lies in H/Fil. At the vector selected in the generic ordinarity proof, D(x) lies outside Fil, so its class is nonzero. A further argument using the generic point supplies a lift of that same vector with zero coefficient in the same filtration. Comparing the two gives the contradiction.

Relative differential forms commute with base change, and exactness preserves the cohomology of the total complex and the image defining the Hodge filtration. As above the residue characteristic is q, and q is nonzero in V. Write 𝔽 = 𝒪F/𝔴 and Q = |𝔽|. A section belongs to A[𝔴] if multiplication by every element of 𝔴 sends it to zero. We shall compare three sets: these sections over V, their generic points over K and their reductions over κ.

Torsion and reduction lemma. For the rank-n unitary datum of algebra degree one, the sections H = A[𝔴](V) form an n-dimensional 𝔽-vector space. Restriction to the generic fibre identifies H with A[𝔴](K). Reduction maps H onto all the points of A[𝔴](κ). This last assertion does not require ordinarity.

Generic points. The field K has characteristic zero. Indeed q is nonzero there, and every other rational prime is already a unit in the base discrete valuation ring. The characteristic-zero torsion theorem for this moduli problem gives |A[𝔴](K)| = N(𝔴)n = Qn. Its exponent comes from the scalar isogeny degree. For each nonzero scalar c ∈ 𝒪F, the norm-degree theorem applied to the torsion module gives |NF/ℚ(c)|n kernel points. The tangent kernel vanishes: a nonzero integer multiple of the identity factors through c and is invertible on the tangent space.

To pass from a scalar to 𝔴, take a positive power 𝔴e = (c) that is principal, using finiteness of the ideal class group (Minkowski’s ideal bound). The torsion filtration for a divisible 𝒪F-module gives |A[𝔴e](K)| = |A[𝔴](K)|e. Divisibility here follows because each nonzero scalar divides a nonzero integer, and multiplication by that integer is surjective on an abelian variety over an algebraically closed field. The scalar count at c gives Qen. Taking the positive e-th root proves the claimed count. The following calculation gives the filtration identity.

Why a new power of 𝔴 contributes the same number of points

Put Tj = A[𝔴j](K), with T₀ = {0}. Choose a in 𝔴 outside 𝔴², so (a) = 𝔴𝔟 for an ideal 𝔟 coprime to 𝔴. Multiplication by a sends Tj+1 to Tj. Its kernel is T₁: an element of Tj+1 killed by a is killed by (a) + 𝔴j+1 = 𝔴(𝔟 + 𝔴j) = 𝔴. The reverse inclusion holds since a ∈ 𝔴.

For surjectivity take y ∈ Tj and choose a point x with ax = y by divisibility. Write 1 = v + u with v ∈ 𝔟 and u ∈ 𝔴j+1. Then vx is killed by 𝔴j+1, since 𝔟𝔴j+1 = (a)𝔴j kills x. Moreover a(vx) = vy = y, as uy = 0. Each fibre of multiplication by a has |T₁| elements, so induction gives |Te| = |T₁|e. Here the groups up to index e are finite since they are contained in the already counted kernel of (c) = 𝔴e.

Properness of A gives a unique V-section extending each K-point. If multiplication by an element of 𝔴 kills the generic point, its product with the section and the zero section have the same generic value. Uniqueness makes them equal over V. Hence restriction identifies the two torsion groups. The action of 𝒪F on either factors through 𝔽. A space of dimension d over 𝔽 has Qd elements, by the unique expansion in any basis. Thus H has dimension n. Stacks Project, valuative criterion for properness[108].

Lifting a prescribed special point. The torsion subgroup scheme A[𝔴] is finite flat over V by the finite flat torsion theorem for the marked abelian scheme. Write it as Spec B, and let χ ∶ B → κ be the prescribed point. Flat going down gives a prime 𝔮 ⊆ ker χ over the zero prime of V. The domain B/𝔮 is finite over V, so its fraction field is a finite extension of K. Since K is algebraically closed, this field is K itself. A valuation ring is integrally closed in its fraction field, hence B/𝔮 = V under this identification. The quotient map B → V gives a section. Its reduction equals χ since χ factors through this same quotient and restricts to the residue map on V. Different sections may thus have the same prescribed reduction. Stacks Project, Lemma 10.39.19[87] and Lemma 10.50.3[109].

Why do points with the same reduction differ by exactly one line?

The special fibre enters through one number. At an ordinary geometric point there are Qn−1 geometric points killed by 𝔴. The residue field κ of our valuation ring is algebraically closed: lift a monic polynomial over κ coefficient by coefficient to V. A root in K is integral over V and hence lies in V. Its reduction is a root of the original polynomial. We can therefore use the ordinary count for A[𝔴](κ).

The reduction line. Write ρ for reduction on H = A[𝔴](V). It respects addition, and the action of each residue scalar is induced by an integral endomorphism. Thus its kernel C is a 𝔽-subspace. By the lifting lemma the image has exactly Qn−1 elements. Subtracting two sections shows that ρ(x) = ρ(y) precisely when x − y ∈ C. Every nonempty fibre is a translate of C, so

Qn = |H| = |C| · Qn−1,   dim𝔽 C = 1.

The same C works for every isogeny at this source point: we defined it using only the abelian scheme and the ideal. Reduction identifies H/C with the group of special torsion points. In particular, for a subspace D of H, its reduced points are indexed by (D + C)/C. Their number is Qj if the j-dimensional D misses C and Qj−1 if D contains C. The quotient comparison explains how much of the subgroup scheme can be recovered from these points.

For a concrete group scheme, take V with fraction field of characteristic zero and residue characteristic three as above. In μ₃ × (ℤ/3ℤ)V the nine generic sections are (ζ3a, b) with a, b ∈ ℤ/3ℤ. All three cube roots of unity reduce to 1 because T³ − 1 = (T − 1)³ in characteristic three. A fixed value of b consequently has three lifts. The line lost on reduction is exactly the first coordinate. Its special coordinate ring κ[t]/(t³), with t = T − 1, still has length three. This product illustrates the point count used above. The experiment fixes b = 1 and tests the resulting component over 𝔽q[ε]/(εe). Its local length is q for every test, while the number of solutions depends on e.

How a section acquires its subspace. For a section of the type-j isogeny correspondence take the elements of H whose marked torsion points belong to its distinguished kernel. They form a subspace D. Over the fraction field the prescribed isogeny type gives Qj such points, hence dim D = j. Two sections giving the same D have the same distinguished kernel on the generic fibre, where it is finite étale. The polarized kernel comparison there identifies the entire quotient isogenies with their markings, so the generic sections coincide. The source of the correspondence is finite over the moduli base and therefore separated. The sections agree over V by the valuative criterion.

Conversely a j-dimensional subspace specifies a finite constant subgroup in the generic abelian variety, stable under the prescribed coefficient action. The marked quotient theorem for the selected type supplies the quotient isogeny realizing that subgroup as its distinguished part. Its moduli point extends uniquely over V because the source map is finite and hence proper. This gives a bijection between sections over our fixed source point and j-dimensional subspaces of H. We will now ask when two such sections acquire the same target on the special fibre. Stacks Project, valuative criterion for properness[108].

Why do two lifts that avoid the ordinary line give the same reduced quotient?

Fix an ordinary valuation-ring point and write κ for its algebraically closed residue field of characteristic q. Write Q = qf for the order of the finite field acting on the torsion space H. Specializing its points gives a map ρ whose kernel is the ordinary line C. A section of the isogeny correspondence, labelled by a subspace D of H, specializes to an isogeny ψD ∶ A → BD of the abelian varieties in the moduli problem. We shall compare two such maps with the same source A. Write tD for the moduli point of the target.

Equality of quotient targets. Suppose D and D′ both meet C only in zero and have the same image U in H/C. Then tD = tD′. For every geometric point of the source abelian variety, the two isogenies also give the same image in the universal abelian variety over this target. These two equalities are needed when the correspondence acts on a tuple of points.

Which part of the kernel is counted? Let KD be the part of ker ψD killed by some power of the distinguished ideal in the split coefficient order. The kernel comparison for the integral isogeny gives two facts. Its coordinate algebra over κ has dimension Qdim D, and its κ-points identify with ρ(D). Indeed, the integral kernel is finite flat of the specified rank. Its points in the special fibre lift to valuation-ring points, and the torsion labels of those lifts are precisely the elements of D. The torsion and lifting argument gives this last passage. Reduction satisfies ρ(x) = ρ(y) exactly when x − y ∈ C. The image ρ(D) is therefore determined by U.

Set r = dim U and d = Qr. Since both chosen spaces avoid the line, each maps bijectively onto U. Both kernel parts have length d and the same d distinct points in A(κ). A finite κ-algebra is a product of its local Artinian factors. Each geometric point contributes a factor of dimension at least one. Here there are d factors and their dimensions sum to d, so every factor is κ. Consequently the two kernel parts are the same reduced closed subscheme of A. This argument is the reason the count of points suffices in this case. Stacks Project, decomposition of an Artinian ring into its localizations[88].

Recovering the whole quotient. The step from this part to the full kernel uses the coefficient action and polarization. For the polarized isogenies in question the polarization multiplier is the same, say qe, and a complementary isogeny makes the composite multiplication by qe in either order. On the resulting torsion the split coefficient action supplies a scalar α with α + ᾱ ≡ 1 modulo qe. Thus a point x in either kernel decomposes into αx + ᾱx. The first term belongs to the distinguished part. For the second, the polarization moves α across the pairing as ᾱ. To write the factorization, call the two isogenies ψ₁ and ψ₂, with targets B₁ and B₂, and denote their complementary maps by ψ₁′ and ψ₂′. Set c = qe. For y in B₂[c], ψ₂′(y) belongs to ker ψ₂. Its α-part belongs to the common distinguished kernel, so ψ₁ ∘ α ∘ ψ₂′ kills B₂[c]. Division through multiplication by c gives a map ν ∶ B₂ → B₁ with ψ₁ ∘ α ∘ ψ₂′ = ν ∘ [c]. Composing with ψ₁′ and cancelling [c] gives ψ₁′ ∘ ν = α ∘ ψ₂′. The adjoint identity now makes the image of ᾱx under ψ₂ pair trivially. Nondegeneracy up to an integer prime to q shows that this integer kills the image. The multiplier qe also kills it, so Bézout’s identity makes the image zero. The full-kernel lemma below records the hypotheses of this argument.

Full-kernel lemma for the polarized datum. For two isogenies of the prescribed kind with the same source, the same multiplier and the coefficient, polarization and level structures of the datum, equality of their distinguished kernels on every test scheme gives equality of their full kernels on every test scheme. The division lemma for abelian schemes supplies the divisibility by the common multiplier used in the adjoint calculation. Equal full kernels then identify the two quotient objects by a structure-preserving isomorphism that intertwines the quotient maps. These assertions use the polarized quotient and rigidity theorems of this moduli problem.

Apply the lemma to ψD and ψD′. The common moduli space represents quotient objects with these structures, so the identified objects give the same map from Spec κ. Uniqueness of their comparison with the universal object intertwines the two maps on points as well. For instance, if H = 𝔽₃² and C is the second coordinate line, the lines generated by (1, 0) and (1, 1) project to the same quotient line. The difference between these two chosen generators lies in C. Each distinguished kernel has length 3 and the same three reduced points. This is the arithmetic count used above, independent of a choice of splitting of H → H/C.

Why does a lift containing the line produce a Frobenius twist?

Keep the same ordinary point, and fix an r-dimensional subspace U of H/C. Choose a lift D₀ missing C, and let D₁ be the full inverse image of U. Write ψ₀ ∶ A → B₀ and ψ₁ ∶ A → B₁ for the specialized isogenies. Both distinguished kernels have the same d = Qr geometric points. Their lengths are d and Qd, respectively. The extra length is the information lost by counting only the geometric points.

Frobenius comparison. Put φ(a) = aQ on κ. Write B₀(Q) for the pullback of B₀ along Spec φ and Frel ∶ B₀ → B₀(Q) for relative Frobenius. There is an isomorphism β of quotient objects satisfying

β ∶ B₁ ≅ B₀(Q),   β ∘ ψ₁ = Frel ∘ ψ₀.

In particular the target for the containing space is the twist of the target for the avoiding space. On κ-valued points of the moduli scheme the formula is t₁ = t₀ ∘ Spec φ. The residue field of the base discrete valuation ring R has Q elements. Its image in κ is therefore fixed by φ. Hence the twisted moduli point is still over the same base point.

Which Frobenius is used? The absolute Frobenius iterated f times raises every local function to its Q-th power, including the scalars in κ. Its factorization through the projection B₀(Q) → B₀ gives the κ-morphism Frel. For any κ-scheme S and any point x ∶ S → B₀, the condition Frel ∘ x = 0 means that x and the zero section agree after precomposition with absolute Frobenius on S, iterated f times. This follows from naturality of absolute Frobenius and the defining pullback of the twist. Over an algebraically closed field the power map on scalars is invertible, so the only geometric point killed is zero. On a nonreduced test scheme the same criterion detects more. For the additive group and S = Spec κ[ε]/(ε²), the nonzero point ε is killed because εQ = 0. Stacks Project, absolute and relative Frobenius[94].

The kernel at the identity. The distinguished kernel of ψ₁ has d geometric points. Translation by those points identifies all its local factors, so the local factor at the identity has length Qd/d = Q. The rank-one conditions on the two auxiliary parameters of the unitary datum (m = a = 1) give a tangent-space bound for the ambient distinguished torsion at the identity. Its cotangent space therefore has dimension at most one. In its Artinian local ring the maximal ideal is therefore principal, by Nakayama’s lemma. If its generator is t, the successive nonzero quotients (tj)/(tj+1) have dimension one over κ. Indeed, an element of (tj) outside (tj+1) is tj times a unit. Every nonzero ideal is generated by an element of least such j. The ideal cutting out the local quotient of length Q is consequently (tQ). On an infinitesimal point of the ambient torsion, membership in this kernel is equivalent to vanishing of the Q-th powers of the functions vanishing at the identity. This is exactly the absolute-Frobenius test just described. Stacks Project, Nakayama’s lemma[92].

Compare this kernel with the one for Frel ∘ ψ₀. On geometric points the two agree because ψ₀ has the same distinguished reduced points as ψ₁ and relative Frobenius adds no geometric kernel points. On local points reducing to zero, applying ψ₀ preserves and reflects the Frobenius test on the distinguished torsion. Indeed, the test applied after ψ₀ puts the Frobenius image of the point into the distinguished kernel of ψ₀. That kernel is étale, so a local point of it reducing to the identity is the identity. The converse follows by naturality. Thus the local tests agree in both directions. Translating each local factor to the identity gives equality of the distinguished kernel functors on every test scheme.

The relative Frobenius is finite and surjective. It commutes with the coefficient action, carries level sections to their twists, and pulls back the twisted polarization line bundle to its Q-th tensor power. The polarized-isogeny theorem gives a complementary map whose composites are multiplication by Q. Thus composing with ψ₀ changes the multiplier from Qr to Qr+1, the multiplier of ψ₁. Applying the full-kernel lemma identifies the two quotient maps as claimed. Representability and the same intertwining equality give the twist both for the base point and for the image of each source point. The marked-target comparison applies these equalities to the full level marking and the fibre coordinates.

How can residue points on the marked fibre power be compared?

The preceding comparisons give an equality of quotient moduli points and an equality of images of points on the abelian varieties. The tower uses a space with additional coordinates. Let Y → M record the auxiliary level structure, with universal family AY pulled back from AM. A point on the k-fold fibre power 𝒵 consists of a point on Y and a tuple of k points in its abelian fibre. Even if two isogenies have the same underlying target in M, they still have to agree on the marking and on that tuple.

Separation by evaluation. Two maps from a test scheme to 𝒵 agree if they have the same composite to M and give the same values in AM on all of the following tests:

  • For every lattice label y, evaluate the auxiliary level section η(y) at the marked base point and project to AM.
  • For each of the k coordinates, project that coordinate from AY to AM.

Indeed the two maps to Y now classify the same object over M and the same marking on it. To compare the markings, pull both objects back to the test scheme. The Cartesian square of universal abelian schemes identifies sections over a fixed base map by their images in the underlying universal family. The equalities on every label therefore identify the marked objects. The representing property of Y gives the same map to Y. Over that common map the same Cartesian square identifies each coordinate. The universal property of the fibre product then gives equality in 𝒵. For k = 0 only the marking tests are needed.

Transporting the tests. Write ψ for the isogeny on the correspondence. If a lifted source point has tuple (x₁,…,xk), the target tuple has entries ψ(xi). For a marking η(y), pull its section back along the source square of the correspondence. The defining compatibility of the marked isogeny says that applying ψ to this pulled-back section gives the target marking. Thus all the tests are evaluated by applying the same isogeny to known points on its source. Formation of these images commutes with passage to the residue field since the square defining each lifted point is Cartesian.

Suppose two subspaces missing the ordinary line have the same image modulo the line. The reduced quotient comparison gives the same base in M and the same images for all the tests just listed. The separation statement gives the same residue target in 𝒵. If one subspace contains the line and the other misses it, the relative Frobenius comparison gives those same equalities after the specified residue twist on the second target. Applying separation to that twisted point gives equality in 𝒵 again. In particular, the conclusion also identifies tuples whose coordinates lie outside the torsion group used to label the kernel.

Which residue target does the subspace count use?

Fix a valuation-ring point of the marked fibre power 𝒵 whose closed point lies over a generic point of the uniformizer divisor as in the integral congruence. The map from 𝒵 to the underlying level moduli scheme M is flat. In fact the marking is finite étale, and a fibre power of the smooth abelian family is flat over its base: for the zeroth power the map is the identity, and each additional factor is obtained by flat base change followed by composition. The generic-point argument then sends the original point to a generic point of a special component of M. The generic ordinarity theorem thus applies at the point used in the correspondence. Stacks Project, going down for a flat map[87].

Let P and R denote the source and target maps on an integral correspondence. A section of P above the chosen point is a lift z over V. The source square on the marked fibre power is Cartesian, so forgetting the marking and the tuple identifies these lifts with the lifts on the underlying isogeny correspondence above the projected point. Conversely an underlying lift and the fixed point upstairs have a unique lift in the Cartesian square. The subspace bijection therefore labels the sections for every j by the j-dimensional subspaces of H. Write v(D) for the residue point obtained by applying the target to the section labelled by D.

Residue target theorem. Let F act on these residue points by precomposition with the map of spectra induced by the Q-power residue automorphism. For a subspace U of H/C, choose any linear section of H → H/C over U. Its image D misses C and projects onto U. Define A(U) = v(D). Changing the section gives another such subspace with the same dimension. Their reduced marked targets agree by the marking and coordinate tests, so this value is independent of the choice. Write π for the projection of H onto H/C. For an arbitrary subspace D we now have

v(D) = A(πD)   if C ∩ D = 0,   v(D) = F(A(πD))   if C ⊆ D.

For the second equality, put U = πD. The chosen section over U and D project onto exactly the same subspace and their dimensions differ by one. They meet the hypotheses of the comparison with relative Frobenius, including its level and coordinate equalities. This gives precisely the one twist on the right. It holds also for D = C, where the chosen section has zero image, and for D = H.

The ordinary subspace count can now be applied to actual residue points. Over each fixed U, the graphs of its linear sections and the full inverse image arrive at the same point after the prescribed number of twists. Their two total weights at that point are equal. Summing over U gives the identity of the even and odd weighted multisets for every allowed test point. Combined with the separately computed generic comparison degree, this supplies the point identity in the integral congruence.

Why do the even and odd correspondences give the same residue points?

The local congruence counts each residue point with its multiplicity. An equality of total degrees would allow an excess at one point to cancel a deficit at another. To prove the identity point by point, we follow the reduction of a single subgroup through the map that divides out the ordinary line.

Ordinary subspace lemma. Let H have dimension n over a field with Q elements, and let C be a line in H. Write π for the quotient map to H/C. Let F be a self-map of a set of points. Suppose that each subspace U of the quotient determines a point A(U). For each subspace D of H of dimension j, its residue point is A(πD) if D misses the line, and F(A(πD)) if D contains it. Apply F another n − j times to this residue point and give it weight Qj(j−1)/2. Then the multiset obtained from even j equals the one obtained from odd j.

Proof. Fix a subspace U of dimension r downstairs. Inside π−1(U) there is exactly one subspace mapping onto U and containing C. It is the entire inverse image, of dimension r + 1. The other subspaces mapping onto U meet C only in zero. Projection identifies each of them with U, so each is the image of a unique linear section. To count the sections, lift one basis of U to get a first section. Every other section is obtained from it by adding a linear map U → C. For each of the r basis vectors one can choose any of the Q elements of the line. This gives Qr subspaces of dimension r.

The second set of subspaces starts at A(U) and receives n − r further applications of F. The single subspace containing C starts one application ahead and receives one fewer thereafter. They arrive at the very same point Fn−r(A(U)). The accumulated weights agree because

Qr · Qr(r−1)/2 = Qr(r+1)/2.

The two dimensions r and r + 1 have opposite parity. This pairs their contributions for the chosen U. All subspaces occur exactly once as U varies. At r = 0 the pair consists of the zero space and the line itself. At r = n − 1 the unique containing space is H. Even if distinct U give the same final point, adding their equal multiplicities preserves equality there.

For instance, let H be three-dimensional over 𝔽₃ and take U a line in the quotient plane. There are three lines above it that miss C and one plane above it that contains C. The three lines supply one copy each of F²(A(U)). The plane supplies three copies of that same point. In the experiment a three-cycle makes the two different numbers of remaining applications of F visible.

In the integral model the set of subspaces of dimension j parametrizes the sections of the j-th source correspondence over a valuation-ring point. The kernel of reduction supplies C, and the marked quotient calculation supplies A and the rule for the residue twist. Thus the lemma proves the pointwise congruence for every enumeration of the sections. The local congruence construction explains where these inputs enter.

How does the residue identity give the initial integral congruence?

Fix the place w and write Q for the size of its residue field and q for its residue characteristic. Thus Q = qf. Choose a uniformizer ϖ of the valuation ring and the integral model with its marking. There is one generic tower mapping to its fibre power. The group-side congruence has already specified an operator γj for every j between 0 and the rank n, as well as a scalar ϑj. We need the actual correspondences on that model and an identity involving their residue points.

Integral congruence theorem. Use the compact unitary datum, a standard base, matching primes under the field identification, and the integral group and level tests at w. Assume the integral moduli and isogeny theorems for this datum, the comparison of sections with subspaces and the ordinary reduction theorem for geometric generic points of the special fibre. Under the group-side congruence conditions, the same model carries n + 1 integral correspondences. Their source maps are finite, and over the open where q is invertible the j-th has finite étale degree equal to the number of j-dimensional subspaces in rank n over the residue field. They satisfy the weighted point identity on the uniformizer divisor. The tower compares with the j-th correspondence with positive multiplicity mj and eigenvalue θ(γj) = mjϑj.

Constructing the legs. At the underlying integral principal level the moduli theorem for isogenies of type j supplies a correspondence with its universal isogeny. Lift the auxiliary marking to it by the marked isogeny theorem. On a fibre power the source retains the tuple on the source abelian scheme, and the target applies the isogeny to each coordinate of that tuple. The source is the pullback of the source on the underlying moduli space. The finite and étale base-change theorem for these correspondences therefore gives the stated degree where q is invertible. Both legs lie over the same point of the valuation ring because the isogeny is defined over that point.

Reading a section at the special fibre. Test the identity at a valuation-ring point as in the definition of the residue comparison. Its fraction field is algebraically closed, q is nonzero in the valuation ring, and its closed point maps to a generic point of the uniformizer divisor. Flatness carries this last condition to the underlying moduli model. At such a point the ordinarity theorem gives exactly Qn−1 geometric points of 𝔴-torsion. Reduction from the Qn generic torsion sections then has a one-dimensional kernel. Comparing the kernels of the isogenies then identifies the sections of the j-th source with j-dimensional subspaces of a single rank-n space over the field with Q elements. There is one distinguished line C for the whole family.

The reduced quotient and the Frobenius quotient supply two equalities of residue targets. For a fixed image U modulo C, any two subspaces missing C give the same target. A subspace containing C gives its residue twist by F. These equalities on a fibre power include the marked moduli point and the images of each coordinate. They determine the entire target point. Choose one subspace missing C over U, for example the image of a linear section, and call its target A(U). The first equality makes this definition independent of the section. The second gives exactly the input to the ordinary subspace lemma. That lemma proves equality of the two weighted multisets for every allowed test point. The coordinate and level tests explain why both identities hold on the marked fibre power.

Reading the tower coefficients. The group test chooses γj with element hj and fine level Mj. Set Hj = K₀ ∩ hj−1K₀hj. It requires that Qj divide Mj, that [K₀ : Hj] give the indicated Grassmannian count, and that the deck transformations occur among the eigenvalue-one operators. By the comparison of Hecke fibres,

mj = [Hj : K(Mj)] > 0,   θ(γj) = mjϑj.

The second equality is part of the original coefficient test. The counting argument identifies the geometric multiplicity with the integer used in that test. This constructs the initial congruence with precisely those coefficients. Restricting the integral model to the components reached by the tower gives the surjective generic cover used later.

Why does an index computed on the generic fibre still count lifts after reduction?

For good reduction we need the degree of a source map over the entire local model. For the rest of the good-reduction construction, write Y for the whole integral fibre power previously denoted by 𝒵, and Y′ for its analogue at a finer level. Let s ∶ Y′ → Y forget the finer marking. The groups of equivalent markings are K₁ ⊆ K₀. At this stage the moduli comparison for forgetting level gives a finite étale map on the integral bases and a Cartesian square of abelian schemes. Passing to their fibre powers is another base change, so s is finite étale everywhere. Its degree still has to be determined.

Integral degree lemma. Assume that a common fine level covers the two generic fibres, that its maps identify precisely the orbits of K₁ and K₀ respectively, and that the stabilizer of a fine lift is its principal level subgroup, contained in K₁. Assume also that the base Y is flat over the valuation ring. Then the number of points in every geometric fibre of s is

#s−1(y) = [K₀ : K₁].

Generic fibre. Choose a geometric point y over the fraction field and a fine lift x. For u ∈ K₀, project Tu−1(x) = x · u to Y′, using the right action. Each point above y is obtained this way, since it lifts to the common fine level and all lifts above y lie in one K₀-orbit. Two choices u, v give the same point when their lifts lie in the same K₁-orbit. The fine-level subgroup is normal in K₀ and lies in K₁, so the stabilizer introduces no further identifications. Equivalently u−1v ∈ K₁. These are precisely the cosets counted by the index. Here surjectivity onto the generic fibres of these particular quotient models comes from the integral level comparison.

Special fibre. Since s is finite étale, its algebra is locally a free module of finite rank. The rank is locally constant on Y. At a geometric point the fibre algebra is a product of copies of its algebraically closed field, one for each point. Its rank is therefore the number we just computed on the generic fibre. Stacks Project, §29.49[110] and Lemma 58.2.2[111].

Take any point of the special fibre and an open neighbourhood on which the rank is constant. Going down for the flat structure map lifts the generic point of the valuation ring to a generalization of the chosen point. Every open neighbourhood of the chosen point contains this generalization. The generic computation gives the value of the rank there, hence also at the original point. This proves the degree formula at every geometric point of the special fibre. Stacks Project, Lemma 10.39.19[87].

The étale hypothesis is used in the equality between rank and point count. For comparison, over ℤ localized at 5 the algebra with equation X(X − 5) = 0 has module rank two everywhere. At 5 its fibre algebra is 𝔽₅[X]/(X²), supported at one point even after algebraic closure. The two integral models at 5 show this collision.

How do the integral correspondences give good reduction for a whole family?

The residue identity involves selected operators. Good reduction asks for an integral correspondence for each operator in the family. Fix a place and a level satisfying the good-reduction group conditions described below. The marked moduli construction supplies a smooth projective fibre power Y over the local valuation ring and a common generic cover. The same Y must work for every operator. Its finer source level may depend on the operator.

Fix one operator. Write h for its translation, K for its group of labels, K₀ for the group at the integral target and K₁ ⊆ K₀ for the group at its finer source Y′. The group hypotheses give principal levels K(M) ⊆ K(N) ⊆ K ∩ K₀, with K(M) ⊆ K₁ normal in K₀. They also give K₀ = (K ∩ K₀)K₁. Thus every marking at the target can be moved to the finer level by an element of the label group. Let s ∶ Y′ → Y forget that finer level. Its degree throughout the integral model is [K₀ : K₁].

Extending a target map. Write h = h₁h₂ as in the group hypotheses. Both factors carry the integral lattice Λ into itself. The source integer level is N₀κ, with κ > 0 and κΛ ⊆ h₂Λ. For a label representative b ∈ K, the group at level one acts by lattice automorphisms, so bΛ = Λ. The same κ works for h₂b. The group conditions supply an intermediate level N₁ ∈ (N₀)𝔞′. Conjugation by h₂b takes K(M) into K(N₁), and conjugation by h₁ takes K(N₁) into K(N). These inclusions make the two successive generic transitions admissible. The integral moduli comparison for such a translation extends it to a map between the marked fibre powers. When h₁ is the identity, this gives the target map directly.

In the other case the hypotheses specify an auxiliary maximal ideal 𝔴′ and an elementary isogeny of type i ≤ n there. The ideal 𝔴′ contains the chosen split ideal (q, ω − r), the refined ideal 𝔞′ lies in 𝔞𝔴′ and N(𝔴′)i divides the intermediate level. These are the level conditions for the integral comparison of that isogeny. Use the intermediate model at the original integer level and refined ideal 𝔞′. Extend h₂b to this model, then extend h₁ from it to Y. Their composite tb extends the generic translation h₁h₂b. This step uses two moduli results about integral extensions. The coset calculation below explains how their maps fit together.

Counting source points. Take one copy of Y′ for each left coset b in K/(K ∩ K₀). Use s on every copy and the corresponding tb as its target. A fine tower label c ∈ K/K(N) maps to its coarser label b. For chosen representatives write c = bv with v ∈ K ∩ K₀. Acting by v before projecting to Y′ leaves the coarse source fixed. Its target is correct because (hb)v = hc. The integral source is a finite disjoint union of finite étale maps. Its degree is

d′ = [K : K ∩ K₀] [K₀ : K₁],   m = [K ∩ K₁ : K(M)].

Counting above one compatible pair. To see why m is the comparison multiplicity, fix a coarse copy b, a point on it and a compatible point in the tower. Choose an origin in the fine fibre. The second marking then has a representative u ∈ K₀. A fine lift has a copy label in K/K(N) and a marking within that copy in K(N)/K(M). After representatives for the first quotient have been chosen, multiplying the two representatives records both as one coset xK(M) in K. The orbit test for the prescribed pair is b−1xu−1 ∈ K₁.

By the factorization of K₀ choose a ∈ K ∩ K₀ with a−1u−1 ∈ K₁. Then ua ∈ K₁. Multiplication on the right by ua changes the test into b−1xa ∈ K₁. This element also belongs to K. Since a normalizes K(M), the substitution y = b−1xa is well defined on the fine cosets, with inverse x = bya−1. It identifies the allowed lifts with (K ∩ K₁)/K(M), giving exactly m > 0 above each compatible pair. Both sources over the generic tower are finite étale, so the comparison is finite étale of this degree by the finite étale fibre argument.

For a small example in which the order of multiplication matters, take K = K₀ = S₃, K₁ = {1, (12)}, both principal marking subgroups trivial and b = 1. With u = (123) choose a = (132). Using right-to-left composition, the two allowed labels are (123) and (23). Right multiplication by a sends them to 1 and (12), precisely the elements of K₁. Here three integral source points each have two lifts.

In general, the factorization of K₀ makes the map from (K ∩ K₀)/(K ∩ K₁) to K₀/K₁ a bijection. The product d′m therefore recovers the upstairs source degree [K : K(M)]. Repeating the construction for each operator gives the initial good-reduction witness at the chosen place. The restriction to the generic image then gives the surjective cover used later.

Which coefficient of the holomorphic trace detects a prescribed degree?

Let g be an admitted Hecke test at the chosen level which satisfies the regularity and vanishing conditions of the definite trace formula. Denote its definite automorphic trace in the given weight by D(g). For a sufficiently large fibre power there is a finite family of coefficients cα, chosen from the weight and its exponent list, independent of g. The label α specifies a nonzero even algebraic integer on each factor of the abelian fibre power. These entries act on their respective factors and give a self-map of the fibre power. In bidegree (a, b), let Ca,b be the sum of its pullbacks over all labels, weighted by cα. Write Ta,b(g) for the Hecke action on Hb(Z, Ωa).

Weighted trace identity. The finite étale fixed-point formula and the comparison of the marked fixed-point count with the definite automorphic trace give the following identity of polynomials in y.

∑a=0d (−y)a ∑b=0d (−1)b tr(Ta,b(g) Ca,b) = D(g) ∑i yhi.

Geometric inputs and their use. Decompose g into a finite sum of double-coset indicators supported where its regularity condition holds. Each indicator and each fibre label give a correspondence on a deeper level. Its two maps to Z are finite étale. At a coincidence of the maps, use the first map to identify tangent spaces and write A for the tangent action of the second. The geometric input identifies the finite fixed locus, proves det(I − A) ≠ 0 there, and compares the resulting sum with the group-side count. For form degree a the holomorphic fixed-point formula gives the local contribution [Xa]det(I + XA)/det(I − A). The notation in square brackets extracts a coefficient. Multiplying this contribution by (−y)a and summing in a simply evaluates the numerator at −y, giving det(I − yA)/det(I − A). In dimension one, a tangent multiplier of 2 contributes 2y − 1. The local numerator is the exterior-power trace appearing in the holomorphic Lefschetz formula. M. F. Atiyah and R. Bott, A Lefschetz fixed point formula for elliptic complexes. II. Applications.[72]

Passing from the deeper level to the normalized Hecke operator divides this sum by the subgroup index. The fixed-point count on the deeper level contains the same factor. It cancels before summing over the indicators. On the group side the weights cα sum the contributions over the marked roots of each regular characteristic polynomial. The weight calculation gives the character of the specified algebraic representation times ∑i yhi. The equality between the weighted fixed-point count and the definite pair count, followed by the equality between the latter count and the automorphic trace, now gives the displayed identity by linearity. This use of the trace identity depends on the geometric fixed-point count, the construction of the weights and both group-side comparisons.

Extracting the coefficient. Number the weight coordinates from 0 to n − 1. The admissible exponent lists have one of two forms, up to an additive constant independent of i. The first requires the conjugate weight list to be constant. It gives hi = constant + λi + n − 1 − i. The second requires the weight at the distinguished embedding to be constant. It gives hi = constant − λ′i + i, using the weight at the conjugate embedding. The weight lists are weakly decreasing. The first exponent list strictly decreases and the second strictly increases. Each exponent therefore occurs once. The fibre power used in the eigenclass theorem can be chosen uniformly. For each embedding and conjugated weight these two formulas give at most two lists, with their constants specified by the weight data. The embeddings of the number field form a finite set and field automorphisms only permute them. Take the maximum of the finitely many thresholds for these lists.

Now suppose D(g) ≠ 0 and put h = hi. The right-hand coefficient of yh is D(g). The left side has degree at most d, so h ≤ d. At that degree the identity reads

∑b=0d (−1)b tr(Th,b(g) Ch,b) = (−1)h D(g) ≠ 0.

At least one summand has nonzero trace. The eigenclass argument applies this calculation to a test g chosen to separate the prescribed Hecke system. This is what gives the nonzero summand its spectral meaning.

How does a trace give a class with all the prescribed Hecke eigenvalues?

Let Z be a smooth projective complex fibre power in the unitary tower, of dimension d. The two indices in Hb(Z, Ωa) record different information. The sheaf Ωa consists of differential a-forms, and b is its cohomological degree. The automorphic weight prescribes the first index. To find the second we use an alternating trace over the possible values of b.

Eigenclass theorem. Use the compact unitary datum of the tower. Its rank is odd, its three parameters a, m and the linked group’s a are all 1, and its complex base is the standard base. Fix a weight whose coordinates are nonnegative integers in decreasing or equal order at each embedding. Assume the geometric and group-side comparisons in the weighted trace identity above. A single fibre power works for all admissible levels and conjugates of this weight. At such a level let f and the Hecke functions ψj be admitted by the tower, and suppose they pass the spectral trace test for the specified scalars θj. For each exponent hi in an admitted list there are an integer 0 ≤ b ≤ d and a class x such that

0 ≠ x ∈ Hb(Z, Ωhi),   Tjx = θjx for every j.

Here Tj is the cohomological action of ψj. The same class satisfies all the equations for the chosen i. The degree b and the class can change with i.

Where the operators commute. Fix h = hi. For 0 ≤ b ≤ d write Wb = Hb(Z, Ωh), Fb for the action of f there, and Tb,j for that of ψj. These spaces are finite-dimensional by coherent cohomology of a proper scheme. Let Ub be the span of the vectors w(Tb)Fbz for z ∈ Wb and every finite word w in the operators, including the empty word. Prepending a letter shows that each Tb,j preserves this space. Convolution of words acts by composition on cohomology. The spectral test permits the first two letters in any word applied to f to be interchanged. Thus the operators commute on every generator of Ub, and hence on that whole space. The Stacks Project, Proposition 30.19.1, finiteness of coherent cohomology.[112]

One polynomial for all the degrees. On the direct sum of the Ub, put all the commuting actions side by side. Adjoin a one-dimensional summand on which operator j acts by θj. This extra line keeps track of scalar evaluation while we choose a polynomial in the operators. If some operator minus its prescribed scalar is not nilpotent on the current space, project to its generalized eigenspace for that scalar. To construct the projection, factor its minimal polynomial as (X − θj)rq(X) with q(θj) ≠ 0. The extra line ensures r ≥ 1. Bézout's identity supplies a multiple of q congruent to 1 modulo (X − θj)r. It fixes the generalized eigenspace, maps the current space into it, and still evaluates to 1 on the extra line. All other operators preserve the image by commutativity.

Every such restriction decreases dimension. After finitely many restrictions, even for an infinite family of operators, the product of the projections is a polynomial s with s(θ) = 1. Its image in each Ub consists of simultaneous generalized eigenvectors with the prescribed scalars. The extra line alone could have survived. We now use the trace to show that one of the cohomological summands survives too.

Finding the class. The spectral test applied to s supplies a second polynomial m such that the function g obtained by applying the convolution words ms to f is admissible for the trace formula and has nonzero definite trace. The coefficient at the prescribed holomorphic degree then gives a b for which

tr(m(Tb) s(Tb) Fb Ch,b) ≠ 0.

The rightmost factor Ch,b is the weighted sum of geometric pullbacks in the trace identity. A nonzero trace implies the composite is nonzero, hence s(Tb)Fb is nonzero. Its image lies in the intersection of the prescribed generalized eigenspaces in Ub. This intersection is stable. On it each difference Tb,j − θjI is nilpotent. Whenever such a difference is nonzero, its kernel is a proper nonzero subspace preserved by all the other differences. Restrict to that kernel and repeat. Dimension decreases until all the differences vanish on a nonzero space. Any nonzero vector there gives the required class.

For example, let T act diagonally on ℂ² with diagonal entries 2 and 3. Its trace is 5. If we prescribe θ = 5, the polynomial s(X) = (X − 2)(X − 3)/6 satisfies s(5) = 1 and s(T) = 0. Every product with this last operator has zero trace. Thus this example fails the spectral test at θ = 5.

For a tower originally defined over a field embedded in ℂ, the comparison also transports the result through the chosen embedding and the complex field automorphism σ of the weight test. The individual correspondence functions count cosets and take natural-number values, so σ fixes these functions. It sends the prescribed scalars to σ(θj). Compatibility of pullback and finite étale trace with base change identifies the resulting equations with those for the actual geometric correspondences. This is the occurrence used in the shifted Hodge degree of the tower.

How is the same Hecke system carried into the geometric tower?

The cohomological eigenspace requires several correspondences to have prescribed eigenvalues on the same nonzero vector. There are two kinds of evidence on the automorphic side. At a finite place a Hecke polynomial records roots. At an embedding a weight predicts degrees in which a joint eigenvector should occur. We describe how these data pass to a single tower once the geometric comparison theorems are supplied.

Conditional transfer theorem. Fix a CM field E, the coefficient identification ι from the algebraic closure of ℚℓ to ℂ, and an automorphic representation of positive odd rank a. Suppose a level, a Hecke test function, and a family of Hecke operators indexed by I have been chosen for it. Write θi for their specified joint eigenvalues, κ for the auxiliary algebraic Hecke character, and mτ for its shift at the embedding τ. The level selection supplies a cofinite congruence among the permitted primes away from ℓ and may impose an additional congruence or weight test at a specified place. Assume the following geometric inputs for these data.

  • Use the standard base over E just constructed. The weighted trace calculation selects a power for this weight. At that power the level transitions give a tower. Its chosen space is smooth and projective and the degree formula counts each source fibre.
  • The comparison at an integral prime sends a group-side good-reduction witness to a smooth projective integral model with a finite étale cover on the generic fibre, and sends a group-side Hecke congruence to the corresponding relation on a cover with the same coefficients. The construction for all operators and the ordinary residue identity for the selected operators give the two initial covering conditions. The image lemma makes the generic cover surjective. The restrictions for good reduction and for the residue congruence preserve the specified data.
  • For this Hecke test and its spectral data, the weighted fixed-point and automorphic trace comparisons must hold. The spectral argument then produces a nonzero simultaneous eigenclass in every holomorphic degree selected by the group-side exponent test. The embedding used for base change must match the field labels of the group datum.

Then the tower carries the same congruences with the same exceptional set. At an embedding τ above any place where the weight test was imposed, each predicted jump j occurs in the shifted holomorphic degree j + mτ, with the conjugation of eigenvalues specified by that test.

Proof at a finite place. Choose the standard base, then the power supplied for this weight, and take the tower at that power. The comparison applies to all its chosen correspondences. At a permitted prime w, take the ideal of the group datum corresponding to w under the chosen field isomorphism. The polynomial test supplies the Hecke coefficients, including a nonzero leading scalar c after applying ι. The geometric congruence uses the same sequence of coefficients, so the polynomial identity passes unchanged. Writing β₁, …, βa for the algebraically normalized Satake parameters, with multiplicity, the identity reads

Pw(X) = c ∏i=1a (X − βi/κ(w)),   c ≠ 0.

For a numerical check, take the three normalized roots 6, 10 and 14, character value 2 and leading scalar 3. The polynomial is 3(X − 3)(X − 5)(X − 7). Multiplying each root by 2 recovers 6, 10 and 14. The scalar 3 multiplies the polynomial once. The local character is unramified at the tested place, so its indicated value on a uniformizer is defined. The leading scalar is retained, and division by it gives the monic polynomial that specifies the roots. This reasoning works separately at every permitted place outside the original finite exception set. For an additionally prescribed congruence the same comparison applies directly at that place.

Proof at an embedding. For τ above the tested prime, the group-side weight test supplies one field automorphism σ of ℂ matching the embeddings of the coefficient datum. For each possible weight of the automorphic representation at τ and each prescribed jump j, it then supplies an exponent list h of nonnegative integers and an index i such that hi = j + mτ. The standard base ensures that σ ∘ τ agrees with the group datum on its designated elements. The Hodge trace comparison therefore applies to the base change along σ ∘ τ and to the joint eigenvalues σ(ι(θr)). It gives some cohomological degree b and a nonzero class in Hb(Ωhi) on which each correspondence r has this eigenvalue. Substitution of j + mτ gives the required holomorphic degree. For instance, if a jump is −1 and the character shift is 3, one looks in holomorphic degree 2. The second degree b is supplied by the comparison and can vary with the jump.

One choice of tower preserves every test carried by the initial level data and its finite exceptional set. The table of level choices distinguishes the type place w₀ from the weight place v′. Every choice retains the weight test at v′. At an additional place above ℓ the weight test and the polynomial test may use separate towers. Applying the transfer to each choice preserves the two conclusions with their own witnesses. The local comparisons and rank extraction explain how these witnesses are used later. The integer level and operator family are constructed above. The integral comparison uses ordinary reduction and the extension of marked isogenies. The weighted counts identifying the geometric trace with the definite automorphic trace are another input.

Which components of the integral model does the tower reach?

Fix a finite place w of the ground field. Write O for its discrete valuation ring, η for the generic point of Spec O, and Y for the smooth projective integral model supplied by the local comparison. Here “integral model” means a model over O. It may have several connected components. Its generic fibre Yη is obtained by allowing division by a uniformizer. The tower space Z maps to this fibre by a finite étale map π. The later cohomological comparison needs every geometric point of the chosen generic fibre to have a lift.

Image lemma. There is a unique open and closed part Y′ of Y for which Y′η is the image of π. The induced map Z → Y′η is finite étale and surjective. The new integral model is smooth and projective over O, with the same relative dimension as the old one wherever it has points.

Proof. The image U of π is closed because a finite morphism is integral and universally closed. It is open because an étale morphism is flat and locally of finite presentation, hence open. Consequently U is a union of entire connected components of the generic fibre. Stacks Project, Lemma 29.45.7[113] and Lemma 29.26.10[114].

The two facts needed to extend U across the special fibre are density and separation of components. Any nonempty open of Y has open image in Spec O by smoothness, so it meets the generic fibre. Moreover O is normal and locally Noetherian. A scheme smooth over it is again normal and locally Noetherian. Its irreducible components are disjoint and open. On any such component C, the intersection with the generic fibre is a nonempty open of an irreducible space and hence is irreducible. Since U is both open and closed there, it contains either all of that intersection or none. Take Y′ to be the union of the components selected by the first alternative. Its complement is the union of the others. Density shows that no different open and closed selection can give the same generic image. Stacks Project, §35.18[115] and §28.7, Lemma 28.7.6[116].

Now π factors through the open subscheme Y′η. Over that part its finite étale fibres are the original ones, and every fibre contains a point. Over an algebraically closed field a nonempty finite étale fibre is a finite collection of rational points, which gives the required lifts. Smoothness and relative dimension restrict to an open subscheme. The inclusion Y′ → Y is also a closed immersion, so composing with a projective embedding of Y gives one for Y′.

Why use smoothness here? Over ℤ localized at 5, consider two generic points labelled 0 and 5. In the model with equation X(X − 5) = 0 their reductions coincide. The indicator of the first branch would have values (1, 0), yet any integral polynomial takes congruent values at 0 and 5. The experiment compares this model with the split model X(X − 1) = 0. Over the fraction field the coordinate X/5 in the first model has values 0 and 1, just as X does in the split model. Thus the two models have the same generic branch indicator. Its ability to separate the reductions depends on the integral model.

Why does the restriction preserve good reduction?

Let s, t ∶ T → Y be the source and target of one integral correspondence representing a tower operator. To restrict both maps to the open and closed part Y′, we must keep precisely the points of

T′ = s−1(Y′) ∩ t−1(Y′).

Intersecting two preimages could in principle discard some points of a source fibre. At a place of good reduction the source is finite étale of a fixed degree d over all of Y. The compatibility with the tower includes a map from the tower correspondence to the pullback of T along π by its source leg. That map is finite étale of positive degree m and its target projection agrees with the tower target after applying π. These properties imply that T′ is the whole inverse image by s of Y′. In particular the restricted source has degree d and the comparison still has multiplicity m.

Proof. Start on the generic fibre. If s(x) belongs to Y′η, lift it by π, then lift the resulting pair over x by the comparison map of degree m. A finite étale map of positive constant degree is surjective, since its geometric fibres have positive cardinality. Following the tower target now writes t(x) as the image of a tower point under π. Thus t(x) also belongs to Y′. On the whole model the possible failure set is open, since Y′ and its complement are both open. The scheme T is smooth over O by composition of the étale map s and the smooth structure map of Y. Every nonempty open of T meets its generic fibre. The failure set has no generic points above η, so it is empty.

The restricted source is therefore the base change of s along Y′ → Y. It is finite étale with the same geometric fibres. Both ends of the comparison map from the tower already land in the chosen parts. The pullback of T along the tower source used for the multiplicity is canonically the pullback with T′ in its place. Its points have the same two coordinates and the same compatibility equation, and the factorization through an open immersion is unique. This preserves m for each operator. Applying the image lemma once to the common model therefore gives a good-reduction witness with surjective generic cover for the entire family.

What happens to the congruence in residue characteristic?

Let p be the residue characteristic of w, q = pf the residue cardinality and n the degree of the congruence polynomial. Here each of the n + 1 source maps is finite on the integral model and étale of known degree on the open where p is invertible. On the special fibre the hypothesis is an identity of multisets of points. We show that restriction to Y′ preserves both assertions.

In the valuation ring O the only prime ideals are zero and the maximal ideal. The latter contains p. A point of Y where p is invertible must therefore lie over η. The generic lifting argument just given applies there to each correspondence. Its intersection T′ has all the old source lifts over this open, so the étale degree there stays fixed. Over the entire model T′ is open and closed in s−1(Y′). Its closed inclusion followed by the finite base change of s is finite. This proves exactly the source-map properties needed at w.

To read the special-fibre identity, take a valuation ring B with algebraically closed fraction field and p nonzero in B. Choose a point y ∶ Spec B → Y′ whose closed point maps to a generic point of the uniformizer divisor. For each index j enumerate the sections over y of its source map. Write vj,a for the residue point obtained by applying the target to section a. Write F for the twist by the residue-field endomorphism z ↦ zq in the test. For each j, count the points Fn−j(vj,a) with weight qj(j−1)/2. The initial congruence says that the even indices and the odd indices give the same multiset, including all repetitions.

As a finite check on these weights, take n = 3, q = 5 and a single point fixed by F. Index the four lists by subspaces of dimensions 0, 1, 2 and 3 in the three-dimensional space over 𝔽₅. There are (5³ − 1)/(5 − 1) = 31 lines. Duality gives 31 planes, and there is one zero space and one whole space. Send every index to the fixed point. Its multiplicity on the even side is 1 + 5 · 31 = 156. The odd side gives 31 + 5³ = 156. In the full identity this equality must hold separately at each residue point.

Every original section over y factors uniquely through the restricted correspondence. Indeed its generic target lies in Y′ by the preceding argument, since p is nonzero in the fraction field. The target of its whole section lies there because Y′ is closed and every point of Spec B is a specialization of the generic point. Its source already lies there by the choice of y. We thus have a bijection between the two lists of sections. The inclusion of Y′ commutes with the residue twist and is injective on residue points. Applying this inclusion to the two weighted lists gives exactly the old identity, so the lists in Y′ are equal. The condition on the generic point of the divisor is preserved by an open and closed inclusion.

The residue degree, uniformizer, indices of the chosen tower operators, multiplicities and polynomial coefficients can therefore be retained. This proves the passage from an initial congruence witness to one with a surjective generic cover. The initial correspondence obtains this point identity from ordinary reduction and the count of subspaces above each quotient subspace.

6.10How can a cohomological piece of unknown dimension determine rank m?

Rank-extraction theorem used here. Let ρ be a continuous semisimple geometric representation of Γ of dimension D. At some place over ℓ and some inducing embedding, its filtration jumps contain a lacunary set of m distinct integers. Let ψ be a continuous character. Suppose that for a dense set of g ∈ Γ there is a monic degree-m polynomial Q with Q(ρ(g)) = 0 and (−1)mQ(0) = ψ(g). Then there exists a continuous semisimple representation r of dimension m, with injective equivariant maps in the following two directions, for some integer k. The set of g where r(g) has m distinct eigenvalues is open and dense. The derivation below passes from the local jumps to a matrix in the Lie algebra of the global image, then from its eigenspaces to the two injections. The argument in each open coset supplies the simple-spectrum condition. The row identity explains why adjoining the other components of the group preserves scalar diagonal blocks.

r ↪ ρ,   ρ ↪ r⊕k.

Here the dense set consists of inverses of arithmetic Frobenius lifts at eligible spherical primes, after finite exclusions. The geometric comparison supplies Q(X) = ∏α ∈ R(X−α), transported to the ℓ-adic field. The determinant character attached to the central character with the Satake normalization takes value ∏α there. Thus the constant-term hypothesis holds, including its sign. The auxiliary weight and the Hodge comparison give the required set of jumps. These facts verify the hypotheses for the cohomological piece.

The first injection passes annihilation to r. Indeed, for the injection A one has AQ(r(g)) = Q(ρ(g))A = 0. It also passes trivial inertia to r. At a tested element of simple spectrum, each of the m distinct eigenvalues of r(g) is a root of Q, by applying the annihilation identity to an eigenvector. Since Q is monic of degree m, it equals the characteristic polynomial there. On that same dense set the determinant of r agrees with ψ, hence it agrees everywhere by continuity.

Different prescribed places may require different geometric pieces. Extract r once from one piece and r′ from another. The two open dense simple-spectrum conditions can be imposed together. In every nonempty open subset of Γ, intersect with those two open dense sets and then choose an inverse Frobenius outside the union of the two finite exceptional sets. Both characteristic polynomials there equal the same Satake polynomial, since both pieces concern the same U′. Continuity gives equality everywhere, and Brauer–Nesbitt identifies the two semisimple representations. Thus the injections for the new piece can be written using the original r. The trace argument for Brauer–Nesbitt.
