Where does the prescribed determinant come from?

The rank-extraction theorem needs a scalar ψ(g) before it produces a matrix r(g). We obtain this scalar from the automorphic representation. Let U be an irreducible automorphic representation of the definite unitary group of rank m ≥ 1 over the CM field E. Fix a prime ℓ and a field identification ι from the algebraic closure of ℚℓ to ℂ. Let Γ be the absolute Galois group of E.

Determinant character theorem. There is a continuous character ψ of Γ with values in the multiplicative group of the algebraic closure of ℚℓ. At every split finite place w where U has spherical Satake parameters, its local parameter is the product of the normalized Satake entries. Away from ℓ this is its value, read through ι, at geometric Frobenius. At w above ℓ the restriction to a decomposition group is crystalline, and the product is the Weil eigenvalue at degree −1.

From the centre to a character. For an idèle z of E, let c be CM conjugation and set ζ(z) = (z/c(z))I. This scalar matrix is unitary because its scalar times its conjugate is one. It commutes with the adelic group. To see that its right translation acts by one scalar on all of U, choose a nonzero form f in U. Its translates under the compact group at infinity span a finite-dimensional space S. A compact open subgroup K at the finite places fixing f fixes S because the finite and infinite translations commute.

Consider the maps from S to U that intertwine the actions at infinity and have K-fixed image. This vector space contains the inclusion. It is finite-dimensional because evaluation at representatives of the finitely many rational classes modulo K and the group at infinity embeds it into one copy of the dual of S per class. An intertwiner is determined there by rational invariance, its finite level and its transformation law at infinity. Composing such maps with translation by ζ(z) preserves their space by centrality. Over ℂ this operator has a nonzero eigenmap. A nonzero value of the eigenmap is an eigenvector in U. Its eigenspace is invariant under every adelic translation, again by centrality, so irreducibility makes that eigenspace all of U. The finite class number and evaluation at representatives.

Call this scalar χ(z). Translation respects products and is invertible, so χ is a multiplicative character. At a point g where f(g) ≠ 0, it equals f(gζ(z))/f(g), hence is continuous. For a principal idèle ζ(z) is rational and central, so left rational invariance gives χ(z) = 1. Thus χ is a Hecke character. It is also one on every idèle fixed by c.

The exponent at infinity. At a pair of conjugate complex embeddings τ, cτ, the last property makes the archimedean character trivial on ℝ×. It factors through the circle via z ↦ (z/|z|)², a surjection with kernel ℝ×. A continuous character of the circle has the form u ↦ un for an integer n. Indeed its image is compact in ℂ×, so has modulus one. Lifting its argument along ℝ → S¹ gives a continuous additive function of the angle, and periodicity makes its slope integral. The exponents of χ at τ and cτ are therefore nτ and −nτ. If the weight of U at τ is λ in the right-translation convention, the scalar uI acts on its highest-weight vector by u∑λj. Evaluating the same central action gives nτ = ∑j λτ,j. The action of the diagonal circle at the chosen embedding.

The value at a split spherical place. An idèle supported at w with value u has conjugate supported at the other place over the same real-subfield prime. Thus ζ sends it to the local scalar uI in the identification with GLm(Ew). Let B be the multiset of unnormalized Satake entries. On a spherical vector, scalar units act trivially. For a uniformizer ϖ the spherical Hecke operator indexed by m is translation by ϖI alone, since its central double coset is a single coset. Its Satake eigenvalue is the mth elementary symmetric function, ∏β∈Bβ. The local irreducible representation maps nontrivially into U by the spherical-component hypothesis. The kernel is invariant, so the map is injective and the spherical vector still detects this scalar in U. Consequently χ is unramified at w and χw(ϖ) = ∏β.

Write q for the residue-field size and t = m(m−1)/2. Normalization multiplies each of the m entries β by q(m−1)/2, so their product gains qt. The idèle norm has local value |ϖ|w = q−1. The Hecke character with the required product is therefore

ξ = χ |·|𝔸E−t,   Dw = ξw(ϖ) = qt ∏β∈B β.

Passing to the Galois group. At a complex place the idèle norm is the square of the complex modulus. The twist therefore subtracts t from the exponent at each embedding. Put n′τ = nτ − t. Form the ℓ-adic character of the idèles by dividing ξ by its archimedean algebraic powers, applying ι−1 to the remaining values, and restoring the same powers at the embeddings into the algebraic closure of ℚℓ. The quotient after removing the infinite powers is locally constant. The restored powers are continuous in the ℓ-adic topology. On principal idèles the removed and restored powers cancel under ι. The corrected character is thus continuous, trivial on principal idèles and on the connected component at infinity. Global Artin reciprocity lets it descend to the abelianized Galois group. Composing with the abelianization of Γ gives ψ. We take reciprocity to send a local uniformizer to geometric Frobenius in the unramified quotient. J. S. Milne, Class Field Theory, Chapter V, §5, Theorems 5.3 and 5.5 and the description of the absolute reciprocity kernel.[117]

At w away from ℓ the corrected character agrees on local idèles with ι−1ξw. Its triviality on units gives trivial inertia. If F acts on the residue field by the qth power, then ι(ψ(F−1)) = Dw. This fixes the sign needed for extraction. The monic degree-m Satake polynomial has constant term (−1)mDw. Once the extracted representation has this polynomial on the dense set of inverse Frobenius elements with simple spectrum, its determinant equals ψ there and hence throughout Γ by continuity. In rank one t = 0, so a single Satake entry β gives ψ(F−1) = ι−1(β).

The comparison above ℓ. Restrict ψ to a decomposition group at a split spherical place w above ℓ. Here the algebraic powers at w enter its action on units. The rank-one comparison theorem identifies its de Rham filtration jump at an inducing ℓ-adic embedding σ with −n′ισ = t − nισ. Since the smooth local character ξw is unramified, the Galois character is crystalline. In the associated Weil representation local reciprocity gives a uniformizer to the power −d modulo units at any Weil element h of degree d. Its characteristic polynomial is consequently

det(X I − WD(ψ)(h)) = X − Dw−d.

At degree −1 this recovers Dw. The equality det r = ψ persists upon restriction to this decomposition group. The determinant is the top exterior power. The Weil–Deligne construction preserves tensor products and the permutation of tensor factors, so it preserves the alternating summand defining this exterior power. This gives the same product of Weil eigenvalues for r. At a place where the Satake parameters also satisfy the multiplicative genericity hypothesis and the geometric annihilation relation holds, the local multiplicity test combines this determinant with that relation to determine the full polynomial. The local input here is the rank-one de Rham and Weil comparison for algebraic characters, together with the crystalline criterion on units. B. How does a local filtration put a matrix in the tangent space of the global image?

We have a representation ρ on a space of dimension D and want one of dimension m. Fix the place over ℓ and the embedding with the separated filtration jumps. Write k₁,…,kD for the full list of jumps, with repetitions. Among these we know m distinct values whose disjoint nonempty subsets have different means. The first task is to exhibit these numbers as eigenvalues of a single matrix subject to the equations of the global image.

Let C be the completion of an algebraic closure of ℚℓ. After choosing the local coefficient model and restricting to the Galois group of a finite extension containing its coefficients, the de Rham comparison gives a basis of C-columns P. Write χ for the cyclotomic character, which describes the action on roots of unity of ℓ-power order, and put θ = χ−1. If g(P) denotes the action on each entry of the basis matrix, the comparison reads

ρ(g) g(P) = P diag(θ(g)k₁, …, θ(g)kD).

The inverse in θ fixes the sign convention. The cyclotomic line itself has its de Rham jump at −1. The Tate–Sen theorem implies that if an element a of C satisfies g(a) = θ(g)da throughout the restricted Galois group for an integer d ≠ 0, then a = 0. A nonzero cyclotomic power still has infinite image on inertia after any finite extension. Brinon and Conrad, Theorem 2.2.7, Example 6.3.1 and Proposition 6.3.2[71].

Take a polynomial f in the matrix entries that vanishes on the global image. We will prove that it vanishes at P diag(tk₁,…,tkD) P−1 for every t ∈ C×. Call this matrix μ(t). Since its diagonal powers multiply coordinate by coordinate, μ(tu) = μ(t)μ(u). Such an algebraic map from the multiplicative group is called a cocharacter. The polynomial q(Y) = f(Y P−1) vanishes at every local matrix ρ(γ)P. Give a matrix entry in column j the weight kj. Multiplying the columns by tkj multiplies a monomial of total weight d by td.

Why does each part of q of a single weight vanish separately? Take all polynomial relations on the points ρ(γ)P, restricting to the finite list of monomials in q. Their coefficient lists form a vector space. Applying g to each coefficient of weight d and multiplying the result by θ(g)d preserves this space. Indeed, evaluating this transformed relation at ρ(γ)P gives g applied to the old relation at ρ(γg)P, by the displayed identity and the choice of a group fixing the matrix coefficients of ρ.

Choose a nonzero relation with minimal support inside the support of q. Normalize one coefficient of weight b to 1. Apply the operation and divide by θ(g)b. Subtracting the original relation cancels its normalized coefficient, so minimality forces the difference to vanish. Each other nonzero coefficient a of weight d thus satisfies g(a) = θ(g)b−da. Tate–Sen forces d = b. Subtract a multiple of this single-weight relation from q to eliminate one coefficient and repeat. This writes q as a sum of single-weight relations. Each vanishes at P by taking γ = 1, and therefore still vanishes after the columns of P are multiplied by their respective powers of t. This proves f(μ(t)) = 0.

The Zariski closure of the image is obtained by imposing all its polynomial relations. The calculation puts the whole curve μ in that closure. To find its tangent at the identity, substitute t = 1 + ε with ε² = 0. This substitution is legitimate because f(μ(t)) is a Laurent polynomial vanishing on the infinite set C×. For every integer k, (1 + ε)k = 1 + kε, using (1 + ε)−1 = 1 − ε for negative powers. Hence μ(1 + ε) = I + εX, where X = P diag(k₁,…,kD) P−1. For every relation f, its first derivative at I vanishes in the direction X. This is the defining condition for the tangent space, also called the Lie algebra of the image closure.

Can the tangent matrix be chosen over the coefficient field?

The preceding matrix has entries in the complete field C. The global representation and its defining equations have coefficients in K = ℚ̄ℓ, the algebraic closure before completion. To work with the global image algebra over K, we need a tangent matrix over K with m lacunary eigenvalues. Treat the D² entries of the matrix Y and the m proposed eigenvalues z₁,…,zm as unknowns. Each tangent equation is linear in the entries of Y with coefficients in K. The equations det(ziI−Y) = 0 are polynomial as well.

For each pair of disjoint nonempty index sets A, B, unequal means amount to requiring that the following polynomial be nonzero. There are finitely many pairs. Multiply all the corresponding polynomials to form L, taking the empty product as 1.

LA,B(z) = |B| ∑i∈A zi − |A| ∑j∈B zj.

Adjoin one further unknown u with equation uL = 1. The known matrix over C, its chosen eigenvalues, and u = 1/L satisfy all the equations, so the ideal they generate is proper. Take a maximal ideal containing it. By Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz, the residue field of this polynomial algebra at a maximal ideal is finite over K. Since K is algebraically closed, the residue field is K itself. The images of the unknowns solve all the equations in K. In particular L is invertible there. Singleton pairs show that the new eigenvalues are distinct, and the remaining factors preserve all the unequal means. From here on, write X and e₁,…,em for this choice. Why can the tangent matrix have only the prescribed eigenvalues?

For a matrix M, let vec(M) be the column of its entries in a fixed order. The assertion that some nonzero polynomial of degree at most m kills M says exactly that the following columns are dependent. A dependence relation supplies the coefficients of such a polynomial, and evaluating any annihilator gives the converse.

vec(I), vec(M), …, vec(Mm).

Dependence is equivalent to the vanishing of every minor of size m + 1 of this column matrix. Indeed, independent columns have full column rank, so row reduction selects m + 1 independent rows. Each minor is a fixed polynomial in the entries of M. At a dense set of Galois elements the given annihilator makes them all zero. The matrix entries vary continuously, so these same minors vanish everywhere on the image. In particular they belong to the polynomial relations defining its closure. This step allows the annihilator to vary with the Galois element.

We now show why the bound also holds for every tangent matrix Y. For a polynomial relation f define a new polynomial by taking the coefficient of s in f(M(I + sY)). At an image matrix M, the polynomial Z ↦ f(MZ) vanishes on the image because it is closed under multiplication. Tangency at I therefore kills that coefficient. Repeating this operation preserves the space of all relations. In the formal power series f(exp(sY)), the coefficient of sn is the value of the n-fold operation at I divided by n!. This follows by differentiating along the formal series, whose derivative is exp(sY)Y. Every coefficient vanishes. Characteristic zero permits the division and the argument requires only formal series.

Apply this to each minor. Over the Laurent series field, the columns for exp(sY) are dependent. Put Z(s) = (exp(sY) − I)/s. Substituting 1 + sT in an annihilator of exp(sY) gives one of the same degree for Z(s), since s is invertible in this field. All the corresponding minors vanish. But the entries of Z(s) are power series with constant term Y. Taking the constant term of each minor gives that minor at Y. Hence Y too admits an annihilator of degree at most m.

For our chosen X, an annihilator must vanish at its m distinct eigenvalues. Its monic minimal polynomial is therefore exactly ∏i(T−ei). Interpolating at those roots gives pi = ∏j≠i(X−ejI)/(ei−ej). At the roots its scalar polynomial takes value 1 at ei and 0 at the others. The identities ∑pi = I, pi² = pi and pipj = 0 for i ≠ j follow, since each difference of the corresponding polynomials vanishes at all the roots and hence is divisible by the minimal polynomial. These give m nonzero eigenspaces. Each can still have dimension greater than one.

Which parts of a tangent matrix can the weights distinguish?

Let K be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Write V for the space of ρ and 𝔤 for the tangent Lie algebra of the Zariski closure of its image. Suppose that every matrix in 𝔤 has minimal polynomial of degree at most m. Fix X ∈ 𝔤 with m distinct lacunary eigenvalues e₁, …, em. Its minimal polynomial must have exactly these simple roots. Write pi for the projection onto the ei-eigenspace along the others. This eigenspace can have dimension greater than one.

Proposition. For every Y ∈ 𝔤 the block piYpj belongs to 𝔤 whenever i ≠ j. Each diagonal block of Y acts by a scalar on its eigenspace.

To distinguish the off-diagonal blocks, take the commutator with X. In a block mapping eigenspace j to eigenspace i, multiplication by X on the left gives the output weight, and multiplication on the right gives the input weight. Thus

[X, piYpj] = (ei − ej) piYpj.

Each nonzero difference belongs to a unique ordered pair. Indeed, an equality ei − ej = ek − el says that the pairs (i, l) and (k, j) have the same mean. If the pairs share an index, cancellation and distinctness give the same ordered difference. Otherwise their supports are disjoint. A repeated entry in either pair has the mean of its singleton support. In every case disjointness would contradict lacunarity. For example, weights 0, 1, 4 produce the six distinct nonzero differences ±1, ±3 and ±4.

Why is the tangent space closed under this bracket? For a tangent Y let DY differentiate a polynomial at M along M(I + sY). As in the formal exponential argument, translation shows that each such derivation preserves the ideal of relations of the image. On a coordinate entry of M, the commutator of the two derivations for Y and Z takes the value of that entry in M(YZ − ZY). Derivations are determined by the coordinates, so this commutator is the derivation for YZ − ZY. It still preserves the ideal. Evaluating at the identity gives the tangent condition for the matrix bracket.

Let Δ be the set of all differences, including zero. For d = ei − ej ≠ 0 form the polynomial Ld(T) = ∏c∈Δ, c≠d (T−c)/(d−c). It takes value one at d and zero at every other difference. Decompose Y as the sum of all its blocks. Applying Ld to the operator [X, ·] selects precisely piYpj. This matrix belongs to 𝔤 because 𝔤 is a vector space closed under commutators.

Subtract these off-diagonal blocks from Y. The remaining block-diagonal matrix Z lies in 𝔤, as does X + tZ for every t ∈ K. On block i the latter has eigenvalues ei + tλ, where λ runs over the eigenvalues of Z on that block. Choose a nonzero t for which the spectra of different blocks are disjoint. Each pair of eigenvalues from different blocks excludes at most one value of t because their intercepts differ. The minimal polynomial of the direct sum is then the product of the block minimal polynomials. Indeed an annihilator must be divisible by each of these pairwise coprime polynomials. Each of the m nonzero blocks costs at least one degree, and the total degree is at most m. Every block therefore has a linear minimal polynomial. It follows that Z, hence the diagonal of Y, acts there by a scalar.

Why is each diagonal block of a product scalar?

Let A be the unital associative algebra generated by the tangent space 𝔤. It contains every spectral projector pi, since interpolation expresses that projector as a polynomial in X. A diagonal block of an element of A starts in one weight space and returns to it. Even the product of two off-diagonal maps can make such a return.

Proposition. For every a ∈ A, the block pi a pi is a scalar multiple of pi, and pi a pj lies in 𝔤 for i ≠ j.

The commutator calculation gives both properties for a tangent matrix. The identity has the same properties, and both are preserved by linear combinations. It remains to check multiplication. Write aik = pi a pk and bkj = pk b pj. Insert the identity between a and b to obtain

pi (ab) pj = ∑k aik bkj.

If k=i or k=j, one factor acts by a scalar on the intervening space. The product has the required property because the other factor does. Suppose now that k differs from both endpoints. If i ≠ j, the reverse product bkj aik vanishes by pj pi=0. Thus aik bkj equals the commutator of two tangent matrices and lies in 𝔤. If i=j, the two orders of multiplication act on different spaces. The commutator lies in 𝔤 and its compression to space i is exactly aik bki. The diagonal conclusion for a single tangent therefore makes this return a scalar on space i. Summing over k proves the proposition.

For example, take two copies of K². Let S carry the second copy identically to the first and vanish on the first. Let T do the reverse. Then ST is the projector on the first copy and TS the projector on the second. Their difference acts by +1 on the first copy and −1 on the second. Compressing the difference to the first copy recovers the product ST. The calculation works even though the space on which the scalar acts has dimension two.

What guarantees an inverse for a nonzero block?

The next step needs the following test. For each nonzero x ∈ A there is some b ∈ A for which bx is not nilpotent. This is a condition on the whole algebra. An individual off-diagonal block can have square zero.

First consider the relation of A to Γ. Conjugation by any ρ(g) preserves the closure of ρ(Γ), fixes the identity and carries its tangent space into itself. The inverse conjugation gives equality. Conjugation therefore preserves the algebra generated by the tangents. Also, if W is Γ-invariant, take v ∈ W and any linear functional λ vanishing on W. The linear equation λ(Mv) = 0 holds on the group image and on its closure. Its derivative gives λ(Yv) = 0 for every tangent Y. Such functionals cut out W, so Y preserves W, as does every element of A.

Let J be the radical of A, the ideal of elements acting as zero on every simple A-module. For a finite-dimensional algebra it is the largest nilpotent two-sided ideal. To see nilpotence, filter the left regular module A by submodules with simple successive quotients. Such a filtration is obtained by choosing a maximal proper submodule at each step, with dimension decreasing. Each factor from J lowers the filtration by one step. A product of as many factors as there are steps annihilates A, hence annihilates its identity. Conversely, a nilpotent ideal I acts by zero on a simple module S, since otherwise IS=S would give InS=S for every n. This also shows that every algebra automorphism preserves J. P. Etingof et al., Introduction to representation theory, Lemma 2.8 and Proposition 2.11.[121]

Write JV for the span of the vectors xv with x ∈ J and v ∈ V. Conjugation preserves J, so JV is Γ-invariant. Semisimplicity of ρ gives a Γ-invariant complement W. Every x ∈ J takes W into W by the preceding calculation and into JV by definition. Thus JW=0. It follows that

JV = J(JV + W) = J2V = ⋯ = JnV.

For sufficiently large n the last space is zero, so J acts by zero on V. Since A consists of actual endomorphisms of V, this gives J=0. Now take x ≠ 0 in A. Some simple module S contains a vector v with xv ≠ 0, by the definition of J. The submodule A(xv) equals S by simplicity, so some b ∈ A satisfies bxv=v. No positive power of bx can vanish in A. This is the required test.

When is a space of block maps one-dimensional?

Let B be any unital matrix algebra containing the projectors. Suppose its diagonal corners are scalar and each nonzero x admits b ∈ B such that bx is not nilpotent. We will apply the result twice, first to the tangent-generated algebra A and later to the algebra containing all group matrices.

Consider the space piBpj of block maps from Vj to Vi, where Vi = piV. Any nonzero member x has an inverse between these two spaces. To see this, choose b ∈ B with bx nonnilpotent, using the assumed test. Then xbx ≠ 0, since otherwise (bx)² = 0. Put z = pjbpi. Both xz and zx lie in diagonal blocks, so each is a scalar times its projector. Their scalars coincide and are nonzero because (xz)x = x(zx) = xbx ≠ 0. Divide z by that scalar to obtain the inverse y. For any other map w in the same block, wy is scalar on Vi and w = (wy)x. Thus a nonzero block space is one-dimensional, even when its maps act on large eigenspaces.

Group indices into classes by declaring i and j related when their block space is nonzero. Identity maps, inverse maps and compositions give reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity. In each class C choose a base index b and isomorphisms ui from Vb to Vi in their block spaces, taking the identity at b. Within the class set Eij = uiuj−1. These are matrix units, with EijEjk = Eik. Write each block of a ∈ B as cij(a)Eij when the indices belong to one class. Take the coefficient to be zero between classes. Inserting the identity ∑ pj between a and b gives

cik(ab) = ∑j cij(a) cjk(b).

Every matrix unit belongs to B. Within each class its entries can therefore be chosen independently by taking linear combinations of these units. Entries between classes vanish. Conversely, all the coefficients together determine the original endomorphism by summing its blocks. Thus the coefficient map identifies B with the product, over the classes, of the corresponding full matrix algebras.

How can one change all the weight projectors at once?

Let A be the algebra generated by the tangent matrices. Its weight projectors pi are nonzero, are pairwise orthogonal and sum to the identity. Let q1, …, qm be a second family in A with the same three properties. Suppose that each diagonal corner for either family is scalar. In the application qi = D−1piD, where D = ρ(g). These corners are scalar because conjugation by D preserves A. We seek a change of basis inside A itself. Scalar corners of products.

Proposition. There are an invertible v in A and a permutation π of the indices such that v pi = qπ(i)v for every i. The permutation can fix every i for which qiA pi contains a nonzero map.

We first describe the coordinates in which to compare the two families. The nilpotence test for A gives, for each nonzero x in A, some b in A for which bx is not nilpotent. Applied with scalar corners, the matrix-unit construction groups the indices into classes C according to whether piA pj is nonzero. Within each class this space has basis Eij, with Eii = pi and EijEjk = Eik. Products with unequal middle indices vanish. Sending these elements to the ordinary matrix units gives

A ≃ ∏C EndK(UC),   UC = KC.

Indeed, each a in A is the sum of its blocks, and any choice of coefficients of the Eij gives such an element. In this model pi projects onto a coordinate line of UC. Its image on the original space of ρ may have higher dimension.

Consider a single projector q from the second family. Write qC for its component on UC. The corner qAq acts there by all endomorphisms of the image of qC, independently in each class. Indeed, an endomorphism of this image extends by zero on the kernel of qC. Thus the dimension of qAq is the sum of the squares of the ranks of the qC. Since qAq = Kq has dimension one, exactly one component has rank one and all others vanish.

For a given class C, let JC be the labels of the qj supported there. Their image lines form a direct sum equal to UC, by orthogonality and completeness. Consequently |JC| = |C|. For i in C, a map in qjA pi can be nonzero precisely when j lies in JC. Within a single full matrix algebra we can send the coordinate vector of i to any nonzero vector on the image line of qj. Maps between distinct factors vanish.

Match the labels of C to those of JC by first fixing their intersection, then pairing the equally many remaining labels in any order. Combining the matchings gives π. In each UC, send the ith coordinate vector to a nonzero vector on the line of qπ(i). These images form a basis, so the maps define a unit v in the product algebra. Checking on this basis gives v pi = qπ(i)v. The fixed labels are exactly the intersections chosen above.

Which part of the change of basis moves the weight spaces?

Proposition. Every unit v of A has a factorization

v = ud,   d = ∑i dipi,   di ∈ K×,

where u is a product of transvections I + N. Here each N belongs to a single off-diagonal block piA pj. It squares to zero, so the inverse transvection is I − N.

In a class C the matrix of v is invertible. Reduce it to a diagonal matrix using row additions. If the next pivot entry vanishes, the remaining square submatrix is invertible, so a lower row has a nonzero entry in that column. Adding this row to the pivot row supplies a pivot and preserves the zeros in the earlier columns. Clear the entries below each pivot in turn, then use the pivots in reverse order to clear the entries above them. All diagonal entries are nonzero. Inverting the transvections gives u = T1−1⋯Ts−1. Since d commutes with all pi, the relation for v gives u pi = qπ(i)u. For qj = D−1pjD, this says that Du carries the image of pi onto the image of pπ(i).

What happens when a group element permutes the weight spaces?

In the rank-extraction argument, the Lie algebra gives m nonzero projectors pi on a space V over the algebraically closed coefficient field K of characteristic zero. They sum to the identity and have pairwise zero products. Their images Vi can have dimension greater than one. We seek a group element in each open part of Γ whose action on the extracted m-dimensional space has simple spectrum. Fix g ∈ Γ and a normal subgroup U of finite index. Let H be the Zariski closure of ρ(U) in the space of matrices, the common zero set of all polynomial equations satisfied by those matrices. We will construct an invertible u ∈ H such that x = ρ(g)u carries each Vi onto Vπ(i) for a permutation π. The diagonal operator with the lacunary weights ei on these spaces belongs to the tangent space to H at the identity. Both assertions concern the original D-dimensional representation.

Here is why passing to U preserves the tangent direction. Work first among invertible matrices, an open neighborhood of the identity. The closure of a subgroup there is a subgroup since inversion and multiplication by a fixed invertible matrix preserve polynomial zero sets in the general linear group. The closure of ρ(Γ) is the union of finitely many translates of the closure of ρ(U), one for each coset in Γ/U. The distinct translates are disjoint closed sets. Thus the translate containing the identity is also open in the full closure. The two closures agree near the identity and have the same tangent space there. In equations, for each other translate choose a polynomial vanishing on it and nonzero at the identity. Take their product Q, or 1 if there are no others. Regular denominators on the general linear group can be cleared by a power of the determinant. If f vanishes on ρ(U), then fQ vanishes on all of ρ(Γ). Differentiating in any tangent direction at the identity gives Q(I) df = 0 there, since f(I) = 0. This proves the required inclusion directly.

The correction u has to lie in H. The matching of the two projector systems in the algebra generated by the tangent matrices first gives an invertible v in that algebra such that ρ(g)v permutes the weight spaces. The factorization by row additions writes v = u∑idipi, with every di nonzero. The right factor rescales each weight space, so ρ(g)u gives the same permutation. The left factor is a product of elementary matrices I + N supported in off-diagonal blocks. The off-diagonal block calculation places these N in the tangent space, hence in the tangent space of H by finite index. Since N² = 0, the formal exponential is simply I + sN. Every relation of H therefore vanishes on the entire line by the formal exponential calculation. Taking s = 1 puts each elementary factor, and hence u, in H.

On a cycle O of π of length a, the return map xa preserves each weight space in that cycle. Rescale the ith space by a nonzero scalar τi and denote this diagonal operator by t. Then y = xt has return map ya = sOxa on the cycle, where sO = ∏i∈Oτi. Choose a nonzero eigenvector v of the return map of x in one of its weight spaces, with eigenvalue β. Invertibility gives β ≠ 0. For every root λ of λa = βsO, form

wλ = ∑0≤j<a λ−jyjv,   y wλ = λwλ.

Each summand lies in a different weight space. Projection onto the starting space gives v, so wλ is nonzero. Multiplication by y shifts all the terms and the return equation supplies the first term again. The a roots are distinct since βsO is nonzero and the field has characteristic zero. To count the roots across cycles too, consider a second cycle O′ of length b with return eigenvalue β′. A common λ would force sOb = (β′a/βb)sO′a. Run over all pairs of distinct cycles and all eigenvalues of their return maps. This gives finitely many equalities to avoid. Every eigenvalue on a cycle satisfies its return equation, by taking the corresponding power and projecting a nonzero component of an eigenvector onto a weight space. Avoiding the whole list separates the entire spectra of different cycles.

Can we avoid every collision while keeping t in H? Start with the formal scalars τi(s) = exp(eis). For any forbidden equality, its constant terms would first force β′a/βb = 1. Its linear terms would then force b∑Oei = a∑O′ei. This contradicts the unequal means of disjoint subsets. Meanwhile the formal diagonal exponential satisfies all equations of H. Indeed the invariant derivative in the given tangent direction preserves the ideal of polynomials vanishing on H, by translating the tangent direction to each group element of ρ(U). Repeated derivatives at the identity give all Taylor coefficients along the exponential, and all vanish. To obtain scalars in K, take the K-algebra generated by the formal scalars and the inverse of the product of the scalars and all the collision differences. It is a nonzero finitely generated algebra inside the fraction field of K[[s]]. A maximal ideal has residue field K by the weak Nullstellensatz. Reduction preserves all the equations of H and keeps the inverted factors nonzero. The resulting t belongs to H and the eigenvalues from the cycles are distinct. The closure H is closed under multiplication, by applying polynomial continuity in each factor successively to ρ(U). Thus M = ut lies in H and ρ(g)M has at least ∑O|O| = m distinct eigenvalues. The Stacks Project, Theorem 10.34.1[120].

One swap and one fixed line. Let x exchange the first two coordinate vectors and fix the third. Take t = diag(1,4,3). On the first cycle, (xt)² is 4 times the identity and the eigenvalues are 2 and −2. On the fixed line the eigenvalue is 3. Replacing the last entry of t by 2 produces a collision. This calculation illustrates just the cycle test, for which the nonzero diagonal entries are specified.

When does the tangent algebra contain a whole row of a group matrix?

Write A for the unital algebra generated by the tangent Lie algebra 𝔤, and let Vi be the image of the weight projector pi. For an operator G, its ith row means the map piG from the whole space V to Vi. The corner piaGpi first applies G to vectors in Vi, then a, then projects back onto that same space.

Proposition. Work over an algebraically closed field K of characteristic zero. Suppose each group matrix has minimal polynomial of degree at most m. Take the m nonzero orthogonal projectors of a tangent matrix with lacunary weights, with sum equal to the identity. Use the tangent-algebra properties proved in the matching of projectors and the separation of cycles. In particular, the projectors belong to A, its diagonal corners are scalar, it is normalized by the group, its off-diagonal corners lie in 𝔤, and each nonzero b in A admits a in A such that ab is nonnilpotent. Then for every G = ρ(g) and every i,

if  piaGpi ≠ 0  for some a ∈ A,   then  piG = piw  for some w ∈ A.

Put qj = G−1pjG. The matching of the two projector systems gives an invertible v in A and a permutation π satisfying vpj = qπ(j)v. This matching keeps the label i fixed whenever qiApi is nonzero. To apply this clause, take the a from the proposition and put b = G−1aG ∈ A. Then qibpi = G−1(piaGpi) ≠ 0. Consequently π(i) = i.

Factor v = ud into a product u of elementary matrices and an invertible diagonal scaling d of the weight spaces. Both factors belong to A. Since d commutes with the projectors, Gu induces π on the weight spaces. Apply the separation of cycles with the full group as the subgroup of finite index. It gives another invertible diagonal scaling t such that u and t lie in the image closure, and the operator y = Gut has disjoint spectra on different cycles. Here the separation applies to every eigenvalue on each cycle. The construction excludes collisions for all pairs of eigenvalues of the return maps. Since the closure is closed under multiplication, y lies there as well. The polynomial equations for the degree bound therefore give a nonzero polynomial P of degree at most m with P(y) = 0.

On each cycle of length k, the cyclic eigenvector construction gives k distinct eigenvalues, each with an eigenvector supported on that cycle. Their union Λ has size m because the cycles partition the labels and have disjoint spectra. Every λ ∈ Λ is a root of P, as one sees by applying P(y) to its eigenvector. Hence P is a nonzero constant times ∏λ∈Λ(T − λ). This counts roots of an annihilating polynomial even when the original space has dimension greater than m.

The fixed label i contributes a single eigenvalue c. On Vi, every y − λI with λ ∈ Λ other than c is invertible. A nonzero vector in its kernel would give the same eigenvalue on this fixed space and on another cycle. Cancel these invertible factors in P(y) = 0 on Vi. The remaining factor gives y = cI there. Since y commutes with pi at a fixed label, we have piy = cpi on all of V. Multiplying on the right by (ut)−1 now gives the promised row,

piG = piw,   w = c (ut)−1 ∈ A.

Indeed t−1 is the sum of the projectors weighted by the reciprocal scalars. The inverse of each elementary factor I + N of u is I − N because N² = 0. Thus the witness lies in the tangent-generated algebra itself. This supplies the row identity used in the passage to the span of the products aρ(g). The scalar-corner and nilpotence properties of A enter separately in the matching of the projectors.

Thus Gt has eigenvalues 2, −2 and 3, and its minimal polynomial is (T² − 4)(T − 3). For the projection p onto the plane, the choice a = I gives pGp = p. The formula gives w = 3t−1, whose row pw equals p. Replacing the action of Gt on the plane by a size-two Jordan block at 3 would preserve these three eigenvalues and raise the degree of the minimal polynomial to four. The bound of three rules out precisely that extra factor.

Why can we adjoin every group matrix and keep scalar corners?

So far the algebra A is generated by the tangent space. To obtain a representation of Γ from block coefficients, we need an algebra containing ρ(Γ). We use the row identity to enlarge A while retaining the two properties used to construct matrix units.

Take R to be the linear span of all products aρ(g). It contains the identity, A and ρ(Γ). It is closed under multiplication because ρ(g)bρ(g)−1 belongs to A for each b ∈ A. Each generator also preserves every Γ-invariant subspace. To compute its diagonal corner, write aρ(g) = ρ(g)b, with b = ρ(g)−1aρ(g) ∈ A. If the corner is nonzero, the row identity replaces piρ(g) by piw. The corner becomes piwb pi, a scalar multiple of pi by the product calculation. The zero corner is already scalar. Taking linear combinations proves the same assertion on R.

We also need to detect nonzero elements of R. Decompose V into irreducible Γ-subspaces using semisimplicity. If x ∈ R is nonzero, choose a summand W and v ∈ W with xv ≠ 0. Since R preserves W, the vector xv lies in W. Its Γ-translates span a nonzero invariant subspace of W, hence span W. In particular some linear combination b of group matrices sends xv to v. We have b ∈ R and bx fixes the nonzero vector v. No power of bx can be zero. This proves the nilpotence test used to construct the matrix units below.

How do the blocks give a representation of dimension m?

Proposition. The semisimple representation ρ contains an m-dimensional representation r and embeds in a finite direct sum of copies of r. Apply the block coefficient construction to the algebra R just obtained.

The identity has coefficient matrix Im. The displayed rule therefore makes r(g) = (cij(ρ(g))) a representation on Km, with inverse r(g−1). It is continuous for the ℓ-adic topology when ρ is continuous. For a nonzero block, choose an entry where Eij is nonzero. Dividing the corresponding entry of piρ(g)pj by that fixed entry expresses the coefficient as a continuous linear function of ρ(g).

Let rC denote the action on the coordinates of class C. Choosing a nonzero vector v ∈ Vb gives one copy of rC inside V. Its coordinate vectors are the independent vectors uiv in the distinct spaces Vi, and the formula for ρ(g) on them is exactly the coefficient matrix. Taking a whole basis of Vb gives a direct sum of dC = dim Vb such copies and spans all the corresponding eigenspaces. Thus

r = ⊕C rC,   ρ ≃ ⊕C rC⊕dC.

Every dC is positive. Taking one copy per class gives r ↪ ρ. With k the largest multiplicity, assign the copies of each class to the first dC of the k available slots to get ρ ↪ r⊕k. Since any subrepresentation of a semisimple representation is semisimple, the first injection also gives semisimplicity of r. Indeed, the intersection with r of an invariant complement in ρ to any subrepresentation of r is a complement in r.

For an example with unequal multiplicities, let Γ = GL₂(ℤ₅) × ℤ₅×. Its element (A, u) acts on a five-dimensional space by diag(A, A, u). The three-dimensional r is diag(A, u). The first injection sends (v, z) to (v, 0, z). The second sends (v, w, z) to ((v, z), (w, 0)). The two-dimensional action occurs twice in ρ and the character occurs once. At the elements A = diag(1, t), u = t⁴ for t ∈ ℤ₅×, these are the weights 0, 1, 4 seen above. In the geometric application the two injections transfer different local information.

Why must an actual Galois element in every open coset have simple spectrum?

The witness M from the cycle calculation satisfies the polynomial equations of ρ(U). To pass from that algebraic witness to elements of gU, use the structure of the extracted module W of dimension m. For every class C and every copy of rC in V, the projection from r onto that class followed by inclusion of the copy gives an equivariant map from W to V. The copies in the direct sum decomposition span V. The extracted representation also comes with an equivariant inclusion A into V, and a linear left inverse B. Let T range over the equivariant maps just described. Write r for the action on W, and define Φ(Z) = Bρ(g)ZA. For Z = ρ(u′) with u′ ∈ U, this gives Φ(Z) = r(gu′). Each intertwining relation ρ(g)ZT = TΦ(Z) therefore holds on ρ(U). It is a system of linear equations in the entries of Z, so it holds on H, in particular at M.

Let q be the characteristic polynomial of Φ(M). By Cayley–Hamilton, q(Φ(M)) = 0. Moving powers through each T gives q(ρ(g)M)T = 0. Since their images span V, q(ρ(g)M) = 0 on the entire space. Applying this identity to an eigenvector shows that each of the m distinct eigenvalues constructed above is a root of q. Its degree is m, so all its roots are simple. The Stacks Project, Lemma 10.16.1, Cayley–Hamilton[46].

Simple spectrum can be tested by a polynomial in the entries of a matrix L. For example, take the determinant of the m-by-m matrix with entries tr(Li+j), starting the indices at zero. If λ₁, …, λm are the eigenvalues with multiplicity, triangularizing L shows that this matrix equals VλtVλ, where row k of Vλ is (1,λk,…,λkm−1). Two equal roots give identical rows. With distinct roots the matrix Vλ is invertible, because a polynomial of degree less than m vanishing at all those roots is zero. Denote the determinant test by Δ. If every element in gU had repeated roots on W, the polynomial Δ(Φ(Z)) would vanish on ρ(U) and hence at M. This contradicts the simple spectrum just proved. Every open neighborhood in Γ contains a coset of the subgroup fixing some finite Galois extension. Such subgroups are normal of finite index, so the simple-spectrum locus is dense in the Krull topology. It is open as well, since the continuous function h ↦ Δ(r(h)) is nonzero there. The finite-extension neighborhoods in the Galois group.

6.11How do the two injections recover the exact data at a prescribed prime?

Consider first a prescribed spherical good prime w away from ℓ. Choose a geometric piece with the annihilation identity at this very prime. For every inverse Frobenius lift there the first injection gives a matrix of size m annihilated by the polynomial with roots R. Its multiset of eigenvalues has m entries, all from R, and its determinant gives the product of the entries. To recover all the multiplicities we use the genericity test imposed at the prescribed prime. For a list α₁, …, αm of its normalized Satake entries it gives

∑ ei = m,   ∏ αiei = ∏ αi   ⇒   e₁ = ⋯ = em = 1.

Indeed, each nonnegative ei is at most m, so there are finitely many exponent lists to test. The genericity polynomial on the unnormalized Satake entries contains a factor given by the difference of these two products for each list other than the all-ones list. A nonzero value excludes every such equality. The common Satake normalization multiplies both products by the same nonzero scalar to the power m. Apply the test to the multiplicities of the eigenvalues to obtain the prescribed characteristic polynomial. For roots {2,3,5}, the determinant 30 forces each prime factor to appear once. With roots {1,2,4}, both diag(1,2,4) and 2I have determinant 8 and are annihilated by (X−1)(X−2)(X−4). Their traces are 7 and 6. This is the collision that the genericity test removes.

Results in this passage. Generic products and a reverse injection recover the local data at a specified prime

Theorems used. Crystalline summands and filtered de Rham periods

At a prescribed spherical w over ℓ outside the two auxiliary real-subfield primes, take a piece that is crystalline there and whose jumps contain the desired m distinct integers. The first injection makes r crystalline at w. Indeed it is a direct summand of the globally semisimple ρ, and each summand of a crystalline representation is crystalline. For the jumps, use the second injection. The space of k copies of r is semisimple as a global representation, so the injection of ρ into it also splits. After restriction to the local group, taking filtered periods preserves these direct sums. Every jump occurring in ρ must therefore occur in r, since the k copies only repeat its jumps. At each inducing embedding the period space of r has dimension m. The m prescribed distinct jumps already use that entire dimension, so each occurs exactly once. Brinon and Conrad, Theorem 5.2.1 and §6.3 on filtered de Rham periods[71].

A further geometric piece can supply the Weil polynomial at the same w. For a Weil element of degree −1, the characteristic polynomial on this piece divides a power of the Satake polynomial. The inclusion of r implies the same divisibility for its Weil polynomial. Thus every root belongs to R. Compatibility of the Weil–Deligne construction with determinants gives the prescribed product, and the same genericity test fixes the multiplicities. Both Weil representations are unramified here, the first by crystallinity and the second by its spherical construction. Each factors through the integer degree map. The eigenvalues at an arbitrary degree are the corresponding powers of those at degree −1, giving equality of the characteristic polynomials at every Weil element.

The geometric input requires the two auxiliary primes to agree on the imaginary quadratic subfield K = ℚ(√(−d)). For the local comparison at w above ℓ choose each auxiliary prime, or its conjugate, to restrict to w|K. There are two primes of K above the split prime ℓ and complex conjugation exchanges them. This choice preserves the underlying primes of E⁺, sphericity, and the cuspidal local type (changing prime identifies the two local unitary groups and transports their compact subgroups). Duality preserves lacunarity of the weight. The preceding uniqueness argument places the comparisons from these choices on one representation attached to U′. The next step needs simultaneous congruences of the eigenvalues to approximate the original system using such representations.

6.12Which evaluations keep a Hecke error small?

At weight zero a Hecke operator is a finite sum of right translations. If all its coefficients have ℓ-adic absolute value at most one, the ultrametric inequality bounds the sum by its largest term. At higher weight, translating the point also changes the vector on which the form is evaluated. We construct a family of test vectors and compute how small each Hecke coefficient must be to compensate for this change.

Let G be the definite unitary group of rank a ≥ 1 attached to the CM field E, viewed over ℚ by restriction of scalars. Fix an identification of the algebraic closure of ℚℓ with ℂ, and use it to read all absolute values ℓ-adically, with |ℓ| = ℓ−1. Realize the weight representation ρ on a finite-dimensional space V of polynomials. Write ‖x‖ for the largest absolute value of a coefficient of x, taking ‖0‖ = 0, and let Λ consist of the polynomials in V with ‖x‖ ≤ 1. A form f(x, g) is linear in x ∈ V and evaluated at an adelic point g.

To transport Λ, record two matrices at each infinite place. The first, c∞(g), reads the archimedean component at the chosen complex embedding. For the second, κ(g), read the finite component at the place above ℓ induced by that embedding and the fixed field identification, then transport its entries back to ℂ. Both constructions respect multiplication. They agree on rational group elements, and κ takes the value 1 on the archimedean subgroup. Put

M(g) = c∞(g)−1κ(g),   eg,x(f) = f(ρ(M(g))x, g),   x ∈ Λ.

Integral evaluation theorem. These evaluations detect every nonzero algebraic form, and each form has a finite bound on all its evaluations. Let λτ,i be the weight entries over all complex embeddings τ of E, with the dual weight at the conjugate embedding. Put D = a ∑τ,i |λτ,i|, using ordinary absolute values of integers in this sum. Consider a Hecke operator with finite support on the finite adelic group and coefficient t(h) at a translation h. For each such h, choose d ≥ 0 so that ℓd clears the denominators of the entries of both h and h−1 at every place over ℓ. If |t(h)| ≤ ℓ−dD for every term, the operator preserves every common bound on the evaluations.

Proof. First we estimate the effect of a matrix on the weight. Suppose every entry of A and A−1 has norm at most B ≥ 1 in every archimedean matrix block, using the transported ℓ-adic norm. Substitution of linear forms into a monomial of degree m gives coefficients of norm at most Bm, by expanding the product. In the block of weight λ₁ ≥ ⋯ ≥ λa, the polynomial part has degree at most ∑i(λi − λa), the sum of its column degrees. The determinant twist contributes at most Ba|λa| by expanding the determinant of A or of its inverse. For each i, (λi − λa) + |λa| ≤ 2∑j|λj|. There is one polynomial block for each conjugate pair of embeddings. The conjugate weight reverses and negates the entries, so the pair contributes 2a∑j|λj| to D, enough for the polynomial degree and the determinant twist together. Adding over the blocks therefore gives ‖ρ(A)x‖ ≤ BD for x ∈ Λ.

For example, take rank two, one infinite place and weight (0, −1). The polynomial part has degree one. The determinant of a two-by-two matrix, or its inverse, costs at most two more powers of B. The two embeddings carry weights (0, −1) and (1, 0), so the uniform formula gives D = 4. Estimating the polynomial and the determinant separately gives B³, within the uniform allowance B⁴.

For detection, take a point g and vector v at which f(v, g) ≠ 0. Multiply ρ(M(g))−1v by a sufficiently high power ℓk to put all its polynomial coefficients in the unit ball. The corresponding evaluation is ℓkf(v, g), which is still nonzero.

For boundedness, take a compact open finite level C fixing f. Borel’s class-number theorem gives finitely many representatives s such that every g has the form γsuk, with γ rational, u archimedean and k ∈ C. Indeed, intersecting the standard finite level with C gives a subgroup of finite index in the standard level, so each standard class splits into finitely many classes. A. Borel, Some finiteness properties of adele groups over number fields, Theorem 5.1.[123]

Left invariance under γ, covariance under u, and invariance under k remove these three factors. In the specified order the matrices satisfy c∞(u)M(γsuk) = M(s)κ(k), which gives eg,x(f) = f(ρ(M(s))ρ(κ(k))x, s). The single exponent d clearing all k ∈ C exists because the denominator conditions form an increasing open cover of the compact group C. Thus ‖ρ(κ(k))x‖ ≤ ℓdD. At each representative s, the functional y ↦ f(ρ(M(s))y, s) is bounded in the coefficient norm. Indeed, coefficient functionals separate points of the finite-dimensional space V, so finitely many form a basis of its dual. Taking the largest bound over the representatives proves the assertion.

Finally take a translation h in the operator. Its archimedean component is the identity, so M(gh) = M(g)κ(h) with the product understood in each block. To evaluate at gh using the vector that was transported to g, apply the inverse change of coordinates and absorb the Hecke coefficient into the vector. This gives

yh = t(h)ρ(κ(h)−1)x,   ‖yh‖ ≤ ℓ−dDℓdD = 1.

By linearity in the test vector, eg,x(Tf) = ∑h egh,yh(f). Every summand is again one of our evaluations. The ultrametric inequality now preserves their common bound, even for a function that is assumed only linear in its weight argument. This allows the same estimate to be applied to every residual in the polynomial approximation.

For an operator supported away from ℓ we can take d = 0. At places over ℓ, any single finite sum can be made integral for this estimate by multiplying it by ℓk. Choose k large enough that ℓ−k|t(h)| ≤ ℓ−dD at each of its finitely many terms. The same multiplier scales its eigenvalue. This accounts for the factors attached separately to the auxiliary Hecke coordinates.

6.13Where do the forms satisfying the local tests come from?

Fix the algebraic weight W of the definite unitary group of rank a ≥ 1, a split auxiliary place w0 above ℓ, and a level K away from w0. The level stays fixed away from w0 throughout the approximation. At w0 we may replace a compact open subgroup by a smaller one. This variation gives the additional forms needed for the approximation.

At each place w of a finite set S, prescribe a nonzero polynomial Φw in the a Satake parameters. Each w is split, lies over a different prime of the real subfield from w0, and has hyperspecial local level. Call a representation admissible here if Φw is nonzero on every ordering of its spherical Satake parameters at every w in S. Write Mgood for the algebraic span of the K-fixed forms of weight W in these representations.

Density theorem at fixed weight and level away from one place. For every K-fixed form f of weight W and every δ > 0, there exist G ∈ Mgood and a scalar function e on the adelic group such that, for every weight vector v and group point g,

f(v, g) − G(v, g) = e(g)f(v, g),   |e(g)|ℓ ≤ δ.

The multiplier is the same for all v at a given g. In particular, every evaluation that vanishes for f also vanishes for G. We derive this statement from two estimates on a finite quotient at w0.

Counting the representations that fail a test. By smoothness choose a compact open subgroup J0 at w0 that fixes f, and a descending congruence tower inside it. The tower construction supplies normal subgroups Jn with finite ℓ-group quotients Hn = J0/Jn. At the full level obtained by adjoining Jn to K, let Bw,n be the span belonging to representations that fail the test at w. The one-place counting estimate asserts that for every η > 0 and every sufficiently large n, this space is finite dimensional with dim Bw,n ≤ η|Hn|. Take η = 1/(2(|S| + 1)) and choose a common depth for the finitely many places. Since each representation failing at least one test belongs to one of these spaces, their sum contains the whole failing span Bn. Hence 2 dim Bn ≤ |Hn|.

One correction. Write H = Hn. The tower provides a label L(g) in H for each adelic point. Right translation by j in J0 changes the label to L(g) times the class of j in H. Multiplying by a function of the label gives a linear map Ψ from functions on H to forms at the refined level,

Ψ(φ)(v, g) = φ(L(g))f(v, g).

Let P be the inverse image under Ψ of the admissible span at this refined level. The automorphic decomposition writes every form there as the sum of admissible and failing contributions. After quotienting by the admissible span, the image of Ψ therefore has dimension at most dim Bn. Its kernel in this quotient is P, so dim P ≥ |H| − dim Bn ≥ |H|/2. Moreover P is stable under right translations of H. Indeed, lift a translation to J0. It fixes f, normalizes the refined level and translates a form inside the same automorphic representation.

Finite-group approximation lemma. A right-translation-invariant subspace of functions on a finite ℓ-group H, of dimension at least |H|/2, contains a function φ satisfying |1 − φ(h)|ℓ ≤ ℓ−1/2 for every h ∈ H. The norm uses the fixed identification of the complex coefficients with the algebraic closure of ℚℓ. Apply this lemma to P. The form Ψ(φ) is admissible by the definition of P. Its error multiplier is 1 − φ(L(g)), so a single correction has a bound strictly smaller than one.

For a two-point example take ℓ = 2 and H = {1, σ}. The sign character spans a translation-invariant line, exactly half the dimension of all functions on H. Taking φ to be that character gives errors 0 at 1 and 2 at σ. The second error has 2-adic absolute value 1/2, smaller than the required 1/√2. Thus a line that contains only functions with values of opposite signs can nevertheless approximate the constant function 1 in this norm.

Iteration. Begin with G0 = 0 and e0 = 1. If the residual is f − Gm = emf, apply one correction to this residual, which still has weight W and level K away from w0. Write B for the resulting admissible form and b(g) for its error multiplier. Set Gm+1 = Gm + B. Then f − Gm+1 = b emf. After m corrections the multiplier has absolute value at most ℓ−m/2 at every point. A finite m achieves any prescribed δ.

By definition of the algebraic span, the resulting G is a finite sum of admissible forms. Group the terms belonging to the same automorphic representation and omit zero sums. When the selected Hecke operators act by scalars on the K-fixed vectors of each representation, each surviving term is a simultaneous eigenform for those operators. With |eg,x(f)|ℓ ≤ R in the integral frame and R ≥ 1, take δ = ε/R. The same list then has residual bounded by ε in every evaluation, as required for the polynomial argument. Simultaneous approximation for all integral polynomials.

The proof uses two different norms. On the tower of auxiliary levels, its separation property allows the complex norm of the test operator to bound the dimension of the failing forms. The resulting dimension inequality is the input to a finite-group estimate in the ℓ-adic norm. That estimate produces the multiplier in the relative error above.

How can each adelic point carry an equivariant label?

The correction at fixed weight multiplies a form by a function on a finite group. To evaluate that function at an adelic point, we need a label that respects rational equivalence and follows right translation at the auxiliary place. The starting level matters because a point can have a stabilizer under this translation.

Let G be the definite unitary group of rank a ≥ 1 attached to a CM field E, viewed over ℚ, and let Γ = G(ℚ). Fix a split place w₀ over ℓ. Its local group identifies with GLa(Ew₀). Fix a compact open level K away from this place, embedded with trivial auxiliary component, and a K-fixed algebraic form f. Smoothness gives an identity neighbourhood N in the local group whose elements fix f. Write 𝒪 for the integers of the local field. Choose s ≥ 2 large enough that the matrices congruent to the identity modulo ℓs lie in N. For n ≥ 0 take Jn to be the congruence subgroup of GLa(𝒪) modulo ℓs+n. These compact open subgroups are normal in J₀ and shrink to the identity through a neighbourhood basis.

Two properties of this choice will be used. First, J₀ is torsion-free. If it contained a nonidentity element of finite order it would contain one of prime order p. Write this element as I + X and take the largest ℓ-adic absolute value of an entry as ‖X‖. Then 0 < ‖X‖ ≤ |ℓ|². In the expansion of (I + X)p − I, the linear term has norm |p| ‖X‖. All higher terms have norm at most ‖X‖², which is strictly smaller since |p| ≥ |ℓ|. The sum cannot vanish. Second, the ℓth power sends Jn into Jn+1. The linear term gains a factor ℓ, and every term of degree at least two is already divisible by ℓs+n+1. Thus every element of Hn = J₀/Jn has order dividing ℓn. This quotient is finite because its open cosets cover the compact group J₀. It is an ℓ-group by Cauchy’s theorem, which says that each prime dividing the order of a finite group occurs as the order of an element. To see the latter assertion for a group of order h and a prime p dividing h, cyclically permute the hp−1 ordered p-tuples whose product is 1. Orbits have size p except for the constant tuples (x, …, x) with xp = 1. Their number is divisible by p and includes the identity tuple, so some such x has order p.

Equivariant label theorem. Write Cn = K Jn, using the split local factor inside the finite adelic group. Projection to the auxiliary component followed by reduction gives a surjection λn from C₀ to Hn with kernel Cn. For every n there is a locally constant label Ln on G(𝔸) such that, for all γ ∈ Γ, g ∈ G(𝔸), u ∈ G(ℝ) and c ∈ C₀,

Ln(γguc) = Ln(g) λn(c).

Proof. Choose one representative b per double class modulo Γ on the left and G(ℝ)C₀ on the right. Assign b the label 1 and set Ln(γbuc) = λn(c). If two decompositions give the same point, then b−1γ₂−1γ₁b belongs to G(ℝ)C₀ and has finite component c₂c₁−1. The intersection of Γ with the conjugate of G(ℝ)C₀ is finite. Indeed, this product is compact by definiteness and the compactness of C₀, and rational matrices form a closed discrete subgroup of the adelic matrices. Our element therefore has finite order. Its auxiliary component lies in the torsion-free group J₀, so λn(c₂c₁−1) = 1. The two labels agree. This verifies precisely the stabilizer condition. Every element fixing a class must act trivially on its label. Multiplication on the right now gives the displayed formula. A label is constant on each open set gG(ℝ)Cn. In particular, multiplying f by any function of the label gives a form at the refined level and preserves its archimedean weight.

For example, inside ℚ₂× start with J₀ = 1 + 4ℤ₂ and J₁ = 1 + 8ℤ₂. The two labels are the residue classes 1 and 5 modulo 8. Right multiplication by 5 exchanges them, since 5² ≡ 1 modulo 8. Although this quotient has an element of order two, the element 5 in the starting group has infinite order. Starting instead at 1 + 2ℤ₂ would admit the torsion element −1, so killing the images of rational stabilizers would require a separate check.

When do different Hecke translates give different points?

The finite quotient also counts the points needed to evaluate a form. Choose a finite set S of representatives at level C₀, using the class-number theorem. For each q ∈ Hn choose an auxiliary lift jq ∈ J₀. At every depth the points bjq, with b ∈ S, cover the double classes of level Cn. Indeed, in a decomposition at level C₀, the auxiliary component differs from its lift by an element of Jn. Move the factors supported away from the auxiliary place and the archimedean component past the lift. The remaining factors belong to G(ℝ)Cn. This gives a cover by at most |S| |Hn| points.

Separation at large depth. Let T be a fixed finite set of finite adelic translations trivial at the auxiliary place, such that the cosets tK are pairwise distinct. For all sufficiently large n, for each b ∈ S and every auxiliary lift j ∈ J₀, distinct t, t′ ∈ T give distinct double classes starting from bj. In the notation [·]n for these classes,

[bjt]n = [bjt′]n   ⟹   t = t′.

Proof. A collision gives bjt′ = γbjtuc for some γ ∈ Γ, u ∈ G(ℝ) and c ∈ Cn. All possible γ lie in one compact set because S and T are finite, j lies in the compact group J₀, and c lies in the fixed compact group C₀. Thus only finitely many γ can occur at any depth. At the auxiliary place, the component of b−1γb equals j cw₀−1j−1, which lies in Jn by normality. For γ ≠ 1 this local component differs from 1 because the field embedding into its completion is injective. The tower eventually excludes all these finitely many nonidentity components, uniformly in b, j and the translations. Then γ = 1, and cancellation gives t′ = tuc. Comparing archimedean components gives u = 1. Comparing auxiliary components puts c in K. Hence tK = t′K, which forces t = t′. The threshold may depend on S and T. This is the separation used in counting the representations that fail a local test.

How can a polynomial equal one on all the bad parameters and have small mean square?

At a split place of rank a a spherical system has an unordered list of a nonzero complex Satake parameters. A given nonzero polynomial Φ can depend on their order. The local test fails if some ordering makes Φ vanish. The operator used in the counting proof must then act as the identity. Its coefficient bound will come from an integral over the unit torus 𝕋a, with each circle carrying its uniform probability measure.

Polynomial estimate. Given any δ > 0, there is a symmetric Laurent polynomial p with p(z)=1 at every failed list z ∈ (ℂ×)a and ∫𝕋a |p(z)|² dz ≤ δ. A Laurent polynomial allows both positive and negative integer powers. Symmetry makes its value independent of how the parameters are ordered.

Form the product P of Φ over all permutations of its variables. Permuting the coordinates permutes the factors. Each factor is a nonzero polynomial, so their product is nonzero. A tuple fails the test precisely when P vanishes there. If P = ∑ν cνzν, let P∗ be the Laurent polynomial with conjugate coefficients and opposite exponents. On the unit torus each inverse coordinate is its complex conjugate, so there P∗(z) is the complex conjugate of P(z). Let M be the maximum of |P| on the compact torus and set c = 1/(1 + M²). For positive integers k put

pk(z) = (1 − cP(z)P∗(z))k.

Both factors of the product PP∗ are symmetric. At every zero of P the displayed value is exactly one for every k, including zeros away from the unit torus. On the torus the quantity being raised to the kth power is the real number 1 − c|P(z)|². It lies between zero and one, and it is strictly less than one wherever P(z) ≠ 0.

Why do the exceptional points have measure zero? In one variable a nonzero polynomial has only finitely many zeros. In several variables expand in the last variable and select a coefficient that is a nonzero polynomial in the others. By induction it vanishes on a set of measure zero. Outside this set, the one-variable slice again has only finitely many zeros. Integrating the indicator of the full zero set one coordinate at a time therefore gives zero. Now |pk|² tends to zero almost everywhere and is bounded by one on a probability space. Dominated convergence makes its integral tend to zero. Choose k large enough to reach δ. S. Axler, Measure, Integration & Real Analysis, Theorems 5.28 and 3.31.[124]

For example take one parameter and Φ(z) = z − 2. Its zero lies off the circle. Here M = 3, and the first power is p1(z) = (5 + 2z + 2z−1)/10. Direct substitution gives p1(2) = 1. On the circle the mean square is (25 + 4 + 4)/100 = 33/100, since all nonconstant integer powers of z integrate to zero. Higher powers keep the value at 2 and drive the mean square to zero. The local Plancherel formula turns that mean square into an estimate for the coefficients of the operator.

Which local operator fixes the forms that fail the test?

Fix a tested split place w, write F = Ew, and let q be its residue-field cardinality. In the split unitary factor we may work with G = GLa(F) and Kw = GLa(𝒪F). Fix a nonzero polynomial Φ in the a Satake coordinates. A representation fails the test if some ordering z of its local Satake parameters satisfies Φ(z) = 0. To bound the dimension of its contribution, we need an operator that acts by one on such a representation and whose complex coefficients have a small sum of squares.

Local operator theorem. For every δ > 0 there is a finite sum of translations at w, with coefficients h(t), satisfying ∑t |h(t)|² ≤ δ. Its supporting elements give distinct cosets tKw. The operator acts as the identity on the Kw-fixed vectors in every smooth irreducible representation with a Satake tuple on the zero set of Φ.

Choose a symmetric Laurent polynomial p equal to one on that zero set and small in mean square on the unit torus. The condition on the zero set concerns all tuples in (ℂ×)a. Only the norm is computed on the unit torus. The following argument determines how small this norm must be. Construction of the polynomial.

From double classes to individual translations. Let μ be a Haar measure on G and put m = μ(Kw) > 0. By the Satake isomorphism there is a compactly supported, bi-Kw-invariant function H whose spherical transform, computed with μ, is p. In this normalization the integrated operator acts by p(z) on the fixed vectors with parameter z. Choose one representative t of each coset tKw in the support. This set T is finite by compactness of the support and openness of Kw. For any fixed vector v in a representation σ, integration on the cosets gives

∫G H(x)σ(x)v dμ(x) = ∑t∈T h(t)σ(t)v,   h(t) = mH(t).

A double class KwxKw contributes one term for every coset it contains. Their number is the index of Kw ∩ xKwx−1 in Kw, since the cosets are kxKw for k ∈ Kw. For GL₂, take x = diag(ϖ, 1) with ϖ a uniformizer. The lattices kx𝒪F² between ϖ𝒪F² and 𝒪F² reduce to the lines in the two-dimensional residue space. Each line occurs and determines its coset, so this double class has (q² − 1)/(q − 1) = q + 1 terms. The factor m in each coefficient is its coset volume. I. Satake, Theory of spherical functions on reductive algebraic groups over p-adic fields, Theorem 3[125].

The measure in the mean square. Give the torus (S¹)a its product Haar probability measure dz. Put s = q−1 and Va(s) = ∏j=1a[(1 − sj)/(1 − s)]. The spherical Plancherel measure on the ordered parameters is represented by the symmetric density

D(z) = (Va(s)/a!) ∏i<j |(1 − zi/zj)/(1 − s zi/zj)|².

Macdonald’s spherical inversion formula gives ∫ φz(y)D(z) dz = 1Kw(y), where φz is the spherical function normalized by φz(1) = 1. In particular D(z) dz has mass one. Since s < 1, the denominators stay nonzero on the torus, and its compactness gives a finite bound C on D. I. G. Macdonald, Spherical Functions on a Group of p-adic Type, Chapter V, §5.1[126].

To extract a single coefficient, use the eigenfunction identity ∑t∈T h(t)φz(yt) = p(z)φz(y). Set y = u−1 for one representative u ∈ T and integrate against D(z) dz. Spherical inversion keeps exactly the term with u−1t ∈ Kw, which is t = u. Thus h(u) = ∫ p(z)φz(u−1)D(z) dz. Multiply by the complex conjugate of h(u) and sum over u. On the unit torus φz(u−1) is the conjugate of φz(u) almost everywhere. The eigenfunction identity at y = 1 then gives

∑u∈T |h(u)|² = ∫ |p(z)|² D(z) dz ≤ C ∫ |p(z)|² dz.

This equality includes all the coset multiplicities and uses the coefficients mH(t). For example, the constant polynomial one has kernel 1Kw/m. Its unique coefficient is one for every normalization of μ. Choosing the polynomial at tolerance δ/(1 + C) proves the coefficient bound, while p(z) = 1 supplies the identity action, including for a failed Satake tuple outside the unit torus.

Transport to the global level. Splitness identifies G with the adelic unitary subgroup supported over the prime of the real subfield below w. The component at w determines the element of this subgroup, including its component at the conjugate place. Lift each representative through this identification and keep its coefficient. The lift is injective, so the squared coefficient sum is preserved. On this subgroup the global level K cuts out Kw, hence the lifted support still consists of distinct cosets modulo K on the right. Its components above the prime of the real subfield below the auxiliary place w0 are trivial because the two underlying primes differ.

To transfer the scalar as well, one needs a local realization. A failed test supplies a smooth irreducible local representation σ occurring in the global representation and an ordering z of its Satake parameters with Φ(z) = 0. The images of the local intertwining maps from σ span the irreducible global representation. Indeed their span is nonzero by occurrence, is stable under the local factor, and is preserved by the other adelic factor, which commutes with it. For a globally K-fixed vector, express it as a finite sum of such images and average over Kw. Smoothness makes this a finite coset average. It fixes the original vector and replaces each local preimage by a fixed vector. The local operator acts by p(z) on each such vector and commutes with every intertwining map. This proves the required identity action on the entire failing span used in the tower count. Counting the forms that fail the test.

How many forms can fail one Satake test?

Let w be the split place where a nonzero polynomial Φ tests the Satake parameters. The level is hyperspecial there. At a second split place w0 above ℓ, refine the level along compact open subgroups Jn normal in J0, decreasing to the identity and eventually contained in every neighborhood of it. The places w and w0 lie over distinct primes of the maximal real subfield. This allows the test at w to be used at every depth at w0, including when both places divide ℓ.

Write K for the level away from w0, Cn for the full level obtained by adjoining Jn, and Hn = J0/Jn. Let Bw,n be the span of the Cn-fixed forms of weight W in the representations that fail the test at w. The count measures the dimension of this space, including the multiplicities of the contributing forms.

One-place counting theorem. For every ε > 0, at all sufficiently large depths n the space Bw,n is finite dimensional and

dimℂ Bw,n ≤ ε |Hn|.

The local input supplies, for every δ > 0, a Hecke operator with complex coefficients h(t) and finite support T such that ∑t∈T |h(t)|² ≤ δ. Its translations act at the tested prime, have trivial components above the prime under w0, and give distinct cosets tK under right multiplication by K. The operator acts as the identity on the K-fixed vectors of every representation that fails the test. Since K is contained in Cn, the operator therefore fixes Bw,n pointwise. All squared norms in this count use the ordinary complex absolute value. The local operator and its normalization.

Cover and separation. A finite set S0 of representatives suffices at depth zero. At depth n the cover has index set Xn = S0 × Hn. Its label y represents an adelic point py up to the actions of the rational group, the archimedean group and the level Cn. Distinct labels may represent the same double class. What the counting argument requires is that for any one starting point py, the translated points pyt for t ∈ T belong to distinct double classes. For the chosen finite support this holds at all sufficiently large depths, uniformly in the starting label. Covering the tower and separating the translates.

The matrix on evaluations. Choose a basis of the weight space of dimension d and evaluate each form at the d basis vectors and all py. These coordinates determine the form. Indeed, for an arbitrary adelic argument the covering expression removes the rational and level factors, while its archimedean factor acts linearly on the weight vector. For each translated point pyt, choose a covering label π(y,t) and write mij(y,t) for the corresponding weight change, so that its ith evaluation is the sum of the jth evaluations at that label with coefficients mij. All these coefficients have absolute value at most a constant L depending only on the weight and basis. The archimedean group is compact and its weight-matrix entries are continuous.

The matrix M computing the translated evaluations of the Hecke sum has entries

M(y,i),(z,j) = ∑t∈T, π(y,t)=z h(t) mij(y,t).

At sufficiently large depth each sum in an entry has at most one term, by separation at the starting label y. Summing squared absolute values first over the target labels, then over the two basis indices and the starting labels, yields the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm

‖M‖HS2 = ∑y,i,z,j |M(y,i),(z,j)|² ≤ |Xn| d²L² ∑t∈T |h(t)|².

The image of Bw,n under evaluation is fixed pointwise by M. Take an orthonormal basis of this image and extend it to the full coordinate space. The sum of ‖Mv‖² on an orthonormal basis is tr(M∗M), independent of the basis and equal to ‖M‖HS2. Each fixed basis vector contributes one. The injectivity of evaluation therefore bounds dim Bw,n by this same squared norm.

Now choose δ = ε/(1 + |S0|d²L²), select the local operator at this precision, and only then choose a depth separating its finite support. Using |Xn| = |S0| |Hn| gives the asserted estimate at every later depth. For a numerical model of the dimension bound, average the N shifts of a cyclic group with coefficient 1/N each and take the scalar weight. In every row the shifts occupy different columns, the squared norm is N·N·(1/N)² = 1, and the fixed space consists of the constants.
