What does the rank of convolution say about the sum of its coefficients?

Let H be a group of order N equal to a power of the prime ℓ. A function a on H prescribes the coefficients of a sum of translations. On a constant function this operator acts by the single number S = ∑u∈H a(u). The rank of the operator bounds the ℓ-adic size of S.

Group determinant bound. Take coefficients in a field k with an ultrametric absolute value, so |x+y| ≤ max(|x|, |y|). Suppose |a(u)| ≤ 1 for every u. Form the matrix M with rows and columns indexed by H, and let r be its rank. Then

Mh,g=a(hg−1),   |S|N ≤ |ℓ|N−r.

For each u let Lu carry the basis vector at g to the one at ug. The only translation carrying g to h has u=hg−1, so M is the sum of a(u)Lu. We first change coordinates for the integer matrices Lu modulo ℓ. In any nonzero quotient by an invariant subspace of the permutation representation over 𝔽ℓ, count the vectors in H-orbits. Each orbit has size a power of ℓ by the orbit–stabilizer formula. The number of fixed vectors is therefore congruent modulo ℓ to the total number of vectors, itself a positive power of ℓ. Since zero is fixed, there must also be a nonzero fixed vector. Its line is invariant. Continuing on successive quotients and lifting the fixed vectors gives a basis in which every Lu is upper triangular with ones on the diagonal. K. Conrad, Group actions, Theorem 4.1.[127]

Lift this basis matrix and its inverse separately to integer matrices P and Q. The entries of QLuP below the diagonal are multiples of ℓ, and its diagonal entries are 1 modulo ℓ. Put A=QMP over k. There is a matrix B with entries of absolute value at most one such that A + ℓB is upper triangular with every diagonal entry equal to S. Indeed, on and below the diagonal each translated matrix differs from the identity by integer multiples of ℓ. Subtract these multiples there before summing with weights a(u). Every integer has absolute value at most one, so the ultrametric inequality bounds all entries of the correction B and of A. The rank of A is at most r by composition.

Expand the determinant of A + ℓB by multilinearity in the rows. A term choosing fewer than N−r rows from ℓB uses more than r rows of A and vanishes by linear dependence. In each surviving term one can factor out at least N−r copies of ℓ. The determinant left after extracting all chosen factors has absolute value at most one by the permutation formula. Since |ℓ| ≤ 1, the entire sum has absolute value at most |ℓ|N−r. The determinant is SN by triangularity.

How do bounds on linear tests produce one approximating function?

On the functions kX on a finite set X, measure distance by the largest absolute difference of the values. A linear test with coefficients ai evaluates v by ∑ aivi. Call it integral when every |ai| ≤ 1. A test of this kind that vanishes on a subspace P distinguishes a vector from that subspace by at most their distance. The converse gives an approximant at the specified radius.

Finite separation lemma. Suppose every integral test annihilating P evaluates on v to a number of absolute value at most R, where R ≥ 0. Then some c ∈ P satisfies |vi−ci| ≤ R at every coordinate.

Let d be the dimension of P. When d = 0, take each coordinate as a test and choose c = 0. Otherwise write a basis of P as the columns of a matrix. Select d rows indexed by I for which the determinant has largest absolute value. That determinant is nonzero because the columns are independent. Every other row j is a linear combination of the selected rows, with coefficients bji. Replace row i of the selected determinant by row j and expand in that row. All terms except the one with coefficient bji have a repeated row. The new determinant divided by the selected determinant is therefore bji, so |bji| ≤ 1.

The invertible selected matrix gives a unique c ∈ P with ci=vi for every i ∈ I. For a remaining coordinate j, the test

x ↦ xj − ∑i∈I bjixi

is integral and vanishes on P by the row relation. Its value on v is exactly vj−cj because c matches v on I. The hypothesis bounds every remaining coordinate for this same c. This finite construction works over the algebraic closure of ℚℓ.

Why does half the space suffice to approximate the constant function?

Finite-group approximation theorem. Let H be a finite ℓ-group, N its order and P a subspace of the functions on H over the algebraic closure of ℚℓ. Assume that P contains the right translate h ↦ c(hg) of each of its functions c for every g ∈ H. If its dimension d satisfies 2d ≥ N, there is a function φ ∈ P with

maxh∈H |1 − φ(h)|ℓ ≤ ℓ−1/2.

Take any integral test a that annihilates P. Its value on the constant function is S = ∑ a(h). For Mh,g=a(hg−1) the coordinate at g of Mtc is ∑h a(hg−1)c(h) = ∑i a(i)c(ig). This is zero because the translated function belongs to P. Thus P lies in the kernel of the transpose and rank M ≤ N−d. Since |ℓ| = 1/ℓ, the group determinant bound gives |S|N ≤ |ℓ|d. Taking the Nth root gives |S| ≤ |ℓ|d/N ≤ ℓ−1/2, including the case d=N/2.

Apply the finite separation lemma to v = 1 and R = ℓ−1/2. It gives one φ meeting the bound at every group element. The automorphic forms have complex coefficients with a fixed field identification between ℂ and the algebraic closure of ℚℓ. Transport the subspace and its basis along this identification. Right translation only permutes coordinates, so both the dimension and the translation hypothesis are preserved. Transferring φ back gives the multiplier in the Hecke correction.

6.14How can one approximation work for every Hecke polynomial?

The Galois construction compares sums and products of Hecke eigenvalues. A finite weighted list of auxiliary systems must work for every polynomial at once. Fix the algebraic weight and the level away from the auxiliary split place above ℓ. At that place the approximants can have deeper level. Write θ for the joint eigenvalues of our form and ηi for those of auxiliary eigenforms. In this passage scalars are read through the fixed identification with the algebraic closure of ℚℓ, and |·| means the ℓ-adic absolute value.

Use the integral family of linear evaluations ex of forms, indexed by a group point and a weight-space test vector. Three properties of this family enter. A nonzero form has a nonzero evaluation, every form in the fixed space has bounded evaluations, and each chosen integral Hecke operator Tj preserves any common bound on the evaluations of a vector. The local denominator bound on each term gives the last property. Normalize the target eigenform f so that e0(f) = 1 at one detecting coordinate. Let R ≥ 1 bound all its evaluations. The density theorem away from the auxiliary place approximates f by a finite sum ∑ifi of allowed eigenforms, with pointwise error given by evaluations of f times a factor bounded by ε/R. Thus the residual has every evaluation bounded by ε.

For any polynomial P with integer coefficients put u(P) = P(θ)f − ∑iP(ηi)fi. For a constant integer this is a multiple of the residual by a scalar of absolute value at most one. Addition preserves the bound ε by the ultrametric inequality. Multiplication by a variable Xj replaces u(P) by Tju(P) because every vector in the sum is an eigenvector for that operator. These three operations construct every integral polynomial. Evaluating at the same coordinate e0 gives

|P(θ) − ∑η cη P(η)| ≤ ε,   cη = ∑i : ηi=η e0(fi).

The finite support and all the coefficients have been chosen before P. The coordinate index set may be infinite because each polynomial uses only finitely many variables. If two forms have the same system, they contribute to the same coefficient. We write θ ∈ 𝒜(S) when for each ε > 0 such a finite weighted list exists in the set S of systems.

6.15How can one remove systems that fail a local test?

Suppose η ∈ 𝒜(T), and let Q be an integral polynomial that is nonzero at η. We want to retain only points x ∈ T with Q(x) ≠ 0. Start with an approximation to η at the finer tolerance ε|Q(η)|. Apply it to PQ and divide by Q(η). The terms with Q(x) = 0 drop out. Each surviving coefficient changes in the same way for every test polynomial:

c′x = cx Q(x)/Q(η),   |P(η) − ∑x c′x P(x)| ≤ ε.

For a finite calculation in ℚ₅ approximate evaluation at 5 by the average of evaluations at 0 and 10. This rule is exact on constants and linear polynomials. On every higher power both the target value and the average are divisible by 25 in ℤ₅. It therefore gives error at most 1/25 on every integral polynomial. Take Q(X) = X. The point 0 disappears and the new coefficient at 10 is (1/2)·10/5 = 1. For P = X the error is now |5−10|₅ = 1/5. It is obtained from the old error on X², namely |25−50|₅ = 1/25, by division by |5|₅. This one finite rule illustrates exactly the precision lost in filtering.

There are two approximation stages in the arithmetic argument. Suppose θ ∈ 𝒜(S) and, for each η ∈ S, η ∈ 𝒜(T) with Q(η) ≠ 0. Choose an outer list at tolerance ε/2 with coefficients aη, and put M = ∑|aη|. For every η on this finite list choose a filtered inner rule with error δ = ε/[2(1+M)]. Sum the rules, giving a shared point x the sum of all products aηc′η,x that reach it. Adding and subtracting the evaluations at η gives

|P(θ) − ∑x c″x P(x)| ≤ ε/2 + Mδ ≤ ε.

The nonvanishing condition holds at the intermediate points where we divide. The outer target θ can lie on the zero set of Q. After filtering we may also forget coordinates. Lift each polynomial in the remaining variables to a polynomial in the original variables, and add the coefficients of all points that project to the same remaining system. The estimate is identical.

6.16Which local conditions survive the approximation?

Keep two split auxiliary places u,v over distinct primes of the real subfield above ℓ. Fix finite sets Z,W of eligible spherical places away from those auxiliary primes, where Z prescribes genericity tests. The power-sum places in W are above ℓ. Both sets consist of split places spherical for the target. In the odd-rank application we test genericity on Z ∪ W. In addition to the original Hecke coordinates indexed by J, introduce one coordinate for every pair (w,n) ∈ W × ℤ, and one detector coordinate for each place z in the finite test set:

θj,   aw,n · power sum at (w,n),   bz · detector at z.

The power-sum operator has the indicated Satake eigenvalue. A spherical Hecke operator at z detects nonvanishing of the chosen genericity polynomial on the Satake parameters. Each nonzero multiplier aw,n or bz puts the corresponding operator within the integral bounds required by the frame. The power-sum multipliers are fixed with Z,W before the family of original Hecke operators is chosen. They may depend on the place and the exponent. The product Q of the detector variables is an integral polynomial because the test set is finite. As each multiplier is nonzero, Q detects simultaneous success at every tested place.

First apply fixed-weight density with generic local systems and the eigenform argument to approximate the extended system by intermediate ones on which Q is nonzero. For each of these, the weight variation at v and the character construction at u provide a second approximation, with the required lacunary weight and auxiliary local type. These operators are supported away from both places, so the same extended eigenvalue coordinates can be tested in this second step. Apply the filtering and composition formula to preserve the first condition while imposing the second. Finally forget the detector coordinates. Each retained system still has a representative that passes every local test, and weighted evaluations approximate all integral polynomials in the original Hecke variables and the scaled powers. On weights outside the specified auxiliary primes the construction keeps the original weights. This supplies the simultaneous approximation used in the trace limit, under the automorphic family hypotheses and the local cuspidality criterion stated below.

Write w0 for the auxiliary place where we will impose a local type, and v for the place where we change the weight. |P(θ) − ∑b cbP(θb)|ℓ ≤ ε   for every integral polynomial P.

The difference is bounded by ε in every frame coordinate. For fixed matrix arguments the functions in the family are K-fixed.

How the local pieces recover the original form. Let C be the compact open level used to construct the family. Write c(g) ∈ C for an equivariant label of the adelic point and φ for the matrix representation of C at the varying place. Put A(g) = φ(c(g))M(g)−1. The construction uses finitely many pieces with representatives cq, a translated form Fq for each piece and a common bound R > 0 on their frame evaluations. At each point the translated form for the piece containing the label agrees with f. Take η = min(1, ε/R). Bν(y₁, y₂)(v, g) = ∑q Pq(Ay₂) Δν(φ(cq)−1Ay₁) Fq(v, g).

Substitute y₁ = y₂ = M(g). Then AM(g) = φ(c(g)). On the selected piece the argument of the weight coefficient Δν is within η of the identity entry by entry. This coefficient is an integral polynomial in the entries times an integer power of the determinant, normalized by Δν(I) = 1. Integral polynomials take integral values on integral inputs, and their values change by at most the largest change in an entry. A determinant unit within η of one remains within η of one after any integer power, by factoring differences of powers and using inversion for negative powers. Thus on the selected piece both multipliers are within η of one. On every other piece the polynomial has absolute value at most η and the weight coefficient at most one. By the ultrametric inequality the full error is at most Rη ≤ ε. This bound holds for every dominant ν with the same polynomials.

The size of the weight error. The family lies in a finite-dimensional span of automorphic functions. Project it into finitely many irreducible automorphic representations, retaining the components on which the family is nonzero. For each such component, let sk(μ) denote the sum of the first k weight entries at τ0. The weight estimate for the family gives |sk(μ) − sk(ν)| ≤ d. These partial sums are the exponents of the highest-weight character when the first k diagonal coordinates are scaled together. Taking differences of consecutive partial sums gives |μτ₀,k − νk| ≤ 2d. At all other archimedean places the family has the original weight. Only τ0 and its complex conjugate lie over the chosen archimedean place, so this gives the weight agreement required in the theorem.

The sum is positive because k < a and N > a² + 4ad. Dominance puts the jumps in increasing order. This proves the claimed separation for every retained component at once. How do all the translated forms acquire a common level and bound?

In the sum defining the weight family, each term uses a form of the original weight W. Which term recovers the original form f depends on the adelic point. As in the weight-variation theorem, let w₀ and v be split places above ℓ with distinct underlying primes in the real subfield. Denote the component at v by prv. By smoothness, an identity neighbourhood at w₀ fixes f. Choose a torsion-free compact open subgroup J inside it by the congruence subgroup construction. Embed J with trivial components away from w₀ and put C = KJ. The two factors commute because they are supported at disjoint places. This gives a compact open level in the finite adeles. Put C′ = C ∩ prv−1(Kv). For c = kj in C′ the v-component is that of k. Hence k belongs to the initial level fixing f, and j also fixes f. Thus C′ fixes f.

The image prv(C) equals GLa(𝒪v). It is compact and contains this integral group by hypothesis. To see the reverse inclusion, use elementary divisors over the local field to write any matrix of the image as two integral invertible factors around a diagonal matrix of uniformizer powers. The diagonal matrix and all its positive and negative powers then lie in the compact image. If any diagonal exponent were nonzero, some sequence of these powers would have an unbounded entry. All exponents therefore vanish. This supplies the integral matrices and inverses required for the polynomial construction.

Reading the finite component from a double coset. Suppose γg = gcx, where γ ∈ Γ, c ∈ C and x ∈ G∞. The element γ lies in the intersection of Γ with a conjugate of the compact subgroup CG∞. This intersection is finite since Γ is closed and discrete in the adeles. Thus cx has finite order. Its w₀-component belongs to the torsion-free J, and consequently equals the identity. The same holds for the conjugate γ. A matrix over E equal to the identity in one completion is the identity over E, so γ = 1. Taking finite components of cx = 1 gives c = 1. This is the stabilizer condition of the equivariant label construction for the entire group C.

Choose a representative s for each double coset in Γ \ G(𝔸) / (CG∞). Write g = γskx and set c(g) = k, where k ∈ C and x ∈ G∞. Two decompositions using the same s give a stabilizer relation at s whose finite component is the quotient of their two k factors. The preceding argument makes that quotient trivial. With the representatives fixed, the label satisfies c(γg) = c(g), c(gx) = c(g) and c(gk) = c(g)k.

Translation to a prescribed label. Fix t ∈ C and send g to g c(g)−1t. This point has label t. For a weight vector u put

Ft(u, g) = f(u, g c(g)−1t).

Replacing g by gk cancels k against the first factor of c(gk)−1. Thus every Ft is fixed by C. It is rationally invariant because the label is. At the archimedean places, the finite correction c(g)−1t commutes with x ∈ G∞ and is unchanged by g ↦ gx. Hence Ft(u,gx) = Ft(W(x)u,g). This gives archimedean continuity and places the archimedean translates in the image of the finite-dimensional weight space. Together with the open finite level and rational invariance these are the defining conditions for an automorphic form of weight W on this definite group.

If t−1c(g) ∈ C′, then its inverse also lies in C′ and fixes f on the right. This gives Ft(u,g) = f(u,g) for every u. In particular, this equality holds when t represents the polynomial piece containing c(g), since each such piece is a left coset of a subgroup of C′.

One bound before choosing the pieces. Use the integral evaluation frame, with test vectors b(g,i). For every form F of weight W the frame gives a bound on |F(b(g,i),g)|ℓ uniform in g and i but possibly dependent on F. To bound all Ft, choose a compact open finite level C₀ fixing the original form. Such a level exists by smoothness, taking a common stabilizer of a basis of the weight space inside a compact open subgroup. Set L = C ∩ C₀. This is open in the compact group C, so the left cosets tL form a finite set. For h ∈ L, right invariance of f gives Fth = Ft. Choose representatives tj and frame bounds Rj for their forms. Then

|Ft(b(g,i),g)|ℓ ≤ R,   R = 1 + ∑j |Rj|.

The cosets of L give a positive R covering every t in C. The subsequent polynomial construction chooses its cosets inside C′ using the tolerance obtained from R. We can therefore prescribe η = min(1, ε/R) before choosing the cosets used for the polynomial approximation. At each point, the error contributed by the selected piece and the contribution of every other piece have absolute value at most Rη ≤ ε.

How do polynomials distinguish the local pieces of a weight family?

The weight-variation argument needs to select one translate of the original form at each point of a compact group. An indicator function selects it exactly. A polynomial in the matrix entries lets us make the same selection to a prescribed ℓ-adic accuracy and keep track of the weights introduced by multiplication. We first construct such a polynomial for two compact sets.

Polynomial separation lemma. Let k be a field with an ultrametric absolute value. Give ks, for finite s, the maximum norm. For disjoint compact sets Z₁ and Z₂ and any η > 0 there is a polynomial P in the s coordinates, with coefficients in k, such that |P(x) − 1| ≤ η on Z₁ and |P(x)| ≤ η on Z₂. We prove the indicator approximation directly. Kaplansky gives the classical approximation theorem for valued fields. I. Kaplansky, The Weierstrass theorem in fields with valuations, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 1 (1950), 356–357.[128]

A polynomial in one coordinate. Write α = min(η, 1). Fix a distance δ > 0 and a compact set Y in k. We seek a polynomial p with three estimates. Its absolute value is at most 1 for |x| ≤ δ, it satisfies |p(x) − 1| ≤ α for |x| ≤ δα, and its absolute value is at most α for x ∈ Y with |x| ≥ δ. The first and third estimates give |p| ≤ 1 on all of Y.

The part of Y where |x| ≥ δ is compact. The closed ball of radius |c|/2 about each of its points c is a neighbourhood of c, so finitely many of these balls cover it. Order their centres by increasing absolute value. Start with p = 1. At each centre c replace p(x) by p(x)(1 − x/c)n. There are three regions to check.

  • On the new ball, |1 − x/c| ≤ 1/2 and |x| ≤ |c|. Writing p(x) = ∑j bjxj, choose n so that 2−n∑j |bj| |c|j ≤ α. The new polynomial then has absolute value at most α throughout this ball.
  • On each earlier ball we have |x| ≤ |c| by the ordering of the centres. This also holds on |x| ≤ δ. Thus the new factor has absolute value at most 1 there and preserves all previous upper bounds.
  • On |x| ≤ δα, put u = 1 − x/c. Then |u − 1| ≤ α and |u| ≤ 1. The factorization of un − 1 by u − 1 gives |un − 1| ≤ α. If the old p was within α of 1, the ultrametric triangle inequality applied to p un − 1 = p(un − 1) + (p − 1) gives the same estimate after multiplication.

Combining coordinates and centres. If either compact set is empty, a constant suffices. Otherwise their distance is positive, since the distance function attains its minimum on Z₁ × Z₂. Take δ equal to this distance and cover Z₁ by finitely many balls of radius δα centred at points t of Z₁. For the compact set Y take the union of the coordinate differences xi − ti as x ranges over Z₁ ∪ Z₂, for each coordinate and each centre. Using a single polynomial p for this finite union, set

qt(x) = ∏i p(xi − ti),   P(x) = 1 − ∏t (1 − qt(x)).

Every factor of qt is bounded by 1 on the two compact sets. For x ∈ Z₁, a covering centre t makes each of these factors within α of 1. A product of such factors stays within α of 1 by the same product identity used above. Thus one factor in 1 − P has absolute value at most α and the others are bounded by 1. For x ∈ Z₂, every centre is at least δ away in some coordinate. This makes every qt bounded by α, so the product of 1 − qt is within α of 1. The two errors are at most α ≤ η.

Left cosets of the compact level. Let Γ be a compact topological group and φ a homomorphism into GLa(k), where k is the ℓ-adic coefficient field. Assume that the entries of φ are continuous and the entries of every φ(g) and its inverse have absolute value at most 1. Fix an open subgroup Γ′ containing ker φ. Let H consist of the g such that all entries of φ(g) − I have absolute value at most η. It is an open subgroup. Indeed, closed balls of positive radius are open in an ultrametric field. Also AB − I = (A − I)B + (B − I) and A−1 − I = −A−1(A − I). The integral entries bound both matrix products entry by entry.

Put J = H ∩ Γ′. Its left cosets form a finite open cover by compactness and disjointness. Choose a representative cq for each coset. The coset and its complement are closed in Γ, so their images under φ are compact. If two elements have the same matrix, their quotient belongs to ker φ ⊆ J and they lie in the same left coset. The two compact images are therefore disjoint. Apply the separation lemma to the a² entries. It gives a polynomial Pq within η of the indicator of cqJ at every φ(g). On the selected coset we also have cq−1g ∈ Γ′ and φ(cq−1g) within η of I. In the application the matrix entries are transported from ℂ to k by the fixed field identification. Transporting the polynomial coefficients back to ℂ preserves the evaluation identity, while the error is measured in k.

For example, take Γ = ℤ₃×, φ(x) = x, Γ′ = 1 + 3ℤ₃ and η = 1/3. There are two classes, represented by 1 and −1. At x ≡ 1 modulo 3 the polynomial P+(x) = (1 + x)/2 is congruent to 1, and P−(x) = (1 − x)/2 is congruent to 0. At x ≡ −1 their roles interchange. Thus degree one suffices for a uniform 3-adic error at most 1/3 on both infinite cosets.

The degree bound for the family. For a target error ε we may choose η = min(1, ε/R), where R > 0 bounds all the values of the translated original form in the chosen evaluation coordinates. The indicator polynomials are now fixed. Write dW for a bound on the absolute values of the exponents in the matrix coefficients of the initial algebraic weight W along the circles diag(z, …, z, 1, …, 1). These coefficients are finite Laurent sums in z and there are finitely many such circles. For fixed matrices A and B, every entry of A diag(z, …, z, 1, …, 1)B is affine in z. A monomial in the entries of total degree j therefore contributes circle exponents between 0 and j. Multiplying by a coefficient of W adds at most dW to the absolute shift. Taking the maximum over the finite set of cosets gives the bound used with the target weight ν,

d = dW + maxq degtot(Pq).

The tolerance and the sets being separated enter through the chosen polynomials. The target weight ν can now vary with this same d.

Which powers can occur when a weight is restricted to one circle?

The family of forms gives functions of a complex number z on the unit circle. To read off a weight from these functions we need to know which powers of z a representation can contribute. For 0 ≤ k ≤ a, let tk(z) be the diagonal matrix with z in the first k positions and 1 elsewhere. Let κ₁ ≥ ⋯ ≥ κa be integers and let sk(κ) = κ₁ + ⋯ + κk, with s₀ = 0. Write Vκ for the irreducible algebraic representation of GLa(ℂ) with this highest weight.

Circle coefficient bound. For any vector w in this representation and any complex linear functional L, the function z ↦ L(tk(z)w) is a finite Laurent sum. Every exponent m with nonzero coefficient satisfies

kκa ≤ m ≤ sk(κ).

The upper bound is attained on the highest-weight vector with any functional that is nonzero there. For the fixed initial weight this supplies a bound in both directions. Changing the embedding to its complex conjugate replaces z by its inverse and reverses the exponents.

Proof. Put b = κa and mj = κj − κj+1 for 1 ≤ j < a. The highest-weight construction realizes Vκ inside a tensor product. Take mj copies of the jth exterior power of ℂa and multiply the action by the determinant to power b. In each exterior factor choose the vector e₁ ∧ ⋯ ∧ ej of the standard basis. Their tensor generates the required irreducible representation. The determinant factor permits negative entries in κ. P. Etingof, Representations of GLₙ, I, Proposition 27.1 and §§27.2–27.3.[22]

A basis vector of the jth exterior power selects j distinct indices. Its power of z counts how many of them lie among the first k. This is between 0 and min(j, k). Exponents add under tensor products, and the determinant contributes kb. The largest possible sum is kb + ∑j min(j, k)mj. To evaluate it, count one copy of mj for each index i ≤ k with i ≤ j. For each i the inner sum telescopes to κi − b. This gives exactly sk(κ). Every term in an expansion in the tensor basis lies in the claimed interval, so taking linear combinations and evaluating L preserves it. The chosen highest tensor selects precisely the first j indices in each factor and attains every maximum simultaneously.

An invertible upper triangular matrix preserves the span of the first j basis vectors. On their top exterior product it acts by the product of its first j diagonal entries. Multiplying over the same tensor factors shows that on the highest vector its scalar is ∏i biiκi for an upper triangular matrix (bij). This gives the triangular transformation used in the weight family.

In rank two take κ = (2, −1). The representation is the third symmetric power of ℂ² twisted by the inverse determinant. The monomial with j copies of e₁ and 3 − j copies of e₂ has exponent j − 1 at t₁. Only the highest monomial attains 2. At t₂ both coordinates scale, and all four monomials have exponent 1. The highest weight specifies the largest exponent available in the representation. A chosen vector may have a smaller one.

Why does the sum over local pieces define a finite family of automorphic forms?

Fix the original weight space W and the finite level K of the weight-variation theorem. The construction of the translates gives a compact open level C containing K, a label c(g) ∈ C and forms Fq of weight W fixed by C. Choose the finitely many indicator polynomials Pq at the required precision. For every dominant integral weight ν, the sum defining Bν then has the following property. As the two matrices y₁, y₂ range over GLa(ℂ) and the vector u ranges over W, its values are automorphic forms in one finite-dimensional complex space. This space may depend on ν. The integer d in the two exponent bounds below can be chosen before ν.

Comparing the two places. Let τ be the chosen complex embedding of the CM field E, let v be the place over ℓ it induces under the field identification ι from the algebraic closure of ℚℓ to ℂ, and let α(g) be the matrix of the infinite component of g at τ. The embedding ι−1τ extends to an embedding of the completion Ev into the algebraic closure of ℚℓ. Apply it entry by entry to the matrix at v, then apply ι, to obtain κ(g). Both α and κ respect multiplication. For a rational point γ they give the same matrix, since both apply τ to its entries. On C the infinite matrix is the identity, and the restriction of κ to C is the homomorphism φ used to construct the polynomials. On the archimedean group the finite matrix is the identity. A. V. Sutherland, Number Theory I, Lecture 12, Corollary 12.24 and its proof.[129]

M(g) = α(g)−1κ(g),   A(g) = φ(c(g))M(g)−1.

Left multiplication by γ leaves M and the label unchanged. For t ∈ C we have M(gt) = M(g)φ(t) and c(gt) = c(g)t. The two copies of φ(t) thus cancel in A(gt). For an archimedean element x, the label stays fixed and M(gx) = α(x)−1M(g), giving A(gx) = A(g)α(x). Finally, if h is finite adelic and its component at v is the identity, both α(h) and κ(h) are the identity. Hence M(gh) = M(g). This last identity lets every term of a Hecke sum use the same pair of evaluation matrices.

How translation acts on the family. Write RxF(g) = F(gx). At finite level both A and Fq are fixed by C, so their product in each summand is fixed by K. At infinity, A acquires the right factor α(x), and Fq(u, gx) = Fq(W(x)u, g). Substitution gives the identity of functions

RxBν(y₁, y₂)(u) = Bν(α(x)y₁, α(x)y₂)(W(x)u).

The first matrix argument also records a character. The coefficient Δν(h) evaluates the image of a highest-weight vector under h against a fixed linear functional. For an invertible upper triangular matrix b, its upper unitriangular part fixes this vector and its diagonal multiplies it by χν(b) = ∏i biiνi. Thus Δν(hb) = χν(b)Δν(h). Replacing y₁ by y₁b multiplies the whole family value by this scalar, since y₁ occurs only in Δν.

One finite span at fixed ν. Write Xq = φ(cq)−1. For a matrix variable n, every function n ↦ Pq(ny₂) lies in the span of the monomials of degree at most deg Pq in its a² entries. Indeed, multiplying by y₂ substitutes linear forms for those entries. The translates n ↦ Δν(Xqny₁) also span a finite-dimensional space. If Δν(h) = L(ρν(h)w), the only factor varying with y₁ is the vector ρν(y₁)w in the fixed finite-dimensional representation. Substitution n = A(g) maps both function spaces linearly into functions of g. The functions Fq(u, ·) are themselves a linear image of the finite-dimensional space W. Products of one basis element from each of the three spaces span every summand at q. Taking the sum over the finitely many q proves the common finite-span assertion.

Each family value is left invariant under rational points and locally constant in the finite variables by its open level. Along the archimedean group, the covariance formula expresses its translates through continuous matrix coefficients and polynomials in the entries of α(x). This gives continuity there, and hence on the product with the finite adeles. All these archimedean translates lie in the common finite span just proved. These are the defining conditions for an automorphic form on the definite unitary group used here.

Two tests on a circle. For 0 ≤ k ≤ a, put T = diag(z, …, z, 1, …, 1) with k copies of z on the unit circle. Let x(z) be its archimedean realization at τ, with the other infinite places fixed, and put uz = W(x(z))u. Write sk(ν) for the sum of the first k entries of ν. All statements about an exponent m refer to a term zm with nonzero coefficient in the indicated Laurent polynomial. For every g, u, y₁ and y₂ the bounds are

Bν(Ty₁, Ty₂)(uz, g)   has exponents   m ≤ sk(ν) + d,
Bν(I, Ty₂)(uz, g)   has exponents   m ≥ −d.

To see this, bound the exponents in the original weight coefficients by −dW and dW. Such a bound exists because each matrix entry of the algebraic representation restricted to a diagonal circle is a Laurent polynomial, and there are finitely many entries and choices of k. At the conjugate embedding the circle parameter is inverted, which preserves this symmetric bound. The factor Pq(ATy₂) has exponents between 0 and its total degree because every entry of ATy₂ is affine in z. When both arguments move, Δν(XqATy₁) is a coefficient of ρν(T) with fixed vector and functional. Its exponents are at most sk(ν) by the highest-weight circle estimate. When the first argument is fixed at I, this same factor is constant in z. Exponents add in products, so d = dW + maxq deg Pq works in both tests and survives summation.

In rank one the two tests can give different exponents even for a single summand. Take W trivial, P(t) = t, ν = −4 and a nonzero constant form. Here Δν(t) = t−4 and we may take d = 1. At k = 1, moving both scalar arguments gives a multiple of z−3, attaining the upper bound −4 + 1. Holding the first at 1 gives a multiple of z, whose exponent is at least −1. To bound the partial sums of a weight actually occurring in an automorphic representation, we will project the family and apply the partial-sum estimate to each nonzero component.

Theorems used. Extending an embedding to a finite completion

How can one decompose every member of the family at once?

Fix a target dominant weight ν in the weight-variation theorem. For each pair of matrices y1, y2 ∈ GLa(ℂ) and each vector v of the original weight space W, the two-matrix family gives an automorphic function B(y1, y2, v). Its dependence on v is linear. All these functions together span a finite-dimensional complex space S. We need one list of irreducible representations valid for every choice of both matrices and of v.

Finite decomposition theorem. On the definite unitary group attached to a CM extension, every finite-dimensional space S of scalar automorphic forms lies in a finite direct sum of irreducible automorphic subrepresentations of the right translation action. The forms are smooth at the finite places and each spans a finite-dimensional space under translations at infinity. The representations in the sum may themselves have infinite dimension.

Here is where admissibility enters. The group at infinity is compact, so the finite-dimensional span of the archimedean translates of a form splits into irreducible types by taking invariant orthogonal complements. Fix one such type A. Its multiplicity space consists of linear maps from A to automorphic functions intertwining the action at infinity. Right translation at finite places acts on this space. Integrating the pointwise Hermitian pairing over the compact adelic quotient gives the positive, translation-invariant Petersson inner product, which induces an inner product on this multiplicity space. At each compact open finite level J its fixed space has finite dimension. Indeed, an intertwiner at this level is determined by one functional on A at each of the finitely many adelic class representatives. This finiteness at fixed type and level is the admissibility property used below. Finite class number and evaluation at representatives.

To see why each vector in the multiplicity space has a finite decomposition, take a vector fixed by J and the representation C generated by its translates. Every invariant subspace N splits off orthogonally in C. For a given vector, choose a compact open stabilizer H and project inside the finite-dimensional fixed space CH onto NH. The remainder is orthogonal to all of N, since pairing an H-fixed vector with n gives the same result as pairing with the average of n over H. This average is a finite sum because the action is smooth and H is compact. If C splits into two nonzero summands, the original generating vector has a nonzero J-fixed projection generating each summand. Both have strictly smaller J-fixed dimension. Induction on this integer gives the finite decomposition.

Pairing each irreducible constituent of the multiplicity space with its archimedean type gives an irreducible representation of the full adelic group. Indeed, the matrix operators of the irreducible finite-dimensional type span its endomorphisms by Burnside’s theorem. Acting by its matrix units on the tensor product isolates each coefficient, so a subrepresentation is the type tensored with an invariant subspace of the multiplicity constituent. Evaluation of the intertwiner is a nonzero equivariant map from this irreducible tensor product to automorphic functions, hence it is injective. Take the union of the finite lists for a basis of S. If an irreducible space in the list meets the sum of its predecessors nontrivially, their intersection is invariant and contains that entire space. Removing such repetitions gives the desired direct sum. P. Etingof et al., Introduction to Representation Theory, Theorem 2.5(i)[130].

For each constituent U let PU take the U-coordinate in this sum. Since every summand is invariant, taking this coordinate commutes with every right translation on the sum. Thus the projected families satisfy the following identity at every argument.

BU(y1, y2, v) = PU(B(y1, y2, v)),   B = ∑U BU.

In particular, the finite level still fixes each value. At the chosen embedding τ let e(x) denote the matrix of an archimedean element x, and let ρ be its action on W. Right translation by x takes a family member to the member with arguments (e(x)y1, e(x)y2, ρ(x)v). Multiplying only y1 on the right by an upper triangular matrix b multiplies the member by χν(b), the product of its diagonal entries raised to the corresponding powers νi. Linearity and commutation with translations preserve both identities.

Projection also preserves the bounds on the exponents of a circle parameter. Indeed, point evaluations F ↦ F(g) span the dual of S. Otherwise a nonzero member of S would vanish at every g. Thus F ↦ (PUF)(g) is a finite linear combination of these evaluations. If each evaluated circle function is a sum of powers zm in a given range, the projected function uses the same range. We now keep the components on which the family has a nonzero value.

Theorems used. Burnside’s density theorem

Why are the highest-weight partial sums bounded on both sides?

Fix a nonzero projected family and write it as F. Its values lie in one automorphic constituent U. Let κ be its highest weight at τ, and write sk(κ) for the sum of its first k entries, with s0(κ) = 0. Vary the first k diagonal entries together using t(z) = diag(z, …, z, 1, …, 1), where |z| = 1. Let x(z) be its lift at the chosen archimedean factor. The character χν(t(z)) is zsk(ν).

Partial-sum estimate. For every k between zero and the rank, the degree bound d chosen in constructing the family satisfies

sk(ν) − d ≤ sk(κ) ≤ sk(ν) + d.

The construction gives two different circle functions. After evaluation at any adelic point, the first has exponents at most sk(ν) + d, and the second has exponents at least −d.

F(t(z)y1, t(z)y2, ρ(x(z))v),   F(1, t(z)y2, ρ(x(z))v).

In the first function the weight coefficient contributes at most sk(ν), while the polynomial in the second matrix and the original weight space contribute at most d together. In the second function the weight coefficient is constant in z. The polynomial has only nonnegative powers and the original weight space has exponents bounded below by −d. These are exactly the two bounds preserved by the finite evaluations above.

To read the weight κ, choose a nonzero value of F and a projection p from U to a copy of the irreducible weight module Vκ that detects this value. The weight detection lemma supplies this projection. The other adelic factors commute with the chosen compact unitary factor, so their translates of one copy of Vκ span a sum of copies of the same type. By irreducibility they span U. The map p intertwines translations by that unitary factor. For any functional L on Vκ, the scalar functional Lp on the finite-dimensional space of family values obeys the same circle bounds by the evaluation argument.

For the upper bound, the vectors pF(y1, y2, v) span Vκ. Their span is nonzero and stable under the compact unitary group by the joint transformation law. The upper bound on every circle coefficient therefore holds for the highest-weight vector itself. Choose a functional nonzero on that vector. Its coefficient is a nonzero multiple of zsk(κ), which gives the upper inequality.

For the lower bound we first find a nonzero value with y1 = 1. Start at any nonzero value with first matrix y1 = ub, where u is unitary and b upper triangular. Gram–Schmidt on its columns gives this factorization. Removing b divides by the nonzero character χν(b). Translating by a lift of u−1 leaves a nonzero value F(1, y, v′). Choose p to detect this particular value and write w = pF(1, y, v′). For the weight action πκ, the character law on the first argument gives

πκ(t(z))w = zsk(ν) pF(1, t(z)y, ρ(x(z))v′).

Every scalar coefficient on the right has exponents at least sk(ν) − d. On the left every weight of Vκ is obtained from κ by subtracting positive roots. Subtracting a root moves a unit from an earlier entry to a later one, so the first k entries can only lose from their sum. Thus every coefficient on the left has exponents at most sk(κ), even for this particular w. Choose L with L(w) ≠ 0. Its coefficient is nonzero at z = 1. Its two exponent ranges must intersect, since a Laurent polynomial vanishing on the circle is zero. This is the circle test on a single nonzero weight-module vector, and it proves the lower inequality. P. Etingof, Highest Weight Modules and Verma Modules, Corollary 8.7 and Proposition 8.8[131].

Subtracting consecutive partial sums bounds the error of a single entry by 2d. The two errors can have opposite signs. For the dominant integer weights ν = (4, 1) and κ = (3, 3), the partial sums change from (4, 5) to (3, 6). With d = 1 their changes are −1 and +1, while the second weight entry changes by 2. This example shows exactly what the two partial-sum inequalities alone imply.

Can a specified nonzero vector be detected at the chosen embedding?

After projecting the family into an irreducible automorphic representation, we obtain functions on the adelic group. The circle calculation applies to vectors in a finite-dimensional weight representation. The next step takes a specified nonzero function to a nonzero vector there while preserving the action of the chosen unitary group.

Detection lemma. Let a group G act irreducibly on a complex vector space U, and let H be a subgroup. Suppose every element of G can be written hc, where h ∈ H and c commutes with all of H. Let V be an irreducible representation of H admitting a nonzero intertwining map into U. For each nonzero u ∈ U there exists a linear map p from U to V with

p(u) ≠ 0,   p(hv) = h p(v)   for every h ∈ H, v ∈ U.

Proof. A nonzero intertwiner from V is injective, since its kernel is an invariant subspace of an irreducible representation. Call its image a copy of V. The sum of all such copies is nonzero. Any c commuting with H carries a copy to another copy, because composing its inclusion with c is still an intertwiner. Every h acts inside each copy. The factorization of elements of G therefore makes this sum G-invariant. By irreducibility it is all of U.

Select a maximal family of copies whose sum is direct. Such a family exists by the maximal principle. The union of a chain of independent families is independent, since every linear relation uses only finitely many members. A further copy meets their sum in an H-invariant subspace. A zero intersection would let us add it, so every copy is already contained in the sum. Thus U is an algebraic direct sum of copies. Some coordinate of u is nonzero. Project onto this coordinate and invert its identification with V. All summands are H-invariant, which gives the required equivariance. M. Zorn, A remark on method in transfinite algebra, pp. 667–670.[132]

In the adelic application H is the unitary factor at the archimedean place of the specified embedding τ. An adelic group element is a tuple of local elements. Taking its component at this place gives h, and the tuple with that component set to the identity commutes with H. Under τ this factor acts by U(a). To say that the weight κ occurs means that the representation of highest weight κ maps nontrivially into U as an H-representation. It is irreducible there: an invariant complex subspace is stable under differentiation by skew-Hermitian matrices, whose complex span is every complex matrix. Thus it is stable under their complex Lie algebra and under exponentials. Elementary row additions and invertible diagonal matrices are exponentials over ℂ and generate GLa(ℂ) by elimination. Irreducibility of the highest-weight module then applies. The algebraic highest-weight representation.

For example, in the restricted representation V ⊕ V a vector (0, w) with w ≠ 0 is killed by projection onto the first copy and detected by the second. The map in the lemma may depend on the given vector. In the lower partial-sum estimate it is chosen after a nonzero value has been transported to the slice where the first matrix is the identity.

Which parts of the original weight survive the projection?

The two matrices in the weight family change under one archimedean factor. At another archimedean place the matrices stay fixed. We show that every nonzero projected component there has the original weight. We then identify the vector giving the required finite level.

Local weights of a constituent. Let U be an irreducible automorphic constituent on the definite unitary group. At any archimedean factor H ≃ U(a), take the span of the H-translates of a nonzero form in U. This span is finite-dimensional by the defining archimedean finiteness of the form. Averaging a positive Hermitian product over the compact group makes it invariant. Orthogonal complements are then invariant, so this space contains an irreducible summand. The Cartan–Weyl classification gives its unique dominant integral highest weight. The decomposition into copies at this factor shows that U is a direct sum of copies of this type when restricted to H. Another irreducible summand projects nontrivially to at least one of these copies. Such an intertwiner between irreducibles is an isomorphism, by looking at its kernel and image. Thus the same dominant weight is obtained however the first vector is chosen. D. Vogan, Theorem 2.12 (Cartan–Weyl for the unitary group).[133]

Keeping the unmodified factors. The original weight space W is the tensor product over the archimedean places of its local weight spaces. Let BU be a nonzero projected family and fix y₁ and y₂ for which the linear map in the weight vector is nonzero. Pure tensors span W, so one pure tensor gives a nonzero value. Choose a place v′ different from the archimedean place of τ. Fix every slot of this tensor except the one at v′. Varying that slot defines a nonzero map from the original local weight space into U.

An element x of the unitary group supported at v′ has matrix equal to the identity at τ. In the archimedean transformation law it changes only the chosen tensor slot. The map just constructed therefore intertwines the two actions at v′. The uniqueness just proved identifies the weight of U there with the original weight. A CM archimedean place has two conjugate embedding labels. Passing to the conjugate embedding conjugates the unitary matrix, negating its torus weights. The dominant member of the opposite extremal orbit is the negative list in reverse order. Applying this operation to the same local weight on both sides gives agreement at the conjugate label as well.

μτ′ = λτ′   if τ′ has a different archimedean place from τ.

For example, if the original weight at a second real place has label (3, 1), its conjugate label is (−1, −3). Both stay fixed as the weight at the selected place varies. Finally, take any nonzero value of BU. It lies in U and is fixed by the required finite level K, by the projection identities. This supplies the level and the unmodified weights for every retained system. At τ itself the two partial-sum inequalities give the separate entrywise error 2d used to choose the gaps.

How does a cyclic character impose a local type?

At the split auxiliary place w₀ above ℓ, we want approximating forms with a nontrivial local character. In the application the map from the local level onto a cyclic group is surjective, so a nontrivial character of the cyclic group stays nontrivial when pulled back. The starting form is invariant under its local level. Averaging its translates against a nontrivial character would therefore give zero. Instead, we multiply the form by each character of an equivariant label. Summing these new forms gives an error whose ℓ-adic size can be computed exactly.

Fixed-weight character estimate. Fix an algebraic weight W on the definite unitary group, a level K away from w₀, and a torsion-free compact open subgroup J of the split local group. Let N = ℓm, with m ≥ 1, and let θ be a homomorphism from J to the additive cyclic group ℤ/Nℤ. If a form f of weight W is fixed by KJ, it admits an approximation G in the span of K-fixed forms of weight W whose representations contain a vector with local character χ ∘ θ for some nontrivial character χ of ℤ/Nℤ. At each adelic point g, the error is a scalar multiple of f there, with multiplier of ℓ-adic absolute value at most ℓ−m.

Proof. The kernel of θ is open even if we start with an abstract group homomorphism. Indeed, on the matrix algebra over the completed number field the derivative of x ↦ xN at the identity sends X to NX. This is invertible in characteristic zero. Apply the multivariable Hensel lemma to the entries of xN − y at the identity. Its Jacobian determinant there is Na². As y approaches the identity the residual tends to zero, so the lemma gives a root approaching the identity, hence a root in J. The image of the power map thus contains a neighbourhood of the identity. Each such power belongs to the kernel. Apply the equivariant label construction with θ on J and the trivial map on K. It gives a label L(g) ∈ ℤ/Nℤ invariant on the left by rational elements and on the right by the archimedean group and K, with L(gj) = L(g) + θ(j) for j ∈ J. K. Conrad, A multivariable Hensel’s lemma, Theorem 3.3.[134]

Choose a primitive complex Nth root of unity ζ. The characters are χb(x) = ζbx for 0 ≤ b < N. For each b ≠ 0 put Fb(v, g) = χb(L(g))f(v, g), where v is a weight vector. The multiplier is locally constant and archimedean invariant. Thus Fb has the same weight as f. Translation by j multiplies it by χb(θ(j)). The automorphic decomposition at a fixed character writes Fb as a finite sum of forms in irreducible representations with this same transformation law. Each nonzero summand has some weight vector at which its value is a nonzero function. That function is a K-fixed vector carrying χb ∘ θ.

Take G = −∑b=1N−1 Fb. Adding the trivial character back gives the finite geometric series ∑b=0N−1 ζbx. Its value is N at x = 0 and zero at every other residue class. Consequently

f(v, g) − G(v, g) = N 1{L(g)=0} f(v, g).

Here 1{L(g)=0} is the indicator of the zero label. Keeping the character sum unnormalized gives exactly |N|ℓ = ℓ−m on this fibre. For instance, with ℓ = 2 and N = 4, the three nontrivial characters at label 2 take the values −1, 1, −1. Their negative sum is 1, and G agrees with f there. At label 0 all three values are 1, so G equals −3f and the error is 4f, of relative 2-adic size 1/4 wherever f is nonzero.

For the simultaneous Hecke approximation, the weight at the second auxiliary place has already been chosen. The local type theorem supplies additional data at w₀. For any identity neighbourhood fixing the current form and any lower bound m₀, it gives m ≥ m₀, a subgroup J inside that neighbourhood as above and a surjective θ. In addition, every smooth irreducible representation of the local general linear group containing a nonzero vector with character χ ∘ θ, for any χ ≠ 1, is cuspidal. Surjectivity ensures that χ ∘ θ is itself nontrivial. Choosing ℓ−m₀ below the requested tolerance now gives approximants with the required local type at the chosen weight. Different summands may carry different nontrivial characters.

Why does each nontrivial character force cuspidality?

The cyclic character sum uses every nontrivial character of a single quotient. Some of these characters have small order. To treat them all, we construct an element mapping to the generator of the quotient in the unipotent radical of each proper parabolic, and in every conjugate of that radical.

Local type theorem. Let F be the completion of the number field at the chosen split place w₀ above ℓ, let G = GLa(F) with a ≥ 1, and fix an identity neighbourhood U and an integer m₀ ≥ 0. There exist m ≥ m₀, a torsion-free compact open subgroup J ⊆ U and a surjective homomorphism θ from J to the additive group ℤ/ℓmℤ with the following property. If a smooth irreducible complex representation σ of G contains a nonzero vector on which J acts by χ ∘ θ for some nontrivial character χ of this quotient, then σ is cuspidal. Here cuspidality means that the coinvariants of σ under the unipotent radical of every proper parabolic vanish.

The level and its cyclic quotient. Write 𝒪 for the valuation ring of F, κ for its residue field and v for the valuation normalized to take value 1 on a uniformizer. Start with a ≥ 2. Choose m ≥ max(2, m₀) sufficiently large that J = 1 + ℓmMa(𝒪) lies in U. These are compact open subgroups because 𝒪 is compact and open, all the displayed matrices reduce to the identity over κ, and the ideals ℓm𝒪 shrink to zero. This uses only v(ℓ) > 0, including at ramified places. To see that J is torsion-free, a nonidentity torsion element would have a power of prime order r, say 1 + Y. Let s be the least valuation of its nonzero entries in Y. In (1 + Y)r − 1 the linear term rY has an entry of valuation s + v(r), while every entry of a higher term has valuation at least 2s. Since s ≥ 2v(ℓ) and v(r) ≤ v(ℓ), that entry survives.

Put M = ℓm. The class of 1 in 𝒪/M𝒪 generates a copy of ℤ/Mℤ. Indeed, for a nonzero integer n, its valuation in F is v(ℓ) times its ℓ-adic valuation, so n lies in M𝒪 precisely when M divides n. On this cyclic subgroup send n to n/M modulo ℤ. Divisibility of the additive circle ℝ/ℤ extends this homomorphism to all of 𝒪/M𝒪. Every value is killed by M, so the extension takes values in (1/M)ℤ/ℤ. Identifying n/M with n modulo M gives an additive retraction φ onto ℤ/Mℤ with φ(1) = 1. Stacks Project, Lemma 15.55.1 (extension into a divisible abelian group).[135]

Identify κa with the degree-a extension of κ. Let B̄ be multiplication by a generator of the multiplicative group of that field. If a B̄-stable κ-subspace contains a nonzero element, the successive powers of the generator carry this element through every nonzero element of the field. Thus the only stable subspaces are zero and the whole space. Lift the entries of B̄ to a matrix B over 𝒪 and define θ by the ordinary matrix trace. K. Conrad, Finite Fields, Lemma 1.6 and Theorem 5.1.[136]

θ(1 + MX) = φ(tr(BX) mod M𝒪).

In the product of 1 + MX and 1 + MY, the coefficient of M is X + Y + MXY. Reduction modulo M removes the last term, so θ is a homomorphism. Its kernel contains 1 + M²Ma(𝒪), hence it is open.

An element mapping to 1 in each radical. Fix the unipotent radical N of a proper parabolic and any g ∈ G. The conjugate g−1Ng acts trivially on the successive quotients of its flag. Choose a nonzero proper step W of that flag. Any map X with image in W and vanishing on W lowers the flag. It kills each step up to W and maps every later step into W. Hence 1 + MX belongs to g−1Ng. To place it in J as well, we need integral entries.

Let L = W ∩ 𝒪a. Clearing denominators shows that L spans W over F. The lattice is saturated. Indeed, if a nonzero multiple of an integral vector lies in W, the vector itself lies in W. Thus 𝒪a/L is a finitely generated torsion-free module over the discrete valuation ring 𝒪, hence free. Lifting a basis of the quotient splits off a complement to L. Consequently the image L̄ of L in κa has dimension dimF W, strictly between 0 and a. Stacks Project, Lemma 15.22.11(3) (freeness over a principal ideal domain).[32]

Since B̄ does not preserve L̄, choose y ∈ L for which By reduces outside L̄. In the free quotient 𝒪a/L at least one coordinate of the class of By is a unit. Pull that coordinate back to an integral linear functional f on 𝒪a. Its extension to F vanishes on W, and u = f(By) is a unit. The rank-one operator below therefore has integral entries.

X(z) = y f(z)/u,   X² = 0,   tr(BX) = f(By)/u = 1.

The square vanishes because f(y) = 0. The trace identity follows by summing the diagonal entries of the rank-one map z ↦ (By)f(z)/u. Its construction puts h = 1 + MX in J ∩ g−1Ng, with θ(h) = 1. Since 1 generates ℤ/Mℤ, this also proves surjectivity of θ.

Vanishing of the Jacquet module. Let v be a nonzero vector of σ with character χ ∘ θ. In the space of N-coinvariants we identify σ(n)x with x for all n ∈ N. For each g choose the element h just constructed, so that ghg−1 ∈ N. Writing brackets for the class in the quotient gives

[σ(g)v] = [σ(ghg−1)σ(g)v] = χ(1)[σ(g)v].

Every nontrivial character takes a value different from 1 on the additive generator, whatever its order. Thus each translate of v has zero class. Their span is a nonzero invariant subspace, hence the whole irreducible representation. This proves that its N-coinvariants vanish for every proper parabolic.

For example, take F = ℚ₂, a = 2 and M = 4. Choose B with rows (0, 1) and (1, 1). Its characteristic polynomial modulo 2 is t² + t + 1, which has no root in 𝔽₂. For the upper triangular parabolic and g = 1, choose X with its only nonzero entry equal to 1 in position (1, 2). Then tr(BX) = 1. The order-two character of ℤ/4ℤ takes the value −1 at 1 and the value 1 at 2. Our element therefore gives [v] = −[v] even for this character. An element mapping only to 2 would give the identity [v] = [v] and yield no information.

Rank one. For GL₁(F) there are no proper parabolics, so every smooth irreducible representation satisfies the stated cuspidality condition. Here we may use the requested exponent m = m₀ exactly. Choose d ≥ max(2, m) with J = 1 + ℓd𝒪 inside U. Send 1 + ℓdx to φ(x mod ℓm𝒪). The product formula again makes this a homomorphism, and 1 + ℓd maps to the generator. For m = 0 the quotient is trivial.

6.17Why do all the original Hecke coordinates lie in one finite extension?

The trace limit needs completeness of its coefficient field. Having each eigenvalue in some finite extension of ℚℓ would allow the degrees to grow with the operator. For a family of rational Hecke operators at the chosen weight and level we can bound the degree of every finite list at once.

Choose a nonzero fixed eigenform for the original system. The polynomial construction below realizes every field conjugate of its eigenvalue system on a nonzero form, all in one finite-dimensional space M. Rationality of the operators is used here so that applying an automorphism of ℂ carries an eigenvalue to its conjugate for the very same operator. The finite adelic values determine the form, so a nonzero such value still detects each conjugate. Distinct joint systems give linearly independent eigenvectors. Indeed, in a finite relation fix one system χ. For each other system ψ choose a coordinate j at which they differ and apply the factor Tj − ψjI. The product kills every other vector and multiplies the chosen one by a nonzero scalar. Thus χ has zero coefficient in the relation. The full tuple of eigenvalues has at most dim M different conjugates.

Transport the tuple back by ι to the algebraic closure of ℚℓ. For every finite set A of coordinates let LA be the field they generate over ℚℓ. It has [LA : ℚℓ] embeddings into the algebraic closure. One can count them by adjoining the generators in succession: each minimal polynomial in characteristic zero has exactly its degree many distinct roots. Each embedding extends to an automorphism of the algebraic closure, hence, through ι, to a field automorphism of ℂ. Distinct embeddings differ on at least one of the generating coordinates, and therefore yield different full conjugate tuples. Milne, Fields and Galois Theory, Proposition 7.4[137].

[LA : ℚℓ] ≤ # conjugate tuples ≤ dim M.

These positive integer degrees have a maximum. Take a finite set attaining it and adjoin any further coordinate. The resulting field contains the previous one and has the same degree, so the coordinate was already there. This gives a single finite extension, complete in its ℓ-adic norm, for all the original rational Hecke coordinates. For instance, in ℚ₅(√2) the infinite sequence 1+n√2, n ≥ 0, has two conjugate tuples. Already the coordinate at n=1 generates degree two, since 2 is a nonsquare modulo 5. The same upper bound of two works for every finite set of indices. A. Sutherland, 18.785, Proposition 10.6, completeness in finite dimension[138].

Why do the conjugate forms fit in one finite-dimensional space?

Let f be a nonzero complex-valued automorphic form on the definite unitary group of rank n attached to the CM extension E/E+. View the group over ℚ by restriction of scalars from E+. Write Γ for its rational points, U for its compact group at infinity and Gf for the finite adelic group. Choose a compact open level K fixing f on the right. For a field automorphism σ of ℂ, the conjugate form fσ must satisfy fσ(s) = σ(f(s)) for every s ∈ Gf, where the component at infinity is the identity. This prescription determines a continuous automorphic form uniquely. Indeed, left Γ-invariance gives its values on ΓGf, which is dense. The density follows from the rational Cayley parametrization at infinity, since the finite component can be chosen arbitrarily.

Proposition. There is a degree D depending on f such that all the forms fσ exist and belong to one complex vector space M. Let h be the number of classes in Γ ∖ G(𝔸) / (U K). The finite class number theorem gives h < ∞. With b = [E ∶ ℚ]n², a common bound is

dimℂ M ≤ h · (b + D)! / (b! D!).

The degree at infinity. Take the matrix entries on U at every complex embedding τ of E. There are b labelled coordinates, including both embeddings of each conjugate pair. Let PD be the span of the products of at most D such coordinates, including the constant 1. The archimedean right translates of f span a finite-dimensional space by the definition of an automorphic form. Choose a basis e1, …, em of this space. Expanding each translate in that basis gives

f(s x) = ∑j=1m ej(s) pj(x),   s ∈ Gf,   x ∈ U.

The functions pj are matrix coefficients of this finite-dimensional action. Each is continuous and its right translates span a finite-dimensional space. Every ej has level K because the finite and infinite translations commute.

Why is each coefficient a polynomial? Let v be such a coefficient and V the span of its right translates Ryv(x) = v(xy). For a coordinate polynomial p, integrate these translates against p(y) using normalized Haar measure on U. The resulting function belongs to V. It is also a coordinate polynomial in x. Indeed, substitution u = xy gives the integrand v(u)p(x−1u). Since unitary inversion is conjugate transpose and the coordinates include conjugate entries, the last factor expands into a finite sum of polynomials in x times polynomials in u.

If v lay outside the span of these integrals, a linear functional L on V would vanish on all of them and have L(v) ≠ 0. Then g(y) = L(Ryv) would integrate to zero against every coordinate polynomial. These polynomials contain the constants, separate the points of U and are closed under complex conjugation. The complex Stone–Weierstrass theorem therefore gives uniform polynomial approximations to the complex conjugate of g. Passing to the limit yields ∫ |g|² = 0. Haar measure gives positive mass to every nonempty open set, so continuity forces g(1) = L(v) = 0. This proves that v itself is a polynomial. Taking the largest degree in the finite list p1, …, pm gives D. M. H. Stone, The Generalized Weierstrass Approximation Theorem[139].

What conjugation preserves. In the expression for pj, apply σ to the coefficients and replace each label τ by σ ∘ τ, keeping its two matrix indices. The resulting polynomial pj,σ still has degree at most D. At the infinite component of a rational matrix γ, its labelled entry is τ(γab), so the new polynomial has value σ(pj(γ∞)). Define

fσ(sx) = ∑j=1m σ(ej(s)) pj,σ(x).

The finite coefficients are locally constant on right K-cosets, and the polynomials are continuous in x. Thus this formula is continuous even for a discontinuous σ. It agrees with σ(f) on ΓGf. There it is left Γ-invariant, and continuity extends that invariance everywhere. Right translates on U substitute linear forms for the matrix entries, so the space of polynomials of degree at most D remains stable and the constructed form is finite under archimedean translations. Conjugation can permute the embeddings that describe the weight. The finite level and the degree bound hold for every σ.

For example, take E = ℚ(i) in rank one. On the unit circle the two embedding coordinates are z and its complex conjugate. A field automorphism sending i to −i interchanges their labels. At the rational point (3 + 4i)/5 the first coordinate becomes (3 − 4i)/5. Both coordinates lie in the same three-dimensional polynomial space of degree at most one, spanned by 1, z and z−1.

Counting the remaining freedom. Take one purely finite representative s for each of the h classes, absorbing its infinite component into U. Let M consist of left Γ-invariant, right K-invariant functions whose restrictions x ↦ F(sx) belong to PD for each representative. This restriction map into h copies of PD is injective because every group element has the form γsxk. The scalar coordinates commute. A monomial is specified by b nonnegative exponents of sum at most D. Adding the unused degree as one more exponent gives (b + D)! / (b! D!) possibilities. Relations among entries or symmetries of a representative may lower the dimension. The displayed bound uses only the form and its chosen level. For a rational Hecke operator, a finite rational sum of translates commutes with σ on the finite adelic values. Uniqueness then gives the conjugate eigenvalue on the constructed form, as required in the common coefficient field argument.

6.18How does an odd-rank Hecke system give a Galois representation?

Let Ω be an algebraic closure of the CM field E and put Γ = Gal(Ω/E). Choose two split places u and v of E above ℓ whose restrictions to the maximal totally real subfield E⁺ are distinct. Keep this pair fixed as the finite sets of test places vary. The construction gives one representation ru,v for all those sets. The three-place argument will identify the companions from different pairs.

The simultaneous polynomial congruences supply one weighted list for all polynomial tests. The rank extraction from cohomology and the local tests give the geometric representations used here. At a spherical split place w away from ℓ, let Bw be the Satake multiset and multiply each entry by (Nw)(m−1)/2. For an arithmetic Frobenius lift σ and a positive integer b, let xj = σ−b. The spherical Hecke operator indexed by these choices measures the sum of the bth powers of the normalized entries. Transport this number back by ι and denote it by θj. We want these numbers to be traces of one representation.

Two arithmetic inputs enter here. The first constructs representations ρi for auxiliary automorphic systems with prescribed local types and suitably separated weights, using geometric Galois representations. For each auxiliary system i the geometric input gives an open dense subset Vi of Γ and finitely many exceptional places. At an eligible spherical place outside the exceptions, the auxiliary representation is unramified. For each arithmetic Frobenius lift σ there that belongs to Vi, the polynomial at σ−1 agrees with the auxiliary Satake polynomial. The input also gives stronger matches at prescribed test places. The second is a congruence theorem for the Hecke eigenvalues ηi of these systems. With any fixed finite set of test places prescribed, it gives this approximation for each ε > 0. There exist finitely many indices F and coefficients ci such that the same bound holds for every polynomial P with integer coefficients in the Hecke coordinates.

|P(θ) − ∑i ∈ F ci P(ηi)|ℓ ≤ ε.

The theorem also places all θj in one finite extension L of ℚℓ because the chosen operators have rational coefficients. To construct a trace at g ∈ Γ, approach g by indices j at which any prescribed finite list of the auxiliary systems agrees with its Galois traces. Such indices exist in every neighborhood. For a neighborhood H of g, take a nonempty open subset of H−1 and intersect it with the finitely many Vi. The intersection is still nonempty and open. Exclude all exceptional places, the primes over ℓ, and the finite fibres above real-subfield primes excluded by the auxiliary level. The degree-one Frobenius argument still supplies an arithmetic Frobenius σ in the intersection. Taking exponent one gives a test xj = σ−1 in H at which all the selected systems match. Taking P to be the single coordinate j puts θj within ε of the continuous sum ∑ ci tr ρi(xj). Shrink the neighborhood until the sum varies by at most ε. Any two such θj then differ by at most ε in the ultrametric norm. Completeness of L gives a limit T(g). The approximation by the same continuous sums is uniform in g, hence T is continuous.

Any integral polynomial in finitely many values T(g₁), …, T(gk) obeys the same estimate. Fix the approximating list F for ε. For each gh, choose indices subject to two conditions. Their group coordinates must belong to a chosen neighborhood of gh, and they must match every system in a chosen finite list containing F. As the neighborhoods shrink and the lists enlarge, the group coordinates converge to gh and the numbers θj converge to T(gh) by the construction of the limit. Make these choices independently for the finitely many arguments of P. Every chosen coordinate matches every system in F, so the original polynomial estimate holds. Polynomial evaluation and the auxiliary traces are continuous, and the ball of radius ε is closed. The estimate therefore holds at the limiting tuple. In particular, a polynomial identity satisfied by every rank-m matrix trace holds for T, since its absolute value is at most every ε > 0. This gives T(1) = m, T(gh) = T(hg) and the alternating trace identity in m+1 variables. These conditions define a rank-m pseudocharacter. The last identity is the alternating sum over permutations, with one trace of an ordered product for each cycle. For matrices it is zero because the antisymmetrizer on the (m+1)st tensor power of an m-dimensional space is zero.

Realizing the trace. Extend T linearly to the group algebra over the algebraic closure of ℚℓ. In each term of the alternating trace identity, every argument appears exactly once. The expression in the extended trace is therefore multilinear, and its vanishing on all tuples of group basis elements implies its vanishing on the whole algebra. Divide by the ideal of elements A with T(AB) = 0 for every B. The pseudocharacter realization theorem makes this quotient a finite product of matrix algebras. On each block a central linear form is a scalar multiple of trace, as one sees on matrix units. If the scalar is c, substituting the same rank-one idempotent into all m+1 slots of the alternating identity gives c(c−1)⋯(c−m) = 0. Thus c is a nonnegative integer. If it were zero, every matrix A supported in that block would satisfy T(AB) = 0 for every B, since AB stays in the block. The trace pairing has zero radical on the quotient by construction. Every surviving block consequently has positive multiplicity. Take c copies of the defining module of that block. The total dimension is T(1) = m and the resulting semisimple representation r has trace T. For continuity, choose group matrices r(hk) spanning their image algebra. The trace pairing on it is nondegenerate because its restriction to each matrix block is the ordinary trace pairing times its positive multiplicity. Hence every entry of r(g) is a fixed linear combination of the continuous functions T(g hk). Rouquier, Caractérisation des caractères et pseudo-caractères, Lemma 4.1 and §4[140].

A rank-three congruence. For s ≥ 1, the representations of the additive group ℤ₅ given by diag((1+5s)g,1,1) have traces congruent to 3 modulo 5s. Integer powers extend continuously to ℤ₅, since taking fifth powers increases the divisibility of the difference from 1 by at least one power of 5. An integral polynomial in any finite list of these traces is consequently congruent to its value on the constant list of threes. Here one system with coefficient 1 gives accuracy 5−s simultaneously for every polynomial, and the limiting companion is the three-dimensional trivial representation.

6.19How does one recover unramifiedness at a specified place?

Keep the chosen pair and its representation r = ru,v and fix w ∈ Qd away from ℓ where U is spherical. In the construction choose the finite test set {w}. The congruence and geometric inputs then supply a family whose every member is unramified at this w and matches its own Satake parameters there. The trace of the same r is uniformly approximated by finite linear combinations of their traces. Indeed the construction of T passed the estimate for any approximating subfamily to Γ, with the original coefficients. We may now use the subfamily attached to {w}.

Choose s in inertia at a place of Ω above w. Every auxiliary ρi in this subfamily sends s to the identity. Its traces at sg and g therefore agree for every g. Letting the uniform trace error tend to zero gives

tr((r(s) − 1)r(g)) = 0   for every g ∈ Γ.

The tested matrices span the image algebra, and r(s) − 1 belongs to it. Nondegeneracy of the trace pairing gives r(s) = 1. The quantifier over g matters. For instance, in the standard two-dimensional representation of SL₂(ℤℓ) plus a trivial line, let s have diagonal entries 1 and upper off-diagonal entry 1 in its two-dimensional block. Let g be its transpose. Both have trace 3 in dimension three, whereas sg has trace 4. Testing the translate g detects the nonidentity s.

The same subfamily gives the power traces at σ−b for every b ≥ 1 and every Frobenius lift σ at w. Here each approximant matches its own Hecke coordinate at the chosen index, so its two weighted sums coincide. Sending ε to zero in the estimates for θj and for T(xj) gives equality of the two limits. The first m power sums pb recover the characteristic polynomial. Indeed for roots αj put H(z) = ∏(1−αjz). Expanding −zH′/H as ∑b≥1 pbzb and comparing coefficients after multiplication by H determines each coefficient from those preceding it. Division by 1,…,m is valid in characteristic zero. Thus r has exactly the normalized Satake polynomial at w.

For example, a rank-three local multiset {1,1,−1} at norm 5 becomes {5,5,−5} after normalization. Its first three power sums are 5, 75 and 125. The elementary symmetric functions are 5, (5²−75)/2 = −25 and (125−5 · 75−25 · 5)/3 = −125. They give (X−5)²(X+5), retaining the repeated root.

6.20How do three places above ℓ give one companion with the full local data?

The odd-rank approximation first chooses two auxiliary places above ℓ, called u and v. They must lie above different primes of E⁺. For the representation ru,v thus obtained, the unramified matches hold at all the allowed spherical places away from ℓ. At a spherical w above ℓ the local theorem also gives crystallinity, the prescribed filtration jumps at each embedding inducing w, and the Weil–Deligne polynomial, provided the prime under w in E⁺ differs from those under u and v.
