Why do the filtration jumps survive a weighted approximation of traces?

Fix a spherical place w above ℓ away from the two auxiliary primes. Write K = Ew for the local field. At each embedding τ of K into the algebraic closure of ℚℓ, every member of the approximating family for {w} has the same multiset of filtration jumps Jτ. A jump h occurs once for each dimension of the graded space Filh/Filh+1 of the de Rham periods at τ. The assertion to prove is that the local restriction of the previously constructed r is crystalline and has precisely those multiplicities. The given convergence concerns linear combinations of global traces. The coefficients can vary with the accuracy, and the representations in a combination can act on different spaces.

From traces to periods. First form the ℤℓ-lattice spanned by the global matrices r(g). Left multiplication by r(g) preserves this lattice, which contains the identity matrix. The lattice comparison theorem uses global semisimplicity and the uniform trace estimates to approximate this action modulo ℓq for each q. Its approximating lattice lies in a finite product of matrix spaces for the auxiliary representations. The lists of representations can be made nested by adjoining the earlier lists and giving the added terms coefficient zero in the current sum. Restrict the resulting actions and comparison maps to the local group at w. On each rationalized approximating lattice, the group acts on the matrix columns by the given auxiliary representations. Thus these columns carry crystalline representations. Taking the maximum of |h| over all Jτ gives a single bound on all their jumps, through every level of approximation.

The bounded-weight Breuil–Kisin comparison for these lattices is the period-theoretic input. It gives integral matrices describing the periods at each level and a frame on the limiting lattice. For every precision a sufficiently deep level agrees with that frame to the required precision under the comparison maps. If the frames on all the levels satisfy the crystalline condition, so does the limiting frame. Its invariant periods span the limiting lattice after extending scalars to the crystalline period ring. To see why this yields periods for r itself, work over a finite coefficient field of definition and view its vector space over ℚℓ. For each vector v, evaluation A ↦ Av on the rational matrix lattice is equivariant and takes the identity to v. After extending scalars to the period ring, this map sends invariant periods to invariant periods. Its image contains 1 ⊗ v, so these invariant periods span the whole target as v varies. This is the period criterion for crystallinity. Brinon and Conrad, Theorem 5.2.1 and Remark 5.2.3 on admissibility over a period ring[141].

Recovering each jump. Fix τ. Choose a local Galois element for which the period construction gives a nonzero ℓ-adic scalar z of infinite multiplicative order. In a period basis adapted to the filtration the associated operator has eigenvalues zh, one for each jump h. Every auxiliary member therefore gives the same nth power trace Sn = ∑h∈Jτ (zh)n, counting repetitions. Write Xn for the corresponding trace on the target representation. Write U for the operator on the auxiliary matrix lattice, whose dimension may exceed the rank of the target. The period comparison bounds its entries and those of the level operators U′ by one constant B ≥ 1. For each precision q it supplies a level and a map Π with ‖UΠ − ΠU′‖ ≤ Bℓ−q, where the norm is the largest absolute value of an entry. The telescoping sum for UnΠ − ΠU′n has terms Ua(UΠ − ΠU′)U′n−1−a. The ultrametric triangle inequality bounds the sum by its largest term. For each fixed power the error thus tends to zero, even if the dimensions of the level lattices grow.

Period operators commute with equivariant evaluation on vectors. If e represents the identity in lattice coordinates, evaluation of Une on each vector therefore gives the nth power of the target operator on that vector. Applying the matrix trace functional to Une recovers Xn. The comparison map preserves that vector and the weighted trace functional to within ℓ−q. Together with the power estimate this gives the following bound with Kn independent of q. The scalar Cq is the sum of the level coefficients in the coefficient embedding used for τ, since every auxiliary member has the very same Sn.

|Xn − CqSn|ℓ ≤ Knℓ−q,   X₀ = S₀ = m.

At power zero this estimate gives |1−Cq|ℓ ≤ K₀ℓ−q/|m|ℓ. Division is valid even when ℓ divides the positive rank. Thus Cq tends to 1. Holding n fixed and letting q increase now gives Xn = Sn. The power-sum recursion recovers the multiset of eigenvalues from its first m positive power sums. Since z has infinite order, zh determines the integer h, including its sign. This recovers the entire multiset Jτ. For an arithmetic check, the lists {0,1,2} and {0,1,4} give identical power sums at z = −1 because 2 and 4 are both even. At z = 2 their first sums are 7 and 19. This is the role of the infinite-order choice.

How does the same companion acquire the local Weil polynomial?

Crystallinity gives the local period space on which Frobenius acts. Its Weil polynomial requires another comparison. For each local Weil element σ, each integer N ≥ 0 and each ε > 0, the congruence theorem supplies a finite set F of these approximants and coefficients cρ in the ℓ-adic coefficient field. How can the chosen place also be one of the original auxiliary places?

Here E contains √(−d), −d is a square in ℚℓ, [E⁺∶ℚ] is even, and E/E⁺ is unramified at finite places. All places above ℓ are split. The remaining field assumption provides three places w₁, w₂, w₃ above ℓ with pairwise distinct underlying primes in E⁺. Fix once and for all the representation from the first two. For an arbitrary spherical target place w above ℓ, at most one of these three lies over the same real-subfield prime as w. Choose the other two for a new auxiliary pair. The corresponding companion now has the strong local conclusion at w. Both companions match the same source polynomial at almost all places of absolute degree one away from ℓ, by the two splitting tests and sphericity. Their characteristic polynomials agree on Γ by continuity and density. Brauer–Nesbitt identifies the semisimple representations. The intertwining isomorphism carries the inertia action, filtered period modules and Weil–Deligne polynomial to those of the companion fixed at the outset. The trace argument for Brauer–Nesbitt.

ru,v ≃ rw₁,w₂   with u, v chosen away from the prime below w.

Why the real-subfield prime matters. Take E⁺ = ℚ(√2,√3), E = E⁺(i), d = 1, and ℓ = 97. The real degree is four. The quadratic extension E/E⁺ is unramified at finite places. Its defining polynomials X²+1 and X²+X+1 have discriminants −4 and −3, respectively. The latter generates the same extension since √3 ∈ E⁺. At every finite place at least one of these discriminants is a unit, so the corresponding quadratic algebra is unramified there. Modulo 97 the numbers 14, 10 and 22 square to 2, 3 and −1, respectively. Their negatives give the other simple roots. Thus the primes of E⁺ above 97 are labeled by sign pairs for (√2,√3), and each splits into two in E. Take the auxiliary real-subfield primes (+,+), (+,−), (−,+). A target over (+,+) uses (+,−) and (−,+), regardless of which root of −1 labels the target itself. This gives the required conclusion for either target on the originally fixed companion. Sutherland, Theorem 12.19 and §12.4 on discriminants of orders[142].

6.21Where do both lifts have the same source parameters?

Fix the two lifts, their common twist κ and the finite lists of auxiliary Hecke characters ψ1,i and ψ2,i. The odd-rank attachment theorem supplies a continuous semisimple representation ρj for each lift. For all but finitely many places in Qd, each ρj already matches the normalized Satake parameters of its lift whenever those parameters exist. This compatibility is an input from the odd-rank construction. We now show that all the hypotheses for applying it to both lifts hold together on a dense set of inverse Frobenius elements.

Each of the finitely many characters is unramified outside a finite set, as is κ. Here is the reason for finiteness. A neighborhood of 1 in the idele group contains every single-place integral unit outside finitely many places, along with every power of that unit. By continuity we can choose the neighborhood so that all its character values lie at distance less than ½ from 1. A complex number with all of its integral powers in this disk must be 1. Its modulus must first be 1 by taking positive and negative powers. For a different point of the unit circle the averages of its first N powers tend to zero by the geometric sum formula, whereas numbers in the disk have real part greater than ½. Thus the character is trivial on the entire local unit group at every remaining place.

Collect in one finite set the places above ℓ, the conductors of all these characters, the exceptions for both odd-rank matches, and the finite exceptional set for sphericity of the source. Outside this union each w ∈ Qd supplies a source Satake multiset Bw. The two lift identities use that very same multiset. Write Bwalg for the result of multiplying each entry by (Nw)(n−1)/2, and Sw for the result of multiplying each entry by κ(w)−1. On applying the fixed coefficient identification, the eigenvalue multiset of ρj at inverse Frobenius is

Sw ⊎ {ψj,1(w), …, ψj,t(w)},   j = 1, 2.

The density result allows this whole finite union to be discarded at once. Adding the other list to each side therefore gives equal polynomials on a dense set. The character-transfer argument extends equality to Γ and isolates the auxiliary lines. The exclusions here serve the density argument. At a particular target place, including one above ℓ, the stronger local conclusion uses the separately prescribed data there and the final untwisting step.

6.22How do good primes identify a character on the entire group?

Fix ℓ and write Γ = Gal(Ω/E), where Ω is an algebraic closure of the CM field E. The two lifts give continuous semisimple representations ρ₁ and ρ₂ of dimension n+t over an algebraic closure k of ℚℓ. Call their respective lists of auxiliary Galois characters A and B. Every character in A differs from every character in B as a function on Γ. Write D(A) for the direct sum of its character lines, and LA(g) for the product of their linear factors X−χ(g).

At a good split place the two Frobenius multisets consist of the same normalized source parameters together with the entries of their respective lists. Add the other list to each side. Now both sides contain the common parameters, every entry of A and every entry of B, with multiplicities. In the local–global application the places belong to the set of good split places just constructed. Its inverse Frobenius elements, allowing all choices of place above each prime, remain dense in Γ after removing any finite set and the primes above ℓ. The argument using finite Galois quotients gives this density for the specified set, and the common local comparison supplies its polynomial identity outside finitely many places. Sutherland, Theorem 28.9[143].

Let Pρ(g) = det(X − ρ(g)). The embedding k ≃ ℂ identifies the polynomials at these Frobenius elements. For any x ∈ k, evaluating both polynomials at x gives continuous k-valued functions of g, since determinants and finite products are continuous. Equality on the dense set extends to every g. Varying x in the infinite field k gives

Pρ₁(g) LB(g) = Pρ₂(g) LA(g)   for every g ∈ Γ.

Brauer–Nesbitt in characteristic zero. Two finite-dimensional semisimple representations of any group over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero are isomorphic if their characteristic polynomials agree on every element. Indeed, their traces agree on the group and therefore on its group algebra by linearity. Take the finitely many distinct irreducible constituents of both representations. By the density theorem for algebras, one group-algebra element can act by a rank-one projection on any chosen constituent and by zero on the others. Its trace counts the copies of that constituent. Characteristic zero recovers these counts as integers. Equal counts for every constituent give an isomorphism of the two direct sums. Etingof et al., Theorem 2.5(ii)[144] and Theorem 2.17(i)[145].

Apply the theorem to the augmented representations. Fix one isomorphism from ρ₂ ⊕ D(A) to ρ₁ ⊕ D(B), and take a basis vector on a line χ in A. Its image is nonzero and transforms by χ under every g. Write its coordinates as (v, (bγ)γ∈B). Projection onto each auxiliary coordinate gives

γ(g) bγ = χ(g) bγ   for every g ∈ Γ.

If bγ were nonzero, γ and χ would agree on all of Γ, contradicting cross-list disjointness. All auxiliary coordinates vanish. Thus v is a nonzero vector in ρ₁ spanning a Γ-invariant line on which the action is exactly χ.

Four group elements. On Γ = (ℤ/2ℤ)² put α(a,b) = (−1)a and β(a,b) = (−1)b. Let ρ₁ = α ⊕ 1 and ρ₂ = β ⊕ 1. Both characters take the value −1 at (1,1), and both take the value 1 at (0,0). At (1,0) their values are −1 and 1. The two original polynomials there are (X+1)(X−1) and (X−1)². Adding β on the first side and α on the second gives (X+1)(X−1)² on each side. For every element the augmented representations have the same three summands, in different order. Removing α from ρ₁ and β from ρ₂ leaves the trivial character in both.

6.23What survives after one character line is removed?

Let V carry the current first representation ρ and let k v be the invariant line just constructed. Semisimplicity means that every invariant subspace has an invariant complement. M−1ρ(g)M = diag(σ(g),χ(g)),   dim W = dim V − 1.

The complement is semisimple. Given an invariant subspace U of W, take an invariant complement Y to U in V. Then W = U ⊕ (Y ∩ W). For continuity, observe that the matrix entries of σ are entries of the fixed conjugate above, and its inverse at g is σ(g−1).

Delete the chosen occurrence of χ from the first list and call the shorter list A′. The block formula factors Pρ(g) by X−χ(g), and the same factor appears in LA(g). It is a nonzero monic polynomial, so it cancels in the integral domain k[X], even when another eigenvalue has the very same value at g. The complement therefore satisfies the shortened identity.

Pσ(g) LB(g) = Pρ₂(g) LA′(g)   for every g ∈ Γ.

At each step both the dimension and the list length drop by one. If χ appears twice in A, the second occurrence remains available at the next step. Only equality across lists was excluded. After all t steps a continuous semisimple representation s of dimension n remains, with ρ₁ ≃ s ⊕ D(A). This removes precisely the prescribed number of copies. The source itself may have further copies of the same character.

6.24Which local statements pass to the rank-n representation?

Fix the two lifts. The residual representation s has already been chosen when we choose a finite place w. Suppose the first lift has prescribed parameters and that each removed character has its own known local parameter ci. Above ℓ, also prescribe the filtration jump mi(τ) of each character for every embedding τ of E into k inducing w. If the first lift has the following multisets, then s has the remaining parameters S and jumps J(τ).

S ⊎ {c1,…,ct},   J(τ) ⊎ {m1(τ),…,mt(τ)}.

Away from ℓ, inertia acts trivially on each block when it acts trivially on the first lift. The block determinant removes one Frobenius factor at a time. Above ℓ, the filtered de Rham period module of a direct sum is the direct sum of the filtered period modules. The de Rham condition therefore passes to each block, and the dimensions of each graded piece add. This subtracts precisely one copy of each prescribed jump at each embedding. Berger’s monodromy theorem makes these de Rham representations potentially semistable. Their Weil–Deligne parameters also form a direct sum. The crystalline condition on the whole gives trivial Weil–Deligne inertia and zero monodromy on both blocks, hence crystallinity of the remainder. For a Weil element of degree d, the cancelled polynomial is X−cid. Berger, Représentations p-adiques et équations différentielles[146] and Fontaine, Exposé VIII, §§2.1.1 and 2.3.3[147].

To recover the original normalization, choose a place w₀ ∈ Q. The two-lift theorem supplies a twist κ and first-list Hecke characters unramified there. For a source Satake multiset at that place, let S₀ be its algebraically normalized multiset and J₀(τ) its predicted jumps. If κ has infinity exponent mτ at the complex embedding corresponding to τ, subtraction leaves the data on the left.

s   (κ(w₀)−1S₀, J₀(τ)+mτ)   ⟶   s ⊗ κℓ   (S₀, J₀(τ)).

6.25The row and its adjoint

An automorphic form is a function on an arithmetic quotient of a group with specified transformation and regularity properties. A theta lift uses an integral kernel to carry such functions between groups. In the part of the proof examined here, the relevant spaces of forms at fixed level and weight are presented as finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces. This allows a precise question about nonvanishing before any local representation is identified.

Fix an index i. It specifies a row number j and a tuple of character data μ. Suppress these two subscripts. Write M for the row space and V for the target space. There is a linear map P from V to M. Its adjoint T goes from M to V. The row space has designated subspaces Mσ for its types σ. A type here labels a component of the space of forms. The target has subspaces Vπ for target types π.

The required Gram hypothesis says that PT acts by a real scalar λσ on Mσ, strictly positive whenever Mσ is nonzero. For every f in that subspace the adjoint identity gives

‖Tf‖2 = Re ⟨f, PTf⟩ = λσ ‖f‖2.

Thus a nonzero row vector survives the upward map. Positive semidefiniteness, which is automatic for an operator times its adjoint, would only yield λσ ≥ 0. Strict positivity is a genuine arithmetic input. The point-condition construction gets the local scalars from its linked isotropy and scalar hypotheses before calling the pairing theorem.

6.26Locating one target type

Call σ and π paired if there are f ∈ Mσ and v ∈ Vπ with ⟨v, Tf⟩ ≠ 0. Assume that the target subspaces span V, are pairwise orthogonal, and that for each σ at most one π can pair with it. The uniqueness property is the upward form of Howe duality in this argument.

Choose nonzero f in Mσ. If every target component were orthogonal to Tf, their span would also be orthogonal to it. This would force ⟨Tf, Tf⟩ = 0, contrary to the Gram identity. Some π therefore pairs with σ. Now take any g in the same row subspace. A nonzero inner product of Tg with a different component would supply a second paired type, contrary to uniqueness. Since the orthogonal components span V, Tg lies in Vπ. The entire image T(Mσ) is a nonzero subspace of Vπ.

In particular r < t, the inequality used in the local classification theorem. These are dimensions of underlying linear groups. The spaces of automorphic forms in the Gram calculation can have different dimensions.

A representation assigns an invertible linear action to each group element. A smooth representation of a group over K is one in which each vector is fixed by an open subgroup. An irreducible representation has no proper nonzero invariant subspace. Unitarisability asks for an invariant positive inner product. The classification step takes a smooth, irreducible, unitarisable representation τ of GLr(K), a smooth irreducible representation Π of GLr+t(K), and a smooth unitary character μ of K×. Its pairing hypothesis asks for a nonzero equivariant bilinear map on test functions and vectors. The test functions are locally constant and compactly supported on the space of (r + t)-by-r matrices. Equivariance says that acting on the function and the target vector is compatible with the source group action. The actual comparison applies this condition to a determinant twist of the target representation.

Given the stated inputs on finiteness and irreducibility of induced representations, the local theorem identifies Π with the parabolically induced product of τ and μ ∘ det on GLt(K). Parabolic induction here uses the subgroup of upper block triangular matrices, with diagonal blocks of sizes r and t. These blocks act on the tensor product of the two input representations. The construction extends this action to the full group by induction. In the application, Π is the twisted target and the comparison removes the twist afterward.

What information survives on the Galois side? A local parameter records the local representation in a form with well-defined direct sums and twists by characters. At each split place w, let Aw denote the source parameter and μw the parameter of the character. Write μw[b] for its real-power twist with exponent b. Let ηw−1 denote the final inverse character in this normalization. The paired target has parameter

(Aw ⊕ ⨁0≤h<t μw[(t − 1)/2 − h]) ⊗ ηw−1.

There are t one-dimensional terms. Their exponents decrease by one from (t − 1)/2 to −(t − 1)/2. They account for the entire increase in rank. The parameter-translation laws turn the induced product into a sum, identify the segment for μ ∘ det, and then remove the determinant twist to give η⁻¹ on the full sum.

A rank check. If k = 6, m = 2 and t = 13, the rank formula gives r = 7 and target rank 20. The extra block has 13 character terms with exponents 6, 5, …, −6. ⟨ΘφF, ΘφF⟩ = vol(Yj+1) · L₀ · I / dS(t/2).

Its Euler product converges and is nonzero at (t + 1)/2 because t ≥ r + 5. Each previous step also contributed a length-t segment. The proof uses the distinct infinity exponents of these characters to obtain an entire partial L-function nonzero at every integer from 1 through t. At the desired point the segment arguments are

t/2 + ½ + (t − 1)/2 − h = t − h,   0 ≤ h < t.

The induction applies the same argument to x with this new family.

For b > 2a, the series identity applies in the convergence region s₀ > a/2. When the two source integrals are paired, the squared norm of each kernel on the target grows at most polynomially. Cuspidal rapid decay makes the absolute triple integral finite, so the target pairing can be performed first. Converting the normalized target mean into the Petersson integral multiplies it by vol([H]). This produces a holomorphic continuation value of the full doubling integral. The proof first works at the frame lattice, then transfers it to the given self-dual lattice.

On the theta side, integrate the doubled kernel over the target quotient [H] and divide by its volume. Its convergence and the region of absolute convergence of the Eisenstein series are two different statements.

The Levi action contributes χB−1(det M) and the normalized absolute determinant to the power s₀ + a/2 = b/2. The compact translates of the Fock vector span a finite-dimensional space. Applying the linear section map to that space gives the same finiteness for the compact translates of f. To move away from s₀, multiply f(g) by the positive Siegel height h(g)s−s₀. In the range b ≤ 2a the proof changes coordinates to a standard Schrödinger model, in which the theta kernel is a sum of a Schwartz–Bruhat function over rational vectors. The chart and a translation put the chosen compact data into standard position and carry the Fock polynomial to a polynomial Gaussian at infinity. Where does the strict half-plane come from?

At the identity, let hγ be the positive height of a representative of a rational Siegel coset. The spherical section to be summed has magnitude hγT, with T = Re s + a/2. Arithmetic reduction assigns to each coset a tuple j of a nonnegative integers. For a base B > 1 and a constant C, its height is at most C B−∑j. For any fixed tuple the number of cosets in any finite sample with this label is at most C Ba∑j. Multiplying those bounds gives a bound for the whole label.

∑γ with label j hγT ≤ C1+T (Ba−T)∑j.

For T > a, summing over the tuple gives a product of a geometric series with common ratio Ba−T < 1. This bounds every finite subsum, establishing summability of the nonnegative spherical majorant. Iwasawa decomposition and the bound for the section on the compact subgroup transfer convergence to the flat section and its translates. The terms vary holomorphically in s through powers of positive heights. Choose a small vertical strip around the point, with both edges inside the half-plane. Each term is bounded in absolute value throughout the strip by the sum of its absolute values at the two endpoint real parts, since a positive height raised to a real exponent is monotone in that exponent. Both endpoint majorants are summable. The holomorphic terms therefore converge locally uniformly.

Choose a dyadic scale ai with ‖φwi‖ ≤ ai < 2‖φwi‖. Dividing each row by its scale bounds every entry of the resulting matrix c. Take all D integral-basis multiples of each of the n selected rows. They span a full-rank sublattice of the original row lattice, of index m ≥ 1. Its squared volume is m² det Gram(φu). Each of the D real rows coming from wi carries the same scale ai. With G(c) the Gram determinant of all the rescaled rows, we get

(m covol(L))² = (∏ aiD)² G(c).

The product of the scales is bounded in the form ∏ aiD ≤ 2rrr/2 covol(L). Cancel the covolume. This bounds m² by a constant times G(c). Since m ≥ 1, it also bounds G(c) away from zero. On the bounded closed set of matrix entries this continuous determinant has a finite upper bound. Its positive lower bound keeps c in an invertible compact set, where inversion is bounded. The upper bound gives a uniform bound for the integer m. Taking the factorial of an integer upper bound makes one integer M divisible by every possible m. Multiplication by M therefore puts every original row in the module generated by the selected rows.

Use the same rows at every finite place. Write Ō for the product of the local integer rings at finite places. Given the finite adelic block β, take Λ = {x ∈ En ∣ xβ ∈ Ōn}. An integer clearing the denominators of β shows that Λ contains a multiple of every coordinate row. Clearing the denominators of β−1 bounds Λ inside one fractional free module. As the ring of integers is Noetherian, Λ is finitely generated. Apply the argument at infinity to Λ and call the selected row matrix Δ. The entries of Δβ are integral by construction. For its inverse, choose positive integers d₁,d₂ clearing the denominators of β and Δ−1, respectively. Approximate a row of β−1 by a rational row x so that their difference belongs to d₁d₂Ōn. Multiplying by β shows that xβ is integral. Hence x belongs to Λ, and Mx is an integral combination of the rows of Δ. Multiplication by Δ−1 gives integral entries for MxΔ−1. The original approximation error still has integral entries after multiplication by MΔ−1. This proves that M(Δβ)−1 is integral at every finite place. Together with the compact real block this is the uniform reduction used for the height label.

Why the second row can require the third minimum

Use E = ℚ(i), n = 2, and the ordinary Euclidean norm on ℂ². Let the finite block be diag(1,1/3) above 3 and the identity elsewhere. Its rational row lattice is Λ = ℤ[i]e₁ ⊕ 3ℤ[i]e₂. The first two independent real vectors can be e₁ and ie₁. They span just one line over E. Every row outside that line has length at least 3, attained by 3e₂. The four real minima are 1,1,3,3. The two chosen field rows have squared lengths 1 and 9, whose product equals the covolume 9. The dyadic scales 1 and 4 give the real block diag(1,3/4). Its inverse is diag(1,4/3). With Δ = diag(1,3), the finite block Δβ is the identity above 3 and diag(1,3) elsewhere. Both matrices and their inverses have integral entries at the places where they occur.

Count the centres for a fixed label. At scalar depth k, subtract a rational element from an adele of F to put it in a fixed compact set. Bound its real components in absolute value by a nonnegative integer R. At each real place use the grid 2−kℤ between −R and R. Its integer numerators have exactly 2·2kR + 1 possibilities. Rounding leaves an error of size at most 2−k. The finite component stays in a fixed compact set. Across the d real places the number of scalar centres is bounded by C₀ bk, where b = 2d, C₀ = (2R + 1)d and B = b².

Choose δ in E with conjugate −δ so that (1,δ) is an F-basis. A skew-Hermitian matrix S can be described by n² scalar adelic coordinates tij. Its (i,j) entry is (tij−tji) + δ(tij+tji). On the diagonal this is 2δtii. Off the diagonal the two ordered entries share two scalar coordinates. Cover tij at depth μi+μj. Its error then carries the factor corresponding to the left and right diagonal scalings. Combining the coordinate choices writes S as a rational matrix plus a centre y plus DμωDμ, where Dμ = diag(sμᵢ) and the entries of ω lie in a fixed compact set. The finite set Yμ of centres is the image of the product of the scalar grids. Its size is at most the number of grid tuples.

|Yμ| ≤ ∏i,j C₀ bμᵢ+μⱼ = C₀n² b2n∑μᵢ = C₀n² Bn∑μᵢ.

A rank-two count. Take one real place, a scalar grid with R = 1 and label μ = (1,0). The four ordered depths are 2, 1, 1 and 0. The corresponding lists of integer numerators have 9, 5, 5 and 3 entries. Their product gives 675 tuples. The formula above permits 3⁴·4² = 1,296. These numbers count candidates and bound their image. Counting rational cosets still requires the multiplicity argument.

Why a centre has bounded multiplicity. Subtract the rational unipotent term and put the compact error into a matrix w(q). In the Cayley coordinates the proof obtains a rational invertible matrix Z(q) = z(μ,y)w(q), with w(q) in a fixed compact set. The map q ↦ Z(q) is injective. In fact, equality of two such matrices makes the original rational representatives differ on the left by an element stabilizing the diagonal subspace. They represent the same Siegel coset.

Fix μ and a centre y. For a nonempty finite collection of cosets using them, choose one member q₀. Multiplying by Z(q₀)−1 cancels the common left factor z(μ,y). The relative matrices w(q₀)−1w(q) are rational and belong to a fixed compact set, independent of μ, y and q₀. Each matrix entry belongs to a finite set of rational points, so there are at most N possible relative matrices. Left multiplication preserves injectivity. Each chosen centre can therefore account for at most N cosets. Summing over all available centres gives an upper bound even when some centres are unused and others occur for multiple cosets.

#{q ∈ A with label μ} ≤ N |Yμ| ≤ N C₀n² Bn∑μᵢ   for every finite sample A.

A uniform finite bound on all finite samples also bounds the full fibre, since a larger fibre would contain a finite sample exceeding it. The summability proof uses exactly the finite-sample statement. Multiplication by the height bound raised to the power T gives the geometric decay when T > n.

How do the Fourier coefficients recover the theta mean?

Consider the lower range of the Siegel–Weil formula. Write n for the source rank and m for the dimension of the target Hermitian space V over the quadratic extension E/F. Thus n < m ≤ 2n and n + w < m, where w is the Witt index of V. The evaluation point s₀ = (m − n)/2 can lie on the boundary of absolute convergence or to its left. Take a test function Φ in the global Fock subspace of the Schrödinger model. With this input we can compare one frequency of the two sides at a time. The frequencies are rational Hermitian n × n matrices β. A frequency is nondegenerate when det β ≠ 0.

For an automorphic function F, move g by the upper unipotent matrix u(b) with diagonal blocks 1 and upper right block b. Invariance under rational unipotent translations makes this function of b periodic. Its domain is the Hermitian adelic matrices modulo the rational ones. Use a fundamental region 𝒟 of volume one. Put ⟨β,b⟩ = ½ TrE/F(tr(βb)), with rational entries embedded in the adeles and the field trace extended to the adeles.

Cβ(F)(g) = ∫𝒟 F(u(b)g) ψ(−⟨β,b⟩) db.

On the theta side, a frequency selects a Gram matrix. Write φ = ω(g)Φ for the translated test function. A rational tuple x of n vectors of V contributes φ(h−1x) to the theta kernel. Translating by u(b) multiplies this summand by ψ(⟨Gram(x),b⟩). The target action of h preserves the Gram matrix. After weighting by the inverse β-character, integration gives 1 if Gram(x) = β and 0 otherwise. Absolute theta convergence justifies grouping tuples by Gram matrix, averaging over [U(V)] and integrating the resulting character series. When det β ≠ 0, every tuple in that fibre has rank n, since rank(x∗Gram(V)x) ≤ rank(x). Thus Cβ(I)(g) is the normalized average of the sum over precisely these full-rank tuples, where I is the theta mean.

On the Eisenstein side, the same frequency selects the open cell. For Re z > n/2 the coset sum has a summable bound on a compact set of representatives. This permits integration of the sum by cells. On each other cell, when det β ≠ 0, there is a translation preserving its contribution and multiplying its character by a scalar different from 1. Its integral is therefore zero. The open-cell cosets are indexed by rational Hermitian translations. Their translates of 𝒟 cover the full adelic Hermitian space, giving the integral below. Here w is the Weyl element interchanging the two isotropic coordinate spaces and fz is the flat section.

Cβ(E(·,z))(g) = ∫Hermn(𝔸) fz(w u(b)g) ψ(−⟨β,b⟩) db.

The Weyl action is a Fourier transform. Evaluating it at zero integrates the translated test function against the Gram character. Consequently the section in this integral is the Gram-character integral of φ times the height H(w u(b)g)z−s₀. This identifies the unfolded family on the right half-plane with the Whittaker integral for β. Its holomorphic value at s₀ is the same full-rank fibre average computed on the theta side. The input used here combines finite-place factors, the unramified Gram-density calculation, a real-place computation, global factorization and a low-rank density identity. Finite linear combination treats the compact argument, then the Iwasawa decomposition transports the identity to arbitrary g.

What can be invisible to all the nondegenerate coefficients?

Take the additive group of symmetric 2 × 2 matrices over the field of three elements. This finite example has 27 elements. Set ζ = exp(2πi/3), T = diag(1,0) and F(B) = ζB₁₁. The normalized β-coefficient is the average of ζtr((T−β)B). At β = T all 27 terms are 1. For β ≠ T, at least one of the three matrix coordinates has a nonzero coefficient in this linear form. Its sum is 1 + ζ + ζ² = 0. The off-diagonal entry appears with multiplier 2, which is invertible in this field. Hence every invertible β has coefficient zero, although F(0) = 1. The missing information sits at the rank-one frequency T.

How does the proof rule out such a discrepancy? At a real place selected using the Witt-index inequality, choose a compactly supported test function η whose Fourier transform vanishes on singular Hermitian matrices. Suppose a continuous automorphic function F has zero full-rank coefficients for all g. Integrate its unipotent translates against η. The β-coefficient of this convolution factors into the β-coefficient of F and the transform of η at the associated local frequency. For invertible β the first factor is zero. For singular β the associated local matrix is singular too, so the second factor is zero. All Fourier coefficients of the convolution now vanish, so Fourier uniqueness on the compact Hermitian quotient makes the convolution zero. Density and continuity give the same vanishing with a group translation on either side of the unipotent argument.

Removing a possible pole and computing the value

At this real place, first take the Gaussian Fock vector (the constant polynomial 1). The local signature condition gives a choice of η and of the two translations for which a compact-group average defines an operator T with nonzero scalar c(0) on the theta mean of this vector. On the corresponding regularized Eisenstein family the scalar is c(z−s₀). Meanwhile, the convolution argument shows that T kills every automorphic discrepancy with zero full-rank coefficients. On a discrepancy with eigenvalue c(0), this forces the discrepancy itself to vanish.

To see where holomorphy enters, write the continued Eisenstein family as A(z)/d(z) with holomorphic numerator and polynomial denominator. Factor d(z) = (z−s₀)kd₁(z) with d₁(s₀) ≠ 0. The full-rank coefficient identities ensure that while a power remains in the denominator, the regularized numerator at the point has zero full-rank coefficients. Its eigenvalue forces that value to vanish, so one can divide the numerator by z−s₀ holomorphically and repeat. After k divisions, the difference between the resulting numerator at s₀ and d₁(s₀)I is killed by T and has eigenvalue c(0). It is zero. Division by d₁ now gives the required value.

What does a full-rank Whittaker factor count at a good finite place?

The open-cell integral compares a Fourier coefficient of the Eisenstein series with the mean of tuples of vectors having Gram matrix T. At a good finite place v, this comparison has a concrete arithmetic content. Count the tuples whose Gram matrix agrees with T modulo increasing powers of a uniformizer. Once the measures are fixed, the normalized count gives the local Whittaker value at z₀ = (M−n)/2, where M is the dimension of the Hermitian space and n is the number of vectors.

Write q for the size of the residue field of Fv. At the places treated here, 2 is a unit, the local quadratic algebra is unramified, the forms J and T are integral with unit determinant, and the scalar character ψv has conductor the valuation ring. The integral lattice is trace-self-dual. Set ε = −1 when the quadratic algebra is the unramified field, and ε = +1 when it splits. The Schwartz function is the characteristic function of the integral M × n matrix lattice. A nonzero rational det T gives this unit condition at almost all places.

Count one Gram fibre. Let Nk be the number of distinct matrices X modulo ϖk satisfying X∗JX ≡ T. Here ∗ is conjugate transpose. There are q2kMn possible input matrices and qkn² Hermitian targets. The density compares the proportion of matrices in this fibre with the proportion one would obtain if every target occurred equally often.

αk(J,T) = Nk · qkn²/q2kMn = ∏j=0n−1 (1 − (ε/q)M−j),   k ≥ 1,   n ≤ M.

At level one a change of basis reduces the unimodular target to the identity. Solutions are orthonormal frames over the residue algebra. Choose one vector of norm one, then choose the next in its orthogonal complement. In dimension r, the norm-one count is q2r−1(1−(ε/q)r). The successive dimensions M, …, M−n+1 give the product above after normalization.

Why does the density stay constant at deeper levels?

Lift a solution modulo ϖk by writing its next representative as X+ϖkY. For k ≥ 1 the quadratic term in Y disappears modulo ϖk+1. The correction must solve the linear equation Y∗JX+X∗JY = H in the residue algebra, with H Hermitian. It is solvable for every H. For instance, since 2 and T are invertible here, take Y = ½XT−1H. The linear map has a domain with q2Mn elements and a codomain with qn² elements. Every fibre has q2Mn−n² elements. Thus Nk+1 gains exactly the factor cancelled by the next density normalization.

A Gram fibre over nine elements. Take ℚ(i) over ℚ at the inert prime 3, J = I₃ and T = I₂. Then q = 3 and ε = −1. In 𝔽₉ the norm of a+bi is a²+b² in 𝔽₃. There are 252 choices for a norm-one column of length three. For each, its two-dimensional orthogonal complement has 24 norm-one columns. This gives 6,048 frames among 9⁶ matrices at the first level. The normalized density is 6,048/3⁸ = 224/243 = (1+3−3)(1−3−2). Each frame has 3⁸ lifts to level two.

Which integral gives this number? Use the self-dual Haar measure on the matrix space for its Weil pairing and the self-dual Haar measure on the Hermitian matrices for their trace pairing. Write ⟨T,b⟩ for half the quadratic-algebra trace of tr(Tb). The source integrates the following expression in b. Inside it the character has positive Gram phase, and the Fourier projection contributes the negative target phase. The height is h(b) = vol(L+bL)/vol(L) for the standard column lattice L. The auxiliary Haar measure in this ratio cancels.

Wv(z) = ∫ h(b)−(z−z₀) ψv(−⟨T,b⟩) (∫integral X ψv(⟨b,X∗JX⟩) dX) db,   Re z > n².

At a good place the Hermitian integral lattice has volume one. Grouping by its cosets rewrites the integral as a sum. The cosets appear in increasing finite sets indexed by a level k. With t = εMq−(2z+n), their sums of absolute values have a geometric majorant because qn²|t| < 1 in the stated half-plane. Each positive-level sum is the same polynomial in t.

How do congruence counts determine a polynomial?

At each positive level the finite Fourier sum is a polynomial Pk(t) whose terms are weighted by the level character at the negative target, and by a nonnegative lattice-index exponent of t. Evaluate it at t = (ε/q)m for each auxiliary rank m ≥ n. Finite Fourier orthogonality and the Gaussian sums identify that evaluation with the density of T for the identity form in dimension m. The counting formula just proved gives ∏j(1−(ε/q)m−j). This equals the evaluation of ∏j(1−t(εq)j) at the same point. Those points have distinct absolute values, so the two polynomials agree everywhere. The auxiliary rank varies only in this interpolation step.

Wv(z) = ∏j=0n−1 (1−εM+jq−(2z+n−j)),   Wv(z₀) = α₁(J,T).

The product extends to an entire function of z. Substituting 2z₀ = M−n gives exactly the density, since εM+j = εM−j. In the example z₀ = ½, while the integral theorem assumes Re z > 4. The continued value is therefore obtained by evaluating the explicit product.

From places to the global coefficient. The pure adelic datum is standard outside a finite set. The global construction multiplies the real factor, the finitely many exceptional factors and the product of the explicit good factors. The last product is holomorphic on Re z > 0. Agreement on a sufficiently far right half-plane identifies the continuation of the global integral. Since n < M, z₀ lies in this positive half-plane. The remaining identification with the theta coefficient uses the global density theorem equating the product of the real and finite densities at T with the normalized mean of the rational Gram fibre. The comparison then returns through Iwasawa decomposition and the open-cell identity to the coefficient at every group argument.

Apply the strict-rank theorem with the extra range assumption n+2 ≤ M or anisotropy of J, and with an integrability hypothesis on a right half-plane. Its general statement also has an implication imposing a Gaussian vacuum condition if a flag is true. In this branch the flag is false, so that particular implication is automatic. The congruence counts, the Whittaker integral and the density-to-mean identity all enter separately. For the example with M = 3 and n = 2 the positive-definite identity form over ℚ(i) is anisotropic over that field.

What replaces the good-place formula at an exceptional finite place?

The good-place count assumes a particular test function, the indicator of the full matrix lattice. A test supported on just one residue class can change the answer even at an unramified prime. The local argument works at every finite place and gives an entire function of the complex parameter z. Its value at s₀ = (M−n)/2 is the density of the chosen test at the target Gram matrix. The global application has n < M.

Fix the local quadratic algebra Ev = Fv ⊗F E, the local component ψv of the adelic additive character, a nondegenerate Hermitian form J of rank M, and a Hermitian target T of size n whose determinant is invertible in Ev. This allows determinants of nonzero valuation. A test Φ is a locally constant, compactly supported function of the M × n matrix X. Use the self-dual measures μ on the matrix space and ν on the Hermitian space for their respective pairings. For a Haar measure λ on Evn and two compact open additive subgroups L₁, L₂, put r(b) = λ(L₁+bL₂)/λ(L₁). It is at least one. Write ⟨b,S⟩ for half the field-algebra trace of the matrix trace of bS. The opposite signs single out the fibre X∗JX = T.

u(b) = ∫ Φ(X) ψv(⟨b,X∗JX−T⟩) dμ(X),   Wv(z) = ∫ r(b)−(z−s₀) u(b) dν(b)   for Re z sufficiently large.

Why can one compact ball determine an entire function? On a shell R < ‖b‖ ≤ 2R, change variables by b ↦ (1+x)∗b(1+x), with x in a small additive matrix ball of radius C/R. These changes preserve the shell, its Haar measure, the lattice index and the integral containing the positive Gram phase. The negative target phase acquires a term linear in x and a term quadratic in x. The latter has norm bounded by a constant times R(C/R)², so the character is trivial on it for large R. Invertibility of T lets one choose C so that at every b in the shell the linear term gives a nontrivial character of the x-ball. Its Haar integral is zero. Averaging the change of variables therefore kills the shell integral for every z, with one cutoff valid for all z. At a singular target the linear term can lose this oscillation, and the stated density hypothesis covers only the regular set.

Choose a ball B₀ beyond that cutoff and double its radius successively. Adding any of the resulting shells leaves the integral over B₀ unchanged. On B₀ the index and its logarithm are bounded, so one can differentiate the compact integral with respect to z. This gives an entire Wv, with no poles. A separate absolute estimate identifies it with the original integral on a right half-plane. For radii growing by a fixed local dilation, the jth outer shell has r(b) ≥ 2j and volume at most a constant times κj. Thus the integral of the absolute value has a geometric majorant when Re z is large. The statement requires existence of a real threshold depending on the data.

How does the test enter the value? Let g be the supplied continuous density of the pushforward of Φ dμ by X ↦ X∗JX on the open set of invertible targets. At z = s₀ the lattice weight is one. Integrating over a large additive ball Λ in b retains those X whose Gram matrix belongs to T+Λ⊥. Indeed, the average of the phase on Λ is one when the difference annihilates Λ and zero otherwise. The annihilator shrinks into the regular set around T, and self-duality gives ν(Λ)ν(Λ⊥) = 1. The integral is therefore an average of g near T. By continuity it approaches g(T). Every sufficiently large ball already gives Wv(s₀).

∫Λ u(b) dν(b) = (1/ν(Λ⊥)) ∫T+Λ⊥ g(S) dν(S)   ⟶   g(T) = Wv(s₀).
Compute the entire factor for one residue class at 3

Take E = ℚ(i), F = ℚ and the inert prime 3. Let J be the two-dimensional identity, n = 1, T = 1 and L₁ = L₂ = 𝒪Eᵥ. Use a character of conductor ℤ₃. The standard integral lattices have self-dual volume one here. Let Φ be the indicator of X ≡ (1,0) modulo 3. There are four scalar coordinates over ℤ₃, so this class has mass 1/81. Its Gram value N(X₁)+N(X₂) belongs to 1+3ℤ₃. For each lift to the next power of 3, the derivative in the real coordinate of X₁ is 2 modulo 3. For each choice of the other three digits, exactly one digit of this coordinate gives the required next Gram digit. Thus the mass is uniform on 1+3ℤ₃, a set of volume 1/3, and the density there is 1/27.

Integration of the character on this coset, including the negative target phase, gives u(b) = (1/81) · 𝟙3⁻¹ℤ₃(b). On ℤ₃ the lattice index is one. On the shell 3⁻¹ℤ₃ ∖ ℤ₃, of volume two, its value is nine because the residue field of Ev has nine elements. In this example the original integral has compact support and converges at every z.

W₃(z) = (1 + 2 · 9−(z−1/2))/81,   W₃(1/2) = 1/27.

Now keep J = I₂ and T = 1, and restore the full-lattice test. There are 24 norm-one columns modulo 3. At every such column at least one scalar derivative of the norm is nonzero modulo 3, so each residue class contributes the same density 1/27. Summing the 24 contributions gives 24/27 = 8/9, the good-place answer in these same dimensions.

Which domain reaches the global coefficient? The local proof uses no rank inequality to construct the entire function once a density is given. The global theorem supplies these densities from the normalized Gram mean when n < M and either n+2 ≤ M or J is anisotropic. It chooses a finite set S outside which the forms, measures, lattices and test meet the good-place conditions. On Re z > 0 multiply the archimedean function, the finitely many entire factors Wv for v ∈ S, and the convergent good-place product. Farther right this equals the adelic integral for the full-rank Fourier coefficient. The point s₀ lies inside the global half-plane by the strict rank inequality. Substituting the local density values gives the normalized Gram mean there. The resulting global continuation is holomorphic on Re z > 0.

Why is the archimedean Whittaker factor entire at a nonsingular target?

At infinity the Fourier variable ranges over Hermitian matrices. For a target with nonzero determinant, integration by parts trades oscillation in this variable for extra decay. Repeating this operation reaches every complex parameter. The value at s₀ = (M−n)/2 recovers the density of the test on the target Gram fibre, as in the finite-place calculation.

Start at one real place. A frame identifies the Hermitian form with J = diag(1p,−1q), with p+q = M. The character on ℝ is u ↦ exp(2πiℓu) for a real ℓ ≠ 0. Set t = 2πℓ and c = 2π|ℓ|. In these coordinates the test on a complex M × n matrix X is a polynomial P in the entries of X and their conjugates, multiplied by exp(−c∑|Xᵢⱼ|²). Define A(Y) by integrating this test against the positive phase exp(it tr(YX∗JX)). The Whittaker coefficient uses the negative phase at the target B. Write D(Y) = det(I+Y²) and w = z−s₀. The integration measure here is Lebesgue measure in the n² real coordinates yᵢⱼ = Re Yᵢⱼ + Im Yᵢⱼ.

W(w) = ∫ D(Y)−w A(Y) exp(−it tr(BY)) dY   for Re w sufficiently large.

One determinant derivative moves the convergence line. Put s = sign(ℓ). Gaussian integration gives A as a polynomial in the entries of (I−isY)−1 and (I+isY)−1, multiplied by the determinants of those inverses to powers p and q respectively. Let Δ be the determinant of the matrix of first derivatives in Hermitian coordinates. Integration by parts shows that the negative Fourier transform of Δf is (it)ndet(B) times that of f, whenever the derivatives are integrable. As det(B) ≠ 0, one can divide by this scalar.

For the decay estimate, diagonalize Y with real eigenvalues λj. Cauchy's derivative estimate uses a radius proportional to √((1+|λi|)(1+|λj|)) in matrix entry (i,j). Each determinant term differentiates once in every row and column. The product of the reciprocal radii thus supplies a factor proportional to ∏j(1+|λj|)−1 ≤ D(Y)−1/2. After N determinants, differentiating the weight D−w leaves that weight times a polynomial in w of degree at most nN with coefficient functions of Y. At integer weights 0 through nN one can absorb the weight into the two determinant powers. Polynomial interpolation transfers the same decay bound to the coefficient functions. On compact parameter sets the differentiated amplitude is bounded by a constant times D(Y)−Re w−(M+N)/2.

Where does the determinant come from in two rows?

Write the diagonal entries of the Hermitian integration variable as x,y and its upper-right entry as u+iv. For a Hermitian target with diagonal a,b and upper-right entry c+id, the trace pairing is ax + by + 2cu + 2dv. Its negative Fourier phase is the exponential of this expression times −it. In these unscaled entry coordinates the determinant derivative is ∂x∂y − (∂u² + ∂v²)/4. Applying it to the phase gives (it)²(ab − c² − d²) times the same phase. Integration by parts twice transfers the derivative to the amplitude with positive sign.

For diagonal entries 2 and 3 and upper-right entry 1 + i, the multiplier is −4t², which we may divide out. For the matrix with every entry equal to one it is zero, although the target itself is nonzero. This is why the hypothesis concerns the determinant. In the derivative estimate the two permutations also have the same decay. The mixed diagonal derivative costs one inverse radius for each diagonal entry, while two off-diagonal derivatives each cost the inverse geometric mean of those radii.

The integral defining WN is holomorphic on UN because D(Y)−σ is integrable for σ > n²/2. On Re w > n²/2 every WN agrees with the original integral by repeated integration by parts. The identity theorem gives equality throughout each connected overlap. The increasing half-planes cover ℂ, giving one entire function.

What fixes the value at w = 0? Now the weight is one. Applying ΔN to A inserts ((it)ndet(X∗JX))N in its defining Gaussian integral. For N = n²+1 the resulting transform is integrable. Fourier inversion with a Gaussian cutoff identifies its inverse transform against compactly supported tests. On the open set det(B) ≠ 0 we can divide by the inserted determinant, obtaining the continuous density g(B) of X ↦ X∗JX for the polynomial Gaussian. The exponent in the Fourier normalization is the real dimension of the Hermitian target.

W(0) = (2π/|t|)n² g(B).
Two complex Gaussian variables and one real Fourier variable

Take n = 1, M = 2, signature (1,1), ℓ = 1, and P = 1 in the one-place Lebesgue model. Then s₀ = 1/2. The Gram value is |x₁|²−|x₂|². Since ∫ℂexp(−a|x|²) dx = π/a for Re a > 0, the two rows give factors 1/[2(1−iy)] and 1/[2(1+iy)]. Thus A(y) = 1/[4(1+y²)]. The absolute integral converges exactly for Re w > −1/2.

In radial coordinates u = |x₁|² and v = |x₂|² the measure is π² exp(−2π(u+v)) du dv. Integrating along u−v = B gives g(B) = (π/4) exp(−2π|B|). For B ≠ 0 this equals W(0). Differentiating the scalar Fourier transform of 1/(a²+y²) with respect to a at a = 1 gives W(1) = (π/8)(1+2π|B|)exp(−2π|B|). At w = −1 the weighted amplitude is the constant 1/4. Its second derivative vanishes, and −1 belongs to U₂, so the continued value is zero. At the singular target B = 0, the phase is constant. As real w decreases to −1/2 the positive integral tends to infinity, since its limiting tail is proportional to 1/|y|. This is where the invertibility hypothesis matters.

Why does a product of local Gram densities give a global mean?

At one finite place a density measures how often a tuple has a prescribed Gram matrix. A rational tuple must satisfy the same equations at every place. To bring these two descriptions together the proof averages over all adelic isometries of a single rational Hermitian space. Let E/F be the CM extension, J the nondegenerate Hermitian form on EM, and T a rational nonsingular Hermitian matrix of size n. The theorem assumes n < M, with either n+2 ≤ M or J anisotropic over E. Anisotropic means that a rational vector of norm zero must itself be zero. The test Φ has a Schwartz factor at infinity and locally constant, compactly supported factors at finite places. Almost all finite factors are the characteristic function of the standard lattice. At every place the two Hermitian matrices come from these same rational forms, and each local additive character comes from one global character.

Let H = U(J), and choose a fundamental domain 𝒟 for its rational points in its adelic group. For each h sum Φ(h−1X) over the rational solutions of X∗JX = T. Replacing h by γh for a rational isometry γ permutes these solutions by X ↦ γ−1X. The sum therefore defines a function on the quotient. Integrate it over 𝒟 using Haar measure and divide by vol(𝒟). Equivalently one can first add the measures obtained by moving each rational tuple under h ↦ h−1X, normalizing their sum by the same volume, then integrate Φ. Countability of the rational tuples and integrability justify this equivalence.

vol(𝒟)−1 ∫𝒟 ∑X rational, X∗JX=T Φ(h−1X) dh = g∞(T) ∏v finite gv(T).
Why can grouping the terms change their weights?

A finite group makes the Haar weights visible. Take H to be the six permutations of three letters and put Γ = K = {id,(12)}. A function constant on ΓhK has just two values. The class of the identity contains two permutations. The class of (13) contains the remaining four. Indeed the size of ΓhK is |Γ||K|/|Γ ∩ hKh−1|, and the two intersection sizes are 2 and 1. If the function takes values 2 and 5, the normalized Haar average is (2·2 + 4·5)/6 = 4. Giving both classes weight ½ would give 3½. The same issue arises when a quotient integral is grouped into classes, whose weights come from their volumes. The definition above keeps that weighting by integrating on a fundamental domain.

What fixes the measure on one Gram fibre?

A global product uses the local integral at a specified target T. An identity averaged over T leaves open what happens at an individual target of measure zero. The extra condition that fixes the answer is continuity of the fibre integrals on the nonsingular targets.

Regular Gram-fibre theorem. Work at a completion R of the base field F of the CM extension E/F. Let V be the space of n-tuples of vectors for the scalar extension to R ⊗F E of a nonsingular Hermitian form J on EM. The Gram map G sends a tuple to its matrix of pairings in the space H of Hermitian n × n matrices. Let B be the open set where the determinant is invertible and fix additive Haar measures μ on V and ν on H. There is a unique family of measures mT carried by G−1{T} for T ∈ B, set equal to zero outside B, with the following two properties.

∫G−1(B) φ dμ = ∫B (∫ φ dmT) dν(T)   for every nonnegative measurable φ.

For every real continuous φ compactly supported inside G−1(B), the inner integral is finite and depends continuously on T ∈ B. An empty fibre carries the zero measure. The integration formula concerns the part of the source lying over B.

How one open set of targets acquires its measures

Fix a nonsingular target T₀. The local congruence-section theorem supplies a subgroup L of changes of basis for the tuple such that h ↦ h·T₀ is a homeomorphism onto an open neighborhood of T₀. Here the target action is congruence, and G(h·z) = h·G(z). A tuple above this neighborhood therefore has unique coordinates (h, z) with z in the reference fibre G−1{T₀}. Recover h from the target and act by h−1 on the tuple to recover z.

Write χV(h) and χH(h) for the factors by which pushing forward μ and ν under h multiplies them. Pull μ back to the product coordinates and multiply by the density χV(h). Translating the group coordinate now preserves the result. Applying the same correction χH(h) to the target measure gives a left Haar measure λ on L. The corrected source measure is λ times a measure m₀ on the reference fibre. Indeed, for each relatively compact measurable fibre set A, the masses of rectangles U × A give a locally finite left-invariant measure in U. Haar uniqueness makes it a constant times λ. A fixed compact neighborhood K of the identity gives that constant as the mass of K × A divided by λ(K). This defines m₀, and exhaustion gives the product identity. Undoing the corrections gives mh·T₀ = [χH(h)/χV(h)] h∗m₀. For a compactly supported continuous test, continuity follows by integration on the fixed reference fibre. Near any fixed h, the translated test supports meet the fibre in a common compact set. Sutherland, Theorem 13.3 on Haar measure[27].

How do the entries of a Hermitian matrix give local coordinates?

Let R be a completion of the totally real field F, and K = R ⊗F E for the CM extension E/F. At a real place K = ℂ. At a finite place it is a quadratic local field or the product R × R with the two factors interchanged. Write * for transpose followed by conjugation. Fix an invertible Hermitian matrix S of size n. We seek a continuous choice of q near the identity that solves q*S q = T as T varies near S.

First choose coordinates in which the centre is diagonal. Even an invertible matrix can have a zero first diagonal entry, as does the two-by-two matrix with ones off the diagonal and zeros on it. A nonsingular Hermitian form of positive dimension has a vector of nonzero length. Indeed, if every length vanished, expanding the lengths of v + w and v + αw, with α an invertible scalar whose conjugate is −α, would force both the sum and the difference of a pairing and its conjugate to vanish. Every pairing would be zero. A vector of nonzero length splits off an orthogonal line. To do this, subtract from any vector its projection onto that line, dividing by the length. The orthogonal complement is nonsingular, so repeating gives S = b*D b with b invertible and D = diag(d₁,…,dₙ), each dᵢ in R×. At a finite place this means nonzero in the local field. The length may have positive valuation.

Triangular coordinates near D. Write the first row of a nearby Hermitian matrix as (p, r), and let C be its lower-right block. If p ≠ 0, direct multiplication gives

(prr∗C)=N1∗diag(p,C−r∗r/p)N1,   N1=(1r/p0I).

The next pivot is the first diagonal entry of the smaller matrix C − r*r/p. At D the successive pivots are exactly the nonzero dᵢ. All these computations are continuous where the earlier pivots are nonzero, so every pivot stays nonzero on an open neighborhood of D. If N′ is the triangular matrix for the smaller block, the full triangular matrix is diag(1,N′)N₁, with N₁ the first upper triangular factor in the displayed identity. Recursion uniquely recovers the pivots pᵢ and an upper triangular matrix N with diagonal entries one. The inverse map sends these coordinates to N* diag(p₁,…,pₙ) N. Both directions are continuous. At size zero there is one empty matrix and no pivot to choose.

How does a chart select one change of basis?

Choose an open subgroup U ⊂ R× on which squaring maps homeomorphically onto an open subgroup U². For real R one may use the positive numbers. Restrict the triangular chart to pᵢ ∈ dᵢU². This is open and contains D. Each ratio pᵢ/dᵢ now has a unique square root uᵢ in U, depending continuously on the pivot. With A = diag(u₁,…,uₙ)N, multiplication gives

A*D A = N* diag(d₁u₁²,…,dₙuₙ²) N.

These matrices A form a subgroup L because triangular multiplication multiplies diagonal entries, and inversion inverts them. In the original basis take Q = b−1L b. Then q = b−1A b satisfies q*S q = b* (A*D A) b. Thus q ↦ q*S q is a homeomorphism from Q onto an open neighborhood of S. Its inverse is the required section, with value 1 at S. Congruence here is a right action on forms. In the fibre integration argument one uses the left action in which h sends a tuple X to Xh−1 and its Gram matrix T to (h−1)*T h−1. Inversion in Q relates the two parametrizations.

Which square root does the chart take above 2?

At any finite place the derivative of u ↦ u² at 1 is 2. The local field has characteristic zero, so this derivative is invertible there, also when 2 has positive valuation. The inverse function theorem gives a continuous inverse on a sufficiently small neighborhood. A small closed ball about 1 of radius less than one is open in the ultrametric topology and forms a subgroup. The chart can use such a ball inside the inverse-function neighborhood. Glöckner, generalized implicit function theorem 5.2[148].

One can see the permitted size directly. Normalize the valuation by ord(π) = 1 for a uniformizer π, set e = ord(2), and take an integer k > e. For u = 1 + πkz, its square is 1 + 2πk(z + αz²), with α = πk/2 in the maximal ideal. The difference of z + αz² at z and z′ is (z − z′)(1 + α(z + z′)). The second factor is a unit. The map therefore preserves distances and is injective modulo every πj. Each residue ring is finite, so the map is also surjective there. The unique solutions for successive precisions are compatible, and completeness gives a unique solution in the local integers 𝒪. Thus (1 + πk𝒪)² = 1 + 2πk𝒪.

For R = ℚ₂ and n = 1, centre the chart at S = 1 and take U = 1 + 4ℤ₂. Its square image is 1 + 8ℤ₂. The target 9 has square roots 3 and −3 in ℚ₂. The section takes −3 because −3 ≡ 1 modulo 4. At the centre it takes 1.

Why do two choices agree at every regular target?

Take two such neighborhoods and a nonnegative continuous test supported compactly over their overlap. Write u(T) and v(T) for its two fibre integrals. On every compact target set K inside the overlap, both integrate to the same quantity, the source integral of the test over G−1(K). If u(T) exceeded v(T) at one point, continuity would give a compact neighborhood on which their difference stays bounded below by a positive number. That neighborhood has positive Haar measure. Its two integrals would differ. Thus u = v throughout the overlap. These tests determine a locally finite measure there: compact subsets can be bounded by continuous cutoffs in arbitrarily small open neighborhoods. Fibre support then gives equality of the two measures at each target.

Choose the measure from any chart containing T. To check the integration formula for the resulting family, take a countable subcover B₁, B₂, …, which exists by second countability. Give each target to the first chart containing it. The measurable pieces Bj ∖ ⋃i<j Bi are disjoint, so their integration formulas add without counting overlaps twice. For continuity near a chosen target, multiply the test by a continuous cutoff in the target that equals one near that point and is supported inside one chart. This leaves the nearby fibre integrals unchanged and gives continuity by the local construction.

One exceptional value. For the complex line with G(z) = |z|², use area on ℂ and length ds on ℝ. In polar coordinates area is ½ ds dθ, so each circle s > 0 has fibre mass π. Doubling just the measure at s = 1 would preserve the integration formula because {1} has length zero. Take a continuous test equal to one near the unit circle and supported in a compact annulus. Its fibre integral would jump from π to 2π at 1. This is precisely the ambiguity that continuity removes. The chart for a scalar length at a finite place uses the same uniqueness argument.

One example checks the direction of the transport factor. For G(z) = ‖z‖² on ℂ² and r > 0, dilation z ↦ rz multiplies the length by r². Its pushforward on the four real source coordinates is r−4 times volume, and on the real target it is r−2 times length measure. The mass transported from the fibre at s to the fibre at r²s therefore acquires the ratio r². Directly, the real ball of radius √s has volume proportional to s². Differentiating with respect to s gives a fibre mass proportional to s, as predicted.

What remains after the first vector is fixed?

Suppose the ambient Hermitian space represents the first target length t ∈ F×. Split off a rational vector of that length. In the resulting coordinates the ambient form is ⟨t⟩ ⊕ J, with J a nonsingular form of dimension r. The prescribed Gram matrix is ⟨t⟩ ⊕ T, with T nonsingular of size n. Thus there are n columns still to choose. Work at a completion R of F with K = R ⊗F E. Use coordinate Haar measures throughout, from one additive Haar measure on R and one F-basis of E.

Let e be the first coordinate vector. A first column y with length t can be written hye for a unitary isometry hy. When K is a field, Witt’s extension theorem extends the isometry between the two lines of length t. At a split place a vector is a pair consisting of a vector u and a linear functional ℓ with ℓ(u) = t. Complete u to a basis with the other vectors in ker ℓ. A change between two such bases carries both the vector and, by its inverse dual, the functional. This gives the required isometry there as well. The remaining columns are orthogonal to y. Applying hy−1 puts these columns into the fixed complement. There they have the form (0,Xⱼ), where the smaller tuple X has Gram matrix T for J. Write ι(X) for the tuple with first column e and remaining columns (0,Xⱼ).

The set of tuples is now described, but the conditional measure still needs its normalization. For a nonnegative measurable test φ, let mt1 be the one-column measure in the full space, and mT⊥ the n-column measure in the complement. The local recursion states

∫ φ dm⟨t⟩⊕T = cv(t)n ∫ (∫ φ(hy ι(X)) dmT⊥(X)) dmt1(y).

The inner integral is independent of the isometry because two choices differ on the right by an isometry fixing e. Its restriction is unitary on the complement and preserves mT⊥. The one-vector orbit is the quotient of the locally compact second-countable unitary group by the closed stabilizer of e. The measurable-section theorem for this quotient supplies a measurable choice y ↦ hy and hence a measurable outer integrand.

Where does the factor for each remaining column come from?

Allow the target to move, so that we can use the defining integration formula for the regular fibre measures. Write its upper-left entry as x, its first row after that entry as b, and its lower-right Hermitian block as B. Near x = t the local square-root branch gives x = a²t, with a = 1 at the centre. In the frame carried by hy the first vector is ae, and each remaining vector is (cⱼ,Xⱼ). Computing their inner products gives

b = at c,   GramJ(X) = B − t c*c = B − b*b/x,   det S = x det(B − b*b/x).

Here S is the full moving target and * is conjugate transpose. The determinant identity follows by subtracting the first row times the appropriate multiple from each lower row. Thus, as long as x is invertible, the smaller Gram matrix is nonsingular exactly when S is. For fixed x and b, passing between the two lower-right blocks is a translation, which preserves their additive Haar measure.

The first row changes volume. Normalize |·|v by the rule that multiplication by u scales the volume of a set in R by |u|v. A coordinate of K has two R-coordinates, so pushing its measure forward by z ↦ at z multiplies the measure by |at|v−2. Indeed, the mass assigned to a target set is the volume of its inverse image. Why is the global normalization one?

Over F = ℚ take E = ℚ(i), the ambient form diag(2,1) and two columns. At the real place fix the first column (1,0) and take the second to be (1 + i,1). Its pairing with the first column is b = 2 + 2i, and its length is 5. Subtracting |b|²/2 = 4 leaves the complement length 1. The full Gram determinant is 2·5 − 8 = 2. Multiplication by 2 in the complex b-coordinate multiplies area by 4, so pushing the original area forward gives the factor ¼. At the place 2, |2|₂ = ½ gives the factor 4. Every other finite place gives one. These two columns in dimension two illustrate the local coordinates and the product of the scalar factors. The global induction below requires at least one extra ambient dimension.

For every rational length t ∈ F×, the product formula gives ∏v|t|v = 1. Hence the product of the local factors cv(t)n is one as well. At almost all finite places the standard lattice test also separates into the standard tests for the first vector and the complement. This latter assertion uses integral isometries at good places. The global induction uses the local recursion in the strict range n + 1 ≤ r, with the full binary space anisotropic when r = 1. The local measure identity itself needs the represented nonzero line and the indicated regular targets. Sutherland, Theorem 13.21 on the product formula[150].

Which lattice points does an adelic box count?

The sum over isotropic lines leaves a rational scalar to count in each shell. We prove a bound for M coordinates over E and then use it with M = 1. Let E/F be a CM quadratic extension and d = [F∶ℚ]. Choose an F-basis of E. It writes an adelic vector in (𝔸F ⊗F E)M as 2M adelic coordinates over F. At each finite place v require every coordinate to belong to N−1𝒪Fᵥ, where N is a fixed positive integer. At each of the d real places take the absolute values of the 2M coordinates. The box BN(R) consists of vectors satisfying the finite conditions whose real absolute values sum to at most R. This sum is the ℓ¹ norm on ℝν with ν = 2dM.

BN(R) = {‖u‖₁ ≤ R} × ∏v finite (N−1𝒪Fᵥ)2M.

The finite factor is compact and open. Away from the primes dividing N, its factors are the usual integral lattices. Every finite adèle has a denominator at only finitely many places, and powers of the rational primes below them clear those denominators. Thus the open finite factors, as N varies, cover any compact family. Take a finite subcover, use a common multiple of its denominators, and bound the continuous real norm on the same family. Every compact Ω is consequently contained in some BN(r) with r > 0. Sutherland, The ring of adeles, Propositions 25.5–25.6 and Definition 25.7[151].

For a rational vector, each of its 2M coefficients c lies in F. The finite condition says exactly that Nc is integral at every finite place, hence lies in 𝒪F. The allowed rational vectors therefore form the additive subgroup ΛN = (N−1𝒪F)2M in the chosen coordinates. Taking differences preserves every finite condition. The real embeddings identify this subgroup with a lattice, so its intersection with a bounded real ball is finite. Sutherland, §14.2, the integer ring in its real embedding space[152].

How many translates of a small ball cover the rational points?

Let PN(R) count the points of ΛN in the closed real ball of radius R, including zero. For 0 < r₀ ≤ R, choose a maximal collection of these points whose pairwise distances are at least r₀. The open balls of radius r₀/2 about the chosen points are disjoint and fit inside the ball of radius R+r₀/2. Dilation by a positive scalar t multiplies volume in ℝν by tν. The number of centres is therefore at most (1+2R/r₀)ν ≤ (3R/r₀)ν.

Every lattice point in the large ball lies within distance r₀ of a centre, since otherwise it could be added to the collection. Subtracting that centre sends the point into ΛN in the small ball. Each centre therefore accounts for at most PN(r₀) points. Using the coefficient 5 in the subsequent shell estimate gives the comparison

PN(R) ≤ (5R/r₀)ν PN(r₀),   0 < r₀ ≤ R.

For an explicit choice take r₀ = min(1, d/(2N)). Indeed, any nonzero coefficient c has |NormF/ℚ(Nc)| ≥ 1 because it is the absolute value of a nonzero integer. AΩ(x) = 0   for x < x₀,   AΩ(x) ≤ C exp(νx)   for x ≥ x₀,   C = (5r/r₀)ν.

At the threshold the actual nonzero count is still zero, while the displayed upper bound is 25. At x = −log 2 the closed radius reaches ½ and admits exactly the four points ±½, ±i/2.

In the shell integral, pairing a tested vector with its transverse dual recovers a scalar in E. The pair and the tested vector vary in compact sets, so the image of their continuous pairing is one fixed compact Ω. Here the dimension in the count is ν = 2d, one scalar over E, and the variable is x = j + log rtest for shell index j and test radius rtest. Why the complementary quotient has finite volume. Borel’s finite-volume theorem applies to a connected linear group over a number field whose characters defined over that field are all trivial. Over E, U(W) becomes GLs. Its algebraic characters are determinant powers. Indeed, on the diagonal torus a character is a monomial whose exponents must be equal by permutation symmetry, and a character is trivial on each elementary unipotent subgroup. Conjugation over F takes the determinant to its inverse. A power descends only when its exponent is zero. Thus 𝒟W has finite volume for any Haar measure on U(W)(𝔸F). The construction by lattice classes below gives an adelic domain with this property. The same argument supplies the finite volume of the complement of dimension M−1 on a nonzero norm fibre. Borel, Theorem 5.6(i), p. 21[123]

For the scalar a, let χ(a) be the multiplier by which conjugation pushes forward the additive measure. The left Haar density contains χ(a) d×a. vol(Cb) vol(Cz) vol(𝒟W) vol×(ω) supω χ · exp(−2d(s+1)j).

Every factor before the exponential is finite and independent of j. The bound grows as j tends to −∞. The compact support of the original indicator and the discreteness of rational scalars supply the lower cutoff in the geometric sum.

Which finite adelic coordinates represent the same lattice?

Removing the hyperbolic plane in the isotropic count leaves a nondegenerate Hermitian space W of dimension s = M − 2 over the CM extension E/F. Its isometries form a group H = U(W,h). Put Γ = H(F), the rational isometries. An adelic isometry has an archimedean coordinate in H∞ and a finite coordinate in Hf. We first show that, up to Γ, only finitely many integral lattice classes occur in the finite coordinate.

Fix coordinates, a reference lattice at the finite places, and its compact open stabilizer K ⊂ Hf. For y ∈ Hf, take the rational vectors in the translated local lattices and multiply them by one fixed nonzero integer to obtain L(y) ⊂ W. This is a finitely generated additive group stable under 𝒪E and spanning W. The finite lattice construction gives two identities

L(γfy) = γL(y),   L(y) = L(y′) ⇔ y−1y′ ∈ K.

The second identity uses recovery of the translated local lattices from their rational vectors by completion. Isometries preserve the pairing, so one integer suffices to make it integral on every translated lattice. The coordinates of the lattices themselves can have arbitrarily large denominators. Clearing denominators in the pairing and its inverse gives one bound D for all y. Explicitly, if L# = {w ∈ W ∣ h(w,L) ⊂ 𝒪E}, then L ⊂ L# and [L# ∶ L] ≤ D. Indeed, one positive integer b sends every such dual into its lattice. A full lattice of additive rank k then satisfies L ⊂ L# ⊂ b−1L and [b−1L ∶ L] = bk.

Finiteness of the lattice classes. In a fixed nondegenerate space, integral lattices with this dual index bound belong to finitely many rational isometry classes. Here is the reduction. Choose a positive Euclidean length that bounds the absolute Hermitian pairings at all archimedean places. When every nonzero lattice vector has length at least 1, lattice reduction with the bounded covolume gives bounded generators. Their Gram entries are algebraic integers bounded at every embedding, a finite set. The Gram entries of spanning generators determine an isometry taking one labelled set to another. If a vector has length less than 1, its Hermitian norm is an algebraic integer of absolute value less than 1 at every embedding. Its field norm forces it to vanish. Split off a hyperbolic plane through the resulting line. Reduction adapted to that line gives finitely many possibilities for the lattices in the two line coordinates and a bounded dual index in the smaller orthogonal complement. Induction gives finitely many models there. For each resulting full split lattice B, the adapted reduction puts the original lattice between B and n−1B for a fixed positive integer n. The finite quotient n−1B/B has only finitely many subgroups.

Choose a representative t for each class attained by L(y). If L(y) = γL(t), the two identities give y ∈ γftK. Thus the double classes Γf ∖ Hf / K are finite. Within the slice tK, exactly the following rational isometries can still identify two points

Γt = {γ ∈ Γ ∣ t−1γft ∈ K} = {γ ∈ Γ ∣ γL(t) = L(t)}.
