Gluing the finite slices into a fundamental domain

Take one t for each double class. For now suppose the archimedean image of Γt has a fundamental domain Dt of finite Haar measure in H∞. The next step proves this for the lattice stabilizers above. Inside H∞ × Hf take

𝒟 = ⋃t Dt × tK.

Given a pair (x,y), move y into tK by a rational isometry. An element of Γt can now move the new archimedean coordinate into Dt while keeping the finite coordinate in tK. Conversely, a rational translate of one rectangle can meet another only in the same double class. In that class, the translating element belongs to Γt. Its archimedean action is faithful, and distinct translates of Dt are disjoint up to measure zero. These statements about coverage and overlap hold almost everywhere. Γ is countable, since its matrices have entries in a number field, so the union of the translated exceptional sets is still null.

Fix factor Haar measures μ∞ and μf. Their product is a Haar measure on the adelic group. For each rectangle its volume is μ∞(Dt) μf(K), because left translation by t preserves μf. This also shows why an archimedean exceptional null set stays null inside each slice. The finite sum gives

vol(𝒟) = μf(K) ∑t μ∞(Dt) < ∞.

Haar uniqueness says that all left Haar measures on a locally compact group differ by a positive factor. Thus the same construction gives finite volume for every choice of adelic Haar measure. A. Weil, Mesure de Haar, §§4–7[153].

Why the smaller unitary quotient has finite positive volume

It remains to verify the archimedean input. The stabilizer Γt is the integral subgroup of the rational algebraic group obtained from U(h) by restriction of scalars to ℚ, using the underlying integer lattice L(t). The arithmetic finite-volume theorem of Borel and Harish-Chandra says that a connected algebraic group over ℚ with trivial rational character group has an arithmetic quotient of finite invariant volume. Here the character condition can be checked directly. Over ℂ the group becomes a product of general linear groups, one for each real place of F. A character on each factor is an integral power of its determinant. Complex conjugation acts on each determinant by inversion, because the defining isometry equation identifies the conjugate matrix with a conjugate of its inverse transpose. A rational character would have every exponent equal to its negative, hence zero. The theorem gives the required finite archimedean covolume. A. Borel and Harish-Chandra, Arithmetic Subgroups of Algebraic Groups, theorem 9.4, p. 522[154].

One can also see where the volume bound enters reduction by short vectors. For an archimedean isometry g measure vectors with the positive length of g−1x. Where the shortest nonzero vector has length ≥ 1, bounded-basis reduction puts representatives in a compact set. Its finite measure bounds this portion of a fundamental domain. Where the shortest length is < 1, choose a shortest vector x. The norm argument above makes it isotropic. Shortest-vector reduction bounds [L ∩ Ex ∶ 𝒪Ex] by a constant depending on the field. Count all nonzero isotropic vectors satisfying that index bound and having length < 1. Their count is at least one on this thin part. The arithmetic unfolding theorem for bounded-index isotropic vectors gives a finite integral of that count over a fundamental domain. Its proof uses finitely many line orbits, parabolic coordinates and finite covolume for stabilizers in smaller dimension. The integral therefore bounds the volume of the thin part, as required.

For the same Haar measure μ, any two fundamental domains 𝒟 and 𝒟′ have the same mass. Partition 𝒟′ by its intersections with γ𝒟 and move each piece back by γ−1. The resulting pieces partition 𝒟 up to null sets. The common mass is positive because countably many translates of a null set could not cover a group with nonzero Haar measure. Thus replacing μ by cμ multiplies this mass by c. For s = M − 2 the isotropic shell estimate uses the smaller quotient volume as a fixed finite factor. Division by the volume of the ambient quotient takes place in the definition of the mean.

A one-dimensional complement. Take M = 3 over ℚ(i)/ℚ, with a hyperbolic plane and the line of norm zz̄. The smaller group at infinity is the circle. Choose K to be the norm-one integral units at the finite places. A norm-one finite idele determines a fractional ideal I with IĪ = (1). Gaussian integers admit Euclidean division, so I = (α). The positive rational number αᾱ generates the unit ideal and must equal 1. Dividing the idele by this rational isometry puts it in K. There is one double class. Its rational stabilizer consists of the four Gaussian units, so a quarter-circle gives an archimedean domain. With circle mass 1 and μf(K) = 1 the adelic covolume is 1/4. Tripling the adelic Haar measure gives 3/4.

How can a primitive column and its dual witness both be kept bounded?

Let E/F be the chosen CM quadratic extension and put K = 𝔸F ⊗F E. A column y with M entries in K is primitive here if there is a row z₀ with z₀·y = ∑i (z₀)iyᵢ = 1. Rows and columns are identified with their ordered lists of M coordinates for membership in Ω.

For every primitive y, there are a ∈ K× and z with ay ∈ Ω,   z ∈ Ω,   z·(ay) = 1.

At a complex component pick a coordinate yᵣ of largest modulus. It is nonzero because the local dot product can equal one. Take a = yᵣ−1 and take z to be the coordinate row with 1 in position r and zeros elsewhere. Every entry of ay has modulus at most one, entry r is exactly one, and z·(ay) = 1. At infinity there are finitely many complex components, and each can choose its own r. Both tuples now belong to a finite product of closed unit discs.

At a finite place where the quadratic algebra is a field, use the same largest-coordinate rule with the multiplicative size |Norm(x)| in the base local field. The base valuation ring is compact because its residue classes modulo each uniformizer power form a finite cover by balls of shrinking radius, and it is complete. To see compactness of the norm ball directly in coordinates, write x = u+wθ with θ² = Δ. The norm is u²−Δw², nonzero on the compact sphere max(|u|,|w|) = 1 because Δ is nonsquare. Its absolute value has a positive minimum there. Dividing by a coordinate of maximal absolute value and using homogeneity of degree two bounds max(|u|,|w|) wherever |Norm(x)| ≤ 1. The ball is therefore closed and bounded in the two-dimensional local field coordinates, hence compact. At a split place the algebra is a product of two fields. Choose a maximum separately on each side, giving one invertible pair of scalars and one pair of coordinate rows. The witness may select different positions in the two factors.

For example, over ℚ(i) at the split prime 5, take k ≥ 1. Write a local two-entry column as y = ((5−k,0),(0,5k)). Each single entry has a zero component. The scalar pair (5k,5−k) sends y to ((1,0),(0,1)). The row with these same two entries evaluates to (1,1), the multiplicative identity. The freedom to replace the row already matters at a complex place. For real R ≥ 1 take y = (R,0) and z₀ = (R−1,R²). After rescaling by 1/R, transporting the old row gives (1,R³). Choosing the new row (1,0) bounds both tuples for the whole sequence.

Why do the local scalings form a single idèle?

Exclude the places over 2, those where Δ is not a unit, and the finitely many denominator primes of the change of coordinates to the chosen basis. At a remaining place where Δ is nonsquare its reduction is nonsquare too. Indeed, an odd-residue-characteristic square root of a unit modulo the uniformizer lifts digit by digit because the derivative 2x at that root is a unit. Thus

|u²−Δw²|v = max(|u|v,|w|v)².

For unequal sizes the largest term gives the value. For equal nonzero sizes, cancellation would give a square root of Δ in the residue field on dividing by w². Hence the local construction produces integral coordinates in the basis 1,θ. In the split case let s² = Δ. The two components of u+wθ are u±sw. Both s and 2 are units, so taking their half-sum and their difference divided by 2s recovers integral coordinates from integral components. The fixed change of basis preserves integrality away from its denominator primes. These conditions leave only finitely many exceptional places.

Fix this finite set S independently of y. Use the compact archimedean box from the first step, the local compact sets constructed there at the finite places in S, and Λv everywhere else. Indeed it lies in one restricted-product chart with the ordinary product topology, where each local lattice is compact and the product of compact sets is compact. Now take an actual witness z₀ for y. Their components both lie in Λv at almost every finite place. Wherever this holds outside S, choose aᵥ = 1 and keep zᵥ = (z₀)v. At the finitely many other places use the local construction to choose aᵥ and zᵥ. Thus aᵥ and aᵥ−1 both equal one at almost all finite places. They assemble to mutually inverse elements of K, so a is an idèle. The rows zᵥ assemble to an adelic row because they are integral almost everywhere. In every component zᵥ·(aᵥyᵥ) = 1. Equality of adèles can be tested in all components, giving the global identity, with ay,z in the fixed Ω.

One example explains why the input row must itself be adelic. Take a rank-one column over ℚ(i) whose component at each rational prime p is p, and whose complex component is one. The column is integral at all finite places and each local entry is invertible in the local algebra. Yet the only possible dual has component 1/p at every p. It fails the restricted-product integrality condition, so this column has no adelic witness.

For the shell estimate, y is isotropic, and ay remains isotropic. The two compactly bounded inputs ay and z now feed the continuous construction of a hyperbolic partner. Its image on Ω × Ω gives the compact family of pairs to which the adelic Gram-fibre lifting argument is applied. The row normalization by itself requires only the displayed primitivity identity. How can a compact family of frames be lifted to isometries?

At a real place of the base field, a Hermitian space is a complex vector space V with a nonsingular form h, conjugate-linear in its first variable. For an ordered tuple of columns X = (x₁,…,xₙ), its Gram matrix T has entries h(xᵢ,xⱼ). Suppose det T ≠ 0. Any linear relation on the columns would give a vector in the kernel of T, so the columns are independent. If Y has the same Gram matrix, the map xᵢ ↦ yᵢ is an isometry of the column spans. Witt’s extension theorem gives an isometry of all of V extending that map. The shell estimate needs more. Given any compact set Ω of tuples, one compact set C in the unitary group must supply a lift g with gX = Y for every Y ∈ Ω of Gram matrix T. First diagonalize T by one fixed change of columns in both tuples. Indeed, a nonzero Hermitian form has a vector with nonzero value on the diagonal, by the polarization identity. Split off its line by orthogonal projection and repeat on the nonsingular complement. The new columns are mutually orthogonal with real squared lengths bᵢ ≠ 0, which may have either sign. Undoing the common column change at the end preserves the equation gX = Y.

Move one column and keep the earlier columns fixed. Suppose the next column is currently x and must be sent to y, with h(x,x) = h(y,y) = b ≠ 0. Set t = h(y,x). For at least one choice of λ = ±1 we have |b − λt| ≥ |b|, since the mean of |b−t|² and |b+t|² is b²+|t|². With u = x−λy and δ = b−λt, define

A(z) = z − u h(u,z)/δ,   B(z) = z − (1−λ)y h(y,z)/b.

Here h(u,x) = δ, so A(x) = λy. To check that A is an isometry, expand h(Az,Aw). The coefficient of h(z,u)h(u,w) in the difference from h(z,w) is [h(u,u)−2 Re δ]/|δ|², which vanishes because h(u,u) = 2b−2λ Re t. The second map acts by λ on the line of y and fixes its orthogonal complement. Thus BA is an isometry sending x to y. Each previously matched column is orthogonal to both and stays fixed.

Keep the lifts in a compact set. The subset of Ω on which the Gram matrix equals T is closed in Ω, hence compact. Start there with the identity matrix. At the first column retain both closed subsets where the corresponding sign satisfies |δ| ≥ |b₁|. They cover the compact set, and on each the displayed matrix depends continuously on Y. At the next column use its image under the current matrix as x and repeat within each subset. After n columns there are at most 2n compact subsets. On each, the product of the successive matrices is a continuous function of Y. The union of their compact images is the required C. At a tie either sign supplies a lift.

In the shell argument the two initial vectors e, f are isotropic, with h(e,f) = 1. Their Gram matrix has determinant −1. The column change (e+f, e−f) gives squared lengths 2 and −2, so both steps have a denominator of absolute value at least 2. For instance, the pairs (a e, a−1f) for 1 ≤ a ≤ 2 lift to the compact family diag(a, a−1) on their plane, extended by the identity on its orthogonal complement. The one-vector orbit mean uses the same real-place assertion for a line of nonzero norm. The next argument explains how the integral choices at finite places enter the compact family of adelic representatives.

Why can the same columns be used at every place?

When their Gram matrix is nonsingular, the columns are independent and form a frame for their span, which may be smaller than the ambient space. Stack them as a matrix and write T = X∗JX, where ∗ means conjugate transpose. Assume det T ≠ 0. Given an adelic tuple Y with this same matrix of pairings at every place, we seek one adelic isometry carrying X to Y. The first change of basis takes place among the n columns. It can be chosen over E before taking any completions.

Consider the pairing h on the space of column coefficients, with matrix T. For n > 0 there is a vector w of nonzero length h(w,w). To see this, suppose every length vanished. Expanding the length of u+v gives h(u,v)+h(v,u) = 0. Choose a nonzero θ with conjugate −θ by taking the difference of an element of E outside F and its conjugate. Expanding the length of u+θv then gives θ(h(u,v)−h(v,u)) = 0. Together the two identities force every pairing to vanish, contradicting nonsingularity. The nonzero length β is fixed by conjugation and therefore belongs to F. For every z, subtract w h(w,z)/β to obtain a vector orthogonal to w. The orthogonal complement is nonsingular because a vector in its radical would pair to zero with the whole space. Repeating the argument gives an invertible rational matrix S of new columns. The identity serves for the empty tuple. Thus

S∗TS = diag(β₁,…,βₙ),   βⱼ ∈ F×.

For example, over ℚ(i) take two columns e, f of lengths 0 and 2 with h(e,f) = 1+i. The Gram determinant is −2. Choose f first and then e−f(1−i)/2. Their lengths are 2 and −1, and their pairing is zero. The division by 2 is valid in every completion. At places above 2 its inverse lies outside the valuation ring, which matters when we ask whether a local isometry preserves an integral lattice.

The tuples XS and YS have the same diagonal Gram matrix. A unitary map g acts on the left, so g(XS) = YS implies gX = Y on multiplying both sides on the right by S−1. The same rational S and its inverse have integral entries outside finitely many places. We can therefore use this one diagonal model in the local tests that follow.

Which denominator is a unit at a finite place?

Let E/F be a CM quadratic extension, with conjugation z ↦ z̄. Let X be a rational frame of n columns in an M-dimensional nonsingular Hermitian space. Assume its n-by-n Gram matrix has nonzero determinant. The columns are then a basis of their span, with n ≤ M. Suppose an adelic frame Y has the same Gram matrix. We want an isometry carrying X to Y that preserves the coordinate lattice at almost every finite place. Fix a common rational change of columns that makes the Gram matrix diagonal, with nonzero entries β₁,…,βₙ in F. Consider one pair of columns of equal squared length β. The real-place construction divides by δ = β − λ̄t, where t = h(y,x) and λλ̄ = 1. To keep this division integral, we need δ to be a unit.

Here are four possible values of λ, fixed once for the extension. Choose a nonzero θ with θ̄ = −θ by subtracting the conjugate of any element of E outside F. Then d = θ² lies in F× and 1, θ is an F-basis of E. Take s ∈ F× with s² ≠ d. Put P = (s²+d)/(s²−d) and Q = 2s/(s²−d). Expanding the squares gives P²−dQ² = 1, so α = P+Qθ has norm one and Q ≠ 0. Our choices are 1, −1, α and −α.

At a finite place v, write 𝒪v for the integers of Fᵥ and Rᵥ for the ring of integers of E ⊗F Fᵥ, a product of two valuation rings at a split place. For the moment suppose 2, d, Q and β are units of 𝒪v and P is integral. Then θ is an integral unit. Each t ∈ Rᵥ can be written a+bθ with a = (t+t̄)/2 and b = (t−t̄)/(2θ) in 𝒪v. Both quotients are integral and fixed by conjugation. For λ = p+qθ, multiply δ by its conjugate to obtain a scalar in the base ring,

Nλ = δδ̄ = (β−pa+qbd)² − d(qa−pb)².

Suppose all four norms vanish in the residue field. Taking differences gives N−1−N1 = 4βa and N−α−Nα = 4β(Pa−Qbd). The first forces a ≡ 0, and the second then forces b ≡ 0 because Qd is a unit. But now N1 ≡ β² ≠ 0. Thus at least one norm is a unit in 𝒪v. For its phase, δ−1 = δ̄/Nλ belongs to Rᵥ.

Why two signs can fail. At an inert place the residue algebra is a field. If β−t and β+t both vanished there, their sum 2β would vanish. At a split place each sign can fail in a different component. For example, 5 splits in ℚ(i). In the residue algebra 𝔽₅ × 𝔽₅, conjugation swaps the factors and i = (2,−2). Take β = 1 and t = (1,−1). The choices λ = 1 and −1 give δ = (0,2) and (2,0). With θ = i and s = 1, we have α = i. For λ = i both components of δ equal 3 modulo 5, so its norm equals 4 modulo 5 and division is integral.

An integral isometry at almost every finite place

We can now specify a finite set S outside which every step works. Include all places above 2 and all ramified places. Include the places where any diagonal entry βᵢ, d or Q fails to be a unit, or P fails to be integral. Also include any place where the form matrix J, its inverse, the rational frame, or the common change of columns and its inverse have a nonintegral entry. Each fixed number-field entry has finitely many denominator primes, and each nonzero diagonal entry, as well as d and Q, is a unit away from finitely many primes. Finally include the finitely many places where the given adelic frame has a nonintegral entry. For a compact family of frames this last set can be chosen uniformly. The open sets of tuples integral outside a given finite set cover the family, so finitely many suffice, and we take the union of their exceptional sets. Sutherland, The ring of adeles, strong approximation, §25.3, Definition 25.7[151].

Fix v outside S. Write h(z,w) = z*Jw, where * is conjugate transpose. For one pair of integral columns x, y with common squared length β, choose λ by the four-norm test and put u = x−λy. For any column w and scalar c, let Tw,c(z) = z−wc h(w,z). The two maps we need are

A = Tu, 1/δ,   B = Ty, (1−λ̄)/β,   x ⟼ Ax = λy ⟼ BAx = y.

Indeed h(u,x) = δ, and B multiplies y by λ̄. To see that the maps preserve the lattice in both directions, write Lz = w h(w,z). This operator is self-adjoint for h and L² = h(w,w)L. Multiplying (1−c̄L)(1−cL) therefore gives the identity whenever c+c̄ = cc̄ h(w,w). This equality holds for A because h(u,u) = δ+δ̄, and for B because (1−λ̄)(1−λ) = 2−λ−λ̄. Thus each map is unitary with inverse Tw,c̄. Every coefficient of the maps and their inverses is integral since w, J and c are integral.

Start with the identity. If g has matched some columns, use x = gXᵢ and y = Yᵢ for the next pair of diagonalized columns. Every earlier matched column is perpendicular to both x and y, so A and B fix it. Replacing g by BAg matches one more column and preserves the lattice. After the last column, undo the common column change to get gᵥX = Yᵥ for the original frames. At each v outside S, gᵥ belongs to the unitary stabilizer of RᵥM, where M is the ambient dimension. The places above 2 enter S because the norm differences divide by 4. The adelic orbit argument supplies the transformations at the remaining places and assembles the local maps.

Which local inverses form an adelic inverse?

A finite adèle of F is a tuple (aᵥ) in the completions Fᵥ with aᵥ in the valuation ring 𝒪ᵥ outside a finite set. Its inverse is an adèle precisely when every aᵥ is nonzero and almost every aᵥ is a unit of 𝒪ᵥ. Indeed the only possible inverse has components 1/aᵥ. At a place where aᵥ is integral, its inverse is integral exactly when its valuation is zero. At the finitely many archimedean places one just needs a nonzero component. As an example over ℚ, take aₚ = p at every finite prime and a∞ = 1. This is an adèle with every component nonzero. Its componentwise inverse has negative valuation at every prime. In contrast, a fixed nonzero rational number and its inverse have a nonzero valuation at only finitely many primes. Sutherland, The idele group, Definition 26.2[157].

Apply this criterion to a denominator in a unitary change of frame. At a finite place put Aᵥ = Fᵥ ⊗F E. This is a quadratic field or a product of two copies of Fᵥ. In both cases the norm of δ is N(δ) = δδ. A nonzero norm gives the explicit inverse δ/N(δ). In a split algebra the norm tests both components. For example, (0,1) is a nonzero element with zero norm. Each of the four candidate phases gives a scalar norm fⱼ. Why do they generate the unit ideal over the full ring of base adèles? For t = a+bθ, their two differences are 4βa and 4β(Pa−Qbd). The scalars 4β and Qd are nonzero elements of F and therefore have adelic inverses. Hence the ideal generated by the four norms contains a and b. For the phase +1 we have f₁ = (β−a)²−db², so β²−f₁ belongs to the ideal generated by a and b. Adding f₁ shows that the ideal of the four norms contains β². Dividing by β² shows that a linear combination of the norms with adelic coefficients equals one. Evaluating this identity at an exceptional place produces at least one nonzero fⱼ. This suffices in the local field even at a ramified or dyadic place. For instance, over ℚ₂(i) take β = t = 1 and the phases ±1, ±i. Their denominators are 0, 2 and 1±i. None is an integral unit, yet 2 is invertible in the field. Where all the coefficients and norms are integral, at least one fⱼ must be an integral unit, since otherwise the sum would lie in the maximal ideal.

Select an admissible index at each place. Both the numerator δ and the inverse of the selected norm are then integral at almost every finite place. Consequently the entries of the elementary unitary corrections, and of their inverses, are adèles in the chosen coordinates. Different places may use different indices. The four indicator functions of the chosen sets take values in {0,1}, hence are integral everywhere. Multiplying each candidate by its indicator and adding realizes the local choices as a single adelic coefficient. This construction applies at each of the finitely many column steps. Each new correction fixes the already matched columns because they are orthogonal to both vectors used in that correction.

How does a pointwise lift give a single compact family?

Write G for the adelic unitary group preserving J. By the column construction and the rational change of basis, every adelic tuple Y of Gram matrix T equals gX for some g ∈ G. Conversely, an isometry preserves all pairings, so the orbit of X is exactly the fibre Z of the Gram map at T. Without the nonsingularity hypothesis, equality of Gram matrices can leave several orbits. In a hyperbolic plane the zero vector and a nonzero isotropic vector both have Gram matrix (0). Every invertible linear map fixes zero.

For the shell bound we need one compact family of such g as Y varies in a given compact set Ω. We first check the topology needed to pass from points to compact sets. In any basis of E over F, an adelic coefficient is a pair of base adèles. Conjugation is linear in these coordinates and multiplication is polynomial. The tuple space is therefore locally compact and Hausdorff, and the entries of the Gram matrix are continuous. The fibre Z is closed. Give an invertible matrix the topology of the pair (g,g−1). In the product of the two matrix spaces, the equations gh = hg = I and g∗Jg = J define a closed set. This gives G local compactness, the Hausdorff property and a countable basis, inherited from the finite powers of the adèle ring. The action is continuous by matrix multiplication.

Why the adelic orbit map is open. Given any neighborhood W of the identity in G, choose a compact neighborhood K with K−1K ⊂ W. The translates of the interior of K cover G, and second countability gives a countable subcover. Transitivity then covers Z by countably many translates of the compact, hence closed, set KX. By the Baire category theorem at least one of these closed translates has nonempty interior in Z. Translating back, choose kX in the interior of KX with k ∈ K. Then k−1 int(KX) is a neighborhood of X inside K−1KX ⊂ WX. Translating this inclusion to each group element proves that g ↦ gX is open onto Z. The Stacks Project, Lemma 5.13.3, Baire category theorem[158].

Take a relatively compact open neighborhood of each group element. Their images under this open map cover Z, so finitely many images cover Ω ∩ Z. The union of the closures of those finitely many neighborhoods is a compact family of adelic isometries giving all the required lifts.

This compactness controls all places together. To see its force, consider the open sets of matrices for which both the matrix and its inverse have integral coordinates outside a prescribed finite set of places. They cover G as the finite set varies. A compact set of representatives meets the requirement for one common finite set, by taking the union from a finite subcover. In coordinates one can enlarge that set to include the finitely many primes in the multiplication table of the chosen rational basis. Applied to the hyperbolic pair, the compact family transports the fixed pair to each of the pairs used in the shell comparison.

Why does a compact set have finite mean on a nonzero norm fibre?

Fix t ∈ F× and a compact adelic set Ω. An unrepresented norm contributes zero. If ⟨e,e⟩ = t for a rational e, the line Ee is nondegenerate. Its orthogonal complement has dimension M−1. The stabilizer G1 of the vector e is the adelic unitary group of this complement. Witt’s extension theorem identifies every rational vector of norm t with γ−1e for some γ ∈ Γ. Two choices give the same vector precisely when they differ by left multiplication by an element of Γ1 = Γ ∩ G1. Thus the classes are Γ1γ in Γ1 ∖ Γ. Unfolding replaces the sum integrated over Γ ∖ G by the integral of f(h) = 𝟙Ω(h−1e) over Γ1 ∖ G, before division by V.

The compact representative theorem supplies a compact set C of isometries such that every norm-t vector in Ω has the form ce with c ∈ C. It uses adelic Witt extension and compact lifting on the closed orbit. Consequently, whenever f(h) = 1, we have h−1e = ce and hc fixes e. Thus the support lies in G1C−1. The compact-cover integral bound for a function ≤ 1 bounds its unfolded integral by a fixed constant times the volume of Γ1 ∖ G1. Finite arithmetic quotient volume in the smaller dimension proves integrability on this fibre.

Finally, the continuous norm maps Ω into a compact adelic set, which meets the closed discrete diagonal copy of F in finitely many points. Add the finite means for those nonzero norms. Enclose Ω in one box and apply the isotropic bound to its nonzero vectors of norm zero. This gives the finite reference mean used in the large-radius packing estimate. Including the origin in that reference box adds exactly one.

Subtract the common term. The zero vector contributes φ(0) to the theta average. The Eisenstein expansion begins with the same term. Take F = ℚ, E = ℚ(i), M = 3 and a single height Y = 4. The innermost ball has radius 1/2. Its two powers in the count are (1/2)³ and (1/2)⁶. Where do the finitely many cusp matrices come from?

Let F be totally real of degree d, with ring of integers 𝒪. A point of the Hilbert upper half-space has one coordinate τw = xw + iyw, with yw > 0, at each real embedding w. For a matrix in SL₂(F) with bottom row (c,b), direct multiplication by the conjugate denominator gives Im(gτ)w = yw/|w(c)τw+w(b)|². We need one row whose denominator is small at every embedding.

Embed 𝒪² in ℝ2d using all its real embeddings. At each place, apply to a pair (a,b) of real coordinates the determinant-one map (a,b) ↦ (√y · a, (xa+b)/√y). The product map preserves the covolume of the lattice for every τ. Choose a cube [−R,R]2d of volume greater than 22d times this covolume. Minkowski’s convex body theorem supplies a nonzero lattice point in it. Adding the squares of the two coordinates at each place gives a pair (c,b) ∈ 𝒪², independent of the place, with

|w(c)τw + w(b)|² ≤ 2R²yw   at every w.

Complete that row. Its two entries generate a nonzero integral ideal I. The class group is finite, so fix an integral ideal J in each class. For the class of I there is a scalar λ with λI = J. Hence |N(λ)| = N(J)/N(I) ≤ N(J), uniformly bounded by a constant B over the fixed finite list. Put (p,q) = λ(c,b). From pJ−1 + qJ−1 = 𝒪 choose a,b′ ∈ J−1 with aq−b′p = 1. This gives a determinant-one matrix g with top row in J−1 and bottom row in J. Choose one such matrix r for each class that occurs. Every entry of r−1g is a difference of two products in J J−1 = 𝒪. Thus g = rk with k ∈ SL₂(𝒪) and r in a fixed finite set. Multiplying (p,q) by a unit preserves the ideal, so the same construction works for every unit multiple. Why can two spheres of different lengths have the same mass coefficient?

Fix a CM extension E/F with conjugation, and an anisotropic Hermitian plane with nonsingular matrix J. Write Q(x) = x*Jx, where * means conjugate transpose. For β ∈ F×, the rational sphere consists of x ∈ E² with Q(x) = β. Average its rational points over the adelic unitary quotient to obtain a measure Θβ. The first mass formula for this length supplies a nonnegative number κ such that, on product tests, Θβ integrates as κ times the product of the local Gram-fibre integrals. A separate choice of κ for each β would leave an unknown weight inside the sum over lengths. A rational change of variables makes the same κ work throughout that sum.

Build the change of variables from two points. Suppose Q(x) = β and Q(x′) = β′, both nonzero. If x*J = (r₀,r₁), put y = (−r₁,r₀)t and take the two columns of Pₓ to be x and y. Then x*Jy = 0 and det Pₓ = r₀x₀ + r₁x₁ = β. Taking determinants in its diagonal Gram matrix gives βQ(y) = β² det J. Thus the two frames give the same diagonal form up to their respective lengths.

Pₓ*JPₓ = β diag(1, det J),   γ = Pₓ′Pₓ−1,   γ*Jγ = λJ,   λ = β′/β.

In particular γx = x′. Its entries belong to E and its multiplier λ belongs to F. This one matrix bijects all rational points of the first sphere with those of the second. On the group used in the average, put h′ = γhγ−1. It is unitary and γ(h−1x) = (h′)−1γx. Pull back the Haar measure and the fundamental domain together under this conjugation. The volume dividing the average is preserved. Reindexing the sum and changing variables gives γ∗Θβ = Θβ′ because the normalized theta measure is independent of these auxiliary choices.

Compute what happens on a fibre. At a place v, write dX for ambient additive Haar measure and db for Haar measure on the scalar length coordinate. The Gram-fibre measures mᵥ(b) recover the ambient integral by integrating over b on the regular locus. Define the positive factors aᵥ and bᵥ by γ∗dX = aᵥ dX and (multiplication by λ)∗db = bᵥ db. Since Q(γX) = λQ(X), the changed family must reconstruct aᵥ dX using bᵥ db. Uniqueness of the normalized fibre measures fixes the quotient, including its direction. Combine all infinite places in F∞.

γ∗mᵥ(β) = (aᵥ/bᵥ) mᵥ(β′),   (a∞/b∞) ∏v finite (aᵥ/bᵥ) = 1.

For the first product formula the proof expresses γ as a linear map in F-coordinates. For the second, scalar congruence on a one-by-one Hermitian matrix acts by λ². Its Haar factor is the square of the positive factor for multiplication by λ, so taking square roots gives the required product formula on lengths. Outside finitely many places the factors are one and γ and its inverse preserve the standard lattice. On a product test enlarge its finite set of places to include these exceptions. All local changes of measure then cancel in the product, leaving exactly the original κ in the formula for Θβ′.

Follow the factor at infinity and at 2 for a sphere of length two

Over ℚ(i)/ℚ take J = I₂, x = (1,0)t and x′ = (1,i)t. Their lengths are 1 and 2. The frame gives γ with rows (1,i), (i,1). Multiplication gives γ*γ = 2I₂ and detℚ(i)γ = 2. In the four rational coordinates its determinant is the norm of 2, hence 4. A pushforward measures the inverse image of a set. At infinity its factor on vectors is therefore 1/4, and on lengths it is 1/2. The fibre factor is (1/4)/(1/2) = 1/2. At 2 the absolute values are |4|₂ = 1/4 and |2|₂ = 1/2, giving pushforward factors 4 and 2 and fibre factor 2. At every odd prime the factors are one. Thus the product of the fibre factors is (1/2)·2 = 1, although the real fibre measure alone changes. This computes the transport of a mass formula without evaluating either sphere’s individual mass.

Which lengths reach the counting theorem? Start with the coefficient supplied for a fixed β ≠ 0. If the infinite fibre measure or any finite fibre measure is zero, its factorization forces Θβ = 0. The local finiteness and summability already supplied let one write the zero factorization with coefficient 1 directly. Otherwise the binary representation theorem gives a rational vector of length β from the nonzero infinite fibre measure. Now consider every β′ ≠ 0. A represented β′ receives the same κ by the preceding argument. For an unrepresented β′ the rational sum is empty, and the contrapositive of that representation theorem gives zero infinite fibre measure. Apply the individual mass formula for β′ to obtain its finiteness and summability conditions. Its zero factorization now holds with the chosen κ as well. For example, length −1 is empty over the reals in the positive definite plane above. The degree-one Gram matrix at β = 0 is singular, and anisotropy leaves only the zero rational vector there. The counting theorem uses precisely the nonzero lengths. Having a common κ on all of them permits the positive-volume comparison that gives κ = 1.

Why does the infinite fibre detect a rational point in this plane?

For a proposed nonzero length t, compare J with diag(t, t det J). Their determinants differ by t², the norm of t from E to F. At an indefinite real place both planes have one positive and one negative direction. At a definite place representing the sign of t makes their signatures agree there too. With all signatures equal, Landherr’s classification gives a rational isometry of the two Hermitian forms. The image of the first basis vector then has length t. Consequently a missing rational length has the wrong sign at some definite real place. The infinite fibre is empty there and its supported measure vanishes. The archive obtains the classification result used here from a quadratic Hasse norm theorem.

Why do the two counts in an anisotropic plane have the same limit?

The binary mass argument has one unknown scalar multiplying the density for every represented nonzero length. To determine that scalar, count the same vectors in two orders. One count dilates four F-coordinates of a vector. The other sums its scalar lengths, which dilate quadratically. Both use the following lattice limit.

εdm ∑x ∈ 𝒪F,Sm Φ(εx) ∏v ∈ S ψv(x)   ⟶   (∫ Φ) ∏v ∈ S ∫ ψv   as ε ↓ 0.

Here 𝒪F,S consists of elements integral away from the finite set S. The tests are continuous and compactly supported. Each finite integer ring has volume one, and the real measure gives the integer lattice covolume one. For S empty the assertion is a Riemann sum. Requiring a translated ideal I in each coordinate multiplies its limit by N(I)−m. To add a place v, approximate ψv to precision u on disjoint boxes of the form c + (𝔭vk𝒪v)m. Each box replaces a modulus I coprime to v by I𝔭vk with a new translate. Its volume qv−km is exactly the extra inverse index. The total box volume stays bounded as u shrinks. At fixed precision apply the previous lattice limit both to the box sums and to their absolute-value majorants. The latter bound the error by u times a quantity with bounded limit. Letting u decrease proves the formula for the added place.

Counting the vectors. Take Φ nonnegative with compact support in the regular Gram locus. Select a compact open regular set Aᵥ at each v ∈ S and the standard lattice elsewhere. Write V = (∫ Φ)∏v ∈ S vol(Aᵥ) using coordinate Haar measures. For each fixed adelic unitary translate, the lattice formula with m = 4 gives the same limit V, since the translation preserves these measures. The exponent is 4d because a binary vector has two coordinates over the quadratic extension. To average, take compact representatives for the anisotropic quotient. One denominator clears their finite supports and one real box contains their rescaled supports. A compactly supported continuous majorant for the box gives an eventual bound for all these translates. Rational invariance extends it across the fundamental domain. Its finite, positive Haar volume permits dominated convergence and division by that volume.

Compute one of the translated lattice sums at the identity

Take F = ℚ, E = ℚ(i), J = I₂ and S = {3}. In the four ordinary integer coordinates impose x ≡ (1,0,0,0) modulo 3. Every such vector has unit Gram value at 3. At infinity use h(t) = max(1−|t|,0) and Φ(x) = h(x₁−2)∏j=24h(xⱼ). Its support stays in x₁ ≥ 1 and its integral equals one. For ε = 1/N, let CN(r) count ordered pairs 0 ≤ u, v < N with u−v ≡ r modulo 3. There are N h(j/N) pairs of difference exactly j. Thus the normalized four-dimensional sum is CN(1−2N)CN(0)³/N⁸. For N = 4 the three pair counts are 6, 5, 5 and the sum is 135/8192. For every multiple of 3 the sum is exactly 1/81. All three ratios CN(r)/N² tend to 1/3, yielding 1/81 for the full limit, the volume of the chosen 3-adic box.

How much mass does one length carry at a good prime?

A Hermitian vector in a plane has two coordinates over E. Each has two coordinates over F. At a finite place v, fixing its length therefore imposes one quadratic equation on four coordinates over Fv. Fix the basis and lattice used in the product formula. Write 𝒪 for the local integers, π for a uniformizer, and q for the number of elements of the residue field. Normalize scalar Haar measure by vol(𝒪) = 1 and use its fourth power on the source. Let gv(s) be the mass on the length-s fibre of the standard lattice.

Good-place mass estimate. Remove the finitely many places where 2 or the determinant of the trace form fails to be a unit, or an entry of its matrix fails to be integral. At each remaining place, for s ≠ 0 one has

gv(s) = 0 for s ∉ 𝒪,   |gv(s) − 1| ≤ 3/q for s ∈ 𝒪,   |gv(s) − 1| ≤ 1/q² for s ∈ 𝒪×.

In the chosen coordinates the length is Q(x) = ½xtBx, where B is the symmetric matrix of the trace of the Hermitian pairing. The factor ½ occurs because the field trace doubles a scalar from the base field. The local Gram-fibre integration formula identifies gv on nonzero lengths with the continuous density of the pushforward of volume on 𝒪⁴ by Q. In particular, if the ratio of the inverse-image volume to target volume is constant on all sufficiently small target balls about s, it equals the fibre mass there. Integrality of B and ½ confines the support to 𝒪. The zero-length vectors also have source volume zero. Choose a vector on which Q is nonzero and take it as the first vector of a basis over the local field. For each choice of the other three coordinates the equation Q = 0 has at most two roots in the first. Singletons have Haar measure zero, so Fubini gives zero volume. An invertible linear change of basis preserves null sets. Thus integrating the regular density gives the entire volume vol(𝒪⁴) = 1.

How is a measure on a single length defined?

Even when a vector of length s exists, the set of all vectors of that length has zero four-dimensional volume. We can still assign it a three-dimensional measure. At a good finite place, choose a primitive residue class C = a + π𝒪⁴. Since B is invertible modulo π, some coordinate of B a is a unit. Keep the other three coordinates y as parameters and use the length in place of that coordinate. For any s in I = Q(a) + π𝒪 and any compatible y, there is exactly one remaining coordinate in its residue class. Indeed, given a solution modulo πk, changing its next digit changes the next length digit by multiplication by that unit. Every required digit has a unique lift, and completeness gives the coordinate. Call this vector x(s,y).

For each fixed y this correspondence preserves one-dimensional Haar measure. It gives a bijection of the residue balls at every precision, and corresponding balls have the same volume. Integration in the length and the three free coordinates now gives, for a locally constant test function φ on C,

∫C φ(x) dx = ∫I (∫y ≡ afree mod π φ(x(s,y)) dy) ds.

The inner integral defines the contribution of this class to the length-s fibre. For φ = 1 it equals q−3 throughout I. For example, over ℚ₃ take the sum of four squares and the class (1,0,0,0) modulo 3. Each of the last three coordinates ranges over 3ℤ₃. The contribution is 1/27 at every length congruent to 1. Integrated over that target ball it gives (1/27)(1/3) = 1/81, precisely the volume of the source class.

Every nonzero integral vector has a unique expression πjz with j ≥ 0 and z primitive. On this shell four-dimensional volume scales by q−4j and length by π2j, so the fibre measure scales by q−2j. At a fixed nonzero integral s only 2j ≤ ord(s) can occur. The shell sum for φ = 1 thus defines a locally constant density near s. It agrees pointwise with the continuous regular Gram-fibre mass used in the product formula by uniqueness on regular fibres. Both integrate to the same volume on every sufficiently small target ball, and every such ball has positive measure.

Why is the error smaller at a unit length?

First count primitive vectors, meaning that some coordinate is a unit. For a residue value a, let N(a) be the number of solutions of the reduced equation Q(x̄) = a in the four-dimensional residue space. Delete the zero vector if a = 0, and write N×(a) for the resulting count. Every remaining solution has nonzero gradient Bx̄ because B is invertible modulo π. Suppose a solution modulo πk is lifted to x + πky. The next digit of the length is determined by the nonzero linear functional y ↦ (Bx̄)·y. Exactly q³ choices give any prescribed next digit. A target ball modulo πk has volume q−k. Its primitive preimage consists of N×(a) q3(k−1) balls of volume q−4k. The ratio is independent of k and equals N×(a)/q³.

Residue count. For a nonsingular quadratic form in four variables over a field of odd cardinality q, one has |N(a) − q³| ≤ q if a ≠ 0, and |N(0) − q³| ≤ q². For a unit length, every solution is primitive. Dividing the first bound by q³ proves the unit estimate. For any integral length the primitive density P(s) therefore satisfies |P(s) − 1| ≤ 1/q + 1/q³, where the last summand allows for deleting the origin.

Why does a nonzero residue save one power of q?

Choose a nontrivial additive character ψ of the residue field and write G(u) = ∑x ψ(uQ(x)). Character orthogonality gives qN(a) = q⁴ + ∑u≠0 ψ(−ua)G(u). Indeed summing ψ(ut) over u gives q for t = 0 and zero otherwise, since translation by an element with character different from one preserves that sum.

Over a field of odd characteristic, completing squares diagonalizes the nonsingular form with four nonzero coefficients. If χ is the quadratic character extended by χ(0) = 0, the equation y² = z has 1 + χ(z) solutions. In each of the four one-variable character sums, changing u from 1 to a nonzero value consequently multiplies the sum by χ(u). The four factors give χ(u)⁴ = 1, so G(u) = G(1). Its modulus is q². To check this, square its modulus and replace the first argument in the double sum by x + y. The sum over x of ψ(xtBy) vanishes unless y = 0, when it contributes q⁴. Finally ∑u≠0 ψ(−ua) equals −1 for a ≠ 0 and q − 1 for a = 0. Dividing by q gives the two count estimates.

What do vectors divisible by the prime contribute?

Write k = ordv(s) for a nonzero integral length. If k is 0 or 1, every vector of length s is primitive, since Q(πy) = π²Q(y). If k ≥ 2, the nonprimitive part lies in π𝒪⁴. Passing from y to πy multiplies source volume by q−4. The matching target ball is scaled by π², which multiplies target volume by q−2. Taking the ratio gives the recurrence

gv(s) = P(s) + q−2gv(s/π²)   (k ≥ 2).

Each application lowers the valuation by two. To verify the uniform error, put w = 1/q ≤ ½ and assume the lower-valuation density differs from one by at most 3w. The primitive bound and the recurrence give an absolute error at most w + w³ + w²(1 + 3w) = w + w² + 4w³ ≤ 3w. The two base valuations already obey this bound. This proves it for every nonzero integral length.

For example, take the positive Hermitian form |x₁|² + |x₂|² over ℚ(i) at 3. The scalar form in four coordinates is a sum of four squares. Modulo 3, each nonzero coordinate contributes 1. To represent 1 there must be one or four nonzero coordinates, giving 4·2 + 2⁴ = 24 solutions. To represent 0 with a primitive vector requires three nonzero coordinates, giving 4·2³ = 32. Thus g₃(1) = 24/27 = 8/9 and g₃(3) = 32/27. At length 9 the vectors divisible by 3 first contribute, giving g₃(9) = 32/27 + (1/9)(8/9) = 104/81.

The reason for keeping both error bounds appears in the average over lengths. At units the error is already at most q−2. The larger bound 3/q occurs only on the nonunits, which have local measure 1/q. Their contribution to the mean absolute error on 𝒪 is at most 3/q². In the global argument, divisibility of a rational length by several primes is counted by the norm of their product ideal.

How does a general Schwartz test reach every regular fibre?

The density at infinity serves a separate purpose. Here the tuple has any number n of columns, the rational form J is nonsingular, and source and target carry additive Haar measures μ and ν. Let mS be their Gram fibre measures. For a complex Schwartz test Φ, its integral over each fibre at an invertible archimedean target S exists and varies continuously with S. The result applies with no inequality between M and n. The archimedean Schwartz theorem for an arbitrary number of columns The compact-test construction fixed the fibre measure before choosing the Schwartz function. When n > M, the rank of a Gram matrix is at most M, so every fibre at an invertible target is empty.

Fix a regular target and choose a neighbourhood O in which congruence carries any one target to every other by continuously varying invertible matrices. In real tuple coordinates of dimension D = 2dMn, put W(x) = (1+‖x‖)−(D+1). This weight is integrable for ambient Haar measure. Disintegration gives a target S₀ in O with ∫ W dmS₀ finite, since O has positive Haar measure. Write S = hS∗S₀hS. Right multiplication LS by hS transports mS₀ to mS up to a positive continuous factor. It is the target pushforward Haar multiplier divided by the source pushforward Haar multiplier. Near the fixed target the inverse maps are bounded, so ‖x‖ ≤ B‖LSx‖ with one B. Schwartz decay of order D+1 now gives |Φ(LSx)| ≤ CW(x) uniformly nearby. Dominated convergence on the single reference fibre proves continuity for the integrals of both Φ and |Φ|.

To recover the density identity, multiply Φ by continuous compactly supported cutoffs between zero and one, eventually equal to one at each point. For each cutoff use the compact-test disintegration. On a compact set K of regular targets, continuity bounds ∫ |Φ| dmS by one constant. Dominated convergence applies on each fibre, on K, and on the source, where |Φ| is integrable. Thus the integral over the preimage of K equals the integral of the fibre densities over K. The global formula uses this theorem first with its coordinate measures, then with source and target measures multiplied by positive scalars a and a′. The density in the second use acquires exactly a/a′.

For the Whittaker integral the two Fourier measures are self-dual. If the measure on matrices is cv times its coordinate measure and the measure on Hermitian targets is ev times its coordinate measure, the density is multiplied by cv/ev. This follows already by integrating over a compact target set. The source integral gains cv, while integration against the new target measure supplies ev. The reference scalar measures give the valuation ring volume one at each finite place and the ring of integers covolume one at infinity. With the chosen global additive character, both families of self-dual scaling constants have product one and equal one at almost every finite place.

gv(T) = (cv/ev) ∫ Φv(X) dmv,T(X),   (c∞/e∞) ∏v finite (cv/ev) = 1.

The coordinate-measure identity, initially tested on nonnegative measurable products, applies to the integrable complex-valued product Φ. Multiplying by the scale ratios gives exactly the displayed normalized mean. This is the equality used at the global Whittaker evaluation point. The count of residue-field frames supplies individual good factors, while the global measure formula fixes their joint normalization against rational tuples.

Let X = [G] be the source quotient and Y = [H] the target quotient, with their quotient Haar measures μ and ν. Each is the space of adelic points modulo rational changes of basis. Write Ki(x,y) for the theta kernel built from Φi. At a fixed y, the lift Θi(y) integrates Ki(x,y)ui(x) over X. Pairing two lifts now integrates over Y. To use the doubling identity we need the reverse order, pairing the two kernels on Y before integrating over the two source variables. What keeps the new integral finite?

Bound one kernel at a time. Take the same polynomial Φ on both sides of the doubled kernel. At (g,g), the doubling identity identifies |K(g,h)|² with the absolute value of that doubled kernel, because the determinant character has modulus one. The Siegel–Weil theorem on these data supplies integrability in h. Its regular Eisenstein value bounds the absolute value of the normalized target mean by a power of the doubled height. The height at (g,g) is at most a constant times a power of the height at g. Multiplying the mean by ν(Y) therefore gives a polynomial bound for ∫Y |K(g,y)|² dν(y). This step uses the rank and Witt-index assumptions of the global formula.

By rational invariance we can take the height H(x) on the quotient, absorbing a constant in the bound. For each kernel choose ci ≥ 0 and an integer ai ≥ 0 such that its squared slice norm is at most ciH(x)aᵢ. Then Ni(x) = 1 + ciH(x)aᵢ bounds the slice norm itself. Rapid decay of the source cusp form means that every required power of H times |ui| is bounded. The source quotient has finite volume, so Mi = ∫X Ni|ui| dμ is finite. At every fixed y, the kernel also grows at most polynomially in x. The same decay proves that each defining lift integral exists there. Continuity and invariance in both rational variables give measurable kernels on the quotients.

Change the order. Put F(x,x′,y) = K₁(x,y)u₁(x) K₂(x′,y)u₂(x′). For fixed x,x′, Cauchy–Schwarz in y gives ∫ |K₁(x,y)K₂(x′,y)| dν ≤ N₁(x)N₂(x′). The remaining bound separates into a function of x and a function of x′. Tonelli’s theorem applies to |F| because it is nonnegative, giving the absolute bound below. With equal kernels and equal inputs this bound also gives Θi ∈ L²(Y). We can now use Fubini for the complex integrand itself.

∫X²×Y |F| ≤ M₁M₂ < ∞.
⟨Θ₁,Θ₂⟩Y = ∫X² ⟨K₁(x,·),K₂(x′,·)⟩Y u₁(x) u₂(x′) dμ(x) dμ(x′).

The Petersson pairing here conjugates the second factor. If g₁ and g₂ represent x and x′, the mixed doubling identity makes the inner pairing the normalized doubled theta mean times ν(Y) and χB(det g₂). Substitution accounts for the single target-volume factor in the norm formula. The absolute bound above exchanges integrations over the two source copies and the target. The preceding Siegel–Weil step supplies the normalized mean, including its own convergence conditions.

Try the two orders on an infinite sum. Give X = {1,2,…} counting measure and Y = {+1,−1} equal probabilities. Let K(n,y) = n yn−1, u₁(n) = 21−n and u₂(n) = (z/2)n−1 with |z| = 1. The target slice norm is exactly n. Its weighted sum is ∑ n/2n−1 = 4, giving an absolute bound of 16. In the reversed order the inner kernel pairing is nm for equal parity and zero for opposite parity. At cutoff 2 and z = i, the two target lifts are (2,0) and (1 + i,1 − i). Pairing them gives 1 − i. Reversing the order gives the same value from the (1,1) and (2,2) terms. For an independent check on the limit, differentiating the geometric series gives ∑n≥1 n rn−1 = (1 − r)−2. At target sign y, take r = y/2 for the first lift and r = yz/2 for the second. The figure gives a bound for the error at every cutoff before taking that limit.

6.32At an unramified finite place

For v outside S, put volume one on the local lattice stabilizer Kv. The spherical section φ on the doubled group has φ(1) = 1 and inducing character χB−1. Let c be a bounded spherical matrix coefficient with the specified Hecke parameters. At a split place the bounds on each parameter and its inverse follow from all integral Hecke sums. For Re s > a the integral of φ((g,1)) c(g) over the local group is

c(1) · Lv(s + ½) / dv(s).

The restriction to the compact stabilizer would contribute just c(1), since the integrand is constant there and its volume is one. Freeing the local variable multiplies that contribution by the displayed quotient. The denominator therefore enters once each time a good place is freed.

The numerator runs over every CM place w above v and every Satake parameter β there. Its factor is (1 − β χB(w)−1 Nw−(s+½))−1, where χB(w) denotes the unramified character value. If η is the quadratic character of the CM extension, the denominator is ∏0≤i<a Lv(2s + a − i, ηb+i). The source gives the local η-factor as a singleton parameter at an unramified place, with value +1 at split places and (−1)b+i at inert places. Every argument of this denominator has real part greater than one when Re s > 0. The resulting dS = ∏v∉S dv is holomorphic and nonzero there. At s₀ the local denominator takes arguments t + 1 through t + a.

Split places. The two places above v have equal residue norms. Their parameter multisets are related by inversion, and their character values multiply to one. Identifying the local unitary group with GLa transports the spherical section to the graph used by the GL doubling calculation. The lattice-fixed source vector and the spherical section make the integrand constant on right Kv-cosets. The sum of these values is the Haar integral because every coset has volume one. Evaluating the GL sum gives exactly the two-place numerator and the split denominator above. The split lattice calculation below derives the required complex sum from the unramified GL doubling theorem.

Inert places. Let q be the residue size at v. The CM residue size is q². Write ε for the value of the inverse target character at a uniformizer and α₁,…,α⌊a/2⌋ for the unitary parameters. Put X = ε q−(2s+a) and y = ε q−(2s+1). For a zonal coefficient normalized to one at the identity the closed expression is

∏h=0a−1 (1 − (−q)hX)   ∏i=1⌊a/2⌋ [(1 − yαi)(1 − y/αi)]−1,

with the additional factor (1 − y)−1 for odd a. To see the source of the powers of X, assign a matrix the lattice length obtained from its elementary divisors. The graph section takes the value X to that length. Summing over the unitary Iwasawa cells uses counts for their unipotent radicals and geometric series for their Levi factors. Pairing each α with its inverse gives the second product. In odd rank the base-change parameters also contain 1. The character restriction gives ε = (−1)b, which converts the first product to the reciprocal of dv. For Re s > a, the half-rank bounds on α and its inverse and |y| = q−(2 Re s+1) place all series in their convergence domain when the coefficient at 1 is nonzero. The adelic comparison restores the factor c(1).

For a local rank-one check take a = 1, b = 8, and set the spherical parameters and twist equal to one. Write x = q−(s+½). At a split place the numerator is (1 − x)−2, while the denominator is (1 − x²)−1. Their quotient is (1 + x)/(1 − x). At an inert place the single CM norm q² gives numerator (1 − x²)−1, hence quotient 1. For |x| < 1 the split answer also reads 1 + 2∑n≥1 xn. To see the cancellation, expand (1 − x)−2 as a sum over pairs of nonnegative integers (u,v). Adding one to both entries preserves their difference and multiplies the term by x². Multiplying by 1 − x² leaves precisely the pairs with one entry zero. This explains the denominator in this rank-one example. Actual chains in this chapter begin at r = k + m − 1 with m ≥ 2 and k ≥ m + 3.

6.33The part that stays inside the integral

For each admissible chain step and each additive measure and fundamental domain of covolume one, choose one polynomial datum φ and one finite-type test vector v. They work for every nonzero vector u of the stage multiplicity space. The order matters. These choices give a nonzero JS(s₀) already before choosing a Hecke eigenvalue. Write F = u(v) and K for the prescribed finite adelic level. We compute the integrand W(g) · pet(R(g)F, F), with R the right translation.

Two restrictions on the finite datum enter the support proof. Its matrix must lie in the summand selected by the split-place idempotent and be integral in the chosen frames. At every selected CM place its top square block must reduce to an invertible block triangular matrix, and the family of upper-left blocks must meet the given subgroup condition. If both a matrix and its translate have nonzero test value, these unit top blocks recover integrality of the transformation in the selected summand. Self-duality gives the conjugate summand, and the two reductions give the required level of the finite transformation. Away from the selected places this already follows from g ∈ U(S). Thus a transformation outside the level moves the support off itself.

For the Weil matrix coefficient one must still transfer this disjointness to the theta vector. A finite sum of additive characters is one on the support and zero on its translate. The corresponding sum of Heisenberg operators fixes the datum. After conjugating the coefficients, transporting by g−1, and reversing the translations, it kills the same datum. The operators commute with the polynomial Fock construction at infinity. Moving the finite sum from one entry of the Hermitian pairing to the other therefore shows W(g) = 0.

On the remaining subgroup, write g = b∞ κ with κ ∈ K. The Weil coefficient acquires the level character χK(κ). The Petersson coefficient acquires the same character before conjugation. Their product contains |χK(κ)|² = 1. The Petersson coefficient also contributes the scalar ⟨u,u⟩ and a product of real discrete-series matrix coefficients. Pushing the restricted adelic Haar measure forward along the projection to the real group gives a Haar measure m∞. Its normalization includes the finite-level volume. If Z∞ denotes the remaining Weil coefficient times the conjugate of that product of real coefficients, the result is

JS(s₀) = ⟨u,u⟩ · ∫ Z∞(b∞) dm∞.

The finite-level computation controls the entire restricted integral, including any relation between the block reductions at the selected places.

6.34A positive contribution at each real place

The actual step vector starts with a nonzero Fock vacuum f. Let I₀ be its squared norm in the chosen covolume-one pairing. At each selected real place τ the gap and weight comparisons allow a polynomial Φτ jointly of highest weight for the two compact groups. Choose a smooth, compact-finite unit highest-weight vector wτ of the source. Glue the Φτ and tensor the wτ to obtain the test data above. On the discrete-series cover, the integral of a Fock coefficient against a conjugate highest-weight coefficient is a positive multiple of a squared norm divided by formal degree. The norm is that of the coefficient projector applied to the normalized joint vector. Its nonvanishing on that vector and positivity of the formal degree make the result strictly positive. Pullback to the cover introduces a positive Haar constant, and the unitary phase cancels against its conjugate. Denote the resulting local value by rτ > 0.

Why the real-place projection has positive mass

Fix one real place τ of a step of the iterated theta chain. Its integral pairs a Weil matrix coefficient with the conjugate of a discrete-series coefficient. Even when both vectors have norm one, the integral can vanish if the two coefficients detect different parts of the representation. Here the Fock model realizes vectors using polynomials with a Gaussian inner product. Restricting a representation to a compact subgroup breaks it into finite-dimensional types. A joint highest-weight polynomial selects a specific type for each of the two compact groups. We must show that this choice survives projection onto the component detected by the source vector. The chain chooses a polynomial Φ of the prescribed highest weights for both compact groups and a unit source vector of its prescribed highest weight. Its real-place comparison identifies the polynomial with a vector in the Fock model of the oscillator representation.

Build the projection. Let G̃ be the double cover of the real unitary group U(p,q) with Haar measure ν. Let σ be the source discrete series on this cover, v its chosen unit vector, and dσ its formal degree for ν. We use the inner product linear in its second entry. Write mv(g) = ⟨v,σ(g)v⟩. For unit v, Schur orthogonality gives ∫ |mv(g)|² dν(g) = 1/dσ. This fixes the scalar that makes the projector send v to itself in σ. For any unitary representation π of the cover define the operator

Pvx = dσ ∫G̃ mv(g) π(g)x dν(g).

The chain’s gap condition ensures absolute integrability of the kernel. The estimate used here requires every pair of source parameters in opposite signature blocks to differ in absolute value by at least 120(p+q)min(p,q)3/2. In polar coordinates the discrete-series decay then pays for the growth of Haar measure. The joint-vector theorem additionally uses the admissible pair of parameters, their matching compact weights and the chain’s further gap and Casimir conditions.

Schur orthogonality gives Pvx = ⟨v,x⟩v in σ itself. In any π, inversion gives Pv* = Pv. Convolving the same kernel on both sides of a translate gives Pvπ(g)Pv = mv(g)Pv. At the identity mv(1) = 1, proving idempotence. Its range is the closed span of the vectors T v for continuous intertwiners T from σ to π. In the Fock representation let η be the normalized joint polynomial vector. Testing the integral operator against η and using η − Pvη ⟂ Pvη gives

∫G̃ ⟨η,π(g)η⟩ mv(g) dν(g) = ⟨η,Pvη⟩/dσ = ‖Pvη‖²/dσ.

The Fock coefficient has absolute value at most one by unitarity, so the same integrability estimate justifies this pairing.

A circle calculation that isolates what the projector measures

Give U(1) Haar mass one and take σ(z) = z, of formal degree one. On ℂ² put π(z) = diag(z,z²) and η = (1,2)/√5. The product of coefficients is ((z + 4z²)/5)z = (1 + 4z)/5. Its integral is 1/5. The operator gives the same answer by sending η to (1,0)/√5. Choosing η = (0,1) would give zero. This calculation checks the conjugation and the squared norm. In the theta chain the following argument supplies the nonzero component.

Why the joint vector survives. Suppose Pvη = 0. Testing against every Fock vector would make every integral ∫⟨z,π(g)η⟩ mv(g) dν vanish. The two source-side highest vectors η and v have the same compact highest weight. Their pair generates a finite-dimensional irreducible representation E of the maximal compact subgroup. Write j₁ and j₂ for its maps to the Fock and discrete-series spaces and give E the norm induced by the injective j₂. Compact translation and irreducibility propagate the assumed vanishing to the integrals of all mixed matrix entries from E.

To see the contradiction, compress π(g) and σ(g) to E, writing A(g) = j₁*π(g)j₁ and B(g) = j₂*σ(g)j₂. In an orthonormal basis, F(g) = tr(B(g)*A(g)) is the sum of exactly those mixed entries, so its integral would vanish. Left compact translation changes the common basis and preserves F. On the noncompact Cartan directions g = exp Y, positivity of the Fock joint harmonics and of the lowest compact type of σ makes both compressed operators positive semidefinite. Diagonalizing one shows tr(B*A) ≥ 0. Since each g is a compact translate of some exp Y, this proves F ≥ 0 everywhere. At the identity B(1) = 1 and F(1) = ∑j ‖j₁ej‖² > 0 because η belongs to the image. Continuity and positive Haar measure on open sets contradict a zero integral. Thus Pvη ≠ 0. When the partner is definite, the stronger local theorem gives Pvη = η and the cover integral equals 1/dσ.

Return to the real integral. Let the cover map send ν to c₀μ for the measure μ chosen on the real group. Let CF > 0 compare the theta pairing with the Fock inner product, and write η = n · ι(κΦ), where κ puts the polynomial in local model coordinates, ι embeds it in Fock space and n = 1/‖ι(κΦ)‖. The original Weil coefficient thus contributes CF/n² times the normalized Fock coefficient. On the cover, both the Weil and discrete-series coefficients carry the same unit-modulus splitting character. Complex conjugation on the discrete-series factor cancels that phase. Passing from ν back to μ therefore gives the positive value

rτ = CF ‖Pvη‖² / (c₀ n² dσ).

The chain uses this number at one real place for its chosen test data. The product over the real places also carries the vacuum normalization and a product-measure constant. The finite-place integrals, the continued L-value and the global Siegel–Weil identity enter separately in the theta norm. The local positivity proof uses discrete-series orthogonality, decay and positivity of its lowest compact type, the Fock positivity on joint harmonics and Cartan decomposition. Its conclusion gives strict positivity for these data, with magnitude depending on the projection and the measures.

The Weil coefficient splits as I₀ times a product, with each real factor divided by I₀. Comparing m∞ with the product of the local Haar measures introduces one constant cHaar > 0. Thus

∫ Z∞ dm∞ = I₀ · cHaar · ∏τ (rτ / I₀) ≠ 0.

The same data supply the convergence assumption to the left of s₀. For each allowed majorant frame, the product h∞ of archimedean heights lies in (0,1]. The norm of the Weil coefficient is bounded by a constant times h∞b/2, and the product of the discrete-series coefficients is integrable. At s₁ = 0, multiplication by h∞−t/2 leaves the nonnegative exponent (b − t)/2 = a/2. At finite places the local height equals one on the level. This proves the weighted integrability required for continuation and the nonvanishing required at s₀.

6.35From partial products to the special point

Inserting a new good place v in S removes its lattice-stabilizer restriction. Write an element of U(S) as an element whose v-component is 1 times an embedded element of Kv. Uniqueness of the normalized spherical section separates the Weil and height factors in that variable. The local integral above applies to the remaining Petersson coefficient. Thus each insertion multiplies the restricted integral by Lv(s + ½)/dv(s). Exhausting the finite places proves, for Re s > a + 1, that the full doubling integral equals LS(s + ½) JS(s)/dS(s).

At the real special point, the normalizing Euler factors have the form (1 − ηb+i(v) q−(t+a−i))−1. Their signs inside the parentheses may differ, but every factor is positive. The exponent is at least t + 1, so the logarithms are absolutely summable and the product is positive. The twisted numerator is a different matter. Its characters can take complex values, and the argument in the preceding chain section proves nonvanishing of the continued special value. On the diagonal the full Petersson pairing is a squared norm.

The integrable height bound at s₁ makes JS holomorphic on Re s > s₁. Uniqueness of meromorphic continuation matches the product just computed to the full doubling integral at s₀, using the supplied holomorphic value L₀ and the nonvanishing of dS. For example, at the second lift a = r + t, so s₀ = t/2 lies even to the left of a/2. Substitution in the far-right Euler identity alone would miss this step. Combining the continued identity with the positive volume, the nonzero residual integral, and the special value proved above forces the chosen lift to survive.

6.36Summing the split local integral one lattice at a time

At a split place, the unitary group can be written as GLa over the local field. A matrix takes the standard lattice to a new lattice, and two matrices give the same lattice exactly when they differ on the right by its stabilizer K. Give K Haar volume one. The local integral is now a sum over lattices. We need to know both what each lattice contributes and whether this infinite sum converges at the complex parameter used by the lift.

Choose a uniformizer ϖ, an element of valuation one, and write q for the residue-field size. The elementary divisors of a lattice give a unique weakly decreasing tuple of integers d = (d₁,…,da). Choosing integral bases separately in the source and the target makes the matrix diagonal with entries ϖdᵢ. Let Sd be the finite set of lattices with that tuple. Two integers extracted from it enter the kernel. The signed sum D = ∑dᵢ gives the determinant valuation and the twist zD, with |z| = 1. The sum k = ∑|dᵢ| measures the total displacement. For d = (1,−1), the twist is one although the displacement is two. With X = q−(a/2+s), the spherical section gives zDXk on every lattice in the cell.

Let v be the spherical vector and write its matrix coefficient as c(g) = λ(π(g)v). By the Hecke eigenvector equation, summing π(g)v over this cell gives a scalar hd times v. Applying λ gives hdc(1). Thus all the information from the representations in this part of the sum fits into a single scalar per tuple. Write Ad = zDhdc(1). If |c(g)| ≤ C, then |Ad| ≤ C |Sd| by the triangle inequality.

Count the first two shells in rank two

Take residue-field size 3 and the trivial coefficient and twist. The two tuples of displacement one are (1,0) and (0,−1). In the first cell, the sublattices of index 3 correspond to the four lines in the two-dimensional residue space. Multiplication by ϖ identifies the second cell with the first. The coefficient of X is therefore 8.

At displacement two the tuples (1,1) and (−1,−1) give one lattice each. The other three are (2,0), (1,−1) and (0,−2), all equivalent by central scaling for the purpose of counting. A lattice of type (2,0) is the kernel of a surjection onto the quotient of the local integer ring by (ϖ²). There are 9² − 3² primitive pairs of coefficients for such a map. Two maps have the same kernel precisely when a unit of the quotient relates them, and there are 9 − 3 such units. Each of the three cells has 72/6 = 12 elements. The counting series begins 1 + 8X + 38X². For the constant coefficient 1 of the trivial representation, the two Satake parameters here are √3 and 1/√3. Thus the product below becomes (1 − X²)(1 − 3X²)/[(1 − 3X)²(1 − X)²]. Its coefficients bound the absolute sum at this one place. To obtain a nonzero norm for a step in the chain, the proof also needs the continued global value and the residual integral.

Fix the standard lattice Λ₀ = 𝒪a and an endpoint Λ = gΛ₀. To sum the split integral, the proof first counts two moves. First enlarge Λ₀ to a lattice H, then shrink H to Λ. Give each move of length k the weight Xk, where length means the module length of the quotient of the larger lattice by the smaller one. Several intermediate lattices give the same endpoint. Their total weight explains exactly which factor must be removed from the product of the two sums.

Write d₁,…,da for the elementary divisors of Λ relative to Λ₀. The smallest possible intermediate lattice is M = Λ₀ + Λ. In elementary-divisor coordinates its exponents are min(dᵢ,0), so the two lengths through M add up to ∑|dᵢ|. For any larger H, additivity of length gives

length(H/Λ₀) + length(H/Λ) = ∑i|dᵢ| + 2 length(H/M).

Taking lattice duals identifies the superlattices of M with sublattices of M∨ of the same quotient length. For an upper triangular basis in Hermite normal form, a diagonal entry ϖuᵢ in row i leaves a − 1 − i entries to its right, each chosen modulo ϖuᵢ. Here 0 ≤ i < a and q is the residue-field size. Summing over uᵢ ≥ 0 gives ∏i(1 − qiX²)−1 after reversing the indices. This common multiplier is the same for every endpoint. To count each endpoint with its required weight X∑|dᵢ|, multiply the two-move sum by ∏i(1 − qiX²).

Check the correction for a pair of rank-two lattices

Take q = 2 and Λ generated by ϖ²e₁ and ϖ⁻¹e₂. The sum M is generated by e₁ and ϖ⁻¹e₂, so the two moves through it have lengths 1 and 2. There are three intermediate lattices one step above M, one for each line in ϖ⁻¹M/M ≅ 𝔽₂². At length two above M, the three possibilities for the diagonal exponents in the dual Hermite form give 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 lattices. Thus the weight at this single endpoint starts X³(1 + 3X² + 7X⁴ + ⋯). Multiplication by (1 − X²)(1 − 2X²) cancels the next coefficients since 3 − 3 = 0 and 7 − 9 + 2 = 0.

Its sum on each double coset agrees with that of a right-K-invariant function whose value on an upper triangular matrix with diagonal valuations uᵢ is ∏iγiuᵢ. Passing to the inverse transpose and reversing the basis turns the enlarging move into a shrinking move, with ratios qiγi−1X. For X = q−(a/2+s), these simplify respectively to αiq−(s+½) and αi−1q−(s+½). The proof first sums for small |X|, where absolute convergence permits either order. Inserting αi = zβi for the determinant twist gives the two sets of factors in the split-place formula.

Why the split-place sum converges at the required parameter

The published unramified doubling input evaluates a zonal integral far to the right. Twisting the representation by the determinant valuation multiplies every Satake parameter β by z. The resulting eigenvalue series gives, initially for small positive real X, the following expression, with Y = q(a−1)/2X and the parameters counted with multiplicity.

∑d Ad X∑|dᵢ| = c(1) ∏0≤i<a (1 − qiX²) ∏β [(1 − zβY)(1 − (zβ)−1Y)]−1.

Why is an identity near zero enough? Apply the same doubling input to the trivial representation. Its Hecke operator counts the lattices in each cell, so its series has coefficient |Sd|. Group the two series by the nonnegative displacement k. Only finitely many tuples have a fixed k. On a positive interval these grouped coefficients determine the Taylor coefficients of their respective rational products. Both products are holomorphic for |X| < q−(a−½). Indeed, if c(1) ≠ 0, the bounds on β and β−1 are qa/2, so each linear Euler term has argument of modulus less than one on that disk. When c(1) = 0 the entire expression weighted by c(1) is identically zero. The counting product has its own Satake bound. Its Taylor series at |X| converges and has nonnegative coefficients. For each individual lattice in Sd, the absolute value of its contribution is at most C|X|k. Summing these bounds over the cell gives C|Sd||X|k. The convergent counting series therefore justifies summing the original complex terms lattice by lattice.

The GL lemma holds for Re s > a/2. In the half-plane Re s > a used by the adelic lifting argument, the value X = q−(a/2+s) lies inside that disk. Substitution gives Y = q−(s+½) and qiX² = q−(2s+a−i). Hence the reciprocal linear factors are exactly the Euler factors at the two CM places over the split prime. The polynomial in X² is the reciprocal local normalizer. At this prime, freeing the integration variable therefore contributes Lv(s + ½)/dv(s) to the product in the lifting formula.
