8.19One integer pays for all the congruences

At the auxiliary automorphic level M, the counting theorem supplies a finite indexed list of Frobenius eigenvalue multisets. Different indices may carry identical multisets. For each index with trace s, form the difference between s and pe+1z₁ + pez₂ + p z₃ + 1, including all simultaneous conjugates of the chosen kth roots of unity z₁, z₂, z₃. For p ≥ 5, e ≥ 2 and y = pe, the purity estimate on the eigenvalues gives |s| ≤ 7y/2. The first summand has size py > 7y/2 + y + p + 1, so every difference is nonzero. The factors are algebraic integers. All field automorphisms permute them. Their product is therefore a nonzero rational integer m. Bounding each factor by p2(e+1) and counting all the factors gives log |m| ≤ cφ(k)[M(e+1)]A log p, with φ Euler’s totient.

Each member of Ξ selects a different index in the product. Equal values at different indices retain their multiplicity. The unused factors have ℓ-adic norm at most one, whence |m|ℓ ≤ ∏r∈Ξ|a(r)|ℓ. Taking negative logarithms bounds the sum by vℓ(m) log ℓ ≤ log |m|. For example, the integer 45 allows at most two powers of 3 across selected integral factors, since 45 = 3² · 5. This elementary divisibility step turns the complex size estimate into the required ℓ-adic inequality.

The auxiliary level grows with the data. Write Q for the conductor of χ, o for its order and X = ℓNe. The construction takes M = ℓ 2n′NP, k = (ℓ−1)2n′(2o). Here P = 1 in case II and is a fixed auxiliary prime determined by χ in case III. In case II, if c₂ is the dyadic conductor exponent of ψ and n₀ = v₂(ℓf₀ − 1), with f₀ the multiplicative order of ℓ modulo lcm(4, ord θ₁) for the auxiliary character θ₁, the integer n′ is the ceiling of the base-two logarithm of max(ℓN4n₀, 2c₂+6oℓ³Q²). The host bounds give 2c₂ ≤ N and 2n₀ < ℓφ(4o). Rounding up to a power of two costs at most a factor two. Together these bounds give 2n′ ≤ X2φ(4o)+10. Case III uses max(ℓQP4n₀, 8ℓ²) and gives the exponent 11 + Q + P + 2φ(4o). The comparison prime satisfies p ≤ 2ℓNP + 10. Thus every factor in 2ck[M(e+1)]A log p is bounded by a power of X whose exponent is fixed once χ is fixed.

The proof may enlarge O to contain enough roots of unity. Independence of normalized length brings the estimate back to the original ring.

8.20The rank-three estimate in case V

Here ℓ belongs to the finite exceptional set for χ, e = 1 and the case-V count applies when 16o(ℓQ)²4n₀ ≤ 2c₂, the conductor threshold denoted by R₁ ≤ 2c₂.

The proof works over the Gaussian field ℚ(i). At a point ξ with components of both signs, rigidity forces every allowed tangent derivation to satisfy D(xj) = b j ξ(xj) on a coordinate of weight j, for a single scalar b. Indeed rescaling that coordinate by (1 + εb)j gives precisely this derivative. For each nonzero d ∈ O the finite-coefficient obstruction embeds into vectors over O/(d) supported in weight −1 and killed by the linearized relations. The resulting bound is uniform in d. Taking d = ℓn bounds the length of the full torsion obstruction because every element is killed by some power of ℓ.

Choose an inert prime p ≡ 3 modulo 4 with 7 ≤ p ≤ 12ℓN and p ∤ ℓN. The Frobenius over this prime has residue norm p². The trace test uses its inverse. Representatives are distinguished up to isomorphism after restriction to the Gaussian subgroup. Group them by the two embeddings of ℚ(i) into the chosen algebraic closure. The unitary counting theorem includes all φ(N)th roots of unity in its integral product. Applying it in each embedding group gives

∑r vℓ(a(r)) log ℓ ≤ 2a φ(N)[N(e+1)]b log p ≤ X2a+1+b+3.

The constants a,b here come from the counting theorem for the fixed field. The inequalities φ(N) ≤ X, N(e + 1) ≤ X and log p ≤ p ≤ X³ explain the exponent. The cotangent estimate introduces a final factor two, absorbed into one more power of X. The final comparison uses the integral automorphic counting statement, a unitary lifting theorem, adjoint rigidity, local and global cohomology theorems, and the commutative algebra length lemma. 8.21One field for all three estimates

The exterior exponent Cout and auxiliary test primes depend on χ. The interior exponents also depend on the layer choices j(ℓ). Bound each by their sum D over Bχ, and put k = |Bχ|. Splitting any finite set of odd primes into its two parts now gives at most k(MD+DB)+MCout. With M ≥ 2, one can take C=Cout+D+k+kD. In particular, 1+k ≤ Mk absorbs the number of polynomial terms and kD ≤ C absorbs the multiple of B. The window chooses j(ℓ)=⌊logℓ Rℓ⌋+3 and B=exp(x4ε/5) before applying this result to any field at x.

Why is M equal to t times the field conductor, as the next theorem requires? Let E be any realization of the four fixing conditions. It embeds into the cyclotomic field of modulus N. If it also embeds at modulus M′ with a smaller exponent at a prime p dividing N, there is a unit c modulo N congruent to 1 modulo N/p outside the fixing subgroup. At the auxiliary primes one can use −1 in the corresponding component, since these primes are 3 modulo 4. At a prime whose exponent comes from χ, primitivity supplies a unit detected at the last power of that prime. In the remaining 2-primary case, 1+2n+1 is 1 at the preceding level and is neither sign at modulus 2n+2. The Chinese remainder theorem puts the chosen component together with the required trivial components.

Pass to lcm(M′,N). The witness lifts to a unit reducing to c modulo N and to 1 modulo M′. Its automorphism would both move and fix the same field. Hence N divides every admissible modulus and the conductor is exactly N. The field is also CM. In the ambient cyclotomic field a quadratic Gauss sum has square −q and transforms by the quadratic character at q. The defining subgroup fixes it, so E contains a square root of −q. An abelian extension of ℚ containing this element is totally imaginary and hence CM. Thus conjugation, the plus estimate, and the minus estimate all refer to this same field. The large-prime hypotheses make q,d coprime to Q and allow the same pair throughout the chosen window.

Which representation results supply these inequalities?

The final call obtains I from the unitary rank-three orbit estimate, II and III jointly from symplectic rank four, and V from a reduced unitary lift with cohomological finiteness, local duality and Euler characteristics. IV is the restriction argument on the bounded-degree layer above. The Z branch uses a trivial-character vanishing theorem. The separate estimate for large R₁ at twist one uses degree two. These distinct calls make clear which proof inputs one would have to strengthen to improve the plus bound.

The product Ak of the αk(χ) over the full selected character set is rational because the set is defined by character kernels and the factors commute with change of coefficient field. Each factor is integral and nonzero, so Ak is a nonzero integer. Every omitted ℓ-adic factor has nonnegative valuation. The sum needed at ℓ is therefore at most vℓ(Ak) log ℓ. How one Bernoulli value bounds a module length

Fix a primitive character ψ of conductor f, an odd prime ℓ prime to its order, and a twist e ≥ 1 with ψ(−1) = (−1)e+1. Write O for the coefficient ring, a discrete valuation ring finite as a module over ℤℓ, v for its additive valuation with v(π) = 1 at a uniformizer π, and A for the cleared Bernoulli value at the conductor. The goal is lengthO ≤ v(A) for this character component. An integer can kill a whole module without controlling its length. For example, 3 kills (ℤ/3)d for every d. The proof needs local tests that measure how much length remains after each one.

Let χ be the ℓ-adic cyclotomic character and ψG the Galois character attached to ψ. The scalar action on the cocycles in the count is α = (χeψG)−1. First consider the case where α(g) − χ(g) is a unit for some g. Choose a nonzero cutoff a₀ ∈ O. Work with cocycles c in the torsion coefficient module O ⊗ℤℓ (ℚℓ/ℤℓ) whose values are killed by a₀. At one auxiliary cyclotomic level, choose δ inducing −1 on the exponents of its roots of unity. Parity gives α(δ) ≡ −1 modulo the maximal ideal. Since ℓ is odd, α(δ) − 1 is a unit. The same δ works for every cutoff. Normalize the cocycles to have c(δ) = 0. Subtracting the coboundary of c(δ)/(α(δ) − 1) achieves this.

Outside the level the scalar action is trivial on inertia, so the local coboundary condition forces the normalized cocycle to vanish there. At a conductor prime p ≠ ℓ the initial condition supplies a witness w on inertia I. Primitivity in this prime-to-ℓ character case supplies t ∈ I with α(t) − 1 a unit. For any d in the decomposition group, d−1td lies in I. Evaluate the cocycle identity on td = d(d−1td). It gives (α(t) − 1)[c(d) − (α(d) − 1)w] = 0. Cancellation extends the same witness to the entire decomposition group. At ℓ a decomposition-group witness is already part of the original condition. Choose a single cutoff killing that witness and the finite image of the continuous cocycle on its compact source. It then kills the witnesses at conductor primes by the same unit cancellation, and conjugation covers the other places over ℓ.

As a₀ runs through powers of π, the images of these spaces cover the locally trivial classes. A bound uniform in the cutoff will therefore bound the entire length.

Choose m after a₀ and put F = fℓ′ℓm, where fℓ′ is the prime-to-ℓ part of the conductor. Outside the primes dividing fℓ this introduces no new ramification. Here F denotes an integer level. Write [t] for the least nonnegative representative of t modulo F. For a suitable b < F and lifts σt acting on Fth roots of unity by the power t, the scalar used in the count is

z = ∑t∈(ℤ/Fℤ)× (⌊[t]b/F⌋ − ⌊[−t]b/F⌋) α(σt)−1.

The evaluation theorem arranges a₀z ∣ ℓm and z ∣ A. Here is the valuation principle behind the second divisibility. The unit-difference hypothesis gives a residue b for which ψ(b)be+1 − 1 is an ℓ-adic unit. The congruence for the floor sum compares it, after explicit scaling, with the nonzero Bernoulli value divided by e + 1. The source takes m large enough that the approximation error is strictly smaller than the norm of the comparison term after scaling. In a nonarchimedean norm, |x−y| < |y| forces |x| = |y|. The resulting norm of z is |Be+1,ψ/(e+1)|. Multiplying by integral factors to get the cleared value A can only increase its valuation.

How multiplication modulo the level produces a Bernoulli value

The length argument needs an integer-like scalar whose ℓ-adic valuation is exactly that of a special value. The floor in its definition records the carry when an integer product is reduced modulo the level. This permits a direct comparison of the two quantities, one residue at a time. Keep the level F = fℓ′ℓm chosen above, put k = e + 1 ≥ 2, and let χ denote the Dirichlet character induced by ψ at level F throughout this calculation. The cyclotomic character will enter again when the sum is compared with the Galois lifts.

For a unit residue, write u for its representative in 1,…,F−1. Choose b prime to F and divide bu by F, obtaining a quotient j and a remainder y between 1 and F−1. The opposite residue is represented by F−u. Its product with b is (b−j−1)F + (F−y). Subtracting the two quotients gives the signed carry θ(u) = 2j − (b−1). Define S = ∑u θ(u)ueχ(u), summed over the unit representatives. The use of ue in place of a lifted cyclotomic character changes the scalar by a multiple of ℓm.

Write C(u) = Fk−1Bk(u/F)/k, where Bk(x) is the Bernoulli polynomial. Let P be the product of the primes at most k + 1 and set D = 2kP. The first two coefficients of the polynomial give

C(u) = uk/(kF) − uk−1/2 + (2F/D)nu,   nu ∈ ℤ.

Indeed the term of Bernoulli index h ≥ 2 has a factor Fh−1. The denominator bound for the Bernoulli number Bh says that PBh is an integer for h ≤ k. Thus the terms after the first two are all multiples of F/(kP).

Compare C(y) and bkC(u) with y = bu − Fj. In the leading power, the first-order change divided by kF is −j(bu)e. In the second power, the surviving term is (b−1)(bu)e/2. Their sum is −θ(u)(bu)e/2. To keep track of the remainder, expand yk modulo F² and ye modulo F. Multiplication by D clears every denominator in the remainder, with one factor F left. In particular the following quantity is an integer multiple of F.

D[beθ(u)ue + 2(C(y) − bkC(u))] ∈ Fℤ.

Multiply by χ(bu) and sum over u. Multiplication by b permutes the units, so ∑χ(bu)C(y) = ∑χ(u)C(u) = TF, the generalized Bernoulli value at level F divided by k. The other terms use χ(bu) = χ(b)χ(u). Every summand on the remainder side is divisible by ℓm in the coefficient ring. This gives the congruence used by the count.

D[χ(b)beS − 2(χ(b)bk − 1)TF] ≡ 0   (mod ℓm).

For example, take the primitive trivial character, ℓ = 5, e = 1, F = 5 and b = 2. The four signed carries are −1, −1, 1, 1, giving S = −1 − 2 + 3 + 4 = 4. In general the change of level multiplies the primitive Bernoulli value by factors 1 − ψ(p)pe. At p dividing the conductor the character vanishes, and at a newly added ℓ the subtracted term has norm less than one. Thus |TF|ℓ equals the norm of the primitive value. The unit-difference hypothesis in the character argument gives a b for which χ(b)bk − 1 is a unit. Since ℓ is odd, 2 is a unit too. The depth is chosen so that |ℓm|ℓ is strictly smaller than |D|ℓ|TF|ℓ, also allowing for the original cutoff. The congruence then forces |S|ℓ = |TF|ℓ. Replacing S by the lifted scalar z preserves that norm. This is the valuation that the successive Frobenius tests spend.

What a Frobenius test measures

Choose a base prime r ≡ 1 modulo F. Let L be a list of distinct auxiliary primes q ≡ 1 modulo F, different from r, at which the multiplicative order of r is prime to ℓ. Call the space at this cutoff, before imposing the base-prime condition, Sbefore. Write SL for its cocycles vanishing on the entire decomposition groups over r and the primes in L. Even S∅ imposes vanishing over r. With each list comes a second function νL in the dual character χα−1. On the subgroup fixing the Fth roots of unity its values are additive and killed by ℓm. Their annihilator is a principal ideal, with generator aL. Put jL = v(aL) and J = v(ℓm). Thus jL ≤ J. The induction uses lists for which the cutoff a₀ divides aL. The initial list has this property, and each new test preserves it.

If SL contains a nonzero c, the prime selection theorem chooses a new q with two properties at once. Evaluation on a Frobenius element φ at q detects c, meaning c(φ) ≠ 0. Every value of νL on the subgroup fixing the roots of unity is an O-multiple of νL(φ). For the longer list L′ there is then an inertia element τ at q for which νL′(τ) equals νL(φ) times a unit. The two values have identical annihilators. Since the entire next system contains this inertia value, aL divides aL′. Denote their quotient by d.

Reciprocity controls the image of the linear evaluation map c ↦ c(φ). In the finite coefficient quotient the characters of the two cocycles multiply to χ. Their cup product is a global degree-two class. At the other primes in the finite ramification set the local coboundary condition makes its restriction trivial. The global sum of local invariants thus leaves zero at q. Local unramified orthogonality, with c zero on inertia there, makes the product of the inertia coefficient of the dual class and the value c(φ) vanish. This conclusion holds in the finite coefficient quotient. The proof first tests it with linear functionals which separate its elements.

Concretely, choose a generator w of the cyclic coefficient subgroup killed by aL′ and write νL′(τ) = y w. Its annihilator is (aL). If the inertia value is nonzero, its order in a cyclic module over a discrete valuation ring gives v(y) = v(d). Thus the reciprocity relation y c(φ) = 0 implies d c(φ) = 0. If the inertia value is zero, its annihilator is the unit ideal and the cutoff dividing aL forces the cutoff space to vanish. The chosen nonzero evaluation therefore forces v(d) > 0. The image of evaluation, lying in cyclic d-torsion, has length at most v(d). An element in its kernel vanishes at the whole decomposition group over q. On the roots-of-unity subgroup it is additive, and the quotient of the decomposition group by inertia is topologically generated by Frobenius. Conjugation transports vanishing to the other places over q. Thus the kernel lies in SL′.

length SL + jL ≤ length SL′ + jL′,   jL′ = jL + v(d) ≤ J.
Check one length loss over ℤ₃

In ℚ₃/ℤ₃ take w = 1/27 modulo ℤ₃. Its annihilator is (27), and the annihilator of 3w is (9). Their quotient is 3. As an example of the evaluation map, send (ℤ/9) ⊕ (ℤ/3) onto the order-three subgroup generated by 1/3 via the second coordinate. The source has length three, the kernel has length two, and the image has length one. Adding this loss to the old annihilator valuation changes 2 to 3. This finite calculation checks the direction and size of one step. Choosing a Frobenius with these properties is the arithmetic assertion above.

Whenever SL is nonzero, the next integer jL′ is strictly larger. It cannot exceed J. Induction on J − jL ends with a zero space and proves length SL + jL ≤ J at every admissible state reached, even before finiteness of the starting length has been established. It remains to remove the condition at the base prime r. Take k = ℓm/z. The initial inertia value is a unit times z w for a coefficient element with annihilator (ℓm), so that value has annihilator (k). Write a∅ = k d₀. In the complementary case α agrees with χ modulo the maximal ideal at every group element. Primitivity and the prime-to-ℓ order imply that α is unramified away from ℓ. At ℓ, an inertia element acting by −1 on ℓth roots of unity gives a unit α(δ) − 1 since ℓ is odd. For a normalized cocycle killed by π, the local coboundary witness over ℓ must be zero. Evaluating its defining equation at δ multiplies the witness by the unit α(δ) − 1 and gives zero. Away from ℓ the cocycle already vanishes on inertia.

To see what these local conditions force globally, apply an additive functional from the π-torsion to the field of ℓ elements. The resulting scalar cocycle s has cyclotomic action. Kummer theory realizes it by a radical β with βℓ = a ∈ ℚ× and gβ/β = ζs(g) for a primitive ℓth root ζ. Vanishing on inertia makes every prime exponent of a divisible by ℓ. Unique factorization in ℚ and oddness of ℓ now give a = uℓ for a rational u, including its sign. For example, −8/125 has exponents 3 and −3 and cube root −2/5. Thus β = uζi, so s(g) = i(χ̄(g) − 1), where χ̄ is the action modulo ℓ. At δ the left side is zero and χ̄(δ) − 1 is nonzero. Hence i = 0. All the scalar tests vanish, and linear functionals separate the π-torsion points. Finally, if πk+1c = 0, apply this first step to πkc and descend on k. The original length here is zero.

The construction of the auxiliary functions gives the unit relating the two local values. The carry congruence gives the valuation against which the length is bounded. Prime selection uses Chebotarev, and the test of each new restriction uses duality and orthogonality.

Which character takes values in the cyclotomic integers?

The Jacobi identity multiplies two algebraic integers. A sum computed only modulo p would lose the ideal it is supposed to measure. Let K = ℚ(ζ), where ζ has order M ≥ 1, and choose a prime ideal of norm p with p ∤ M. Its quotient has p elements. Identify it with 𝔽p and call the resulting reduction π. The algebraic integer ζ satisfies the cyclotomic polynomial ΦM. Its reduction satisfies the same polynomial modulo p. As p ∤ M, the roots of XM − 1 are simple, and the cyclotomic factors for the divisors of M have disjoint roots. A root of ΦM therefore has exact order M. In particular πζ has that order and M divides p − 1.

Put h = (p − 1)/M. For each nonzero x in 𝔽p, the element xh is an Mth root of unity. The M powers of πζ are distinct and list every such root. Find the exponent 0 ≤ a < M with xh = (πζ)a and set χ(x) = ζa. Set χ(0) = 0. Multiplying two residues adds their exponents modulo M, so χ is multiplicative. Its order is exactly M. Indeed, if χk = 1, a generator g of 𝔽p× satisfies ghk = 1 after reduction. Hence Mh divides hk, so M divides k. Conversely all nonzero values have Mth power one. This explains why the nontriviality checks on the Jacobi characters reduce to exponent checks.

Lift the residue 2 at level five

Take M = 5 and p = 11, with πζ = 3. The powers of 3 starting at exponent zero are 1, 3, 9, 5, 4 and then 1. Since h = 2, square the input 2 to obtain 4. The required lift is χ(2) = ζ⁴. Squaring this value gives χ(4) = ζ³. Checking the other way, 4² ≡ 5 ≡ 3³ modulo 11. For the other reduction π′ζ = 9, the input 2 still gives 2² = 4. Since 9² ≡ 4 modulo 11, its lift is now χ′(2) = ζ². The prime ideal is part of the construction.

Why every prime above p occurs only once

For each invertible residue t modulo M let σt(ζ) = ζt and put Pt = ker(π ∘ σt). This inverse-image convention is what sets the indices in the signed divisor. Every reduction is onto, since ordinary integers already give all of 𝔽p. Its kernel is therefore a maximal ideal of norm p. If two kernels agreed, subtract from any algebraic integer the ordinary integer representing its first reduction. The difference would also belong to the second kernel, forcing both reductions to agree on that element. Applying this to ζ gives (πζ)s = (πζ)t, hence s = t.

These φ(M) distinct maximal ideals are pairwise coprime, and each divides (p). Their product divides (p) and already has norm pφ(M). This equals the norm of (p), because [K : ℚ] = φ(M). The leftover integral ideal has norm one and is the unit ideal. Thus (p) = ∏tPt. For a Jacobi sum J dividing p, this gives ordPₜ(J) ∈ {0,1}. Testing π(σtJ) = 0 tells exactly which exponent is one. In the example at 11 the four reductions send ζ to 3, 9, 5 and 4. A repeated prime would exhaust too much of the norm.

To tell which primes occur, reduce σt(Jj) modulo P. The result is ∑ xA(1 − x)B with A = h[t]N and B = h[jt]N. Both exponents lie strictly between 0 and p − 1. Expand the binomial. In degree A + k the sum of powers over the field vanishes unless p − 1 divides the degree. Since all degrees are positive and below 2(p − 1), only k = p − 1 − A can contribute. When this index is in the expansion its binomial coefficient is nonzero modulo p, since B < p. Thus the residue is zero exactly when A + B < p − 1, or [t]N + [jt]N < N. Each addition without a carry contributes one factor of Pt to (J).

Let e(t) count these additions. For b ≥ 1 there are b − 1 steps. The number of carries is ⌊b[t]N/N⌋, since each new addition increases the integer quotient by one precisely when a carry occurs. Hence e(t) = b − 1 − ⌊b[t]N/N⌋. Conjugation exchanges Pt and P−t, so the exponent in (c(J)/J) is e(−t) − e(t) = θN(t). The product with its complex conjugate is 1 by cancellation. At b = 0 the Jacobi product is empty and XP = 1, as all the floor weights vanish.

Take N = 5, b = 3 and p = 11, so h = 2. At t = 1 the Jacobi factors for j = 1,2 give exponents (A,B) = (2,2),(2,4). Both sums vanish modulo 11 because their degrees stay below 10. At t = 4 the pairs are (8,8),(8,6). Both reach degree 10. The surviving terms give −28 ≡ 5 and −15 ≡ 7 modulo 11. Thus e(1) = 2 and e(4) = 0. The quotient c(J)/J has exponent −2 at P1, +2 at P4, and 0 at the other two primes. This agrees with θ5(1) = ⌊3/5⌋ − ⌊12/5⌋ = −2.

Why each Jacobi sum divides the split prime

The cyclotomic construction determines a signed ideal by testing a product of Jacobi sums at the primes above p. A zero residue proves that one such prime divides a factor. How can we tell that its square does not? Each factor has an explicit partner whose product with it is p. At a split unramified prime, the order of p is one, so the nonnegative orders of the two partners sum to one. This turns the residue test into an exact exponent.

Let χ and φ be multiplicative characters of 𝔽p× taking values in a characteristic-zero integral domain R, extended by zero at zero. Assume χ, φ and χφ are all nontrivial. Define J(χ,φ) = ∑x∈𝔽pχ(x)φ(1−x). The partner uses the inverse of each character. Its values already lie in R, since every nonzero character value is a unit.

J(χ,φ) J(χ−1,φ−1) = p.

To compute the product, pass to the fraction field of R and then to a cyclotomic extension containing a nontrivial additive character ψ of 𝔽p. Write Gψ(ρ) = ∑xρ(x)ψ(x). In the product Gψ(χ)Gψ(φ), group pairs (x,y) by t = x+y. At t = 0 their total is φ(−1)∑x(χφ)(x) = 0. At t ≠ 0 put x = tu. The two characters contribute (χφ)(t)χ(u)φ(1−u). Summing yields Gψ(χφ)J(χ,φ).

A second orthogonality identity says Gψ(ρ)Gψ−1(ρ−1) = p for nontrivial ρ. To see why, expand the two sums and put x = uy for y ≠ 0. At each y the summand becomes ρ(u)ψ(y(u−1)). We can include y = 0 because its total is ∑uρ(u) = 0. Summing over all y now leaves only u = 1, contributing p. Apply the first identity twice, once with ψ and once with its inverse and the inverse multiplicative characters. Multiplication and the second identity give pJ(χ,φ)J(χ−1,φ−1) = p². Cancelling p and using injectivity of the two field embeddings gives the claimed identity in R.

Take the level M = 3, b = 2 and p = 7. In ℤ[ω], with ω²+ω+1 = 0, choose the cubic character determined by χ(3) = ω, since 3 generates 𝔽₇×. At the prime where ω reduces to 2 it satisfies the required reduction χ(x) ≡ x². Here the Jacobi product has one factor, J(χ,χ). The inputs 0 and 1 contribute zero. For x = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 the five contributions are ω², 1, ω², 1, ω². The sum and its inverse-character partner are 2+3ω² and 2+3ω. Their product is 4+6(ω+ω²)+9 = 7. At ω ≡ 2 modulo 7 the first is zero and the second is one. At ω ≡ 4 their roles reverse. Each factor has order exactly one at the prime where it vanishes.

How to choose the prime in the inverse ideal class

The Jacobi sum uses a prime ideal P whose residue field has a prime number of elements. To apply that calculation to an arbitrary nonzero integral ideal 𝔞, the same P must make 𝔞P principal. For a prime of a number field K above a rational prime p, its absolute norm NP is the residue field size pf. Thus absolute residue degree one means NP = p. We can require this degree, prescribe the ideal class [P] = c and exclude any finite set of prime ideals of K.

Let H be the Hilbert class field of K. Its Artin isomorphism sends [P] to the arithmetic Frobenius at a prime above P, acting on residues by x ↦ xNP. Apply the degree-one prime theorem to H/K with target automorphism Art(c). The Frobenius supplied by the theorem restricts to this precise automorphism. Two Frobenius lifts at the same place agree modulo inertia, and inertia in H/K is trivial. Applying Art−1 gives [P] = c. In the cyclotomic application take c = [𝔞]−1 and exclude the primes dividing N𝒪K, where N is the cyclotomic level. This set is finite because N ≠ 0. Then p ∤ N, reduction preserves the order of ζN, and N divides p − 1 as the character construction requires. The inverse on [𝔞] comes from [𝔞][P] = 1.

How can the proof still impose absolute degree one?

Write L/K for the finite Galois extension and g for the requested automorphism. The proof chooses an auxiliary prime ℓ with [L : K] dividing ℓ − 1 and Φℓ irreducible over L. In L(ζℓ) choose an automorphism h restricting to g on L and raising ζℓ to a generator τ of (ℤ/ℓℤ)×. Irreducibility permits this choice by adjusting a lift of g with an automorphism fixing L. Take the fixed field Z of ⟨h⟩ inside this compositum. The powers of h realize every exponent on ζℓ, so Φℓ is still irreducible over Z.

Above the finite exclusions and the ramified primes of L/K there are only finitely many primes of Z. Away from these, seek a prime w with Nw ≡ τ modulo ℓ. A prime-distribution result gives divergence of the sum of reciprocal prime-ideal norms in this residue class. Primes of absolute degree at least two contribute at most [Z : ℚ]∑p primep−2, since at most [Z : ℚ] primes of Z lie above each p. The finite exclusions also contribute a finite amount. Hence a remaining w has prime norm p. For P below w, the equality Nw = (NP)f(w/P) forces NP = p.

A Frobenius lift at w fixes Z and acts on the ℓth roots by the pth power, since p ≠ ℓ and those roots remain distinct after reduction. Its action in the compositum is therefore hj with τj = τ. Thus j ≡ 1 modulo ℓ − 1. The order of g divides [L : K], which divides ℓ − 1, so gj = g. The equality of norms lets the same lift serve as an arithmetic Frobenius at P.

Their norms 2 and 3 multiply to N(ω) = 6, hence 𝔞P = (ω). Here the inverse class is genuinely different. The norm form a² + ab + 6b² never takes the value 2, so 𝔞 is nonprincipal. The element ω − 2 has norm 8 and is nonzero modulo the other prime (2,ω − 1) above 2, giving (ω − 2) = 𝔞³. Thus [𝔞] has order three and [P] = [𝔞]².

Given 𝔞, choose a degree-one prime P outside the primes dividing N, in the inverse ideal class [𝔞]−1. It follows by applying degree-one Chebotarev in the Hilbert class field. Now 𝔞P = (y) for a nonzero algebraic integer y. For a principal ideal the formula is immediate. Put Z(y) = ∏t σt−1(y)θN(t). Its ideal has the required factors for (y), and pairing t with −t gives Z(y)c(Z(y)) = 1 by antisymmetry. Divide this element by XP. At each conjugate prime the factors contributed by P cancel, leaving exactly the fractional ideal prescribed for 𝔞. The identity with complex conjugation survives division.

How much does the choice of generator matter? If X and X′ solve the same problem, their quotient w generates the unit ideal. It is an algebraic unit, and wc(w) = 1. Under every complex embedding this says |w| = 1. Kronecker’s theorem then makes w a root of unity. The torsion order of the units in KN divides 2N, hence w2N = 1. Both conditions on the generator enter this argument. For example, (3 + 4i)/5 in ℚ(i) has complex absolute value one, but its trace 6/5 rules out integrality.

What happens to the exponents under the norm?

Let q be a prime with q ∤ N, and let u be its residue modulo N. For b < q, sum the weights of the units upstairs lying over a fixed t downstairs. Among the q possible lifts [t]N + iN, exactly one is divisible by q, namely q[u−1t]N. Its missing floor is ⌊b[u−1t]N/N⌋. Summing before removing that lift gives ⌊b[t]N/N⌋ plus a constant independent of t. For 0 < b < q, this follows because the residues ib run once through all residues modulo q. Taking the difference at t and −t cancels the constant. At b = 0 both sides vanish.

∑t′ ↦ t θqN(t′) = θN(t) − θN(u−1t).

Take a nonzero ideal 𝔞′ upstairs and elements X′ and X satisfying the two defining conditions for 𝔞′ and its relative norm downstairs. The field norm of X′ multiplies its conjugates over KN. Grouping the factors of their ideals by the fibres t′ ↦ t gives the sum on the left. On the right the first weight is the exponent for X and the second gives the exponent for σu−1(X). The principal fractional ideals of the field norm and of X/σu−1(X) therefore coincide. Both generators have product one with their complex conjugates, so their quotient is a root ξn in the smaller field with ξn2N = 1.

Which degree counts the conjugates, and which degree counts the ideal?

Put N = Fd and enlarge the level to qN by a fresh prime q coprime to N. The construction chooses its two cyclotomic fields inside one algebraic closure. Even if the two embeddings were initially chosen separately, every Nth root of unity is a power of a primitive root of order qN. This puts the smaller field inside the larger one in precisely one way compatible with the chosen embeddings. Restricting the same place above the rational prime r then gives primes 𝔭′ above 𝔭.

The field norm counts conjugates. A relative automorphism fixes the roots of order N and can act by any nonzero residue on a primitive qth root. Indeed, for a generator g modulo q, the Chinese remainder theorem gives an exponent equal to 1 modulo N and to g modulo q. The resulting power map on roots gives an automorphism τ of KqN over KN. Its first q − 1 powers are distinct on the primitive qth root. They exhaust the relative Galois group since the degree is φ(qN)/φ(N) = q − 1, where φ counts invertible residues. Hence the product of τi(Xqd) for 0 ≤ i < q − 1 is its field norm.

The ideal norm counts residue-field degree. For r ∤ qN, write ordn(r) for the least positive k with rk ≡ 1 modulo n. At either level the prime is unramified, and Frobenius acts on the roots by the rth power. Its order is the absolute residue degree. Write κ(𝔭) for the residue field at 𝔭. Degrees multiply in the tower of residue fields, giving

s = [κ(𝔭′) : κ(𝔭)] = ordqN(r) / ordN(r),   Norm(𝔭′) = 𝔭s.

Thus Xds satisfies the two generator conditions for Norm(𝔭′). Raising to the power s multiplies each ideal exponent by s and preserves the identity with complex conjugation. This explains its exponent in both the norm formula and the congruence. The denominator in the norm formula uses the inverse of the qth-power action on the lower roots. The admissible auxiliary primes have orders of r prime to ℓ, and r ≡ 1 modulo F. By the Chinese remainder theorem their least common multiple is ordqN(r), so ℓ ∤ s.

8.24Why the Bernoulli factor is integral

To combine several primes in the minus estimate, the proof discards some character factors from an ℓ-adic product. This step is safe when each discarded factor has nonnegative valuation. Where does that integrality come from? At twist j put k = j + 1 ≥ 2. If χ has level N, conductor f and primitive character χ*, its denominator-cleared Bernoulli value is α = NPkBk,χ*, where Pk is the product of the primes at most k + 1. The two integer multipliers pay for different denominators.

Expand the Bernoulli polynomial in ordinary Bernoulli numbers Bh. The rational coefficient attached to one residue a is

fk−1Bk(a/f) = ∑h=0k binom(k,h) Bh fh−1ak−h.

At h = 0 the factor f−1 can introduce a conductor denominator. Multiplying the entire sum by f changes every exponent to the nonnegative integer h. For a positive even h, the von Staudt–Clausen formula expresses Bh as an integer minus a sum of 1/p over primes with p−1 dividing h. Each such p is at most h+1 ≤ k+1, so it divides Pk. The remaining indices give B₀ = 1, B₁ = −½ and Bh = 0 for odd h > 1. Thus PkBh is integral throughout, and fPk times the displayed coefficient is an integer, residue by residue.

Multiplying these integers by χ*(a) and summing keeps the result in the ring generated by the character values. A unit value is a root of unity, hence an algebraic integer, and a nonunit contributes zero. Each unit modulo f lifts to a unit modulo N, so the values of χ* belong to the ring generated by the original χ. Finally f divides N. Multiplying by the integer N/f proves the required integrality of α in that ring.

The same scaling also allows a single archimedean bound. For k ≥ 2 the Fourier expansion on [0,1] pairs the positive and negative frequencies. Each pair of unit complex phases has absolute value at most 2. Its reciprocal-power sum is bounded by 2∑m≥11/m² = π²/3 < 4. Consequently |Bk(x)| ≤ 4k!/(2π)k. There are f terms in the primitive sum, each carrying fk−1 and a character value of absolute value at most 1. Using f ≤ N, Pk ≤ 4k+1 and 4/(2π) ≤ 1 gives |α| ≤ 16Nk+1k!. The denominator bound uses von Staudt–Clausen and the primorial estimate. The absolute-value bound uses the Fourier series and the sum of reciprocal squares.

For a localization-kernel class x, choose a power ℓs killing x. At a sufficiently high cyclotomic level the congruence for z holds modulo ℓs and the restriction of the approximating element vanishes on x. The error acts by zero on x. Descent gives z(φ(H)x) = 0. On the sign component c acts by (−1)k, so the determinant of multiplication by z on the quotient imposing this sign also kills φ(H)x. This last deduction uses the adjugate identity in the quotient.

A denominator-cleared nonzero integer multiple of this determinant has absolute value at most the determinant bound raised to ⌊n/2⌋. Its ℓ-adic valuation bounds an exponent r₀ for the determinant. With r₁ = vℓ(φ(H)), the power ℓr, r = r₀ + r₁, annihilates the minus summand. Bounding the logarithm of the determinant bound together with log(Nℓ) gives

r log ℓ ≤ 30n(j+1) log(jℓN).

For the other factor in the length estimate, pass to the first cyclotomic layer of degree m over ℚ, with m ≤ ℓn. The ℓ-torsion of the ambient cohomology injects into a finite Selmer quotient of size at most ℓ2m times that layer’s class number. The class-number estimate gives a torsion length g ≤ 8ℓn log(ℓN). For the minus submodule M killed by ℓr, multiplication by ℓa−1 embeds each layer M[ℓa]/M[ℓa−1] into M[ℓ]. The bottom layer is finite by the Selmer count. Induction through at most r layers proves that M is finite and its length is at most rg. For ℤ/9 ⊕ ℤ/3, the subgroup killed by 3 has order 9, and the next quotient has order 3. Its length is 2+1=3, within the allowance 2·2. The annihilating determinant bounds the number of layers and the Selmer count bounds the size of each. Combining these inequalities gives mℓ,j log ℓ ≤ 240ℓn²(j+1) log²(jℓN). The constant in the public theorem is existential. The factors 30 and 8 exhibit one witness.

Each automorphism of the ambient cyclotomic field, raised to 2e+1o, fixes E. This follows from the 2-power congruence, the kernel condition defining the base field, and the two quadratic character conditions, which are killed by squaring. The Galois quotient has order n. If an odd prime ℓ divides n, Cauchy’s theorem gives a quotient element of order ℓ, hence ℓ divides o. Summing the preceding estimate over 1 ≤ j < t bounds the contribution of each such prime by 240ℓn²t² log²(tℓN). All terms are nonnegative, so the sum can be enlarged to the fixed odd prime divisors of o. In particular, for o a power of two the first term alone suffices.

Counting the generators before bounding the length

Fix an odd prime ℓ dividing the degree of the field E. The determinant calculation above tells us how many powers of ℓ annihilate the minus group. One also needs to bound how many independent classes can survive a single multiplication by ℓ. Write X for the ambient twisted first cohomology group and X[ℓ] for its subgroup killed by ℓ. The argument counts this subgroup even though it only needs a bound for the minus classes.

Let F = E(μℓ) and put m = [F:ℚ], n = [E:ℚ]. Choose, for each class in X[ℓ], a cocycle taking values in the order-ℓ subgroup of ℚℓ/ℤℓ. Indeed, if ℓ times a representative is the coboundary of a coefficient b, choose b′ with ℓb′ = b in the divisible group ℚℓ/ℤℓ. Subtract the coboundary of b′. The new representative is killed by ℓ pointwise. Over F the cyclotomic character is 1 modulo ℓ. Restricted to this subgroup of values, the twisted cocycle rule becomes ordinary addition. One obtains an additive character of the absolute Galois group of F, unramified outside the primes over ℓ because the original cocycle factors through the Galois group with that ramification condition. If two chosen cocycles give the same character, their difference restricts to zero. The index [F:E] divides ℓ − 1, so averaging over the cosets is allowed in ℤℓ. The coboundary lemma then identifies their classes over E. This gives an injection of sets. If E embeds in the cyclotomic field of level N, then F embeds at level ℓN.

Choose a primitive ℓth root ζ in F. Kummer theory attaches to such a character φ a nonzero radical β with gβ = ζφ(g)β and βℓ = a in F×. Unramifiedness makes the valuation of a divisible by ℓ at each prime outside S, where S is the set over ℓ. Changing a by an ℓth power in F leaves the character determined by the radical unchanged. Indeed the two resulting radicals, after scaling, differ by a root of unity fixed by every g. The characters therefore inject into the multiplicative group of allowed a modulo ℓth powers.

To count this quotient, remove the primes in S from the fractional ideal of a and divide the remaining prime exponents by ℓ. Its class in the ideal class group with these primes inverted belongs to ClS(F)[ℓ]. Every such class occurs because its ℓth power is principal away from S, and a generator gives an admissible a. The kernel consists of S-units modulo powers. These are the elements with valuation zero outside S. For a concrete count, take ℚ, S = {3} and cubes. After removing a rational cube every allowed number is represented by exactly one of 1, 3 and 9. The sign is already a cube. This illustrates the quotient being counted. The earlier injection uses a field containing μℓ.

Over F, the S-unit factor has order ℓr₁+r₂−1+|S| |μℓ(F)|, where r₁ counts real embeddings and r₂ counts conjugate pairs. The root-of-unity factor is at most ℓ, both r₁+r₂ and |S| are at most m, and the order of ClS(F)[ℓ] is at most the ordinary class number hF. If g is the dimension of X[ℓ] over the field with ℓ elements, the count gives the following inequality.

ℓg ≤ ℓ2mhF.

The cyclotomic comparison gives log hF ≤ 3m log(ℓN). Taking logarithms, using m ≤ ℓn and log ℓ ≥ log 2 > 5/8, gives g ≤ 8ℓn log(ℓN). Finally, if ℓr kills the group being bounded, its length is at most rg. For successive kernels of ℓi on X, multiplication by ℓi injects the next quotient into X[ℓ]. There are r quotients. This explains the product of the constant 8 from the dimension estimate and the constant 30 from the determinant estimate. Put z = Yε/5 and z′ = z(log Y)². Take q ≡ 3 modulo 8 with z/2 < log q ≤ z. For this q, let B be q times the product of the odd primes at most z. Why the progression still contains enough primes

The selection argument spends a fraction of the primes in one residue class. It needs a positive lower bound for the denominator even when the modulus grows with the first chosen prime. As in both stages, 8 divides m and a is coprime to m. Put L = log U, let π(U;m,a) count all primes up to U congruent to a modulo m, and write li(u) = ∫₂ᵘ dt/log t. The progression theorem supplies a main term B. Without an exceptional zero it is li(U)/φ(m). With an exceptional pair (χ, β) it is

B = [li(U) − Re χ(a) li(Uβ)] / φ(m).

Here χ is a nontrivial quadratic character modulo m with a real zero β between 1 − 1/(8 log m) and 1. Keeping this term matters for a progression on which χ(a) = 1, because it subtracts almost the whole main term if β is close to one. The relative prime-number estimate bounds the error by B times a constant times [exp(−c₃L/log m) + exp(−√(c₃L))]. Uniformly over the admitted data this multiplier is at most ½ for sufficiently large Y. Indeed L/log m ≥ (log Y)²/4 and L ≥ Yε/6. The lower and upper admitted bounds on L also give log m ≤ 4Yε/5, which puts L in the theorem’s range C₀ log m · log(log m + 2) ≤ L.

How can the error shrink with the exceptional main term?

Write d = log m, L = log U, and φ = φ(m). When an exceptional pair exists, set η = min{1, (1−β)d} and s = χ(a) ∈ {−1,1}. In its absence take η = 1, s = 0 and β = 1. The difficulty occurs at s = 1. As β approaches one, both the expected number of primes and the permissible error in this class shrink. We need the same factor η in two estimates.

Lower bound for the corrected main term. Suppose U ≥ 16 and L ≥ d. Then B ≥ P, where

P = Uη/(2φL).

Indeed β ≥ ½ and Uβ ≥ 2. If s ≤ 0, integrating 1/log t from U/2 to U already gives φB ≥ U/(2L). If s = 1, integrate from Uβ to U. Throughout this interval 1/log t ≥ 1/L. Its length is U[1−exp(−(1−β)L)] ≥ Uη/2. Here (1−β)L ≥ η and 1−exp(−η) ≥ η/2 for 0 ≤ η ≤ 1, by concavity and the endpoint values. This gives the bound for both signs.

The corresponding saving in the error. Let Ψ(t) sum log p for each prime power pk ≤ t congruent to a modulo m. Its model is F(t) = (t − s tβ/β)/φ. The analytic input, obtained by summing the errors for Dirichlet characters and applying their orthogonality, gives constants A, c > 0 such that

|Ψ(t) − F(t)| ≤ A tη[exp(−c log t/d) + exp(−c√(log t))]/φ.

This holds for 8 ∣ m, gcd(a,m) = 1 and log t ≥ C d log(d+2) with an absolute C large enough. To see where η enters for large moduli, recall that the contribution from a zero ρ, after dividing the weighted explicit formula by t, contains tRe ρ−1. A very close exceptional zero forces the remaining zeros farther to the left by the Deuring–Heilbronn theorem. The density estimate at this modulus counts zeros separated in height for each character. A local count restores their multiplicities. Once the weighted bound is available, partial summation converts it to a prime count. After the exceptional zero has been set aside, these two inputs bound the relevant weighted zero sum by a constant times η dN exp(−c′ log t/d) for fixed N and c′ > 0. The remaining power of d can be paid for explicitly. Once log t ≥ (2N/c′)d log(d+2), we have dN exp(−c′ log t/(2d)) ≤ 1. Half the exponential decay and the whole factor η survive. When d is at most a fixed small multiple of √(log t), the small-modulus argument recovers η while summing the character errors. The explicit formula, zero-density and repulsion estimates are the deeper analytic inputs to this step. A published zero-density theorem incorporating repulsion is given by Thorner and Zaman, Refinements to the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions, Theorem 2.1[173].

How does the square-root exponential arise for one character?

Write d = log m, s = √(log y), and ψχ(y) = ∑n≤y Λ(n)χ(n). In the small-modulus range, d is at most a fixed small multiple of s. Take cZ to be the smaller of 1/20 and a positive constant provided by the ordinary zero-free-region theorem. Its region is Re z ≥ 1 − cZ/log(m(|Im z| + 2)), with 0 < cZ ≤ 1/20. Let Bχ consist of the zeros of L(·,χ) in this region. Across the characters of this modulus there is at most one such zero. If present, it is simple, real, and belongs to a nonprincipal quadratic character. The product over all characters is what makes uniqueness simultaneous. See Koukoulopoulos, The Distribution of Prime Numbers, Theorem 12.3[174]. There are constants c, C > 0 such that for y ≥ 2 and d ≤ cs,

|ψχ(y) − 𝟙χ principaly + ∑β∈Bχ yβ/β| ≤ Cy exp(−cs).

For a nonprincipal χ, smooth by weighting Λ(n)χ(n) with y/n − 1 for n ≤ y. Denote this sum by S(y). The contour formula for it has a linear term D(1)y, where D = −L′/L, and a term −yβ/[β(β − 1)] for each β in the region. To see the rate of decay of the remainder, take height T = exp(cZs/2) and put J = log(m(T + 2)). For d ≤ cZs/4 we have J ≤ 3cZs/4 + 2. The shifted line can be chosen with real part σ ≤ 1 − cZ/(4J). Truncation and the shifted line together cost at most a constant times (s + 2)³(y/T + Tyσ). For sufficiently large s, J ≤ s/4, so Tyσ ≤ y exp(−cZs/2). Absorbing the cubic factor and increasing the constant on bounded s gives a remainder of order y exp(−cZs/4).

To undo the smoothing take u = y(1 + h). The expression [yS(u) − uS(y)]/(u − y) gives weight one to n ≤ y, and a weight between zero and one to the at most yh + 1 integers in (y,u]. This costs at most (yh + 1)log u. The linear term cancels. The difference of the β term is −yβ/β with error at most 2yh, uniformly up to β = 1 from below. Indeed the difference quotient for S(x)/x averages xβ−2 over [y,u], with a factor −yu/β. The relative factor multiplying −yβ/β lies between (1 + h)β−1 and 1 + h, hence within h of 1 since ½ ≤ β < 1. The two contour remainders, after differencing, are of order y exp(−cZs/4)/h. These competing errors explain why the width of the averaging interval matters.

For the principal character, the unrestricted smoothed zeta sum has main term x log x − (1 + γ)x, where γ is Euler’s constant, and error of order x exp(−cζ√(log x)). This zeta estimate also follows from the ordinary prime number theorem. If ψ(t) = t + E(t), partial summation gives S(x) = x ∫1x ψ(t)dt/t². The bound |E(t)| ≪ t exp(−b√(log t)) makes ∫x∞ |E(t)|dt/t² exponentially small in √(log x), after decreasing b. Its constant ∫1∞ E(t)dt/t² equals −1 − γ. Indeed −ζ′(w)/[wζ(w)] − 1/(w − 1) is the integral of E(t)t−w−1 for real w > 1. Taking w down to 1 in the integral and the Laurent expansion gives the constant. See Koukoulopoulos, proof of Theorem 8.1[174] and DLMF (25.2.4)[175].

The difference of the principal main term gives y(1 + h)log(1 + h)/h, between y and y(1 + h). Remove the powers of primes dividing m. At each exponent their weights sum to at most log m, and there are at most log y/log 2 exponents. Now put c₀ = min(1, cζ, cZ/4) and h = exp(−c₀s/2). Both h and exp(−c₀s)/h equal exp(−c₀s/2). The logarithms in the short interval and the deleted prime powers fit within Cy exp(−c₀s/4) when d ≤ c₀s/4. This proves the displayed estimate with c = c₀/4. The large-modulus formula below uses the same elementary weights with a different contour and a longer list of zeros.

Results in this passage. A uniform character estimate in the square-root range

Where does the exceptional factor come from at small modulus?

Suppose 8 divides m. The progression theorem chooses one pair (χ₁,β) for the entire modulus when there is a nonprincipal quadratic character with a real zero 1 − 1/(8d) < β < 1. It chooses the pair in the ordinary zero-free region first if one exists. This rule makes the main term the same in both modulus ranges. For a single character let Mχ(y) be y if χ is principal and zero otherwise, with yβ/β subtracted if χ = χ₁. Put η = min(1,(1 − β)d) if a pair was chosen and η = 1 otherwise.

Set cA = min(c/4,cZ) and assume d ≤ cAs. If a selected β lies in the region, the character bound already contains its contribution. If the selected β lies outside, the regional list for χ₁ is empty. The additional term in Mχ₁ has modulus at most 2y exp(−s/2). Indeed β ≥ ½, and 1 − β > cZ/log(2m) ≥ cZ/(2d) ≥ 1/(2s). Since log y = s², this is precisely the loss in the exponent of yβ. If no pair exists every regional list is empty.

Summing the absolute errors over the φ(m) ≤ m characters costs one factor of m. To retain η, use the exceptional-zero bound η ≥ b/m for a fixed b > 0. This is the exponent-one case of Siegel’s lower bound. For a real primitive character of conductor f and a real zero β near 1 one has 1 − β ≥ bεf−ε. A character modulo m is induced from conductor f ≤ m, and its additional Euler factors have no zeros of positive real part. The factor d in η is at least log 8. Thus introducing η costs at most one further factor m/b. But m² ≤ exp(2cAs), with 2cA ≤ c/2 and 2cA ≤ 1/10. Both exponentials survive. See Kedlaya, Notes on analytic number theory, Theorem 10.9[176].

∑χ mod m |ψχ(y) − Mχ(y)| ≤ [(C + 2)/b] yη exp(−c′s),   c′ = min(c/2, 2/5).

For a reduced class a, multiply each error by the conjugate of χ(a), whose modulus is one, and divide the sum by φ(m). Character orthogonality gives the small-modulus contribution to the weighted progression estimate. The error still falls with η in a class where the exceptional term subtracts from the main term. See DLMF §27.8, Dirichlet characters and orthogonality[177].

Check the loss from primes dividing the modulus

For m = 8 and y = 16, the unrestricted count includes 2, 4, 8 and 16. Each contributes log 2, so passing to the principal character removes exactly 4 log 2. The general bound counts four possible exponents, with allowance log 8 at each. This checks the correction to the principal sum independently of any exceptional zero.

Why does repelling the other zeros save the exceptional factor?

Fix the modulus m, with 8 ∣ m, and put d = log m, Y = log t. In the large-modulus part of the progression estimate, the explicit formula is truncated at T₀ = m12. Its finite zero lists satisfy 1 − κ < Re ρ < 1 and |Im ρ| ≤ T₀ + 1, with a fixed positive κ ≤ 1/20 chosen within the range of the repulsion theorem. Put H = log(m(T₀ + 3)), so d ≤ H ≤ 14d. For a listed zero set v = H(1 − Re ρ). Its weight in the error after division by t is exp(−vY/H). We sum over all characters modulo this one modulus, counting multiplicities and subtracting the one exceptional occurrence if it is present in the lists. Call the sum W. When the exceptional zero occurs, its multiplicity is at least one. Removing one copy leaves every remaining weight nonnegative.

Results in this passage. Fixed-modulus density and the multiplicity of each zero strip

Why does a smoothed prime sum produce this list of zeros?

Fix a modulus m ≥ 3, a Dirichlet character χ modulo m, a height T ≥ 2 and a strip width 0 < κ ≤ 1/20. The sharp sum we seek is ψχ(y) = ∑n≤y Λ(n)χ(n), where Λ equals log p on positive powers of a prime p and vanishes elsewhere. Start with the continuous weight y/n − 1 on 1 ≤ n ≤ y, zero beyond that range. Call the weighted sum Sχ(y).

For Re s > 1, integrating (x − 1)x−s−1 from 1 to infinity gives 1/[s(s − 1)]. Mellin inversion recovers the weight at x = y/n. Multiplying by Λ(n)χ(n) and summing gives Perron’s integral for Sχ(y), with integrand (−L′/L)(s,χ)ys/[s(s − 1)]. On the initial vertical line Re s = 1 + 1/log y the Dirichlet series converges absolutely and the kernel decays quadratically with height. Mellin inversion, DLMF 2.5.2[178].

Move this line left to σ₁ between 1 − κ and 1 − 3κ/4 and truncate at a height T′ between T and T + 1. The left side and both heights are fixed before y varies. The right side moves with y but stays to the right of 1. All enclosed zeros therefore stay in the same list at both arguments of the difference. The local expansion of the logarithmic derivative bounds the number of zeros, counted with multiplicities, in the strip Re ρ ≥ 9/10, |Im ρ − t| ≤ 1 by C log(m(|t| + 2)). Adding these estimates along the strip bounds the number of zeros up to T + 3 by a constant times (T + 1)log(m(T + 2)). Exclude short intervals around their real parts and absolute ordinates when choosing the sides. Their total length leaves room for a clearance of at least κ/[C(T + 1)log(m(T + 2))].

Write Zχ for the zeros strictly inside the resulting rectangle and aρ for their orders of vanishing. Every listed zero satisfies 1 − κ < Re ρ < 1 and |Im ρ| ≤ T + 1. Every zero with Re ρ ≥ 1 − κ/2 and |Im ρ| ≤ T is included. Between those two boundaries the list may depend on the chosen rectangle. At a zero of order aρ, −L′/L has residue −aρ. To read the term at 1, put Fχ(s) = (s − 1)L(s,χ) with its value continued at 1 for the principal character, and Fχ = L(·,χ) otherwise. Then Fχ(1) ≠ 0. Put Kχ = −F′χ(1)/Fχ(1). The residue at 1 contributes yKχ. For the principal character there is also the double pole from the kernel times 1/(s − 1). Differentiating ys/s at 1 gives y(log y − 1). The residue theorem equates the sum of these contributions to the integral around the rectangle. Dividing by y gives the following identity for every y ≥ 2. Residue theorem, DLMF 1.10.8[179].

Sχ(y)/y = Kχ + 𝟙χ principal(log y − 1) − ∑ρ∈Zχ aρyρ−1/[ρ(ρ − 1)] + Rχ(y),
|Rχ(y)| ≤ C[(mT)Cy−κ/2 + (log y)(log(mT))²/T].

Here C depends only on κ. On the three new sides the local logarithmic-derivative estimate costs a factor of at most a constant depending on κ times T(log(mT))², apart from the known principal pole. Each horizontal segment gains T′−2 from the kernel. The omitted tails of the original line gain 1/T′ after integrating the inverse square. These give the second error. The left side has length 2T′, and after division by y it contains yσ₁−1 ≤ y−3κ/4. Its cost fits inside a constant times (mT)⁴y−κ/2. Enlarging C gives the displayed bound. The same local counts give the multiplicity estimate used in the count of zero strips.

Theorems used. Perron inversion for the ramp

How much of a logarithmic derivative comes from nearby zeros?

A zero of order a gives a term a/(s−ρ) in f′/f. To move a contour near many zeros, we need to bound both their total multiplicity and the part of the derivative left after removing them. Both follow from the same comparison of the size of f at the centre of a disk with its size on the boundary.

Local zero expansion. Let f be analytic on a neighbourhood of the closed disk of centre z₀ and radius r > 0. Suppose f(z₀) ≠ 0 and |f(z)| ≤ B|f(z₀)| throughout the disk, with B ≥ 1. Let Z consist of all zeros at distance at most r/3 from the centre. Write aρ for the order at ρ and N for the sum of these orders. At every s within r/6 of the centre where f(s) ≠ 0,

N ≤ log B / log 2,   |f′(s)/f(s) − ∑ρ∈Z aρ/(s−ρ)| ≤ 72 log B / r.

The zeros in the smaller closed disk are finite, since an accumulation point there would force f to vanish identically. Divide f by the polynomial P(z) = ∏(z−ρ)aρ. At each zero its Taylor expansion shows that the quotient g extends holomorphically with a nonzero value. At the centre, |P(z₀)| ≤ (r/3)N. On the outer circle each zero is at least 2r/3 away. There |P| ≥ (2r/3)N, hence |g| ≤ B 2−N|g(z₀)|. The maximum-modulus principle carries this inequality back to the centre. Cancelling |g(z₀)| gives 2N ≤ B. Maximum-modulus principle, DLMF §1.10(v)[180].

On the disk of radius r/3 the quotient is zero-free. Choose the analytic logarithm H of g/g(z₀) with H(z₀) = 0. Its real part is at most log B by the preceding bound. The Borel–Carathéodory inequality gives |H| ≤ 6 log B on the disk of radius r/4, since 2(r/4)/(r/3−r/4) = 6. For |s−z₀| ≤ r/6, the circle of radius r/12 about s stays in that disk. Cauchy’s estimate bounds |H′(s)| by 72 log B/r. Since f′/f = P′/P + H′, this is exactly the remainder in the displayed formula. Siu, the Borel–Carathéodory theorem[181] · Cauchy’s integral formula for derivatives, DLMF §1.9(iii)[182].

For example, take f(z) = exp(z)(z−1/9)² on the unit disk about zero. At the centre f′/f = −17. The zero contributes 2/(0−1/9) = −18, and the remaining 1 is the logarithmic derivative of the exponential. Counting the zero once would leave an extra pole in the remainder.

Which disk controls a Dirichlet character at height t?

Fix an integer m ≥ 3, any Dirichlet character χ modulo m, and any real t. Set z₀ = 101/100 + it and r = 2/5. For the principal character take F(s) = (s−1)L(s,χ), continued at 1. For the other characters take F = L(·,χ). All these functions are analytic on the outer disk. For σ = Re s > 1 the Euler product gives |1/L(s,χ)| ≤ ζ(σ) ≤ 1 + 1/(σ−1), the last inequality by comparison with an integral. Hence |L(z₀,χ)| ≥ 1/101. In the principal case |z₀−1| ≥ 1/100. The uniform centre bound is therefore |F(z₀)| ≥ 1/10100. Dirichlet series, analytic continuation and Euler products, DLMF §25.15(i)[183].

The whole disk lies in σ ≥ 1/2. For a nonprincipal character the complete period sums to zero, so |∑n≤xχ(n)| ≤ m. Partial summation expresses L(s,χ) as s times the integral of this partial sum against x−s−1 on [1,∞), giving |L| ≤ 2m|s|. For the principal character the finite factors ∏p∣m(1−p−s) have product of absolute values at most ∏p∣mp ≤ m. Applying the same partial summation to the integer count ⌊x⌋ = x−{x} gives ζ(s) = s/(s−1) − s∫₁∞ {x}x−s−1 dx. The integral is bounded by 1/σ. After removing the pole we obtain |F(s)| ≤ C₀m(1+|s|)² with an absolute constant C₀ ≥ 1.

Since |s| ≤ |t|+2 on this disk, the preceding lemma applies with B = 10100C₀m(|t|+3)². Its logarithm is at most a fixed multiple of log(m(|t|+2)). Thus the disk of radius 2/15 contains at most that order of zeros, with multiplicity. For |s−z₀| ≤ 1/15, s ≠ 1 and F(s) ≠ 0, the sign needed in the contour integral is

−L′(s,χ)/L(s,χ) = 𝟙χ principal/(s−1) − ∑|ρ−z₀|≤2/15, F(ρ)=0 aρ/(s−ρ) + E(s),   |E(s)| ≤ 180 log B.

If the contour stays at distance at least δ from each listed zero, the pole sum costs at most N/δ. In the smoothed progression formula, only zeros with real part at least 9/10 need to be avoided. The contour has real part at least 19/20, so all other zeros are already at least 1/20 away. To the right of 107/100 the absolutely convergent series for −L′/L supplies a uniform bound.

To count the zeros in the window |Im ρ−t| ≤ 1 and 9/10 ≤ Re ρ < 1, take the fifteen centres with real part 101/100 and heights t+k/7 for −7 ≤ k ≤ 7. Choose the nearest of these heights to Im ρ. Its vertical distance is at most 1/14 and the horizontal distance is at most 11/100. Since (11/100)²+(1/14)² < (2/15)², the zero belongs to one of the counting disks. Summing the fifteen disk bounds counts every zero at least as many times as its multiplicity. Their heights differ from t by at most one, so the window count is still bounded by a constant times log(m(|t|+2)). This gives the short-interval multiplicity count. The power-sum argument uses the disk lemma with centre 26/25 + it and radius 12/25, then differentiates the analytic remainder by Cauchy’s formula.

How does the difference recover the sharp prime count?

Choose 0 < δ ≤ ½, put u = (1 + δ)y and b = yu/(u − y) = y(1 + δ)/δ. Multiply the difference Sχ(u)/u − Sχ(y)/y by b. For every n ≤ y, the two weights differ by 1/y − 1/u = 1/b. Thus these terms contribute exactly ψχ(y). An integer in (y,u] contributes with weight b(1/n − 1/u) between zero and one. Their total in absolute value is at most (δy + 1)log(2y).

Check the weights at 4, 5 and 6

Take the principal character modulo 3, y = 4 and u = 6. Then b = 12. Every integer up to 4 has weight one in the scaled difference. Only 2 and 4 contribute, giving 2 log 2. At 5 the weight is 12(1/5 − 1/6) = 2/5. At 6 it is zero. The difference equals 2 log 2 + (2/5)log 5, so its entire discrepancy from ψχ(4) comes from the short interval.

What does a zero force a finite sum to do?

Fix a modulus m ≥ 3 and a height T ≥ 2. We count pairs (χ,ρ) with χ a character modulo m, L(ρ,χ) = 0, σ ≤ Re ρ < 1 and |Im ρ| ≤ T. Assume ¾ ≤ σ < 1. Two distinct zeros of the same character in this list must have ordinates at least one apart. The strip argument explains how to put the multiplicities back afterwards. The problem here is to bound the number of these separated pairs.

Take q = ⌈mT⌉, V = q³, J = 8(⌊log₂ q⌋ + 1), and N = 2J. Thus q⁸ ≤ N ≤ 256q⁸. For a character χ let PN(s) = ∑n≤N χ(n)n−s. Multiply it by MV(s) = ∑d≤V μ(d)χ(d)d−s. Here μ is the Möbius function. It is zero on integers divisible by a prime square and equals (−1)k on a product of k distinct primes.

In the product the coefficient of χ(n)n−s is bN(n) = ∑dk=n, d≤V, k≤N μ(d). This equals 1 at n = 1. For 1 < n ≤ V every divisor occurs, and their Möbius sum is ∏p∣n(1 − 1) = 0. The product is consequently 1 + DN, where the remainder runs over V < n ≤ VN. Partition it into J sums on doubling intervals. With U = V2j their common form is

BN,U(χ,ρ) = ∑U<n≤2U bN(n)χ(n)n−ρ.

Nonprincipal detector. At a zero of a nonprincipal character, |PN(ρ)| ≤ 8qN−Re ρ. Indeed, complete periods of χ sum to zero, so partial sums on every interval are bounded by 2(m + 1). Partial summation of the tail of the L-series bounds it by 2(m + 1)(1 + |ρ|/Re ρ)N−Re ρ, and 1 + |ρ|/Re ρ ≤ 3T. These bounded partial sums give locally uniform convergence on Re s > 0, so the series there agrees with the continued L-function. Since L(ρ,χ) vanishes, the finite sum equals the negative of the tail. Also |MV(ρ)| ≤ V. Thus |1 + DN| ≤ 8q · q−6 · q³ = 8/q² ≤ ½. The remainder must have absolute value at least ½. At least one of its J blocks therefore has absolute value ≥ 1/(2J).

Check the cancellation before grouping the blocks

Use small cutoffs V = 3 and N = 4 just to check the coefficients. At n = 2 and 3 they are 1 − 1 = 0. At n = 6 the admissible pairs (d,k) are (2,3) and (3,2). Each contributes −1, so the coefficient is −2. The cutoff has removed the pairs (1,6) and (6,1) that would complete the divisor sum. How does a real zero control the mass of prime powers?

We want to keep track of its size on entire intervals. For this purpose introduce the divisor sum r(n) = ∑b∣n χ₁(b), the coefficient of ζ(s)L(s,χ₁). The Dirichlet convolution formula gives this identity and the multiplicativity of r. See DLMF (27.5.1)[184].

For n = ph, r(n) = 1 + χ₁(p) + ⋯ + χ₁(p)h. It equals h + 1 when χ₁(p) = 1. When χ₁(p) = −1 it alternates between zero for odd h and one for even h. For other positive n, Λ(n) = 0 and r(n) ≥ 0 by multiplicativity.

∑y<n≤x r(n)/n ≤ |L(1,χ₁)| log(x/y) + 400m(1 + log y)/√y   (1 ≤ y ≤ x).

Subtract this identity at N₀ = ⌊y⌋ and N₁ = ⌊x⌋. The constant γ cancels. The character has χ₁(2) = −1 and χ₁(7) = 1. At 2 and 4 the divisor sums are 0 and 1, and the prime coefficients are 0 and 2 log 2. At 7 the divisor sum is 2 and the prime coefficient is 2 log 7. At 3 the divisor sum is 1 but the prime coefficient is zero. Thus the divisor sum can count more mass while still detecting the cancellation at 2.

Removing failed twists

First remove primes for which some such character has a zero in the box of height H. Choose one offending character for each removed prime. Its conductor determines the prime uniquely. Indeed if fp = f′p′, primality forces p to divide f′ or p′. The first possibility contradicts 0 < f′ ≤ F < p, so p = p′. The zero-density theorem bounds the number of offending primitive characters by C H1/4. Dividing by the number of candidates makes the loss tend to zero.

#primes removed / |P| ≤ C(FU)1/4/U9/10 ≤ C U−21/40.

Thus the same exclusion works for every member of Ξ. The fixed exponent 1/4 counts characters admitting a zero in this particular rectangle.

How can one count characters whose L-function has a zero?

Write Q for the height H of the box in the preceding prime selection. Consider all primitive characters of conductor at most Q that have at least one zero ρ with Re ρ > 399/400 and |Im ρ| ≤ Q. The number of these characters is at most CQ1/4 for every real Q ≥ 3 and a single absolute constant C. One zero, chosen separately for each character, suffices. The argument turns it into a large finite sum on one interval, then bounds how many characters can give large sums on the same interval.

Detecting one zero. For large Q take X = ⌈Q⌉, Y = X⁴, J = 8(⌊log₂ X⌋ + 1) and N = 2J. Here Y is the length of an auxiliary sum within this proof. Multiply the first N terms of L(s,χ), denoted P(s), by M(s) = ∑d≤Y μ(d)χ(d)d−s, summing over positive integers. The Möbius function μ is zero on multiples of squares of primes. On a product of k distinct primes it is (−1)k, including μ(1) = 1. In the product the coefficient multiplying χ(n)n−s is

a(n) = ∑db=n, 1≤d≤Y, 1≤b≤N μ(d).

For 2 ≤ n ≤ Y every divisor occurs, since Y ≤ N. The sum is zero by expanding (1−1)k over the distinct prime divisors. At n = 1 it is one. Thus PM = 1 + D, where D uses only Y < n ≤ YN. For a short calculation set Y = 3 and N = 4. At 6 only (2,3) and (3,2) qualify, so a(6) = −2. At 4 only (1,4) and (2,2) occur, and their contributions cancel. Truncating the product can leave either outcome beyond the initial range.

Why must at least one block be large at a zero?

For a primitive character of conductor q > 1, complete periods of χ sum to zero. The remainder estimate by partial summation gives, at the chosen zero with σ = Re ρ, |P(ρ)| ≤ 2(q+1)(1+|ρ|/σ)N−σ. Every term of the second polynomial has modulus at most one, so |M(ρ)| ≤ Y. When Q ≥ 20 we have q+1 ≤ 2X and 1+|ρ|/σ ≤ 3X. Also N ≥ X⁸ and σ > 15/16, so Nσ ≥ X⁷√X ≥ 4X⁷. Multiplication by Y = X⁴ gives |PM| ≤ 3/X ≤ 1/2. Since PM = 1 + D, the reverse triangle inequality forces |D| ≥ 1/2. Split (Y,YN] into J successive blocks (U,2U] with U = Y2j. At least one block sum has modulus ≥ 1/(2J).

How many characters can select the same block?

Write σ₀ = 399/400. Suppose T characters selected one block (U, 2U]. Place their values in rows vχ(n) = χ(n)n−(ρχ−σ₀), and put b(n) = a(n)n−σ₀. Multiplying each row by this same column gives its selected large block. The squared norm of a row is at most U. For two different rows the character χψ̄ at their common product modulus is nonprincipal: equality of the induced characters would identify their conductors and then the original primitive characters. Complete periods of this product sum to zero, so its partial sums have modulus at most the product of the conductors, at most Q². Partial summation against the complex power gives the bound 2Q²(1+|w|) for the inner product, with w = ρχ−σ₀ + conj(ρψ−σ₀). Each of these nonprincipal zeros has real part below 1, and the two imaginary parts have absolute values at most Q. Thus the inner product has modulus at most 8Q³.

The number of divisors of n bounds |a(n)| and is at most a constant times n1/400. Squaring after multiplying by n−σ₀ and summing the U terms gives ∑|b(n)|² ≤ C U−99/100 ≤ C U−197/200. The matrix of row inner products has absolute row sums at most U + 8TQ³. This bounds its operator norm: in its quadratic form use 2|xᵢxⱼ| ≤ |xᵢ|² + |xⱼ|² and the symmetry of the absolute entries. Applying the bound to the rectangular matrix and the column b gives

T/(4J²) ≤ ∑χ |∑n b(n)vχ(n)|² ≤ (U + 8TQ³)C U−197/200.

Since U ≥ Q⁴, the coefficient of T on the right is at most 8CQ−47/50. Above a single threshold independent of the characters, this is at most 1/(8J²), so we can subtract it and obtain T ≤ 8CJ²U3/200. Summing over the J blocks gives at most 8CJ³(YN)3/200. Here YN ≤ 2²⁰Q¹² and, eventually, J³ ≤ Q7/100. The exponents add to 12·3/200 + 7/100 = 1/4. The only primitive character of conductor one costs at most one further character. For bounded Q, the finite number of characters below the fixed threshold can be absorbed into the same absolute constant. In the prime selection we apply this bound at Q = FU, where U again denotes the upper limit on candidate primes.

How accurately does a finite character sum approximate the value at a zero?

Let χ be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character modulo q. Write A(n) = ∑1≤k≤n χ(k) and PN(s) = ∑1≤n≤N χ(n)n−s. A complete period of χ sums to zero. Deleting whole periods bounds |A(n)| uniformly, and we may take B = q+1. For any complex s with σ = Re s > 0, put f(x) = x−s on the positive real axis. The point of using the partial sums A(n) is that the differences of f are absolutely summable throughout this half-plane.

Indeed, integrate f′(x) = −s x−s−1 from n to n+1, and take absolute values inside the integral. This gives |f(n)−f(n+1)| ≤ (|s|/σ)(n−σ−(n+1)−σ). Moreover, on any compact subset with σ ≥ σ₁ > 0 and |s| ≤ K, the difference is at most K n−σ₁−1. Thus G(s) = ∑n≥1 A(n)(f(n)−f(n+1)) converges locally uniformly and defines a holomorphic function there. For finite N, replacing χ(n) by A(n)−A(n−1) gives

PN(s) = ∑1≤n≤N A(n)(f(n)−f(n+1)) + A(N)f(N+1).

The last term tends to zero. For σ > 1, the limit on the left is the absolutely convergent Dirichlet series for L(s,χ). By uniqueness of analytic continuation G therefore gives L throughout σ > 0. Subtracting the displayed identity from G leaves the sum of differences beginning at N+1, followed by minus A(N)f(N+1). In the bound for the sum, the consecutive differences of n−σ telescope to (N+1)−σ. The boundary term costs B(N+1)−σ. Hence for all integers N ≥ 1,

|L(s,χ)−PN(s)| ≤ B(1+|s|/σ)(N+1)−σ ≤ 2B(1+|s|/σ)N−σ.

The second, deliberately weaker bound is the one used in the detector. It applies at a zero even on the left of the line of absolute convergence. One can see the boundary term already with the quadratic character modulo 4, s = 1 and N = 2. Here A(1) = A(2) = 1, so the first two differences give (1−1/2)+(1/2−1/3) = 2/3. The boundary term is +1/3 in the finite identity, giving P₂(1) = 1. Kiran Kedlaya, Notes on analytic number theory, Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.5 and equation (3.2.3)[186].

Why are there exactly J possible blocks?

Fix Q ≥ 20 and a primitive character of conductor 1 < q ≤ Q. It is nonprincipal because the principal character is induced from conductor one. Take a zero ρ with σ = Re ρ > 399/400 and |Im ρ| ≤ Q. For this step the lower bound on σ suffices. Put X = ⌈Q⌉, Y = X⁴, J = 8(⌊log₂ X⌋+1) and N = 2J. The number 2⌊log₂ X⌋+1 is strictly larger than X, including when X is a power of two. Its eighth power is N, so N ≥ X⁸ ≥ Y.

At ρ the remainder bounds |PN(ρ)|. Since |ρ| ≤ σ+Q and σ > 1/2, we have 1+|ρ|/σ ≤ 2+2Q ≤ 3X. Also q+1 ≤ 2X. The weaker inequality σ ≥ 15/16 already gives Nσ ≥ X15/2 = X⁷√X ≥ 4X⁷. The other factor in the detector is MY(ρ) = ∑1≤d≤Y μ(d)χ(d)d−ρ. Each summand has modulus at most one, so |MY(ρ)| ≤ Y. All four estimates hold simultaneously for every allowed character and zero. Multiplying them gives

|PN(ρ)MY(ρ)| ≤ 2(2X)(3X) X⁴/(4X⁷) = 3/X ≤ 1/2.

By the finite Möbius product identity, the same product is 1+D, where D sums the coefficients a(n)χ(n)n−ρ over Y < n ≤ YN. The reverse triangle inequality gives |D| ≥ 1/2. Partition these integers with endpoints Y, 2Y, 4Y, …, Y2J = YN. There are J+1 endpoints and exactly J intervals. For index j = 0,…,J−1, write Bⱼ(ρ) for the sum on (Y2j, Y2j+1]. The first integer included is Y+1. Each internal endpoint belongs to the earlier interval, and the last interval includes YN. Thus

1/2 ≤ |D| ≤ ∑j=0J−1|Bⱼ(ρ)| ≤ J max0≤j<J|Bⱼ(ρ)|.

For the small product example Y = 3, N = 4 = 2², the two intervals are (3,6] and (6,12]. The coefficient a(6) = −2 belongs entirely to the first block, and a(12) = −1 belongs to the second. In the zero count, each character supplies at least one block of modulus ≥ 1/(2J), with equality allowed. Choosing one such index per character produces the families in the block mean-square estimate. That estimate also needs Re ρ < 1. The Euler product excludes zeros with Re ρ > 1, and the classical nonvanishing theorem excludes the whole line Re ρ = 1 for a nonprincipal character, including the real point ρ = 1. Every chosen zero of conductor greater than one therefore lies strictly to the left of that line. Kedlaya, equation (3.2.1) and Theorems 3.8, 3.10 and 3.11[186].

How do two different characters interact in the same detector block?

Fix a real Q ≥ 3. Take a finite set S of distinct primitive Dirichlet characters of conductors at most Q. For each χ choose one complex point ρχ with σ₀ = 399/400 < Re ρχ < 1 and |Im ρχ| ≤ Q. The zero detector assigns one such zero and one block to each selected character of conductor greater than one when Q ≥ 20. For the mean square itself the points may be anywhere in that strip, even at the same height. Fix a positive integer U and use the same U integers U < n ≤ 2U for every row. Set vχ(n) = χ(n)n−(ρχ−σ₀). For any complex coefficients b(n), the block mean square satisfies

∑χ∈S |∑U<n≤2U b(n)vχ(n)|² ≤ (U + 8|S|Q³) ∑U<n≤2U|b(n)|².

Write Gχψ = ∑ vχ(n) conj(vψ(n)). The diagonal is at most U since each term is at most one. For χ ≠ ψ let m be the product of their conductors. The sequence ξ(n) = χ(n) conj(ψ(n)) is a character modulo m. On units it is the quotient of the two induced characters. On a nonunit at least one factor vanishes. If ξ were principal, the two induced characters would agree on every unit. Uniqueness of the primitive character inducing a given character would force χ = ψ. A complete period of ξ therefore sums to zero. Multiplication of the unit classes by some a with ξ(a) ≠ 1 leaves the sum unchanged and multiplies it by ξ(a). Deleting complete periods gives |A(r)| ≤ m for A(r) = ∑0≤n<r ξ(n). Andrew Sutherland, Theorem 18.13 and Corollary 18.15[187].

The complex weights vary across the block. Put w = ρχ−σ₀ + conj(ρψ−σ₀), so 0 < Re w < 1 and |Im w| ≤ 2Q. For f(x) = x−w, the derivative has modulus |w|x−Re w−1 ≤ |w|/U throughout the block. Substituting ξ(n) = A(n+1)−A(n) and shifting the second sum leaves endpoint terms f(2U)A(2U+1)−f(U+1)A(U+1), followed by −∑U<n<2U (f(n+1)−f(n))A(n+1). Each endpoint costs at most m and the full difference sum costs at most m|w|. Hence |Gχψ| ≤ 2m(1+|w|) ≤ 8Q³, using m ≤ Q² and |w| ≤ 1+2Q.

It remains to pass from pairwise comparisons to the sum of squares. Write V for the row matrix and Δ = U + 8|S|Q³. Every absolute row sum of G = VV∗ is ≤ Δ, and the same holds for columns by Hermitian symmetry. For any vector z, bound each term in z∗Gz by |Gχψ| (|zχ|²+|zψ|²)/2. Summing gives ‖V∗z‖² ≤ Δ‖z‖². Take z = Vb. Cauchy–Schwarz gives ‖z‖² = |⟨V∗z,b⟩| ≤ √Δ ‖z‖ ‖b‖. For z ≠ 0 division and squaring give the stated inequality. For z = 0 it already holds.

For a small check of that matrix argument, use the unweighted quadratic characters modulo 3 and 4 on the integers 5, 6, 7, 8. Their rows are (−1,0,1,−1) and (1,0,−1,0). The off-diagonal entry equals −2 even though the complete product period of length 12 sums to zero. The diagonal entries are 3 and 2, so one may take Δ = 5. Against b = (1,0,−1,0) the row outputs are −2 and 2. Their squared sum 8 is bounded by 5‖b‖² = 10. This example checks the finite matrix inequality for arbitrary coefficients.

For odd primes dividing m it also fixes the residue of q modulo that prime. Hence for a sign σ depending on the pair and the progression,

(n/q)(n′/q) = σ(q/s),   σ ∈ {−1,+1}.

For example, 53 and 101 are both 5 modulo 24. The pair (4,3) has s = 1 even though 12 is not a square. Its symbol is −1 at both primes. For (3,5) the symbol is −(q/5), giving +1 at 53 and −1 at 101. These two terms cancel exactly. The example illustrates the correlation on two primes.

9The one-sided window theorem

Suppose the arithmetic argument repeatedly finds a stretch of scales on which a centered prime sum stays below a small power of the scale. A zero of an associated L-function would force a pole of its transform. How can a bound on scattered stretches rule out even one pole? High derivatives let us choose where the integral sees the function.

9.1The hypothesis in logarithmic coordinates

Fix 0 < θ < 1 and δ > 0. Write g(u) = GF(exp u) for a real weighted sum from a finite character family F. The abstract theorem below allows any real measurable g with |g(u)| ≤ C0 exp(2u) for u ≥ 0. Every point of the half-plane must have a punctured neighborhood free of Z, including points outside Z. At each pole the residue is nonzero, and at each real pole it is real and strictly positive.

Put U = log Y. Then [Y, Y1+δ] becomes I = [U, (1 + δ)U]. For every η > 0 and every lower limit U0, suppose there exist U ≥ U0 and a majorant R on I with R ≥ max(g, 0), such that R(u) exp(−θu) is integrable there and

∫I R(u) exp(−θu) du ≤ exp(ηU).

Theorem. Every ρ ∈ Z satisfies Re ρ ≤ θ. The window and its majorant may depend on η and U0. Between windows the growth estimate still holds. An arithmetic upper bound GF(y) ≤ C yθ on arbitrarily distant windows suffices. Take R(u) = |C| exp(θu). Its weighted integral equals |C|δU, which is at most exp(ηU) once U is large.

Test the hypothesis on a single pole. Take θ = ½, δ = ½ and g(u) = exp(¾u). Its Laplace transform is 1/(s − ¾). On [U,3U/2] even the smallest admissible majorant has weighted integral 4(exp(3U/8) − exp(U/4)). For η = ⅛ this eventually exceeds exp(ηU) on every window. Change the sign of g and R = 0 works on every window, although the transform still has a pole at ¾. Its residue is now −1. This example explains the sign hypothesis at real poles and why the arithmetic only needs an upper bound.
